This article from the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy (Land Lines magazine, January 2020 issue, written by Gregory Scruggs, December 16, 2019) examines how U.S. municipalities are adapting to the changing retail landscape as shopping malls decline and online retail grows. 

Key case studies include:
- **Bangor, Maine**: The struggling Bangor Mall, built in 1978 on a former dairy farm, once contributed $1.2 million annually to local taxes. Its assessment fell from $60.9 million (2017) to $46.3 million (2018) to $34.6 million (2019), with the mall now accounting for just 1.31% of the city's taxable valuation. The mall was sold at auction in February 2019 for $12.6 million—less than half its assessed value—after owner Simon Property Group defaulted on an $80 million loan. However, Bangor's thriving downtown, including a $22 million Bangor Savings Bank campus and new downtown apartments, has compensated for the mall's decline.
- **Onondoga County, New York**: ShoppingTown Mall (opened 1954) saw its assessment drop from $53 million (2008) to $36 million (2014). Owner Moonbeam LLC owes $9.7 million in back taxes and sought bankruptcy protection in 2019.
- **Sheboygan, Wisconsin**: Lost $1.3 million in annual tax revenue when Memorial Mall challenged its assessment; the mall closed in 2017. The city offset losses through Acuity Insurance's corporate expansion and downtown revitalization (innovation district, pop-up retail program) without increasing residential property taxes.
- **Chapel Hill, North Carolina**: University Place mall transformed with a children's museum, health club, CrossFit studio, and specialty food store (Southern Season), supported by flexible zoning and local government partnership.
- **Nashville, Tennessee**: Hickory Hollow Mall (rebranded Global Mall at the Crossings) failed to revive despite $50 million in investment, and a planned "innovation district" collapsed in November 2019.
- **Plano, Texas**: Colin Creek Mall, bought for $10 million, will be redeveloped into $1 billion in commercial development with 15-20 restaurants, aided by a property tax incentive.

Key statistics: Property taxes account for 72% of local tax revenue (2015); retail is about one-quarter of commercial property value; there are 8.5 billion square feet of retail space in the U.S. (24.5 sq ft per capita vs. Europe's 4.5); retail real estate is at over 95% occupancy; e-commerce represents only about 10-11% of retail sales (projected to grow to just over 15% by 2022); sales tax accounts for about 12% of municipal tax revenue; vacancy rates are predicted to increase 20% over the next five years.

The article emphasizes that the retail transition is less dire than media narratives suggest. Municipalities that invest in downtowns, flexible zoning, service-oriented retail (restaurants, gyms, coffee shops, salons), and redevelopment of mall sites can maintain fiscal health. Experts cited include Lincoln Institute Fellow Ron Rakow, Bangor City Assessor Philip Drew, Denton (Texas) assessor Marc Moffitt, and LSE professor Lindsay Relihan. Big-box retailers like Walmart have filed tax assessment appeals in at least 21 states over the past decade.
args.key_excerpts: "In some communities dependent on malls, they can make up 20 to 30 percent of their tax base and other taxpayers may have been paying relatively less," says Lincoln Institute of Land Policy Fellow Ron Rakow, former assessor for the City of Boston. "If the mall isn't doing as well, the community is either going to have to reduce services or increase taxes for others.", "Malls as a property type are dead," says Moffitt. "It is not *if*, it's *when* they go under and are ready for redevelopment." "What malls are worth right now is their dirt. Their structures have little to no value," Moffitt adds. "Investors view malls as mixed-use redevelopment opportunities better able to serve the community, and they are going to provide a much more robust sales and property tax base.", "While in the past it was one of the higher valued properties, the loss of value affects the mindset more than the pocketbook," says Sheboygan City Assessor Mike Grota., "There's a lot of stuff you don't buy on Amazon." — Marc Moffitt, "Policies that support a transition to service-oriented retail, and the density and accessibility of that retail, are likely to be key to local retail health," says LSE professor Lindsay Relihan. "Transitions are very disruptive in the short run, but I don't see any reason why fiscal health should necessarily decline in the long run."

# The Death and Reinvention of American Malls

_Written By_ Reena Jari

Before the 2000s, shopping malls were places of congregation for younger generations to not only shop, but to watch movies, eat, and hang out. Malls are typically owned by real estate investment trusts (REITs), companies that own or operate real estate assets. These REITs lease out their retail spaces to tenants, and they pay the REITs in the form of base pay, operating expenses and a percentage of their sales. Bigger department stores, such as Macy’s or Nordstrom are called “anchor stores” as they drive foot traffic, and as a result they normally get charged a lower rent (CFI, 2020). Malls have recently experienced a decline in retail sales and are no longer seen as strong investments because of the many economic and technological changes over the past few decades. This decline is due to many factors, including the rise of e-commerce, the effects of COVID-19, and competition from other malls, which have all contributed to store closures, bankruptcies, and the deterioration of many malls. However, with the new generation of shoppers and promising new investors, malls may still have a future.

One of the largest contributors to the decline of malls is online shopping. In the early 2010s, as Amazon and other big e-commerce companies were launching their platforms, consumers switched to online retail platforms. A study examining the impact of e-commerce on retail noted that, “E-commerce sales are increasing because of how convenient online buying is, how accessible it is, and how many different things are available” (Kothari, 2018). This convenience and lower pricing reduced the competitiveness of brick-and-mortar sales. This has made it difficult for many retailers to turn a profit. Another driving factor of mall closures was the COVID-19 pandemic, as many people started working from home and no longer needed to travel as frequently. According to a quarterly JP Morgan Chase Institute report, there was a decrease in consumer foot traffic because less people were commuting to work, and employment centers were unable to support the same level of retail establishments from before the pandemic. This report noted that other establishments, like grocery stores and restaurants have bounced back since COVID, however retail spaces are still lagging because of the rise of e-commerce (Wheat, 2023). COVID-19 and the rise of e-commerce have shifted consumer retail behavior patterns to online, which has significantly impacted the performance of malls across America.

In addition to the external factors, the internal pressure of competition between malls has caused many vacancies. Malls with poor asset management are being forced out of business, as they are struggling to compete with newer malls that have more amenities and a broader selection of stores (Fung, 2017). For example, a struggling mall was recently acquired by Dillard’s after their previous owners were known for their poor management practices and “not paying their utility bills, [and] not paying property taxes” (King, 2025). Poor management structure causes stores to collapse, as it leads to financial instability making it very difficult to retain tenants. The closure of major retail stores also has a significant effect on the mall’s overall success. For example, the bankruptcy of Forever 21 led to the tenant loss of more than 200 stores in the United States. These stores often occupy very large spaces within the mall making it difficult for mall owners to fill the space once they close (King B, 2025). When large stores become vacant, it is easier for surrounding stores to then also break their leases or negotiate the rent, further weakening the overall occupancy and revenue of the mall (Thomas, 2019). The loss of an anchor store like Forever 21 shows how malls can be destabilized quickly and go into bankruptcy. Similarly, San Francisco Centre mall used to be a major retail location for the city. However, in recent years the mall has entered a “death spiral”. The mall has struggled with years of homelessness, shoplifting, and drug use which has caused nearly all of its retailers to leave the store. Once anchor stores such as Nordstrom and Bloomingdale’s closed, the mall ultimately collapsed as they lost significant foot traffic (King A, 2025). These examples demonstrate that both internal and external factors lead to deterioration of malls.

However, some investors and analysts see redevelopment potential in underperforming malls, in some cases the closure of struggling retail stores allows for stronger brands or a new type of business. As the Wall Street Journal explains, “That optimism reflects a surprisingly strong landscape for the mall industry. High-end malls are nearly fully occupied and rents are rising” (King B, 2025). Vacant spaces are being converted into restaurants, gyms, entertainment venues or alternative uses (Young, 2024). The mall owners have seen they need to adapt to economic and technological advances, so malls are evolving into entertainment centers rather than purely retail. The department store, Dillard’s, recently purchased the Longview Mall in Texas and is going to renovate and maintain the property unlike the previous owners that allowed it to collapse (King, 2025). Dillard’s decision to acquire this struggling mall and repurpose it shows how they understand the needs of the mall and are finding innovative ways to attract customers by enhancing consumer experience and foot traffic.

Lastly, younger generations are making malls more popular again. Studies show that “shoppers between the ages of 18 and 24 bought 62% of their total general merchandise purchases in stores last year. Shoppers ages 25 and older, by contrast, made 52% of their purchases in person, according to Circana” (King, 2026). Many younger shoppers want instant gratification when shopping and value the ability to try on the clothes in store. After the pandemic, Gen Z shoppers have shown an increased interest in demand for in person social retail experiences. The clothing brand Edikted was originally an online store, however, Gen Z has pushed for it to open physical mall locations. Overall, while many malls have struggled to adapt to e-commerce, changes post-COVID and bankruptcies, the industry might be making a comeback. Malls are adapting to consumer demand rather than disappearing entirely.

args.summary:
This article from the Michigan Journal of Economics (published April 13, 2026, written by Reena Jari) examines the decline and potential reinvention of American shopping malls. 

**Background & Structure:** Malls are typically owned by real estate investment trusts (REITs) that lease retail space to tenants in exchange for base pay, operating expenses, and a percentage of sales. Large department stores like Macy's and Nordstrom serve as "anchor stores" that drive foot traffic and receive lower rent.

**Causes of Decline:**
1. **E-commerce rise:** Online shopping platforms like Amazon, launched in the early 2010s, offered convenience, accessibility, and variety at lower prices, reducing brick-and-mortar competitiveness.
2. **COVID-19 pandemic:** Remote work reduced commuting and consumer foot traffic. A JPMorgan Chase Institute report noted that grocery stores and restaurants bounced back post-pandemic, but retail spaces continued lagging due to e-commerce.
3. **Competition between malls:** Malls with poor asset management struggled against newer malls with better amenities. Poor management practices (e.g., not paying utility bills or property taxes) caused financial instability and tenant loss.
4. **Anchor store bankruptcies:** Forever 21's bankruptcy resulted in over 200 store closures in the US, creating large vacant spaces difficult to fill, destabilizing surrounding tenants and occupancy.
5. **Example - San Francisco Centre mall:** Entered a "death spiral" due to homelessness, shoplifting, and drug use, causing nearly all retailers to leave; when anchors Nordstrom and Bloomingdale's closed, the mall collapsed.

**Signs of Reinvention:**
- High-end malls are nearly fully occupied with rising rents per the Wall Street Journal.
- Vacant retail spaces are being converted into restaurants, gyms, entertainment venues, and alternative uses, evolving malls into entertainment centers.
- Dillard's acquired the struggling Longview Mall in Texas and is renovating it, demonstrating investor optimism.

**Gen Z Revival:** Younger shoppers are driving mall resurgence. Circana data shows shoppers aged 18-24 bought 62% of total general merchandise in stores (vs. 52% for ages 25+). Gen Z values instant gratification and in-person try-ons, pushing online-only brands like Edikted to open physical mall locations.

**Conclusion:** While many malls have struggled to adapt to e-commerce and post-COVID changes, the industry may be making a comeback as malls adapt to consumer demand rather than disappearing entirely.

--- SOURCE 1: E-commerce penetration by category, Q1 2026: where DTC has won (and where it hasn't) | Eightx ---
URL: https://eightx.co/blog/ecommerce-penetration-by-category-2026

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an analytical article from Eightx (a fractional/interim CFO firm) by Matt Putra, Managing Partner, examining US e-commerce penetration by retail category in Q1 2026 and what it means for DTC brands.

KEY HEADLINE DATA:
- US e-commerce reached 16.9% of total retail in Q1 2026 (seasonally adjusted, Census CB26-81, released May 18, 2026), with $326.7B in e-commerce sales on $1,929.0B total retail.
- E-commerce grew 9.8% YoY vs. 3.9% for total retail.
- Share gain from Q1 2025 to Q1 2026 was +0.9 points, vs. only +0.1 points the prior year — though part of this apparent acceleration is a benchmark artifact (the April 2025 Census benchmark dropped nonemployer establishments from the series; Q1 2025 reads 16.0% on the restated basis vs. the original 16.2%).

THREE-BUCKET CATEGORY SPLIT (based on 2022 Annual Retail Trade Survey data, the most recent available):
1. SATURATED: Nonstore retailers (NAICS 454) at 70.7% (up from 65.6% in 2019); Electronic shopping & mail-order (4541) at 77.9% (up from 74.6%). These capture pure-play digital sellers and marketplaces — near a ceiling by definition.
2. MID-CYCLE: Clothing & accessories (448) at 6.9% (up from 4.6%); Sporting goods/hobby/books (451) at 6.0% (up from 4.3%); Furniture & home furnishings (442) at 3.3% (up from 1.9%); Electronics & appliances (443) at 3.0% (up from 2.0%). These categories added 1-2 points of share between 2019-2022 and still have runway.
3. STUCK: Food & beverage stores (445) at 2.9% (up from 1.1%); Building material & garden (444) at 0.8% (up from 0.6%). Motor vehicle, health/personal care, gas stations, and general merchandise were suppressed in 2022 under Census "D" disclosure rules. Beauty/health & personal care is estimated at ~17% online penetration by trade-press estimates despite being suppressed in Census data.

WHY CATEGORIES ARE STUCK:
- Grocery loses on last-mile cost ($8-15 fully loaded on a $40 basket, unaffordable on 1-3% retail margins).
- Building materials lose on bulk weight and project urgency (can't economically ship a 150-lb appliance).
- Gas stations are a definitional problem (can't pump gas online).
- The data is consistent with trade-press coverage: Modern Retail (April 15, 2026) flagged home/furniture as saturated; Retail Dive (May 23, 2026) said home retailers face a "weak will get weaker" 2026; eMarketer frames food & beverage as the biggest single-category online growth engine.

THREE OPERATIONAL MOVES FOR 2026:
1. Mid-cycle categories (apparel, sporting goods, furniture): Keep paid acquisition aggressive; benchmark against your category's e-commerce growth rate (~8-12% YoY), not total e-commerce.
2. Saturated nonstore categories (70%+ online): Growth must come from share-take, not category drift; go deeper on existing channels before diversifying.
3. Stuck categories (food, beauty, pet): Treat retail media as a core budget line — Kroger and CVS are planning massive in-store digital-screen rollouts in 2026; retailer-owned advertising (Instacart, Amazon Ads, Walmart Connect, Kroger Precision Marketing) is now core, as paid social CPMs keep climbing.

METHODOLOGY NOTES:
- Census 16.9% differs from Digital Commerce 360's 23.1% due to different definitions (Census excludes nonemployers post-April 2025 and covers retail NAICS 44-45; DC360 uses a broader goods-and-services basis).
- ARTS 2023 not yet released (typically lands January 2027), so category-level data stops at 2022.
- MRTS growth multiples (March 2026 vs March 2020): Nonstore retailers 2.03x, total retail 1.55x, food & beverage 1.05x, furniture 1.45x, clothing 2.52x (inflated by COVID baseline).

AUTHOR BACKGROUND: Matt Putra is Managing Partner of Eightx, managing $650M+ in revenue across 35+ ecommerce/DTC/CPG brands across the US, Canada, Australia, and the UK; former PE investor with $500M+ deployed.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The 16.9% headline isn't the story. The story is which bucket your category sits in. If you sell apparel or hobby/sporting goods, the channel is still doing some of your growth work for you. If you sell food or beauty, online channel-share isn't moving and you have to take share. If you sell pure-play digital, you're already at 70%+ and the only lever is going deeper on the channel you already own. Pick your bucket. Plan against it."

**2024 Furniture and Home Furnishings:** This category struggled to stay positive for most of the year but ended on a high note with all three months of Q4 up YOY. Foot traffic increased in Q4 with a 3.5 percent YOY increase.

**2025 Q2 Outlook:** E-commerce YOY growth has remained consistently positive as more consumers shop online, making a solid digital presence and online strategy increasingly crucial regardless of economic conditions. The article promotes Nationwide's OneShop platform for growing online sales.

Both men and women saw gains in Nonstore Retailers, Motor Vehicle and Parts Dealers, and Building Material and Garden Supply Stores. The analysis notes that women's sustained retail job losses over the last year represent the longest stretch of losses in the industry for either gender since the Great Recession, with men's retail declines preceding women's before the recession and men's gains preceding women's during recovery. The report was prepared by Jennifer Clark, Emma Williams-Baron, and Heidi Hartmann, Ph.D., at IWPR.

--- SOURCE 4: Retail trade employment: before, during, and after the ... ---
URL: https://www.bls.gov/opub/btn/volume-11/retail-trade-employment-before-during-and-after-the-pandemic.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics' "Beyond the Numbers" publication (Vol. 11, No. 4, April 2022) by Daniel Dorfman examines retail trade employment trends before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic, using data from the BLS Employment Projections program.

KEY TRENDS AND FINDINGS:

**Pre-Pandemic (2010-2019):**
- Retail employment grew from a Great Recession low of 14.4 million workers in 2010 to a peak of 15.8 million in 2017 (1.3% average annual growth), then declined by approximately 200,000 jobs from 2017-2019 (0.7% annual decline) due to e-commerce competition, thin sales margins, and technological disruption.
- Seven retail industries drove the 2017-19 contraction. General merchandise stores and clothing stores each accounted for ~29% of the decline; sporting goods, hobby, musical instrument, and bookstores accounted for 19.3%. These three together accounted for 77.6% of the sector's decline.
- Supporting industries grew significantly: couriers and messengers grew 54.4% and warehousing and storage grew 86.1% from 2010-2019, versus retail's 8.1% growth.

**During the Pandemic (2019-2020):**
- The retail sector lost almost 800,000 jobs in 2020 (vs. ~200,000 from 2017-19). E-commerce support industries (couriers/messengers, warehousing/storage) gained a combined ~300,000 jobs.
- Clothing stores accounted for 38.6% of total retail sector employment loss in 2020. Six industries (motor vehicle and parts dealers, gasoline stations, miscellaneous store retailers, clothing stores, furniture stores, and health/personal care stores) accounted for more than three-quarters of retail jobs lost.
- General merchandise stores fared relatively better (only 1.5% decline in 2020 vs. 29.2% in 2017-19), because warehouse clubs and supercenters selling essential goods experienced employment gains.

**Projections (2020-2030):**
- Retail trade is projected to lose ~587,000 jobs (4.0% of 2020 employment) over 2020-30, the largest projected employment decline of any sector. Retail trade's share of total employment is projected to fall from 9.7% (2020) to 8.6% (2030).
- Largest projected declines: food and beverage stores (-257,500 jobs, -8.3%) and general merchandise stores (-233,500 jobs, -7.7%), together accounting for 83.7% of retail jobs lost.
- Projected to gain employment: nonstore retailers (+85,600, +14.6%, the only industry projected to exceed prepandemic levels), motor vehicle and parts dealers (+76,100, +4.0%), clothing stores (+42,800, +4.5%), and furniture/home furnishings stores (+19,900, +4.9%).
- Other projected declines include: electronics and appliance stores (-15.0%), miscellaneous store retailers (-11.6%), sporting goods/hobby/book stores (-7.3%), gasoline stations (-4.7%), health/personal care stores (-4.0%), and building material dealers (-4.0%).
- By 2030, motor vehicle and parts dealers are projected to grow their share to 13.9% of retail employment (from 12.8%); nonstore retailers to 4.7% (from 3.9% in 2020). Clothing stores are projected to recover to 7.0% share (between prepandemic 8.5% and pandemic 6.4%).
- E-commerce sales increased 32.0% from Q4 2019 to Q4 2020, growing from 11.0% to almost 14.0% of total retail sales.

**Conclusions:**
The pandemic accelerated pre-existing trends driven by e-commerce and automation. Most retail industries will continue long-term declines, while those insulated from e-commerce (building material dealers, motor vehicle dealers) and those accelerated by e-commerce (nonstore retailers) will fare best. BLS projects 3.9% average annual productivity growth in retail trade from 2020-30, versus 2.3% from 2010-20.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 6: COVID-19 ends longest employment recovery and expansion in CES history, causing unprecedented job losses in 2020 : Monthly Labor Review : U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics ---
URL: https://www.bls.gov/opub/mlr/2021/article/covid-19-ends-longest-employment-expansion-in-ces-history.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a June 2021 Monthly Labor Review article by BLS economists Ryan Ansell and John P. Mullins documenting how COVID-19 ended the longest employment recovery and expansion in U.S. Current Employment Statistics (CES) history, causing unprecedented job losses in 2020.

KEY FINDINGS:
- Nonfarm payroll employment declined by 9.4 million in 2020, the largest calendar-year decline in the history of the CES employment series (which began in 1939).
- Total nonfarm employment ended 2020 at 10.0 million below its February 2020 peak of 152.5 million.
- The U.S. had experienced over 9 years of steady employment growth before the pandemic, the longest recovery/expansion in CES history.
- January and February 2020 added a combined 604,000 jobs before the pandemic hit.

CHRONOLOGY OF THE 2020 DOWNTURN:
- January 21, 2020: CDC announced the first U.S. COVID-19 case.
- March 11, 2020: WHO designated COVID-19 as a pandemic (312 new daily U.S. cases that day).
- March 2020: State/local governments imposed restrictions (stay-at-home orders, social distancing, travel restrictions, school closures, business capacity limits). Nonfarm employment fell by 1.7 million — a loss only surpassed by a 1945 post-WWII demobilization decline.
- February 2020 was designated as the economic peak (start of recession).
- April 2020: Employment plummeted by 20.7 million — the largest decline in CES history. Combined March-April losses totaled 22.4 million, a 15 percent decline. By contrast, job losses in the previous four recessions since 1981 averaged 3 percent (largest was 6 percent in the Great Recession of 2007–09).
- Recovery began May 2020 (+2.8 million) and June 2020 (+4.8 million). May, June, July, and August brought the four largest monthly job gains in CES history.
- As COVID-19 surged later in 2020 and restrictions tightened, gains shrank, and December ended with a job loss.

INDUSTRY IMPACTS (2020 employment changes):
- Leisure and hospitality: -3,677,000 (largest losses; fell 48.6% Feb–Apr, recovered 51.1% Apr–Dec)
- Government: -1,273,000
- Education and health services: -1,184,000
- Professional and business services: -860,000
- Manufacturing: -578,000
- Retail trade: -459,000
- Other services: -450,000
- Wholesale trade: -282,000
- Information: -238,000
- Construction: -157,000
- Mining and logging: -97,000
- Transportation and warehousing: -93,000
- Financial activities: -58,000
- Utilities: -10,000
- Every major industry lost jobs in 2020.

WOMEN'S EMPLOYMENT:
- Women's nonfarm employment fell 5.2 million in 2020.
- In March-April, women's employment declined by 12.2 million, accounting for 55 percent of total employment decline.
- Losses concentrated in industries with large female workforces (leisure and hospitality: women = 53% of employment; education/health services: 77%; government: 58%; other services: 53%; retail trade: 50%; professional/business services: 46%).
- In education/health services, women accounted for 84% of total employment declines in March-April; in leisure/hospitality, women accounted for 54% of job losses.

EARNINGS:
- Average hourly earnings of all private employees rose $1.55 (5.5%) in 2020; production/nonsupervisory rose $1.31 (5.5%) — largest annual changes in CES history.
- Earnings rose because job losses concentrated in low-wage industries. Leisure and hospitality (Feb avg hourly earnings $16.90, lowest of any industry) accounted for 39% of Feb–Apr private employment decline; retail trade ($20.18, second lowest) accounted for another 11%.
- This compositional effect pushed up average private earnings.

HOURS:
- Average weekly hours of all private employees rose 0.4 hour to 34.7 hours (largest annual increase since 2010); production/nonsupervisory rose 0.7 hour to 34.2 hours (largest in CES history).

DIFFUSION INDEXES (breadth of employment change):
- In April 2020, the 1-month total private diffusion index fell to 4.5 — lowest reading in 30-year history; manufacturing fell to 3.3 — lowest in its history.
- In March, 221 of 257 total private industries lost jobs; in April, 244 did. In manufacturing, 61 of 75 industries shed jobs in March, 72 in April.
- Index surged back above 50 from May onward, indicating most industries adding jobs monthly.
- However, December 2020 12-month index stood at 14.6 (total private) and 11.3 (manufacturing): 219 of 257 total private industries lost jobs during 2020 (only 37 gained); 66 of 75 manufacturing industries shed jobs (only 8 gained).

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This July 2020 fact sheet from the National Women's Law Center (NWLC), authored by Amanda Fins, examines the disproportionate impact of the COVID-19 pandemic and ensuing recession on women working in the U.S. retail sector.

KEY FINDINGS ON JOB LOSSES:
- Nearly 20.7 million people lost jobs in April 2020 alone; retail was hit particularly hard.
- Women make up 48.7% of the retail workforce (7.8 million women), but accounted for 65.2% of all retail trade job losses between February and June 2020.

Examples: Food and Beverage Stores (100% of losses were women's despite being 50.3% of the subsector workforce), Health and Personal Care Stores (85% of losses; 71.9% share), General Merchandise Stores (74.8%; 58.3% share), and Clothing Stores (70.8%; 71.1% share).

WAGE AND BENEFIT DISPARITIES:
- Women in retail earn $34,000 annually vs. $42,000 for men (81 cents per dollar). Black women, Latinas, and Native American women earn $30,000 annually—just 61 cents per dollar paid to white, non-Hispanic men ($49,000). Women with disabilities and women born outside the U.S. earn 71 cents per dollar.
- In 2018, 32.5% of women in retail worked part-time vs. 20.1% of men. By June 2020, one in four women (25.2%) working part-time wanted full-time work but couldn't get it for economic reasons (up from 11% in February).
- 8.9% of women in retail lived in poverty in 2018—nearly double the overall worker poverty rate. Poverty rates were notably higher for Black women (12.5%), Latinas (12%), Native American women (10.5%), and women with disabilities (16.5%).
- Women hold 66% of cashier/retail salesperson jobs in grocery stores (paying ~$11.40/hour) and 71% in general merchandise stores (~$12.11/hour). Temporary $2-3/hour hazard pay boosts largely expired.
- Only ~40% of workers in large retail/grocery stores had paid sick days pre-pandemic; companies with 500+ employees are exempt from federal emergency paid sick leave provisions.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the Michigan Journal of Economics (published April 13, 2026, written by Reena Jari) examines the decline and potential reinvention of American shopping malls. 

**Background & Structure:** Malls are typically owned by real estate investment trusts (REITs) that lease retail space to tenants in exchange for base pay, operating expenses, and a percentage of sales. Large department stores like Macy's and Nordstrom serve as "anchor stores" that drive foot traffic and receive lower rent.

**Causes of Decline:**
1. **E-commerce rise:** Online shopping platforms like Amazon, launched in the early 2010s, offered convenience, accessibility, and variety at lower prices, reducing brick-and-mortar competitiveness.
2. **COVID-19 pandemic:** Remote work reduced commuting and consumer foot traffic. A JPMorgan Chase Institute report noted that grocery stores and restaurants bounced back post-pandemic, but retail spaces continued lagging due to e-commerce.
3. **Competition between malls:** Malls with poor asset management struggled against newer malls with better amenities. Poor management practices (e.g., not paying utility bills or property taxes) caused financial instability and tenant loss.
4. **Anchor store bankruptcies:** Forever 21's bankruptcy resulted in over 200 store closures in the US, creating large vacant spaces difficult to fill, destabilizing surrounding tenants and occupancy.
5. **Example - San Francisco Centre mall:** Entered a "death spiral" due to homelessness, shoplifting, and drug use, causing nearly all retailers to leave; when anchors Nordstrom and Bloomingdale's closed, the mall collapsed.

**Signs of Reinvention:**
- High-end malls are nearly fully occupied with rising rents per the Wall Street Journal.
- Vacant retail spaces are being converted into restaurants, gyms, entertainment venues, and alternative uses, evolving malls into entertainment centers.
- Dillard's acquired the struggling Longview Mall in Texas and is renovating it, demonstrating investor optimism.

**Gen Z Revival:** Younger shoppers are driving mall resurgence. Circana data shows shoppers aged 18-24 bought 62% of total general merchandise in stores (vs. 52% for ages 25+). Gen Z values instant gratification and in-person try-ons, pushing online-only brands like Edikted to open physical mall locations.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Coresight Research report (published 2023, with a 2026 follow-up report referenced) examines the state of the American mall, challenging the popular narrative of "dying malls" by showing that top-tier malls are thriving. Key findings include:

- Physical retail bounced back after pandemic restrictions lifted, with 2022 seeing more store openings than closures for the first time since 2016.
- Retail sales at malls grew more than 11% in 2022 to nearly $819 billion.
- Malls capture a greater share of sales than their share of space, with high sales productivity especially pronounced at top-tier malls.

MARKET SCALE AND OPPORTUNITY:
- Malls make up a shrinking proportion of total US retail gross leasable area—down to 5.5% in 2023 from 5.7% in 2014, driven by low-tier mall closures.
- ICSC estimates 12.9% of US consumer expenditure on retail goods and services went through malls in Q1 2023.
- Mall expenditure totaled $728.9 billion in 2021 and $818.7 billion in 2022 (11.2% YoY increase).

CORESIGHT RESEARCH ANALYSIS:
- Occupancy: Top-tier malls averaged 95.1% occupancy in 2022 (based on public mall operators, S&P Capital IQ data), still slightly below pre-pandemic levels; non-top-tier malls lagged more meaningfully.
- Rent: Average minimum base rent at top-tier malls grew in the mid-teens percentage range for four consecutive quarters from Q4 2021.
- Revenue: Both top-tier and non-top-tier public mall operators saw CAGRs in the mid-to-high single digits between 2020 and 2022.
- Traffic: Based on a Placer.ai sampling of 120 malls, traffic at top-tier malls was up 12% on average in 2022 versus pre-pandemic 2019; non-top-tier malls were up 10%. Top-tier mall traffic growth was driven by long-distance visitors. Coresight's US Consumer Tracker found 40.3% of respondents visited a mall in the prior two weeks in the December 28, 2022 survey.

DRIVERS OF MALL GROWTH:
1. Multichannel halo effect: Brands with both online and offline presence see sales boosts, reduced customer acquisition costs, and better margins. Rising online advertising costs (driven partly by data privacy features like Apple's app tracking transparency) push brands to physical retail. 61% of retailers and 66% of digital-first retailers cite rising customer acquisition costs as the top obstacle to 2022 e-commerce goals (CommerceNext study). 45% of tracked DNVBs have opened physical stores (Coresight DNVB Databank). BORIS (buy online, return in-store) cuts shipping costs and boosts loyalty.
2. Brand synergy: Brands generate more value in proximity to other high-value brands, driving foot traffic.
3. Reinvestment: Top-tier mall operators like Simon Property Group (Phipps Plaza Atlanta redevelopment with Nobu Hotel/Restaurant, Life Time facility, Citizens Market, office tower) and Taubman ($200 million renovation of The Mall at Green Hills in Nashville, 2019, including 132,000 sq ft of inline retail, new Dillard's, and 70,000 sq ft RH store) continually reinvest.
4. Omnichannel investment by mall owners: Cadillac Fairview partnered with Swyft (CF Delivery same-day/next-day shipping) and ReturnBear (multi-retailer returns). Simon Property Group's Simon Search provides real-time mall inventory data; its Shop Premium Outlets (SPO) platform provides access to 35 million online shoppers and 2 billion in-store shoppers globally, and partnered with Tmall Global (Alibaba) in late October 2022 for Singles' Day. Simon also partnered with Leap (November 2022) to support DNVBs entering brick-and-mortar.

CONCLUSION: Top-tier malls are outperforming the average mall in revenues, occupancy, and foot traffic. The combination of physical retail and e-commerce creates a halo effect benefiting brands. Coresight expects that omnichannel strategies and investments will disproportionately benefit top-tier mall growth going forward.

Contributors: Charlotte Rothschild and Daniel Rodden, Analysts at Coresight Research.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the Michigan Journal of Economics, written by Reena Jari and published April 13, 2026, examines the decline and potential reinvention of American shopping malls. 

**Background/Context:** Malls are owned by real estate investment trusts (REITs) that lease retail spaces to tenants who pay base rent, operating expenses, and a percentage of sales. Large department stores like Macy's and Nordstrom serve as "anchor stores" that drive foot traffic and receive lower rents. Malls have faced declining retail sales due to multiple factors.

**Key Causes of Mall Decline:**
1. **E-commerce:** The rise of Amazon and other online retailers in the early 2010s shifted consumer behavior to online shopping due to convenience, accessibility, and product variety, reducing competitiveness of brick-and-mortar retail.
2. **COVID-19 pandemic:** Work-from-home trends reduced commuting and foot traffic. A JP Morgan Chase Institute report found grocery stores and restaurants recovered post-COVID, but retail spaces lagged due to e-commerce.
3. **Internal competition between malls:** Poorly managed malls struggle against newer malls with better amenities. Examples include a mall in Texas acquired by Dillard's after previous owners failed to pay utility bills and property taxes.
4. **Anchor store bankruptcies:** Forever 21's bankruptcy caused the loss of 200+ stores in the US, and large vacant spaces are difficult to fill. The San Francisco Centre mall entered a "death spiral" due to homelessness, shoplifting, and drug use, leading to anchor store closures (Nordstrom, Bloomingdale's) and collapse.

**Reinvention & Recovery:**
- Some investors see redevelopment potential; high-end malls are nearly fully occupied with rising rents according to the Wall Street Journal.
- Vacant spaces are being converted into restaurants, gyms, entertainment venues, and alternative uses — malls are evolving into entertainment centers.
- Dillard's purchased and renovated the Longview Mall in Texas to enhance consumer experience.
- Gen Z is driving a mall comeback: Circana data shows shoppers aged 18-24 bought 62% of total general merchandise in stores (vs. 52% for those 25+). Younger shoppers value instant gratification and in-store experiences, with the online clothing brand Edikted opening physical mall locations due to Gen Z demand.

**Conclusion:** While many malls have struggled to adapt to e-commerce, post-COVID changes, and bankruptcies, the industry may be making a comeback by adapting to consumer demand rather than disappearing entirely.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"E-commerce sales are increasing because of how convenient online buying is, how accessible it is, and how many different things are available" (Kothari, 2018).
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Bed Bath & Beyond is closing hundreds of stores. But they won’t be empty for long | CNN Business ---
URL: https://www.cnn.com/2023/04/24/business/bed-bath-beyond-stores-bankruptcy-real-estate/index.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
CNN article (updated from an original March 21 piece) reports on Bed Bath & Beyond's bankruptcy and the real estate opportunities created by its store closures. The company filed for bankruptcy on Sunday and will close its remaining 360 Bed Bath & Beyond stores and 120 buybuy Baby locations, adding to 400 stores already closed over the past year. Rather than remaining vacant, these stores are being rapidly scooped up by other retailers and businesses due to historically tight commercial real estate conditions.

Key context: total new commercial retail construction hit a record low in 2022 (third consecutive year), and the retail space vacancy rate fell to 4.9% at the end of 2022 — the lowest since CBRE began tracking in 2005. Bed Bath & Beyond stores are attractive because they're located in all 50 states (most in California, Texas, New Jersey, and Florida), mostly in suburbs of mid-size and large cities, and average around 30,000 square feet (under 50,000 sq ft), aligning with the retail trend toward smaller spaces. In some cases, landlords are eager to replace old leases because Bed Bath & Beyond was paying below-market rent.

Chains already moving into former locations include TJ Maxx, HomeGoods, Ross, Burlington, Five Below, Nordstrom Rack, and budget gym Planet Fitness (which opens ~200 new gyms a year). Growth is most pronounced in the discount retail segment as budget-conscious shoppers seek low prices. Physical store openings exceeded closings last year for the first time since 2016 (Coresight Research), and Dollar General, Family Dollar, Dollar Tree, and Five Below lead opening announcements this year.

Federal Realty, a REIT owning nine Bed Bath & Beyond stores, is negotiating with chains like TJX, Burlington, Ross, Nordstrom Rack, and Container Store. Once agreements are finalized, new retailers typically take 18-24 months to open. Meanwhile, Tuesday Morning will also close more than 250 stores this year, with A&G Real Estate Partners auctioning off leases (10,000-20,000 sq ft spaces), with discount chains interested due to their small, already-built nature. With limited new development, growth is coming from "second-generation space."
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"E-commerce scared a lot of people off from building retail. A lot of great real estate is going to come available into a market where there's been no vacancies. It will not take long for retailers to occupy those spaces." — Brandon Isner, head of retail research at CBRE. "For us, the biggest source of new store locations comes from other retailers closing stores. So many of our most productive locations were formerly Circuit City or Toys 'R' Us or Sports Authority." — Burlington CEO Michael O'Sullivan. "There is good interest for Bed Bath & Beyond stores that are closing given desirable locations and an average size of around 30,000 square feet." — Telsey Advisory Group retail analysts. "We feel pretty bullish based on the demand that we've seen that we'll be able to release all of these spaces to other retailers." — Lance Billingsley, senior VP of anchor leasing at Federal Realty. "With not a lot of new development going on, everyone's growth will come from second-generation space." — Mike Matlat, A&G Real Estate Partners senior managing director.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Dead/Dying Malls in Your Area and Predictions ---
URL: https://www.retailwatchers.com/viewtopic.php?t=2660

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a forum thread from Retail Watchers (retailwatchers.com) titled "Dead/Dying Malls in Your Area and Predictions," posted in the Shopping Centers subforum. The thread was started on November 24, 2020, by user "architect" and contains 91 posts across 10 pages. The purpose is for users to share observations about dead or dying shopping malls in their regions and predict which malls will next decline. The thread opens with a prediction that up to 50% of malls could close over the next five years.

Key observations by region:

**Dallas-Fort Worth, TX (architect):** The Shops at Willow Bend in Plano has deteriorated noticeably, with 30-40% of in-line spaces vacant. It opened around 9/11 targeting an upscale demographic with anchors including Neiman Marcus, Saks, and Lord & Taylor. Apple closed its store there (the third to open in the nation) due to patent-troll litigation strategy, causing traffic to decline. Other dead/dying DFW malls include Music City Mall, Irving Mall, Ridgmar Mall, and Village at Fairview. Golden Triangle Mall and Hulen Mall are at risk long-term.

**Portland, OR (babs):** Lloyd Center, interior of Mall 205, interior of Cedar Hills Crossing (exterior businesses successful), and Three Rivers Mall in Kelso are all struggling.

**Phoenix, AZ (arizonaguy):** Dead malls include MetroCenter (only Harkins, Dillard's Clearance Center, Walmart remain), Fiesta Mall (fully closed, being converted to medical offices), and Paradise Valley Mall (Dillard's closing). Dying malls include ChrisTown Spectrum, Desert Sky/Westridge, and Superstition Springs Center (wounded by Macerich building SanTan Village nearby). Healthy malls include SanTan Village, Biltmore Fashion Park, and Scottsdale Fashion Square (the Phoenix area's flagship mall). Notably, nearly all Phoenix malls are owned by Macerich.

**Pacific Northwest (Super S, Brian Lutz):** Struggling malls include Shoppes at Riverside (Aberdeen, WA), Willamette Town Center (Salem), Lewis County Mall (Chehalis), and Yard Birds "Mall" (Chehalis). In Seattle, Northgate Mall is being converted from indoor to outdoor (with a Seattle Kraken practice facility and new light rail station). Healthy Seattle malls include Bellevue Collection, Alderwood, Southcenter, and Crossroads Bellevue. So-so malls include Pacific Place, Westlake Center, Marketplace at Factoria, Everett Mall, Redmond Town Center, and Commons at Federal Way.

**Texas (pseudo3d):** Post Oak Mall (College Station) has seen better days, with Macy's upper level converted to Backstage, an outdated JCPenney, closed Sears (partially converted to Conn's HomePlus), and former Bealls became Gordmans then closed. The mall is about 85% full, with a small food court and demographic shifts.

**Northern California (lake52, Alpha8472, storewanderer):** Strong malls include Galleria at Roseville, Stanford, and Hillsdale Mall. Struggling malls include Fountains at Roseville, Arden Fair (which experienced a mass shooting around the time of posting), Sunrise Mall (city of Citrus Heights planning redevelopment away from retail), Downtown Commons, Tanforan, and Stonestown (in transition). Sunvalley Mall in Concord is near death with 80% of stores closed, and Hilltop Mall in Richmond is near death (only kept alive by a Walmart). Crime is cited as a major factor in several Bay Area mall declines. Arden Fair is discussed in depth, with suggestions that it needs to pivot to a lower-middle-class tenant mix and mixed-use/housing redevelopment, including adding a grocery operator.

--- SOURCE 4: The Great American Store Closure Tracker, 2026 Edition - MMCG Invest ---
URL: https://www.mmcginvest.com/post/the-great-american-store-closure-tracker-2026-edition

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive citation-grade research article (April 2026, "The Great American Store Closure Tracker, 2026 Edition") analyzing the 2025 U.S. retail closure cycle. The central thesis is counterintuitive: while media portrayed American retail as "collapsing," the data show a CONCENTRATED contraction, not a broad collapse.

KEY HEADLINE DATA:
- Coresight Research counted 8,270 U.S. store closures in 2025 vs. 5,270 openings (net loss ~3,000), far below the projected 15,000
- National retail vacancy was 5.7% (Q4 2025), only 40 bps above the cyclical low of 5.3%
- Simon Property Group ended 2025 at 96.4% mall/outlet occupancy with rents up 4.7%
- Five bankrupt brands (Joann, Party City, Big Lots, New Rite Aid, Forever 21) drove more than half of all 2025 closure square footage (~127M sf closed through July 2025)
- Top ten chains accounted for ~5,500 of 8,270 closures (~two-thirds)

MAJOR BANKRUPTCIES AND CLOSURES:
- Rite Aid: second Chapter 11 (May 5, 2025), full liquidation of all ~1,240 stores by Oct 3, 2025; ~15.5M sf vacated
- Joann: second Chapter 11 (Jan 15, 2025), full liquidation of all ~800 stores; ~18M sf
- Party City: Chapter 22 (Dec 21, 2024), ~700 stores liquidated; ~8.4M sf
- Big Lots: converted to Chapter 7 (Nov 10, 2025), ~340 net closures after Variety Wholesalers rescue; ~9M sf
- Forever 21: Chapter 22 (Mar 16, 2025), all 354 U.S. stores liquidated
- Saks Global: Chapter 11 (Jan 13, 2026, Southern District of Texas), $3.4B funded debt, ~5.6M sf coming off market; post-closure footprint ~13 Saks Fifth Avenue, 32 Neiman Marcus, 2 Bergdorf Goodman stores
- Walgreens: ~500 closures FY2025; Sycamore Partners $23.7B take-private (Aug 28, 2025) decelerated closures to <100 in 2026
- CVS: ~271 closures in 2025, ending its 900-store program; first net-add year in five
- Starbucks: ~520 North American closures (Q1 FY26 only 3 more)
- Advance Auto Parts: 727 closures (5.45M sf), exited 5 Western states entirely
- GameStop: 727 closures FY2025, cumulative >50% of fleet since FY2023

STRUCTURAL INSIGHTS:
- Chapter 22s (second filings) dominated — companies emerged from prior Chapter 11 but failed to restore trade credit/vendor terms
- 71% of largest consumer discretionary bankruptcies of 2025 involved private equity ownership at filing
- Casual dining in worst distress since 2009 (Red Lobster, TGI Fridays, Hooters, FAT Brands/Twin Hospitality filing Jan 2026 with $1.3-1.4B debt, QVC Group prepackaged Chapter 11 Apr 16, 2026 targeting $5.3B debt reduction)
- 9% of full-service restaurant units and 4% of limited-service units flagged "at risk" of 2026 closure

GEOGRAPHIC BIFURCATION:
- Most stressed markets: New Orleans (+240 bps to 6.3%), Buffalo (+240 bps to 10.8%), Pittsburgh (+200 bps to 6.4%), Providence (+170 bps), Milwaukee (+170 bps)
- Sun Belt winners: Charlotte (+7.6% rent growth to $27.29/sf, 3.4% vacancy), Raleigh-Durham (3.1% vacancy), Phoenix (+964,553 sf absorption)
- Heavy closure concentration in California, Florida, Ohio, New York, Michigan
- Stagnant/declining population states lose retail; high-growth Sun Belt states gain it

BACKFILL COHORT (who absorbed closed boxes):
- Aldi: ~180 new stores 2025 toward 800-store target
- Burlington: 104 net new stores 2025, >40% from bankrupt-tenant recaptures
- Planet Fitness: 181 new clubs 2025 (highest ever); Crunch Fitness: 91 clubs, leased 4.27M sf
- Dollar Tree: +388 net stores to 9,269; Dollar General: +196
- AutoZone: 304 net new stores (record); O'Reilly: 207 net new with 225-235 guided for 2026
- Dave's Hot Chicken: Roark Capital $1B valuation majority stake (June 2025)
- Dick's Sporting Goods: 16 new House of Sport + 20 Field House in 2025

LANDLORD OUTCOMES:
- Best landlords turned bankruptcy into alpha: Brixmor full-year 2025 new-lease cash spreads 38.7%; Kimco ~90% of Party City/Joann/Big Lots/Rite Aid space re-leased at 30-40% releasing spreads; Simon re-tenanted Saks Off 5th at +67% mark-to-market spread
- Kimco upgraded to A- (S&P) and A3 (Moody's)
- 2025 saw the largest embedded rent mark-to-market in a decade driven by bankruptcy recapture
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Ask a casual observer what happened to American retail in 2025 and the answer is usually some version of 'it collapsed.' The images from the year support the impression. Joann liquidated. Party City liquidated. Rite Aid liquidated for the second time in nineteen months. Forever 21 liquidated. Big Lots collapsed into Chapter 7. Starbucks shuttered more than five hundred North American stores in a single fiscal quarter. Advance Auto Parts walked away from five Western states entirely. The data tell a different and more useful story."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: List of Retail Company Bankruptcies & Closing Stores - CB Insights ---
URL: https://www.cbinsights.com/research/retail-apocalypse-timeline-infographic

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a CB Insights research report (published April 26, 2023) that analyzes 154 retail bankruptcies from 2015 through early 2023, examining why major retailers failed. The report argues that Amazon is not the only cause of physical retail's troubles—mounting debt, retailers' own missteps, and lack of adaptability are also to blame.

Key context: The Covid-19 pandemic accelerated the fall of many retailers facing dwindling sales and growing debt. Department stores proved most vulnerable (e.g., Neiman Marcus, JCPenney). There were 52 retail bankruptcies in 2020, 21 in 2021 (a 60% drop YoY), and only a handful in 2022. Reports indicated bankruptcies may flare up again in 2023 due to rising prices and pullback in consumer spending.

Notable 2023 bankruptcies:
- Bed Bath & Beyond (April, home goods): Lagged competitors in e-commerce, faced declining revenue, debt, supply chain disruption; closed stores to sell parts of the business.
- David's Bridal (April, bridal apparel, second bankruptcy): Hit by pandemic and post-pandemic change in consumer preferences for wedding apparel; laid off 9K+ employees.
- Boxed (April, wholesale e-commerce): Struggles exacerbated by Silicon Valley Bank crisis where it held most cash deposits; wound down retail, sold software business.
- Independent Pet Partners (February, pet supplies): Consumers shifted away from grain-free/high-protein dog food; exited Natural Pawz and Loyal Companion brands.
- Tuesday Morning (February, discount home goods, second bankruptcy): Decreased consumer spending and high interest rates.
- Serta Simmons Bedding (January, bedding): $1.9B debt load, litigation over pandemic funding, aimed to cut debt to $300M.
- Party City (January, party supplies): Helium shortage (2019), inflation slowdown, big-box competition; $1.7B debt and $122M liquidity as of Sept 2022.
- Forma Brands (January, beauty/Morphe): Moved away from influencer partnerships after scandals; brands failed to hit revenue projections.

Notable 2022 bankruptcies:
- M&Co (December, UK apparel): Inflation, decreased consumer appetite; ~2,000 employees at risk.
- Sears Hometown (December, home goods): Pandemic aftershocks, drop in sales, increased costs.
- Joules (November, UK apparel): Bought out of insolvency by Next in partnership with founder Tom Joule (operated ~80% of stores).
- Olympia Sports (September, sporting goods): Faulty order management system, executive flight, pandemic; total closure after ~50 years and 230 stores at peak.
- Secoo (August, luxury e-commerce, China): Heightened competition, decreased spending, sales contract disputes, false advertising charges.
- Future Retail (July, India): Court admitted to bankruptcy despite Amazon's opposition (Amazon sought control of FR since 2019).
- Revlon (June, beauty): Declining sales, pandemic supply chain disruption, growing competition from startups like Glossier; Citigroup accidentally wired $900M instead of $8M in interest payments.
- Missguided (May, UK womenswear): Bought by Frasers Group for ~$24M.
- Escada America (January, luxury womenswear): Overexpansion, deficient leadership, overpriced leases; closed 5 of 10 US locations.
- BH Cosmetics (January, beauty): Pandemic-driven changes in beauty routines; sold IP for $4.3M; bought by Revolution Beauty.

Notable 2021 bankruptcies:
- ABC Carpet & Home (September, high-end home goods): 124 years in business; $80M unsecured and $8M secured debt; sales down 50% from 2018 to $25M.
- Lorna Jane (September, Australia activewear): Brick-and-mortar sales dropped 56% in 2020; $3.7M fine for falsely advertising Covid-19 protection claims; used bankruptcy to cancel 21 US leases.

- Alex and Ani (June, jewelry): $1B valuation in 2016, then legal complications, executive turnover, mismanagement, ransomware attack, pandemic; revenue fell 40% in 2020.
- Washington Prime Group (June, mall REIT): Rental income dropped $127M in 2020; income fell from $10M to $3.3M (March 2020–March 2021); secured $100M DIP financing, deleveraged $950M.
- The Collected Group (April, womenswear: Joie, Current/Elliot, Equipment): Emerged with KKR funding.
- Paper Source (March, stationary): Awarded executives $1.5M in bonuses during pandemic; acquired by Barnes & Noble.
- Belk (February, department store): Founded 1888; entered with $1.9B debt; emerged in one day, reduced debt by $450M, received $225M fresh capital for 291 stores.
- Solstice (February, sunglasses): Sales down 50%+ at 66 stores; emerged with $6.5M exit financing from Second Avenue Capital Partners.
- L'Occitane US (January, beauty): Behind on $15M rent, exited 29 "burdensome" leases.
- Christopher & Banks (January, womenswear): Closed most of 450 stores; sold online business to Hilco Merchant Resources affiliate.
- Loves Furniture (January, furniture): Warehouse/inventory problems, lost furniture, canceled orders.
- Stock+Field (January, farming/agriculture): Closed 25 locations after 55+ years; acquired by R.P. Acquisition Corp.

Notable 2020 bankruptcies:
- Francesca's (December, womenswear): Closed roughly half of 551 mall locations; sold to TerraMar Capital and Tiger Capital Group for $18M.
- Furniture Factory Outlet (November, furniture): Sun Capital Partners-owned; closed 37 of 68 stores; acquired by American Freight.
- Guitar Center (November, musical instruments): $1.3B debt, online competition; emerged after capital infusion wiped out $800M of debt.
- YouFit Health Clubs (November, gym): Sold to former lenders; 24 Hour Fitness and Gold's Gym also filed earlier that year.
- Century 21 (September, discount department store): Closed all 13 stores; CEO blamed insurers for failing to pay $175M.
- Stein Mart (August, discount department store): 112-year-old chain, 8,000+ employees; liquidated all stores; TJ Maxx and Ross reportedly grew amid pandemic.

</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Modern-day retail is at an inflection point as retailers face struggling physical storefronts, massive debt, and inefficient operations, among other issues., Department stores proved to be the most vulnerable, with the pandemic felling iconic names such as Neiman Marcus and JCPenney., While there were 52 retail bankruptcies in 2020, 2021 saw just 21 — a 60% drop year-over-year, according to Axios., As we'll see, Amazon is not the only reason that physical retail is troubled — mounting debt and retailers' own missteps and lack of adaptability are also to blame, among other factors., While the company grew its physical footprint considerably in the aughts, it lagged behind competitors like Target, Amazon, and Walmart in building out its e-commerce presence.

--- SOURCE 6: Retail Vacancy in New York City - Office of the New York City Comptroller
Mark Levine ---
URL: https://comptroller.nyc.gov/reports/retail-vacancy-in-new-york-city

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is from the New York City Comptroller's Office (comptroller.nyc.gov) and presents a comprehensive report titled "Retail Vacancy in New York City: Trends and Causes, 2007-2017." The report was authored by New York City Comptroller Scott Stringer and provides a data-driven analysis of retail vacancy across all five boroughs of NYC using administrative data from property tax filings (RPIE), commercial leasing data from Compstak, MasterCard merchant data, and regulatory approval data from the NY State Liquor Authority and NYC Department of Buildings.

KEY FINDINGS:
1. Vacancy Rates Have Risen: The citywide retail vacancy rate increased from a low of 4.0% in 2007 to 5.8% in 2017. Vacancy rates rose across all five boroughs, most dramatically in Staten Island (from 4.3% to nearly 11%). Reported vacant retail space roughly doubled from 5.6 million sq ft to 11.8 million sq ft over the decade. The highest vacancy rates are in the outer boroughs, particularly Staten Island, Queens, and the Bronx.

2. Internet Shopping Changed Retail Space Usage: Amazon sales rose from $14.8 billion in 2007 to $177.9 billion in 2017. NYC retail establishments grew 19%, but personal services grew ~50% and bars/restaurants rose 65%. Regression analysis shows Amazon sales positively and significantly associated with retail vacancy, driving vacant retail square footage higher by nearly 1 percentage point between 2007-2017.

3. Rising Rents Contributed to Vacancy: Average retail rents rose 22% citywide (from $42 to $51 per sq ft). Rents doubled in Soho (10012) from $60 to $126 and rose 87% on the Upper East Side (from $79 to $146). A 1% increase in average retail rents is associated with 0.33% increase in vacant retail square footage. Property taxes paid by retail tenants doubled from $1.1 billion in 2007 to $2.2 billion in 2017 (rising from 20% to 23% of total retail rents).

4. Regulatory Hurdles Impede Turnover: The share of Department of Buildings alteration permits unapproved after 30 days is a significant driver of vacancy (1% increase associated with 3.28% increase in vacant retail footage). Liquor license approval times rose from ~50 to ~75 days in 2018. A 1% increase in liquor license approval time is associated with 0.17% increase in retail vacancy.

5. Landmark status was NOT found to contribute to vacancy; in fact, regression analysis shows landmarked retail is associated with lower vacancy rates.

RECOMMENDED ACTIONS:
- Provide tax incentives (tax credits up to 20%) for independent merchandise retailers in high-vacancy retail corridors
- Create single point-of-contact customer service task force for businesses occupying retail space, and waive permitting/inspection fees for businesses taking over long-vacant space
- Incorporate retail demand analysis into neighborhood planning and rezoning decisions

The report includes appendices with regression methodology (fixed effects OLS regression of log vacant retail square footage on explanatory variables at zip code level), neighborhood definitions, and detailed notes on data sources and methodology. Key limitations noted: RPIE data excludes ~25% of retail square footage (smaller buildings under $40,000 assessed value); increased penalties for non-filing beginning in 2014 improved reporting by about 1 million sq ft.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The citywide retail vacancy rate has increased substantially, from a low of 4.0 percent in 2007 to 5.8 percent in 2017."

--- SOURCE 7: Retail real estate outlook: PwC ---
URL: https://www.pwc.com/us/en/industries/financial-services/asset-wealth-management/real-estate/emerging-trends-in-real-estate-pwc-uli/property-type-outlook/retail.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is the Retail property-type outlook from PwC and the Urban Land Institute's "Emerging Trends in Real Estate® 2026" report. It examines the state of the U.S. retail real estate market heading into 2026, characterized by "uncertainty fatigue" rather than outright pessimism, with pandemic-earned confidence in retail resilience.

U.S. retail real estate in 2025 is characterized by near-record occupancy, steady (if modest) rent growth, and reviving capital flows, underpinned by a decade of constrained supply. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from RockStep Capital, dated March 10, 2025, is an educational blog article by Belen Worsham explaining the mall grading system used to classify shopping centers into Class A, B, or C categories. The article is aimed at beginner investors in shopping center/retail real estate.

**Origin of the Mall Grading System:** The concept emerged in the late 20th century. Malls were initially categorized by size (regional, super-regional, community centers). Investment research firms like Green Street Advisors pioneered revenue-based classification, and by the 1990s-2000s, REITs and firms like CBRE and JLL adopted these standards. The International Council of Shopping Centers (ICSC) continues to refine these standards today, and while not legally required, they are widely recognized as industry standard.

**Six Key Classification Factors:**
1. Sales Per Square Foot (most important metric)
2. Tenant Mix and Anchors (e.g., Apple, Gucci, Tesla vs. discount shops)
3. Location and Demographics
4. Occupancy Rates
5. Physical Condition and Amenities
6. Market Perception and Shopper Experience

**Class A Malls (Luxury High-Rises of Retail):** High sales exceeding $700-$1,000+ per square foot; premium tenants like Louis Vuitton, Gucci, Apple, and Nordstrom; occupancy at 95% or higher; located in major metro areas and affluent suburbs; offer experiential retail (fine dining, entertainment, unique attractions). Considered like blue-chip stocks—stable and resilient in downturns, but with high price tags that are less accessible to beginner investors.

**Class B Malls (Suburban Workhorses):** Moderate sales of $400-$700 per square foot; diverse tenant mix of national retailers, discount stores, and regional brands; occupancy around 85-95%; located in secondary markets (mid-sized cities or suburbs). More accessible to investors with value-add opportunities (renovations, re-tenanting), but require active management and face pressure from e-commerce trends.

**Class C Malls (Fixer-Uppers):** Low sales below $400 per square foot; high vacancy rates of 20% or more; declining foot traffic; outdated infrastructure; often viewed as redevelopment opportunities (mixed-use spaces, office hubs, or e-commerce logistics centers). High-risk, high-reward investments requiring heavy repositioning efforts and clear redevelopment strategy.

**Investor Takeaways:** The article recommends that beginner investors seek well-located Class A or B malls as the safest entry point, offering strong tenant demand and steady rental income. Those willing to take on more risk may pursue Class C repositioning, but success requires careful planning and market expertise. The page also promotes RockStep Capital's free webinar replay on "The Blueprint for Shopping Center Investments" and a free 50-page ebook on alternative investing. The article belongs to the "Investing Basics" topic category.
</summary>

## Introduction

**Gen Z shopping habits** are reshaping the entire retail landscape at unprecedented speed. As the first truly digital-native generation enters peak earning years, understanding **Gen Z shopping habits** has become essential for retail survival.

The challenge facing brands today isn’t simply understanding what Gen Z buys—it’s grasping how they discover, evaluate, and ultimately choose where to spend their money. Traditional retail playbooks built for Millennials and Gen X fall flat with a generation that grew up with smartphones in hand and algorithms curating their world.

What makes **Gen Z shopping habits** so different? This generation expects seamless digital experiences, demands authentic brand relationships, and prioritizes sustainability in ways previous generations never did. In this comprehensive guide, we examine the fundamental shifts **Gen Z shopping habits** are driving across the retail landscape. Drawing on current [market research](https://www.researchandmetric.com/what-we-do/services/online-data-collection/) and consumer intelligence, Research and Metric reveals the key patterns reshaping retail in 2025 and beyond.

## Understanding Gen Z Consumer Behavior: The Digital-First Discovery Journey

**Gen Z shopping habits** begin differently than any previous generation—they don’t browse, they scroll, swipe, and discover. Unlike older consumers who might start their shopping journey with a Google search or mall visit, Gen Z consumers increasingly encounter products through social media feeds, influencer content, and peer recommendations.

According to [Forbes research on Gen Z consumer behavior](https://www.forbes.com/sites/forbesagencycouncil/2024/01/18/how-gen-z-is-reshaping-the-retail-landscape/), over 60% of Gen Z discovers new brands through social platforms rather than traditional advertising channels. This statistic alone demonstrates why understanding **Gen Z shopping habits** is crucial for modern retailers.

### Social Commerce Dominates Gen Z Retail Trends

The path from discovery to purchase has compressed dramatically due to evolving **Gen Z shopping habits**. Social commerce features allowing in-app purchasing mean the gap between “I want this” and “I bought this” shrinks to seconds. Platforms like TikTok, Instagram, and Pinterest have transformed into powerful shopping destinations.

Key characteristics of **Gen Z shopping habits** in social commerce include:

TikTok has emerged as a primary product discovery engine, with the hashtag #TikTokMadeMeBuyIt generating billions of views. Instagram Shopping enables seamless browsing and purchasing without leaving the app. Pinterest serves as a visual search engine where **Gen Z shopping habits** translate inspiration into purchases instantly.

Retailers who create friction in this journey—requiring multiple clicks, app switches, or cumbersome checkout processes—lose sales to competitors who meet consumers where they already are. Our [consumer research services](/services/consumer-research) help brands map these critical touchpoints and optimize for **Gen Z shopping habits**.

**Key Takeaway:** Retail success with Gen Z requires treating social platforms as primary discovery and conversion channels, not supplementary marketing touchpoints.

## Authenticity: The Non-Negotiable Factor in Gen Z Brand Loyalty

For Gen Z, brand authenticity isn’t a nice-to-have—it’s a filter determining whether they engage at all. **Gen Z shopping habits** include sophisticated vetting processes, and this generation has developed sharp radar for detecting performative marketing. They respond to perceived inauthenticity by disengaging entirely or actively sharing criticism across their networks.

### What Authenticity Means for Gen Z Consumer Behavior

What constitutes authenticity within **Gen Z shopping habits**? Consistency between stated values and actual business practices ranks highest. They research companies before purchasing, checking for alignment between marketing messages and reported corporate behavior.

The [National Retail Federation’s consumer research](https://nrf.com/research-insights/consumer-research) confirms that **Gen Z shopping habits** are increasingly shaped by brand transparency and verified claims. A brand promoting sustainability while using excessive packaging, or championing diversity while lacking leadership representation, faces swift backlash.

### User-Generated Content Trumps Traditional Marketing

User-generated content and peer reviews carry more weight than polished brand messaging in shaping **Gen Z shopping habits**. Gen Z trusts real customer experiences over professional marketing, making review management and community building essential retail competencies.

# The Gen Z paradox: Spending less, expecting more

![Hero Image](/us/en/industries/assets/gen-z-paradox-hero.jpg)

Gen Z’s expected spending power by 2030

expected drop in Gen Z holiday shopping

of Gen Z say they plan to purchase “dupes” this holiday season

Gen Z has become a riddle that many retailers can’t quite crack. Their arrival in the consumer marketplace coincided with the explosion of smartphones and social media — and with economic headwinds like inflation, rising interest rates, a tough job market and the resumption of student loan payments.

The result is a generation defined by contradictions. Gen Z is digitally native, yet drawn back to physical stores. Fiercely brand-aware, yet ready to abandon brands for private labels. Cautious with money, yet quick to spend when the purchase carries emotional weight.

According to PwC’s analysis of nearly a million consumer transactions, Gen Z cut overall spending by 13% between January and April 2025 — particularly in categories like apparel, accessories and electronics. And in [PwC’s 2025 Holiday Outlook survey](/us/en/industries/consumer-markets/library/holiday-outlook-trends.html), they reported plans to slash holiday spending by 23% this year, after expecting to boost spend by 37% in 2024. Even so, Gen Z still plans to spend an average of $1,357 this season. Understanding this shift is important, considering that Gen Z’s spending power is expected to grow to [$12 trillion by 2030](https://nielseniq.com/global/en/landing-page/spend-z/), according to NielsenIQ and GfK in collaboration with World Data Lab projects.

While Gen Z’s pullback may look like a simple case of belt-tightening at first glance, it actually reveals something more complex. It’s a generational shift in how value is defined and where money feels worth spending.

![planned holiday chart]()

## What Gen Z is buying

It turns out Gen Z isn’t just price-conscious. They’re value-conscious, with an emphasis on emotional and social value, not just discounts. PwC's five-year view of Gen Z indicates that more than 79% wait for products to go on sale, and only 21% regularly pay full price. Deal hunting is rising — searching for discount codes is up 14%, browsing up 17% — but this is less about frugality than intentionality. Increasingly, as Gen Z also turns to AI tools for help finding deals, whether it’s asking for the “best value-for-money mascara” or more tailored recommendations, their path to purchase could become more algorithmically curated. To stay ahead, retailers need to start thinking about optimizing discoverability within AI-driven environments now.

With all this in mind, the answer to the Gen Z riddle appears to be about offering affordable affluence. This is like the lipstick effect, something that appeared in the aftermath of 9/11 and again in 2008, updated for the social media era. Micro luxuries like a pricey matcha, a resale sneaker drop or cosmetics that double as skincare can telegraph cultural relevance without breaking the bank. But to stay in the “must-buy” category, these items need more than aesthetic appeal. They need to feel smart — endorsed by creators, justified by value transparency and surfaced through algorithmically tailored feeds.

Timing also matters. A trending item can rise and fall within days — and for retailers, converting interest means meeting Gen Z expectations for social-to-shelf speed. The window for “what’s worth it” is short. While this generation is saving for big milestones and managing tight budgets, they still want purchases that spark joy, earn social currency and align with their own sense of identity.

Gen Z isn’t spending less across the board. They’re reallocating — trading down on everyday expenses in order to afford meaningful indulgences.

Gen Z’s selectivity doesn’t stop at products — it extends to brands themselves. This generation isn’t inherently brand loyal. They’re brand agnostic until given a reason to commit. For example, according to PwC’s analysis, more than half of Gen Z (59%) still prefer known brands but nearly half (41%) are willing to buy less expensive, private-label alternatives and 49% want customized products. For the holidays, [according to our Holiday Outlook survey](/us/en/industries/consumer-markets/library/holiday-outlook-trends.html), 82% of Gen Z say they plan to purchase less expensive alternatives (commonly known as “dupes”) and 63% plan to shop for vintage or upcycled products. These choices aren't just about saving. They reflect a generation that rewards relevance over recognition and expects brands to keep up.

When asked where they’d cut back over the next six months, Gen Z pointed to restaurants and takeout (51%), clothes (33%), and alcohol (29%). But fewer said they’d trim “high-value” items this year compared to last. What emerges is not across-the-board austerity, but selectivity. They’re willing to trade down — or trade out — on everyday expenses in order to afford meaningful indulgences.

#### Gen Z's tradeoffs: What they're cutting back on

## Where Gen Z is shopping: From clicks to bricks — again

For years, the assumption was that Gen Z would live entirely online. But that assumption is already outdated. PwC’s analysis shows that 61% of Gen Z now prefers to discover new products in-store, a reversal that speaks volumes about what this generation wants: experience.

Why? Because shopping has become an event. Our [2025 Holiday Outlook survey](/us/en/industries/consumer-markets/library/holiday-outlook-trends.html) shows a 10-point rise in how many Gen Z consumers plan to shop in-store more frequently than usual this holiday season — up from 27% in 2024 to 37% this year. Their preferred reasons are to touch and see products (41%, up from 34% last year), to experience holiday displays and store atmospheres and, yes, to chase promotions.

43% of Gen Z expect to use social media to discover gifts this holiday, compared to 30% overall. They’ll also use it to research (39% vs 27%) and compare items before purchasing (32% vs. 22%).

At the same time, Gen Z’s digital behaviors remain intense, but the path to purchase is no longer linear. They might, for instance, discover a product on social media, price compare in-app and transact in-store. This expectation of instant gratification — from social scroll to in-store shelf — is likely to increasingly shape omnichannel merchandising and inventory strategies.

![]()

## The illusion of affordability

Buy-now-pay-later (BNPL), which accounts for 1.5% to 2.5% of all transactions, has become another Gen Z paradox. According to LendingTree, 64% have tried it at least once, and BNPL loans surpassed credit card use during peak holiday periods. But beneath convenience lies risk. More than 40% have made a late payment, up seven points from a year earlier. And according to PwC’s Holiday Outlook, 11% say it’s one of their top three preferred payment methods this holiday season, up from 5% in 2024.

The trend may signal a revealing tension: Gen Z’s desire to keep spending, while flirting with fragility. Retailers who offer BNPL may find opportunity, but they also inherit responsibility — to make payment options easy to understand, rather than fueling debt cycles.

## The opportunity for retailers is hiding in plain sight

There’s no universal decoder ring for Gen Z, but there are patterns in what they choose to buy and [in the experiences they gravitate toward](/us/en/services/consulting/business-transformation/library/2025-customer-experience-survey.html). For a generation fluent in self-curation, and sensitive to economic uncertainty, budgeting and discernment are critical filters. To sell something with a premium price tag, it needs a story of sustainability, exclusivity, craftsmanship and social validation. And if something isn’t showing up on social media, in group chats or through influencer drop culture, it may not feel worth the stretch.

Retailers once wary of private labels and dupes can now lean into them, not as fallback options but as creative options. Gen Z doesn’t see “affordable” as generic. They see it as smart. They want curated alternatives that feel personal, not mass-produced. Limited drops, house-brand collabs and design-led value options offer novelty without overextending inventory. The win isn’t in cutting cost alone. It’s in delivering value that feels intentional, not leftover.

But speed is the real unlock. Spotting a trend isn’t enough if you can’t act on it. Relevance now depends on turning consumer signals into shelf decisions quickly and at scale. That takes more than instinct. It takes merchandising models that flex weekly, forecasting that adapts in real time and pricing strategies grounded in what Gen Z actually values: the thrill of a smart find.

### What forward-thinking retailers are doing differently

## A preview of what’s to come

Gen Z’s behavior isn’t just a puzzle. It’s a preview. Their emphasis on value, experience and novelty may be the early signal of where consumer psychology is heading. Retailers that study Gen Z aren’t just preparing for one cohort. They’re future-proofing. What Gen Z demands today, other generations may begin expecting tomorrow.
