  The Rise of the Vertical Shopper Consumers used to be reliably horizontal. Horizontal in the sense that they spent in price bands, from value at the bottom to luxury at the top. This pattern was directly linked to income; consumers spent at the quality level they could afford. There was always an incentive to stretch upwards as far as possible, to reach something a little better.  The predictability of this arrangement was useful for brands. They could position at a point in the hierarchy, and then expand sideways into related offers around the same price point. Big supermarkets have been the most obvious proponents of this approach, as they expanded their ranges across categories.  But now, we’re all vertical shoppers. We buy value veg, but premium ready meals, middling coats, but luxury handbags. We pick and choose, muddling the previously clean horizontal lines. There are lots of reasons for this change: overall increases in quality mean that cheaper does not necessarily mean worse, the trend towards self-treating up around selected items, and the cost-of-living crisis driving more people to search for value, to name only three.  For brands, the temptation is to chase their consumer up and down the pricing scale. But this risks de-positioning themselves and confusing their audience. Better to stick to your idea, but actively welcome the new consumers dipping into your area. Another idea is to use brand architecture to develop a range of offers at different price points.  Consumer’s may have gone vertical, but brand ideas are better to stay horizontal. [#ConsumerTrends](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fconsumertrends&trk=public_post-text) [#BrandInsights](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fbrandinsights&trk=public_post-text) [#RetailTrends](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fretailtrends&trk=public_post-text)

args.summary:
This LinkedIn post by Jonathan Mark examines how Gen Z's spending habits are transforming the retail landscape, particularly heading into the Holiday 2025 season. Gen Z, despite being digital natives, shows a notable preference for brick-and-mortar stores and tangible shopping experiences. Their brand loyalty is tempered by willingness to explore private labels, and while they are financially cautious, they readily invest in purchases with sentimental value. Key data points from PwC reveal a 13% reduction in Gen Z's overall spending earlier this year (particularly in apparel, accessories, and electronics), a planned 23% decrease in holiday spending for 2025 (despite a prior 37% increase intention in 2024), with average seasonal expenditure projected at $1,357. Gen Z's purchasing power is forecast to reach $12 trillion by 2030 (per NielsenIQ, GfK, and World Data Lab).

The post also aggregates related retail insights from various industry voices: Deloitte's 40th Holiday Survey finds consumers plan to slash holiday spending ~10% YoY with a shift toward "value-seeking" behaviors; Placer.ai research highlights a "two-tier economy" and volatile retail traffic; and broader trends show average U.S. shopper spending at $1,595 (down 10% YoY), only 17% expecting to spend more, and 57% expecting economic worsening in 2026. Additional themes include the rise of "valuespending" (92% of consumers make purchases aligned with their values; 70% of shoppers aged 18-24 say brand values will influence future purchases), the emergence of "vertical shoppers" who mix value and premium purchases across categories, and Australian retail data showing 51% of consumers visit stores more often when loyal to a brand. Holiday 2025 strategies emphasize earlier shopping (50% start before Thanksgiving), bigger Black Friday discounts (30%+ markdowns, $14.7B projected Cyber Monday), AI adoption (33% of shoppers plan to use AI, double last year), and value differentiation beyond price.

# Gen Z spending habits: The trends marketers need to know in 2025

![Picture of Georgie Walsh](https://www.gwi.com/hs-fs/hubfs/Website/Blog%20Authors/Georgie%20Walsh.png?width=50&name=Georgie%20Walsh.png)

[Georgie Walsh](https://www.gwi.com/blog/author/georgie-walsh)  Content Marketing Manager

**SHARE**

   [Gen%20Z%20spending%20habits:%20The%20trends%20marketers%20need%20to%20know%20in%202025&body=Check%20out%20Gen%20Z%20spending%20habits:%20The%20trends%20marketers%20need%20to%20know%20in%202025">](mailto:?subject=Check%20out%20<span%20id=)

Gen Z have been called everything from the TikTok generation to the loneliest generation. But the truth is they’re a lot more complex than any simple label can capture.

Born between the late ‘90s and 2012, they’re a mix of high schoolers figuring out life, and young professionals stepping into their prime career years. And while they’re not a monolith, one thing *is* clear: they know what matters to them.

They’re not just chasing trends; they’re shaping them. They prioritize experiences over material things and they’re far more likely to scroll and shop on their phones than browse in-store.

With their digital-first, value-driven mindset, they’re flipping the script on how brands should engage with them. So let’s dive in and take a closer look.

## **Why Gen Z’s spending habits matter**

Gen Z may not outspend millennials just yet, but they’re the next-most dominant consumer force. Even those still in school know what they want and what they expect from brands. Ignore their motivations, and you’ll be left out before the conversation even starts.

Shaped by the 2008 recession and the pandemic, Gen Z are financially savvy and brand-conscious. They’ve grown up with social media, trusting influencers and peer recommendations over traditional ads. They don’t just scroll; they shop, interact, and set trends in real time.

For them, spending centers on digital convenience. Mobile banking, digital wallets, and Buy Now Pay Later aren’t just nice-to-haves - they’re the norm. They expect seamless, cashless transactions that fit into their fast-moving world. If brands want to win Gen Z’s loyalty, they need to back it up with effortless digital experiences.

## **Key Gen Z spending trends for 2025**

Here are six key Gen Z spending habits for 2025. Want the full picture? Check out our deep dive into [Gen Z characteristics](/blog/generation-z-characteristics).

### **1. Value-driven shopping: Gen Z wants ethics** ***and*** **affordability**

Call them demanding - or just particular - but Gen Zers know what they want and what matters.

They’re sometimes said to be the “green generation”, but it’s not that simple. Gen Z aren’t any more willing than the average consumer to pay extra for eco-friendly products. In EU5 markets, the number willing to pay more has dropped 15% since 2020.

It’s not that Gen Z don’t care, they just want brands to do the heavy lifting. Of all US generations, they’re the least likely to feel personally responsible for the environment and the most likely to say brands should do more. Discounts for reusable cups, buy-back programs for pre-loved furniture, and trade-in rewards for tech waste are all great ways for brands to win Gen Z’s approval.

Gen Z are both budget-conscious and tech-savvy, but price still rules; 51% say it’s the top factor when buying household essentials.

For other goods, Gen Z blends cost-consciousness with ethics. They believe eco-friendly choices shouldn’t come with a hefty price tag. One way for brands to respond to this is to double-down on discounts — 2 in 5 Gen Z actively search for coupons before buying.

In the US, Gen Z are 8% more likely than the average consumer to buy secondhand. And despite Facebook's older-skewing reputation, visiting Facebook marketplace is the second most popular action taken in the past month among US Gen Z.

So is fast fashion over for Gen Z? Not yet, but platforms like Depop, Poshmark, and Vinted are undoubtedly making an impact. Depop use has grown 8% since 2022, and Vinted has seen a 47% surge in visits from Gen Z in the UK and France.

### **2. Digital-first consumers: Online shopping and social commerce dominate**

Gen Z grew up with smartphones, and now they’re a leading group in ecommerce with a clear mobile-first mindset. In the past week, 27% bought new or secondhand products using their mobile phones. Additionally, in the US, 32% of Gen Z use their mobiles to shop or browse for products online. Mobile grocery shopping is another area seeing major growth with Gen Z, up 40% since 2021.

While older generations use social media to connect, Gen Z mixes social with shopping. Over a quarter say they use social platforms to find products. To keep up, brands need to make their social presence engaging and shoppable.

And they’re not just researching products on social media, they’re buying there too. Gen Z in North America and Europe are 16% more likely than the average consumer to use Instagram Shopping Bag. In the past year, the number of Gen Z outside China using TikTok Shop has jumped 14%.

As digital natives, many Gen Z are keen to embrace AI. Over half say they would consider using it for price comparisons, and 2 in 5 say they would use AI for shopping support, with AI-powered recommendations reshaping how Gen Z interacts with brands. As we’ve seen elsewhere with Gen Z, money matters - they’re 22% more likely than the average consumer to say budgeting support would make them consider using AI while shopping online.

[![Say hi to Agent Spark   Your AI insights analyst. Instant insights, endless possibilities.    ](https://no-cache.hubspot.com/cta/default/304927/interactive-213257080944.png)](/hs/cta/wi/redirect?encryptedPayload=AVxigLL3i5d52b3wg%2BCn2jbZZ4TkOzIKrF1w22dC6dIDEWJ7TRqa0FkSzKmRt3wPH6ZvevDQzK1D0sgLIbx2gfrWZ6H3Z6NsYuOBnhtWx%2FeQj%2BZyM9%2B2dkbUii2EEShU3dieO8g8osppauh8oMyHyYxlIzRWlv8K3o6difptv7bwWD%2FbXcCHFXE%3D&webInteractiveContentId=213257080944&portalId=304927)

### **3. Buy Now, Pay Later (BNPL) and flexible payment preferences**

Gen Z are changing the payment game. While older generations like baby boomers rely more on traditional payment methods, Gen Z are embracing flexible alternatives like Buy Now, Pay Later. Buy Now, Pay Later (BNPL) services like Klarna and Afterpay are steadily growing - no surprise given Gen Z’s focus on saving money.

BNPL continues to grow in certain markets. Indonesia leads the league, while markets like the UK have seen a jump of 16% since 2021. In the US, BNPL is still gaining traction, with at least 10% of Gen Z using it weekly.

As you’d expect from a group who’re glued to their phones, Gen Z are particularly comfortable with mobile payments and digital wallets. Nearly a quarter have used services like Apple Pay or Samsung Pay in the last month. Mobile payments aren’t just growing, they’re *surging*, up 46% among Gen Z since 2021, making them 60% more likely than the average American to have used Apple Pay.

The point is that brands targeting Gen Z need to keep up and give them what they want. Flexible payment options like interest-free splits and subscriptions aren’t just nice-to-haves, they’re the new normal this financially savvy generation expects.

### **4. Experience over possessions: Where Gen Z prioritizes their spending**

Similar to previous generations, Gen Z prefers to splurge on experiences rather than material goods.

So where does their disposable income actually go? Travel, dining, and entertainment are all contenders. Naturally social media trends play a big role in shaping their choices.

30% of Gen Z outside of China turn to social media for travel inspiration, including domestic trips. And they’re not just looking, they’re also booking, with over a quarter having reserved a domestic vacation online in the past 3-6 months.

Gen Z are also more likely than other generations to travel solo when they find a destination they love. 34% are planning a trip alone, compared to 29% of millennials, 23% of Gen X, and 21% of baby boomers.

But it’s not just about vacations; Gen Z seek unique, shareable experiences. In the US they’re 23% more likely to be interested in food and drink festivals. Elsewhere they’re 19% more likely to spend on experiences like a spa day or a day out.

Gen Z also dive deep into digital media and gaming, from streaming to metaverse purchases. If a game’s free, they’re all over it, with nearly half having played or downloaded a free-to-play game at some point.

But while Gen Zers love a freebie, they’re also willing to spend when it counts. They’re 36% more likely to have purchased an in-game item or feature using microtransactions. And once they’re immersed, they’re 31% more likely to have bought a game add-on or DLC in the past year.

Bottom line? As brands move away from in-store physical media, Gen Z are right there with them. In fact they’re 33% more likely than average to buy video games from online stores or digital platforms.

### **5. Financial anxiety is reshaping Gen Z spending behavior**

Gen Z has weathered economic storms, from the 2008 crisis to the pandemic, shaping how they approach education, careers, and money. A combination of rising inflation and student debt means that many have become financially cautious, focusing on stability and value-driven spending.

How worried are Gen Z about the economy? It’s a mixed picture. The cost of living is a concern for many, but despite the challenges, they’re optimists at heart. Over the next six months, 55% believe their country’s economy will improve. They’re also 15% more likely than the average s to say their personal finances will get better.

Still, Gen Z aren’t diving into big, life-changing purchases just yet. Only 6% are planning to buy property. They’re also holding off on major life milestones. Since early 2024, the number of Gen Zers planning to get engaged has dropped 25%, while those planning to marry is down 16%.

As a value-driven generation, Gen Z wants to make every dollar count. Financial education and money management are top priorities. Many seek out resources to improve their financial literacy, with 22% wanting their bank to offer a financial advice hotline and 38% wanting access to online financial courses.

For financial brands this is a huge opportunity. Gen Z aren’t just looking for a bank - they want a financial partner that helps them reach their goals. Finance brands who take on that role will prosper.

### **6. Loyalty is earned: How Gen Z engages with brands**

Brands must work hard to earn Gen Z’s trust, and even harder to keep it. They’re the least brand-loyal of all generations and don’t think twice about switching.

What does Gen Z look for most? In a word, reliability. They expect brands to be authentic and consistent across every touchpoint. Social media and user-generated content play a huge role in building trust; Gen Z want real connections, not marketing speak.

Over half of Gen Z use social media to explore brands, and they’re 31% more likely than average to use vlogs to find information on a company.

They’re also deeply influenced by online conversations and social proof. Gen Z are 12% more likely than the average to say‘likes’ and positive comments on social media would make them more likely to buy online. Clearly peer validation is a key part of their buying process.   
  
Gamified shopping and reward programs also work, with 24% of Gen Z saying loyalty points would make them more likely to buy online.

## **Implications for marketers and businesses**

Gen Z undoubtedly values authenticity. To earn their loyalty, brands need to lead with transparency, storytelling, and shared values. Want to know how your brand stacks up? Track your [brand health](/services/brand-tracking) and gauge consumer perception.

Gen Z’s loyalty is hard-won and easily lost. They’re quick to jump between brands, so staying connected is key. Engage directly, personalize conversations, and create experiences that make them feel valued.

Social proof matters. Gen Z relies on social media and peer opinions, making influencer marketing a powerful way to connect. To find out which platforms matter most just check out our latest [social media stats](/blog/social-media-statistics).

As we’ve said, they also love a good deal and they’re not afraid to shop around. Loyalty programs and rewards keep them coming back, while seamless mobile shopping and flexible payments make buying easier. And while they care about sustainability, price still comes first - they won’t pay extra just because something’s eco-friendly.

## **How to use GWI Spark for insights on Gen Z spending habits**

Gen Z shopping habits can be hard to pin down. Navigating these nuances isn’t easy, but GWI Spark helps you spot the trends and craft the right message.

Here’s one example: Gen Z aren’t any more likely than other consumers to pay extra for eco-friendly products. They expect brands to step up, but without passing the cost onto them.

GWI Spark shows that Gen Z loves second-hand shopping, a key insight that could inspire a brand to sell refurbished items or create products made from recycled materials.

And that’s just the start. With GWI Spark, you’ll uncover insights to shape your marketing, strengthen connections, and meet Gen Z on their terms.

## **Final thoughts**

Winning over Gen Z isn’t just about knowing what they buy. It’s also about recognizing the beliefs, priorities, and emotions that influence their purchasing behavior.

Brands aiming to make a splash in 2025 can tap into Gen Z’s preferences. Focus on immersive experiences, second-hand goods, and cutting-edge technology. Above all, to win over Gen Z, brands must build authenticity. As more Gen Zers enter and advance in their careers, brands that meet their expectations will be the ones that thrive.

# Gen Z Shopping Trends and Habits for Retailers

Mar 9, 2026

Understanding Generation Z’s shopping habits is essential for retailers looking to capture valuable market share. As their purchasing power increases, they reshape how products are discovered, evaluated, and bought.

While digital fluency is a given, Gen Z’s behavior reflects a nuanced balance between online discovery and offline loyalty, tradition and disruption, values and pragmatism, as well as individualism and community.

In this article, we’ll explore the results from some of our 2025 case studies to unpack the latest insights into how Gen Z chooses between brands, and what retail insights leaders need to know

## Key Findings

* Omnichannel retail is non-negotiable: Gen Z blends digital discovery (TikTok, YouTube, social media) with in-store experiences, expecting seamless access across channels.

* Values drive spending: Gen Z doesn’t just buy products, they buy what the products represent. Authenticity, sustainability, and social impact matter as much as price, making brand ethics a key purchase driver.
* Wellness and community shape choices: From fitness and beauty to alcohol alternatives, Gen Z prioritizes self-care and shared experiences that align with their identity and are willing to spend on it.

## Gen Z Gravitates Toward Experiential Retail

Gen Z shoppers are drawn to retailers that offer a more experience-oriented environment, such as Target or Barnes & Noble, at higher rates than older generations who are more typically associated with those retailers. This aligns with the generation’s broader preference for experiences, a theme echoed throughout the research. Most Gen Z respondents still shop at Walmart, but less often than older generations, showing they’re less tied to the purely practical and value-oriented retailer.

Our research also illuminates just how important social media, especially YouTube and TikTok, are as gateways to brand and product awareness. 49% of Gen Z respondents say they discover new brands/products on social media and 44% call out YouTube specifically.

The takeaway for retailers: Invest in seamless omnichannel strategies. Gen Z buyers look for inspiration online but expect meaningful experiences in-store or via an app. Bridging virtual and physical experiences is key to driving consideration and strengthening brand loyalty.

## Purpose, Ethics, and Social Proof

Gen Z doesn’t just buy products, they also buy what the product represents. Authenticity, sustainability, and social impact strongly influence purchase decisions. When asked about the most influential factor in shaping how they approach life and decision-making, Gen Z respondents were most likely to select “making a positive impact on their personal and professional lives”. This is more than previous generations, who tend to prioritize family bonds and religious beliefs as their primary drivers.

Takeaway for retailers: Be authentic! As younger generations are well-equipped for doing their own research, proof of impact, sustainable practices, or meaningful partnerships resonate more than marketing slogans.

## Aspirational Wellness & Curated Image

Gen Z’s interest in wellness goes beyond fitness; it blends appearance, health, and identity. They are fueling growth in categories like gym memberships, personal care, and beauty, investing not just in how they feel but how they present themselves.

According to our data, Gen Z values body image and physical appearance higher than previous generations. 27% of Gen Z respondents selected “building muscle/getting toned” and 26% “having better looking skin” as their highest priorities related to health and wellness. On the other hand, previous generations are more concerned with losing weight, strengthening their immune systems, and reducing pain/inflammation.

This doesn’t mean they’re vain in a shallow sense. Rather, looking good, feeling strong, and projecting an image aligned with their values are deeply interconnected. Retailers in beauty, fashion, and accessories have opportunities to position their products as part of a holistic wellness journey.

Takeaway for retailers: Reframe your products within the broader narrative of self-care, wellness, and self-expression. Success lies in offering solutions that help Gen Z look *and* feel good.

## Belonging as a Wellness Driver

Wellness for Gen Z isn’t only an individual pursuit, it’s also a social one. Fitness studios, wellness apps, and even group classes serve as “third places” where health and community intersect. Social accountability and peer support are integral to staying motivated.

Digital communities also play a big role. From influencers to peer reviews, Gen Z’s trust in products often hinges on seeing others in their circle endorse or experience them first.

Takeaway for retailers: Position health and wellness products within a community framework. Highlight stories, create shared challenges, or foster in-person and digital spaces that support belonging and wellbeing.

## Alcohol Use Down, Alternatives Up

Gen Z respondents reported drinking 6.96 drinks per week on average compared to 11.63 for Millennials, a 40% decrease. When asked about their reasons for cutting back, 19% of Gen Z respondents cited a preference for non-alcoholic alternatives compared to 16% of Millennials and just 9% of Gen X respondents.

For brands, this opens an opportunity to join in the fast-growing category where wellness meets lifestyle. Alcohol-free drinks that fuel energy, relaxation, and connection are set to drive the next wave of market growth.

Takeaway for retailers: Stocking and promoting alcohol-free or low-alcohol alternatives isn’t just niche anymore, it’s meeting younger buyers where they are. [Download our Health and Wellness Study](https://www.thelangstonco.com/research/alcohol/) to get more insights on alcohol intake across different segments.

## Balancing Fun with Financial Pressures

Gen Z is known for prioritizing experiences such as travel, live events, and wellness activities. Even in the face of rising living costs and economic uncertainty, 22% of Gen Z respondents choose to invest in experiences and items that bring them joy at the expense of savings, more than any generation before them.

At the same time, financial wellness is top of mind. Many are struggling to balance higher expenses with the desire to save. This tension creates a push-pull: experiences remain a priority, but long-term savings may be sacrificed.

Takeaway for retailers: Prioritize products and experiences that create lasting, positive memories but stay mindful of [price sensitivities](/solutions/innovation-pricing).

## Closing Thoughts

Gen Z is often painted as a purely digital generation, but the reality is far more nuanced. They embrace tradition while demanding innovation, value authenticity while remaining budget-conscious, and balance personal wellness with community connection. For consumer insights professionals, the challenge is not just to understand these dichotomies, but to translate them into strategies that create meaningful connections.

<webpage_content>
# Secondhand Isn't a "Trend" Anymore. What Comes Next, After Resale's Record Growth?

### I talk to ThredUp's SVP of Marketing about key insights from the 2026 Resale Report, including why she thinks the "buy, wear, resell, reinvest" cycle is the industry's most durable shift.

[Emily Stochl](https://substack.com/@prelovedpod)

*I’m Emily Stochl, the secondhand industry’s top resale reporter, and this is **[Pre-Loved](https://prelovedpod.substack.com/)** 🎤 the must-read newsletter for vintage dealers, thrifters, collectors, and circular fashion professionals, where we unpack the business and culture of vintage and secondhand.*

PS: If you work in resale, your **[$5 subscription](https://prelovedpod.substack.com/subscribe)** is likely a business expense.

***Hey hi hello.*** I’m back from New Orleans — my first true vacation in *years!* … The Big Easy delivered! — and back in your inbox. New [Pre-Loved Podcast](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/pre-loved-podcast-with-emily-stochl/id1435719708) episodes will return next Monday. 🎧

More on New Orleans to come, but I basically spent the week [drinking Barq’s rootbeer from a glass bottle](https://substack.com/@prelovedpod/note/c-238609937?utm_source=notes-share-action&r=3r6ct) and reading by the pool, or getting my 20,000 steps a day checking out the city’s vintage. By the way, I updated **[Pre-Loved’s Global Directory of Vintage & Secondhand Shops](https://prelovedpod.substack.com/p/pre-loveds-global-directory-of-vintage)** with 20+ spots from NOLA. Bookmark it for your next trip (there or anywhere), as the internet’s largest list of vintage is always growing!

→ [Follow me on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/emilymstochl/?hl=en)  
→ [Follow me on TikTok](https://www.tiktok.com/@emilymstochl)

**💌 In today’s letter:** ThredUp dropped its 14th Annual Resale Report last week, and — *[like I’ve done for nearly a decade!](https://prelovedpod.substack.com/about)* — I’m breaking it all down for you into key trends and takeaways. **[Read the full report here.](https://www.thredup.com/resale?srsltid=AfmBOoquiRJukqwtWu7u18nUGd8KfZEuOV8WKiauWd0v5jnMzzZW3YdU)**

# **Key Resale Trends & Takeaways:**

The global secondhand market is projected to hit **$393 billion by 2030**, growing more than twice as fast as overall apparel. In the U.S., resale grew **19%** in **2025** alone — nearly **four times** faster than traditional retail. But “the global secondhand market is no longer just a ‘high-growth story’,” **[ThredUp](https://prelovedpod.substack.com/p/thredup-enters-a-new-era-marking?utm_source=publication-search)** co-founder and CEO **[James Reinhart](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jamesgreinhart)**writes in this year’s Resale Report, “it’s entering a more competitive, structurally complex phase.”

We’ve moved past the era of resale as “trend.” It’s no longer a secondary, “second-best” option — it’s increasingly where consumers *start* their search.

**[Pre-Loved](https://www.instagram.com/emilymstochl/)** readers, you already knew this. You’ve been living it.

Where this year’s findings get interesting are the *details* — what's shifting underneath the growth story, and what it actually means for resale to be entering a new and "more complex" phase. The report’s release is timely: I've just spent several weeks on my own version of similar research. Pre-Loved's first-ever **[Secondhand Shopping Survey](https://prelovedpod.substack.com/p/i-asked-200-dedicated-secondhand)**, published last month, polled nearly 200 active secondhand shoppers — **83%** of whom have wardrobes that are majority secondhand, **67%** of whom have resold their own clothing. Where [ThredUp’s Resale Report](https://www.thredup.com/resale?srsltid=AfmBOopbkY8_GvbzIXFr0goX-OMhhzWbxXma8MPuwJYQGdvc-1ioH8vU) charts mass market adoption, my findings dial in on the behavior of super-users who’ve been at this for years.

I’ll be pulling findings from both throughout, plus input from [ThredUp’s Senior Vice President of Marketing](https://prelovedpod.substack.com/p/thredup-enters-a-new-era-marking?utm_source=publication-search), **[Kristen Brophy](https://www.linkedin.com/in/kbrophy)**, who spoke to Pre-Loved last week, prior to the report’s release.

**Here's what stood out to me this year. →**

## **The search bar is losing its job.**

For the past decade, resale platforms have been built around the assumption that you know what you want to buy, you type it in to a marketplace search bar, and you find it — depending on how hard you were willing to sift through results.

The 2026 Resale Report suggests that assumption is cracking. **Nearly half** secondhand discovery now happens *outside* resale marketplaces — through social feeds, creators, livestreams, and in-person browsing. The “want” is being manufactured somewhere else before a shopper ever opens a marketplace, and the search bar is no longer where the journey starts for a growing share of buyers.

“Consumers used to think of resale as a ‘needle-in-a-haystack’ browsing experience,” Brophy told me, “where you wander until you found something. But today it has become incredibly intent-led.”

**Social media is now the user’s primary starting place** — when a creator shares viral style inspiration, ThredUp sees same-day search spikes, sometimes within minutes. Self-fulfilling that reference loop, their **[Trend Report](https://prelovedpod.substack.com/p/thredup-enters-a-new-era-marking?utm_source=publication-search)** tool, launched last year, begins surfaces surging styles to users right as they start to peak.

## **Quality supply is the industry’s bottleneck.**

Demand for resale is well-established. Where the constraint on industry growth remains is the sell side: **$23.3 billion** in U.S. market value will be unlocked by 2030, per ThredUp, by making *selling* easier. Even among buyers who select “nothing” would motivate them to resell clothing, a third changed their answer when presented with a simpler, more automated listing process.

Brophy says friction on the supply-side falls into two buckets. The first is “mechanical” — things like photography, pricing, shipping logistics — where she believes the industry has made the most real progress. The second is psychological: “it's that internal friction of asking, ‘is selling this actually worth my time?' or 'will I regret letting this go?'" she explains. The unlock, she says, will be removing the mental burden of decision-making to ease resale.

## **AI is making secondhand shopping easier — but it’s not a silver bullet.**

From discovery to pricing to authentication, AI tools are fully incorporated into the secondhand shopping and selling experience, whether users are aware of them or not. **48%** of Gen Z already use AI shopping tools and **63%** say they’re comfortable with agentic buying. **6 in 10** shoppers of all ages say they’d use AI to negotiate deals on their behalf, and **69%** say they’d delegate 24/7 platform monitoring to AI to find them specific items.

For platform operators, the pressure to integrate AI tools that make secondhand shopping and selling meaningfully easier is only going to increase with time.

Yet [Pre-Loved's own survey respondents](https://prelovedpod.substack.com/p/i-asked-200-dedicated-secondhand), who have been using secondhand search tools since long before AI entered the conversation, still cite search as a top frustration, with several specifically asking for the ability to filter out low-quality clothing, starting with fast fashion brands. This request points at something bigger. **63%** of Pre-Loved’s respondents named “too many low-quality items to search through” as their top frustration in the secondhand market overall. The fast fashion flood, in thrift stores and on resale platforms, is real and ongoing. Worsening even. Surfacing quality — for example, a high-quality sweater buried under thousands of cheaper pieces — is not a problem AI has solved yet. Nor is turning off the faucet of over-produced, low-quality fashion in the first place — going back to the fundamental issue of quality supply.

## **The market is heavily fragmented, setting the table for consolidation.**

Despite its scale, resale is still a long-tail market: thousands of platforms, individual sellers, consignment shops, vintage dealers, thrift store chains, and everything in between. **43%** of secondhand shoppers have purchased items via [social commerce platforms or livestream formats](https://prelovedpod.substack.com/p/a-vintage-dealers-most-used-app-more?utm_source=publication-search) this year, for example. The Resale Report posits fragmentation sets the stage for increased competition and potential consolidation. The next phase of resale won't be defined by attracting new participants — there are plenty — but by competing for wallet share and supply among the people *already here.*

For independent sellers, consolidation pressure creates room for differentiated, community-rooted businesses that larger operations can't easily replicate — the vintage dealer who remembers your name, whose specific eye for curation you trust. **77%** of Pre-Loved’s survey respondents said they return to sellers they’ve had a good experience with, and **32%** have a handful of favorites they buy from repeatedly. In a consolidating market, loyalty like that is not a small thing.

## **"Holy grail" is replacing the haul.**

According to ThredUp, **62%** of Gen Z shopped secondhand in 2025, and **67%** of them consider the resale value of an item before buying. The report finds they've shifted from high-volume “haul” behavior toward what they dub "holy grail hunting” — fewer purchases, higher intention, and a sharper eye for that ‘one specific item.’

ThredUp's own platform tools back this up. Their **[Daily Edit](https://prelovedpod.substack.com/p/thredup-enters-a-new-era-marking?utm_source=publication-search)** — an AI-powered feature that surfaces a personalized selection of 100 items per user per day — has the highest engagement of any feature on the platform. Daily Edit users purchase at **more than twice** the rate of non-users, with a **23%** conversion rate, Brophy told me. “It's shifting the entire conversation from ‘how many things did I get?' to 'did I find *the one* I've been looking for?'" she said. ThredUp’s search data also reveals more specific search queries and longer session depths where shoppers are hunting for one meaningful item, rather than filling a cart.

Pre-Loved’s survey cohort skewed older — Millennials and Gen X primarily — and they’re several laps ahead of this behavioral shift. **Quality** and **craftsmanship** of vintage items was the top motivator for **57%** of our respondents. One even described this as “holy grail hunting” before ThredUp even published this framing. Another wrote: “I’m old enough to have the experience of a full trend cycle, decline of item quality, and a solid understanding of my personal style. New retail pieces often feel uninspired, poor quality, or I already own a better example.” **These shoppers know what they're looking for, and will wait for it.**

## **Shoppers understand the resale value of their closets.**

On the selling side, **57%** of ThredUp’s sellers say they're reselling for **income** — **more than double** last year's figure — and **60%** of *all* consumers now factor “resale value” into their new apparel purchases, **up 13 points** year-over-year.

This is a genuine shift in how people think about their wardrobes.

> “We’re seeing consumers moving away from just looking at the price tag, toward starting to calculate the lifetime value of a garment,” said Brophy.
>
> “It’s made users more savvy and price-elastic, meaning they buy better brands because they know the resale demand for them, and they take better care of their pieces. They’re mentally offsetting the cost of a new purchase with what they expect to get back later.”

She told me ThredUp’s most engaged users are those who both buy and sell — participating in resale’s whole “flywheel.” **[Clean Out Kit](https://www.thredup.com/cleanout)** requests from these existing sellers were up **34%** year-on-year in 2025, with supply from those users up **14%.**

Every year when the ThredUp Resale Report drops, mass-market adoption keeps charting upward, which makes headlines. But in 2026, we’re well past covering secondhand as a trend story — what comes next, after resale’s record growth? What's different about these findings, is the documented shift from “growth” to maturity — from proving *that* resale works to understanding *how* it works.

As these trends show, a growing share of people are now participating in the full "buy, wear, resell, reinvest" cycle of circularity — and Brophy says it’s one of the biggest changes of this new era. “The mindset of ‘return on investment’ is a much more durable and sustainable foundation for the industry than bargain hunting and fast fashion trend cycling," she told me. Meaning a more evolved resale industry isn't just *bigger* than it was. It's built on something that might actually hold.

As resale matures, growth figures will keep making headlines. But what happens within its *culture* is the more interesting question. That's the one I'll be chasing.

args.summary:
This article from Emily Stochl's "Pre-Loved" newsletter breaks down key insights from ThredUp's 14th Annual Resale Report (2026), supplemented by Pre-Loved's own Secondhand Shopping Survey of nearly 200 active secondhand shoppers. The central thesis is that secondhand fashion has moved past being a "trend" story and is entering a more mature, structurally complex phase of growth.

KEY STATISTICS AND FINDINGS:
- Global secondhand market projected to hit $393 billion by 2030, growing more than twice as fast as overall apparel.
- U.S. resale grew 19% in 2025, nearly four times faster than traditional retail.
- $23.3 billion in U.S. market value will be unlocked by 2030 by making selling easier.
- Nearly half of secondhand discovery now happens outside resale marketplaces (social feeds, creators, livestreams, in-person browsing).
- 48% of Gen Z use AI shopping tools; 63% comfortable with agentic buying; 6 in 10 shoppers would use AI to negotiate deals; 69% would delegate 24/7 platform monitoring to AI.
- 62% of Gen Z shopped secondhand in 2025; 67% consider resale value before buying.
- 57% of ThredUp sellers resell for income — more than double last year's figure.
- 60% of all consumers factor "resale value" into new apparel purchases, up 13 points year-over-year.
- 43% of secondhand shoppers purchased via social commerce or livestream formats this year.
- ThredUp's Daily Edit (AI-powered personalized selection of 100 items/day) has highest engagement of any platform feature, with users purchasing at more than twice the rate of non-users (23% conversion rate).
- Clean Out Kit requests up 34% year-on-year in 2025, with supply from existing sellers up 14%.

MAJOR TRENDS IDENTIFIED:
1. **The search bar is losing its job** — Discovery increasingly starts on social media; ThredUp sees same-day search spikes after creators share viral style inspiration.
2. **Quality supply is the industry's bottleneck** — Friction on the sell side falls into "mechanical" (photography, pricing, shipping) and "psychological" (time-worthiness, regret) buckets. A third of shoppers who said "nothing" would motivate them to resell changed their answer with a simpler, more automated listing process.
3. **AI is helpful but not a silver bullet** — 63% of Pre-Loved's respondents named "too many low-quality items to search through" as their top frustration; the fast fashion flood continues and AI hasn't solved quality surfacing.
4. **Market fragmentation sets the table for consolidation** — The next phase will compete for wallet share and supply among existing participants rather than attracting new ones. 77% of Pre-Loved respondents return to sellers they've had good experiences with; 32% buy repeatedly from a handful of favorites.
5. **"Holy grail" hunting replaces the haul** — Fewer purchases, higher intention, hunting for one specific item rather than volume. Pre-Loved's older cohort (Millennials/Gen X) showed this shift earlier — 57% cited quality and craftsmanship of vintage as top motivator.
6. **Shoppers understand the resale value of their closets** — Consumers are moving from looking at price tags to calculating the lifetime value of a garment, buying better brands due to known resale demand, and taking better care of pieces.

The article concludes that resale is shifting from proving "that" it works to understanding "how" it works, with the "buy, wear, resell, reinvest" cycle and return-on-investment mindset representing a more durable foundation than bargain hunting and fast fashion trend cycling. ThredUp CEO James Reinhart notes the market is "entering a more competitive, structurally complex phase."
args.key_excerpts: "Consumers used to think of resale as a 'needle-in-a-haystack' browsing experience, where you wander until you found something. But today it has become incredibly intent-led." — Kristen Brophy, ThredUp SVP of Marketing

“The global secondhand apparel market continues to burgeon — a testament to the intrinsic value shoppers find in the secondhand experience and proof of the seismic shift towards a more circular fashion ecosystem,” James Reinhardt, CEO of ThredUp, said in a press release sent to Fashion Dive.

[In-house resale is a trend to watch](https://www.fashiondive.com/news/7-fashion-industry-trends-2024/703597/) for brands as well. The report found that 39 brands launched resale programs in 2023, including [H&M](https://www.retaildive.com/news/hm-preloved-thredup-resale-program/644926/), J. Crew, [American Eagle](https://www.fashiondive.com/search/?q=online+resale), [Toms](https://www.fashiondive.com/news/toms-amy-smith-q-and-a/689643/) and Kate Spade. The total number of brands with resale programs is now 163, up from 5 in 2019, per the data. 

Based on a survey of the top 50 fashion brands in the U.S., 74% of executives at brands that don’t have resale programs are considering or planning to create ones, according to the report. 

Of the approximately 55,000 brands on ThredUp, the top five brands for resale in 2023 were Lululemon, Patagonia, Vuori, Reformation and Free People. Both Lululemon and Free People [also made the top five in 2022](https://www.fashiondive.com/news/thredup-us-resale-market-projected-to-reach-70b-by-2027/646922/). Zara, Johnny Was, Sézane, Anthropologie and Skims rounded out the top 10 in 2023. 

“With more than half of all consumers shopping for secondhand apparel last year, it’s evident that resale is now firmly embedded in the fashion landscape,” Neil Saunders, managing director of GlobalData, said in a press release sent to Fashion Dive. The report also found that 55% of consumers said they plan to “spend more on secondhand apparel if the economy doesn’t improve.”

If 2023 was a good year for the secondhand market as a whole, it was also a strong one for ThredUp. Earlier this month, [ThredUp reported Q4 revenue of $81.4 million](https://ir.thredup.com/news-releases/news-release-details/thredup-announces-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2023-results), up 14% year-over-year, and full fiscal 2023 revenue of $322.0 million, up 12% from 2022. The company expects to see full fiscal year 2024 revenue in the range of $340 million to $350 million, per their March earnings report. Increasing consignment sales and expanding their resale-as-a-service business [helped ThredUp narrow their losses](https://www.retaildive.com/news/thredup-the-realreal-different-paths-profitability/690366/) in 2023.

**Dive Brief:**

**Dive Insight:**

Inflation and economic uncertainty contributed to store count growth in retail’s discount sector. 

Those trends “will likely continue to expand in 2023, given [the] current forecast of further economic slowdown, including a possible recession,” the report, which was authored by Coresight Research CEO and founder Deborah Weinswig, data analyst Aaron Mark Dsouza and analyst Daniel Rodden.

Store closures declined by just over 50% in 2022 [compared to 2021](https://www.retaildive.com/news/as-2022-kicks-off-store-closures-are-down-65-coresight/618020/). In contrast with 2019 and 2020, when numerous retailers filed for bankruptcy due to the pandemic, the number of retail-related bankruptcies declined in 2021. This trend helped bring closures closer to pre-pandemic levels.

“The retailers of the post-pandemic world are more robust, given their ability to survive lockdowns, supply chain problems and high inflation,” the report’s authors said. “As such, store closures in 2023 are unlikely to reach the numbers seen in 2019 and 2020, even if economic conditions worsen. Still, we expect the current economic environment to have some impact on store closures this year, likely resulting in a slight increase in store closures in 2023 compared to 2022.”

Four retailers led store openings in the sector last year. Dollar General opened about 1,024 stores and recently marked its [19,000th store opening](https://www.retaildive.com/news/dollar-general-store-expansion-rei-corporate-layoffs/641916/#:~:text=The%20dollar%20store%20chain%20opened,over%20the%20past%20several%20years.). Family Dollar and Dollar Tree, which are owned by the same parent company, opened 393 and 206 stores, respectively. Youth-oriented retail discounter Five Below opened an estimated 134 stores in 2022.

Coresight said 10 retailers accounted for 73% of estimated apparel store closures in 2022:

The news wasn’t all down for the apparel sector though. TJX Cos., parent of TJ Maxx, and Burlington Stores opened an estimated 133 and 113 respective stores in 2022. 

In other retail sectors, CVS Health closed an estimated 300 locations in 2022, leading closures in the drug store sector. Sears Hometown closed 204 stores, and also filed for bankruptcy late in 2022. Family Dollar closed about 100 stores and Amazon closed 57 locations in a move to focus on physical grocery stores.

CVS plans to close an additional 300 stores, Bed Bath & Beyond – which [narrowly avoided bankruptcy](https://www.retaildive.com/news/bed-bath-beyond-secures-funding-avoids-bankruptcy/642278/) – plans to close more than 150 stores, and American Eagle plans to close 83 locations.

Dollar General has aggressive opening plans in 2023 with more than [1,000 openings planned](https://www.businessinsider.com/dollar-general-family-dollar-dollar-tree-dominate-us-store-openings-2023-1), according to Insider. Five Below plans to open 237 locations. Other retailers with announced openings in the double digits include Uniqlo, Dollar Tree, VF Corp. – parent of Vans, The North Face, Timberland and Dickies – and Academy Sports and Outdoors.

If the report’s projections come to fruition, the US will gain 82.6 million square feet of retail space but lose 41.7 million square feet through store closures. The estimates are based on historical data, consumer behavior outlooks, announced store openings and closings and data-based modeling.

This Retail Dive article, written by Nate Delesline III, reports on a Coresight Research analysis finding that retail store openings outpaced closures in 2022. Key findings include:

- Store closures declined by just over 50% in 2022 compared to 2021, bringing closures closer to pre-pandemic levels, as retail bankruptcies declined in 2021 following the pandemic-era surge of 2019-2020.
- Inflation and economic uncertainty drove growth in the discount retail sector, a trend expected to continue into 2023 given forecasts of further economic slowdown and possible recession.
- Four retailers led store openings in 2022: Dollar General (~1,024 stores, marking its 19,000th store), Family Dollar (393 stores), Dollar Tree (206 stores), and Five Below (~134 stores).
- Ten retailers accounted for 73% of estimated apparel store closures in 2022, though TJX Cos. (parent of TJ Maxx) opened ~133 stores and Burlington Stores opened ~113 stores.
- In other sectors: CVS Health closed ~300 locations, Sears Hometown closed 204 stores (also filing for bankruptcy late 2022), Family Dollar closed ~100 stores, and Amazon closed 57 locations to focus on physical grocery stores.
- Announced 2023 closures include: CVS (additional 300 stores), Bed Bath & Beyond (150+ stores, after narrowly avoiding bankruptcy), and American Eagle (83 locations).
- Announced 2023 openings include: Dollar General (1,000+), Five Below (237), plus double-digit openings from Uniqlo, Dollar Tree, VF Corp. (parent of Vans, The North Face, Timberland, Dickies), and Academy Sports and Outdoors.
- Projections: the US will gain 82.6 million square feet of retail space but lose 41.7 million square feet through closures in 2023.
- The report was authored by Coresight Research CEO Deborah Weinswig, data analyst Aaron Mark Dsouza, and analyst Daniel Rodden, based on historical data, consumer behavior outlooks, announced openings/closings, and data-based modeling.
- The report notes post-pandemic retailers are "more robust" given their survival of lockdowns, supply chain problems, and high inflation, so 2023 closures are unlikely to reach 2019-2020 levels, though a slight increase in closures is expected.

The page also includes standard Retail Dive site content such as newsletter signups, editors' picks (including articles on distressed retailers facing bankruptcy in 2026, Allbirds' decline, and retail's response to GLP-1 weight-loss drugs), and most popular stories.

# 2021 was a turning point for retailers, with store openings outpacing store closures

Major retailers announced 5,083 store openings compared to 5,079 store closures in 2021, after nearly two years of stay-at-home orders, social distancing measures and the rise of online shopping.

Some companies who originally sold exclusively online, like Warby Parker, have either opened their own stores or started to sell on physical shelves.  Warby Parker

[Add NBC News to Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=nbcnews.com)

By [Leticia Miranda](https://www.nbcnews.com/author/leticia-miranda-ncpn1068566)

Just one year after a record number of stores closed for good at the height of the pandemic, the retail store has made a comeback, with more store openings than closings in 2021.

This year through Dec. 16, major retailers announced 5,083 store openings compared to 5,079 store closures, signaling that retailers are reaching a balance between online and in-store shopping in the age of e-commerce, according to Coresight Research, a global advisory and research firm specializing in retail and technology.

Major retailers including Walmart, Target and Home Depot beat profit expectations over the last quarter despite supply chain woes slowing down inventory. Tapestry, which owns brands such as Coach and Kate Spade, showed a rebound from the crushing pandemic in the last quarter [reporting](https://tapestry.gcs-web.com/static-files/57b40af6-c37f-4a74-9c07-9abb825df95d) a 26 percent increase in revenue from last year.

“The fact that retailers are flush with more cash means they are able to stay in some of their physical leases longer and they have more patience to do and think differently,” said Deborah Weinswig, CEO and founder of Coresight Research. “The thing is, you need to have a physical space to mean something to the consumer.”

The slight growth in store openings marks a turning point for retailers in the pandemic. For nearly two years, brick-and-mortar stores have gone cold amid stay-at-home orders, social distancing measures and the rise of [online shopping](https://www.nbcnews.com/business/consumer/retail-has-been-life-support-coronavirus-could-pull-plug-n1178356). This forced out weaker retailers and bolstered heavyweights, largely based on how well companies adjusted to the new digital world before the virus struck the country, said UBS retail analyst Jay Sole.

“The pandemic pulled forward a lot of stores that were going to close over time,” he said.

Last year, iconic retailers and department stores fell into bankruptcy as the coronavirus ripped across the country. High-end department store Neiman Marcus filed for bankruptcy in May. Y2K mall staple True Religion Apparel filed for bankruptcy in April. The hip minimalist American arm of Japanese-owned Muji filed in July. But by the end of 2020, all three companies had emerged from bankruptcy.

“We are taking a relationship that exists with a customer in-store and strengthening it digitally,” Neiman Marcus CEO Geoffroy van Raemdonck [told](https://www.voguebusiness.com/consumers/out-of-bankruptcy-neiman-marcus-ceo-plans-a-comeback) Vogue Business last September. He added that the company is “very focused on being present for the customer, however and whenever they want.”

What a shopper wants in a store has radically shifted over the last two decades, said Mark Mathews, vice president of research development and industry analysis with retail trade group National Retail Federation. Retail stores traditionally were places shoppers visited to browse and buy, Mathews said. But, even as e-commerce increases its share of total retail sales, the physical store continues to be a place for shoppers to browse new products, make a return or pick up online orders. An annual consumer survey [published](https://www.pwc.com/gx/en/industries/consumer-markets/consumer-insights-survey.html) in December by professional services firm PwC found 55 percent of shoppers reported they shopped in-store weekly or daily compared to 36 percent of shoppers who said they shop that often on their phones.

What a shopper wants in a store has radically shifted over the last two decades.

Physical stores also play a role in ramping up sales, even if they’re made online, Weinswig said. When retailers close down a brick-and-mortar store, online salesplummet by 50 percent on average in that market, she said. Mathews compared it to concerns that the [popularization of the ATM would drive out bank branches](https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/archive/2015/03/a-brief-history-of-the-atm/388547/). Like bank branches, physical retail stores aren’t solely about throughput, he said.

“It’s about brand value,” he added. “It’s about creating experiences and connecting with the brand and about people being able to go to Best Buy and learn about the product they’re trying to buy.”

Some companies who originally sold exclusively online, like Warby Parker, Casper, Allbirds, Bonobos and Dollar Shave Club, have now all either opened their own stores or started to sell on physical shelves. Some previously online-only companies have chosen to add on to their real estate footprint with new stores. For instance, home-furnishings retailer Wayfair plans to open three stores in Massachusetts in 2022, which would bring their total store count to four. Beauty brand Glossier opened a second permanent store in the U.S., in Los Angeles, last month.

“It does appear that mass store closures over the last couple years have kind of settled down,” said Brandon Isner, Americas head of retail research with commercial real estate investment firm CBRE. “[Digital retail brands] now see brick-and-mortar retail as a way to build the brand and get a whole new population of customers that they may not have been able to get from online sources.”

But as retailers tighten their footprint, stores of the future will not be the same. Retailers like Walmart and Allbirds are experimenting with new shopping platforms including livestream shopping on Pinterest TV, TikTok and Twitter. Nike is testing out what’s called “ghost retail,” where shoppers jump into a virtual queue to speak with a store associate who can talk them through products they have at a store without ever leaving their home.

“You build bridges with customers wherever they are, that’s kind of what retail has always represented,” Weinswig said. “We got a little far outfield … [but] to me it is all just retail and I don’t think you can take out the heart and soul."

The new retail landscape even has space for beleaguered brands such as Toys R Us, which opened up a new 20,000-square-foot flagship store in the American Dream shopping center in East Rutherford, New Jersey, earlier this month. Other retail companies are planning to reopen flagship stores as well, Weinswig said.

“Those stores held different value than realized by retailers,” she said. “Even if those locations are not cash flow positive, they serve a higher purpose.”
