args.summary:
This is a PNAS research article titled "The impact of COVID-19 on small business outcomes and expectations" by Alexander W. Bartik, Marianne Bertrand, Zoe Cullen, Edward L. Glaeser, Michael Luca, and Christopher Stanton. Published July 10, 2020, in PNAS Vol. 117, No. 30, pp. 17656-17666 (DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2006991117). It is an open-access research article in Economic Sciences with 2,225,366 total views and 1,129 citations.

**Study Overview:** The researchers surveyed more than 5,800 small businesses (members of Alignable, a network of 4.6 million small businesses) between March 28 and April 4, 2020, to understand the early economic impact of COVID-19 on US small businesses.

**Key Findings:**
1. **Mass layoffs and closures occurred within weeks of the crisis onset**: 43% of businesses had temporarily closed (nearly all due to COVID-19), and employment fell by 39% on average from January levels. The Mid-Atlantic region (including NYC) was hardest hit with 54% of firms closed and employment down 47%. Retail, arts/entertainment, personal services, food services, and hospitality saw employment declines exceeding 50%.
2. **Financial fragility**: The median firm with monthly expenses over $10,000 had only about 2 weeks of cash on hand. Three-quarters of respondents had enough cash for 2 months or less. Firms with more cash were more optimistic about surviving to year-end.
3. **Wide variation in crisis duration expectations**: 50% of respondents believed the crisis would last at least until mid-June, but beliefs varied widely. For a crisis lasting 4 months versus 1 month, only 47% of businesses expected to be open in December versus 72% under the shorter duration.
4. **CARES Act response**: Over 70% of respondents anticipated using aid resembling the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP). Many anticipated bureaucratic problems and eligibility difficulties. Using experimental variation, researchers found traditional loans with speedy delivery and sufficient liquidity meaningfully shifted survival expectations, suggesting liquidity provision (not grant vs. loan form) was paramount. The CARES Act had modestly greater take-up than straight loans but at much higher government cost.
5. **Projected job losses**: Closures alone could lead to 32.7 million job losses if the crisis lasts 4 months and 35.1 million if it lasts 6 months—potentially larger than anything since the Great Depression or the 1918 influenza epidemic.

**Methodology:** Survey conducted via Alignable in partnership with Harvard Business School researchers, with 7,511 total responses (5,843 from US-based businesses). The survey included 43 questions, an experimental module randomizing policy scenarios, and skip logic. The sample was compared to the 2017 Census of US Businesses and found reasonably representative on firm size (64% had fewer than 5 employees vs. 60% in Census), though it overrepresented coastal states and retail/service industries. A follow-up phone screen of 400 businesses found 42% of survey respondents were still open versus 56% of non-respondents.
args.key_excerpts: "Across the full sample, 43% of businesses had temporarily closed, and nearly all of these closures were due to COVID-19."

<webpage_content>
High Frequency Business Dynamics in the United States During the COVID-19 Pandemic by Catherine Buffington U.S. Census Bureau Daniel Chapman U.S. Census Bureau and University of Maryland Emin Dinlersoz U.S. Census Bureau Lucia Foster U.S. Census Bureau John Haltiwanger University of Maryland CES 21-06 March 2021 The research program of the Center for Economic Studies (CES) produces a wide range of economic analyses to improve the statistical programs of the U.S. Census Bureau. Many of these analyses take the form of CES research papers. The papers have not undergone the review accorded Census Bureau publications and no endorsement should be inferred. Any opinions and conclusions expressed herein are those of the author(s) and do not necessarily represent the views of the U.S. Census Bureau. All results have been reviewed to ensure that no confidential information is disclosed. Republication in whole or part must be cleared with the authors. To obtain information about the series, see www.census.gov/ces or contact Christopher Goetz, Editor, Discussion Papers, U.S. Census Bureau, Center for Economic Studies 5K038E, 4600 Silver Hill Road, Washington, DC 20233, CES.Working.Papers@census.gov. To subscribe to the series, please click here. Abstract Existing small businesses experienced very sharp declines in activity, business sentiment, and expectations early in the pandemic. While there has been some recovery since the early days of the pandemic, small businesses continued to exhibit indicators of negative growth, business sentiment, and expectations through the first week of January 2021. These findings are from a unique high frequency, real time survey of small employer businesses, the Census Bureau’s Small Business Pulse Survey (SBPS). Findings from the SBPS show substantial variation across sectors in the outcomes for small businesses. Small businesses in Accommodation and Food Services have been hit especially hard relative to those Finance and Insurance. However, even in Finance and Insurance small businesses exhibit indicators of negative growth, business sentiment, and expectations for all weeks from late April 2020 through the first week of 2021. While existing small businesses have fared poorly, after an initial decline, there has been a surge in new business applications based on the high frequency, real time Business Formation Statistics (BFS). Most of these applications are for likely nonemployers that are out of scope for the SBPS. However, there has also been a surge in new applications for likely employers. The surge in applications has been especially apparent in Retail Trade (and especially Non-store Retailers). We compare and contrast the patterns from these two new high frequency data products that provide novel insights into the distinct patterns of dynamics for existing small businesses relative to new business formations. * * Any opinions and conclusions expressed herein are those of the authors and do not represent the views of the U.S. Census Bureau. All results in this paper use publicly available data from Census Bureau websites. The Census Bureau has reviewed the public domain products for unauthorized disclosure of confidential information and has approved the disclosure avoidance practices applied to this release (Approval ID: CBDRB-FY20-259, CBDRB-FY-20-357, CBDRB-FY-20-214, CBDRB-FY21-094). We thank John Eltinge, Scott Ohlmacher, and Nick Orsini for helpful comments. 2 1. Introduction In the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States, the Census Bureau introduced new data products designed to capture its impacts on the American economy and population (see Buffington et al. (2021)). These data products were designed to provide geographically granular, timely, and high frequency information about the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on businesses and households. We describe the results from two new business data products: the Small Business Pulse Survey (SBPS) and the weekly and monthly Business Formation Statistics (BFS).2 We report results from the first three phases of the SBPS (April-June, August-October, and November-January) and there are distinct patterns in each of the three phases. The SBPS shows that existing small businesses experienced very sharp declines in activity, business sentiment, and expectations early in the pandemic. While the indicators of net growth, business sentiment, and expectations have become less negative since the early weeks of the pandemic, the indicators are still in a substantially negative range by the first week of January 2021. This improvement has not been monotonic: conditions improve in the Summer of 2020 but worsen at the end of 2020.3 The patterns for new business formations from the BFS are in sharp contrast to those for existing small businesses. After an initial decline, there has been a strong surge in new business applications for both likely employers and nonemployers. For overall applications, 2020 is the highest year on record for new business formations with most of this surge occurring in the second half of 2020. Both the SBPS and BFS show substantial sectoral variation. Existing small businesses in some service sectors have been especially hard hit. The SBPS provides insights into changes in revenue, employment, and hours in these sectors. In order to illuminate these differences, we focus on two extremes of the sectoral experience in the SBPS section of the paper: Finance and Insurance and Accommodation and Food Services. We show differences in the changes in revenue and employment as well as differences in their future needs and expectations of a return to normal level of operations. Small Business Pulse Survey The SBPS complements existing Census Bureau surveys conducted at higher frequencies that are also intended to measure the impact of the pandemic on businesses. As its name suggests, the SBPS focuses on small businesses. As context, there are about 5.3 million employer firms in the U.S. in 2018 consisting of 7.1 million establishments and 130 million workers. 6 See North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) U.S. Census Bureau. 5 While the number of “small” businesses (defined here as less than 500 employees) dominates the total number of establishments and firms (81% and more than 99%, respectively), the share of workers at “small” firms so defined is about 47%.7 Thus, the target pool of businesses is an important part of the economy. Moreover, many COVID-19 relief policies targeted businesses of this size. The SBPS sample is drawn from the 2017 Economic Census for all single-location businesses with 1-499 employees and $1000+ revenue that report an email address.8 The survey divides the sample equally across the nine weeks of each phase of the survey. Thus, each week of the survey, about 100,000 emails are sent out to businesses asking them to participate in the survey. Each of the nine subsamples is used only once each phase but are reused across phases (thus some businesses may have responded three times, once in each phase). With a response rate of about 25%, there are approximately 25,000 businesses responding each week. The survey is designed to be representative and the results are re-weighted to be nationally representative.9 The focus on single-location businesses allows the Census Bureau to publish detailed geographic (at state and selected MSA levels) information. The focus on small single-locations businesses makes it more likely that the business is operating in one sector which facilitates publishing detailed sectoral (at 2-digit NAICS and selected 3-digit NAICS) information. It is important to provide granular information to accurately capture the heterogenous impact of the pandemic on businesses. As noted above, the sample of the SBPS complements other existing Census Bureau surveys conducted at higher frequencies. This is also true for its content. The trade-off is that the SBPS is higher frequency and more timely, but less comprehensive in terms of coverage than the Monthly Retail Trade Survey (which is not as frequent or timely). Many of the questions in the SBPS have checkbox responses that capture only whether a business is impacted and not the size of the impact. The survey has an internal narrative structure that leads the respondent through the questions; the substantive section of the survey starts by asking about the overall effect of the 7 From 2018 Business Dynamics Statistics. The survey content was developed in partnership with eight other agencies and interested stakeholders.10 Their subject matter expertise was especially helpful in developing content useful for policymakers as they develop programs intended to assist small businesses. The content of the survey varies over Phase 1 and Phases 2-3, but there are about 20 questions on the survey (as shown in Table 1). A guiding principle is to maintain consistency across phases where possible to allow for longitudinal analysis. However, questions are edited, added, or dropped as analysis of results and changing conditions warrants (these are discussed more below). One critical feature of the SBPS is that it requests confirmation of the respondent’s Employer Identification Number (EIN,) the last four digits of which are pre-printed in the invitation to respond. If the provided EIN does not match that for the company, the respondent is asked to provide the correct EIN. The EIN enables the use of existing Census Bureau information on sector and geography, allowing survey information to be released by sector and geography while minimizing respondent burden. This also means that the SBPS survey results can be linked to other Census Bureau collections at the micro-level (which may allow us, for example, to provide information concerning owner demographics collected on other surveys). Another important feature of the SBPS is the time frame of the questions. Many of the questions are designed to capture changes in behavior over the weeks of the pandemic and thus ask about changes “in the last week.” For example, questions concerning changes in hours, employment, and revenue use this time frame. This time frame allows us to capture flows of changes, but it means that we will miss changes that precede the week in question. The survey started in late April 2020, so some of the businesses’ changes in response to the pandemic may have already taken place.11 Other questions are designed to capture changes in behavior since the start of the pandemic and thus ask about concepts “Since March 13, 2020.” Questions related to 10 The Small Business Administration, the Federal Reserve Board of Governors, International Trade Administration, Minority Business Development Agency, Bureau of Transportation Statistics, National Telecommunications and Information Administration, Office of Tax Analysis of the Treasury Department, and the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Finally, the two more holistic questions that bookend the survey have more open-ended time frames. A number of other surveys have been conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic to capture some of these same concepts. First, BLS conducted one phase of the Business Response Survey (BRS) from July-September 2020 asking businesses about the impact of the pandemic and their responses through seven questions over three areas: “1) business experiences and payroll decisions, 2) worker benefits and their ability to telework, and 3) whether a business received a loan or a grant from the government tied to the payroll.”12 Second, Bartik et al. (2020 conducted a survey early in the pandemic of about 5,800 small businesses through Alignable asking about impact, actions, and expectations. args.summary:
This is a CES research paper (CES 21-06, March 2021) by Catherine Buffington, Daniel Chapman, Emin Dinlersoz, Lucia Foster (U.S. Census Bureau) and John Haltiwanger (University of Maryland) examining high-frequency business dynamics during the COVID-19 pandemic using two new Census Bureau data products: the Small Business Pulse Survey (SBPS) and Business Formation Statistics (BFS).

KEY FINDINGS:
1. Existing small businesses experienced sharp declines in activity, sentiment, and expectations early in the pandemic. While indicators improved somewhat, they remained substantially negative through the first week of January 2021. The improvement was not monotonic—conditions improved in Summer 2020 but worsened at the end of 2020.
2. There is substantial sectoral variation: Accommodation and Food Services were hit especially hard compared to Finance and Insurance. Even in Finance and Insurance, small businesses exhibited negative growth indicators for all weeks from late April 2020 through early 2021.
3. After an initial decline, there was a strong surge in new business applications in 2020 (highest year on record), particularly in Retail Trade and Non-store Retailers (e-commerce). The surge was most apparent in the second half of 2020.
4. The pandemic may lead to lasting structural changes: sectors hit hard for existing small businesses are seeing surges in new business applications.
5. Adverse impact on revenue was greater than impact on employment, partly due to decreases in hours rather than employment (suggestive of labor hoarding). By the last week of Phase 3, 84.1% of businesses did not change employment.
6. About 74% of small businesses in the SBPS received PPP loans. Cash on hand was limited, highlighting the precarious nature of small business operations.
7. Remote work increased significantly but varied by sector (Information had highest at 79.6%; Accommodation and Food Services lowest at 21.7%). Some businesses pivoted to new goods/services (especially Educational Services, Accommodation and Food Services, Information) and many more pivoted to new delivery modes.
8. Geographically, the initial decline in business applications was concentrated in the Northeast and West, with recovery emphasized in the South and Midwest.

SBPS METHODOLOGY:
- Sample drawn from 2017 Economic Census for single-location businesses with 1-499 employees and $1000+ revenue
- ~100,000 emails sent weekly; ~25,000 responses weekly (25% response rate)
- Three phases: April-June, August-October, November-January
- Overall Sentiment Index (OSI) ranges from -1 (most negative) to +1 (most positive)
- Sectors consistently at top of OSI: Finance and Insurance, Construction, Retail Trade. At bottom: Arts/Entertainment/Recreation, Educational Services, Accommodation and Food Services
- By end of Phase 3, 64.9% of Accommodation and Food Services businesses had large negative effects vs. 13.7% in Finance and Insurance

KEY SECTOR STATISTICS:
- First week of Phase 1: 74.0% of businesses saw revenue decreases vs. 5.9% increases. Last week of Phase 3: 56.1% of Accommodation and Food Services had revenue decreases vs. 22.1% in Finance and Insurance.
- Employment: Finance and Insurance grew by ~50,000 jobs in 2020; Accommodation and Food Services shrank by ~3 million jobs (BLS data).
- By end of 2020, Finance and Insurance revenue was close to pre-pandemic levels; Accommodation and Food Services remained below.
- Supply chain issues: Retail Trade had largest percentage with domestic supplier issues (48.0%); Finance and Insurance smallest (5.0%).
- Operating capacity: about half of businesses noted decreased capacity relative to one year ago by end of Phase 3; 42.9% reported no change.

LIMITATIONS/CAVEATS: Seven considerations for interpreting SBPS results include non-response bias for business closures, reliance on email addresses, single-location business focus, willingness to respond to federal surveys, overrepresentation of adversely impacted businesses, and representation of young businesses.

This summary will be used by a downstream research agent, so it's crucial to maintain the key details without losing essential information.

Here is the raw content of the webpage:

<webpage_content>
# US Store Closings Outstrip Openings in Break From Past Two Years

![So far this year there will be 122 net U.S. store closings, according to Coresight Research. (Getty Images)](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcostar.brightspotcdn.com%2Fdims4%2Fdefault%2F46e7721%2F2147483647%2Fstrip%2Ftrue%2Fcrop%2F2100x1575%2B0%2B0%2Fresize%2F2100x1575!%2Fquality%2F100%2F%3Furl%3Dhttp%253A%252F%252Fcostar-brightspot.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%252Ff3%252F71%252F6dfbd68c4eff846545198c11ebf7%252Fgettyimages-1940030669-1.jpg&w=3840&q=75)

## RELATED ARTICLES

### RELATED ARTICLES

U.S. store closings have surpassed openings for the first time this year, the result of a surge of bankruptcy filings by struggling retailers that has extended into the back half of 2024.

Year to date, the 4,548 stores shutting their doors have outpaced the 4,426 announced openings, resulting in 122 net store closings, according to a Coresight Research report dated Aug. 9. The data marks a shift from the previous two years’ annual totals where openings edged closings.

One of the reasons closings are now outpacing debuts is because furniture and home goods seller Big Lots, based in Columbus, Ohio, has significantly increased the number of locations it plans to shut, by 258, John Harmon, managing director of technology research at Coresight, a data-driven retail analytics firm, told CoStar News on Tuesday.

"Until two weeks ago, the lines [of closings and openings] were just tracking each other as expected," he said.

Around the time of the [ICSC national](https://product.costar.com/home/news/shared/1372106200) [retail real estate](https://product.costar.com/home/news/shared/1372106200) [conference in May,](https://product.costar.com/home/news/shared/1372106200) there had been wave of retail Chapter 11 filings and store closings. In the past few months there's been another spurt of bankruptcy filings, with more vacant retail space being thrown onto the market. But at least one retail analyst said there hasn't been any tipping point now — that despite the new round of closings the demand for retail space will continue to outstrip the supply. The national retail vacancy rate is 4.1%, according to CoStar data, making that sector very tight in terms of available space.

"It's not, in my opinion, a resumption of the retail apocalypse that we saw in 2018, 2019, 2020 where we were seeing so many stores closed," Brandon Svec,national director of U.S. retail analytics for CoStar Group, told CoStar News. "There are still a substantial amount of tenants from a broad range of sectors looking for space. And the longer-term imbalance between the space needed in retail and the space that we have, I don't think has shifted."

Of course, it remains to be seen how many more retailers shake out this year and what effect that will have on retail leasing. Several analysts said they expect more stores to be shuttered and more Chapter 11 filings.

# Closing Up Shop

# 

In recent weeks, in addition to Big Lots, the flock of retailers and chains shuttering locations has grown to include [Conn's HomePlus,](https://product.costar.com/home/news/shared/1005420379)Badcock's Home Furniture & More,[LL Flooring Holdings,](https://product.costar.com/home/news/shared/1297436783) [Buca di Beppo,](https://product.costar.com/home/news/shared/1144920131) Rubio's, and World of Beer. The LL Flooring closings, 94 stores, just happened this week so aren't included in Coresight's report.

Coresight said that department store chain J.C. Penney had closed 12 stores year to date. The retailer plans to close three more stores in 2024: one in the Shoppes at Bel Air shopping mall in Mobile, Alabama; one in the Sikes Senter shopping mall in Wichita Falls, Texas; and one in the Elm Plaza shopping mall in Waterville, Maine. J.C. Penney also plans to close one store in the Westfield Annapolis shopping mall in Annapolis, Maryland, at some point in 2025, according to Coresight. It now operates 660 stores.

Discount giant Target plans to close one store in East Palo Alto, California, on Sept. 28, taking the company’s U.S. store count to 1,965, according to Coresight. And Party supplies retailer Party City has opened one store and closed 18 year to date, with plans to close one store in Albany, Georgia, later in this year, according to Coresight's report.

Still, this year's store closings pale compared to prior years. In 2020, the peak of the pandemic, there were only 3,704 openings compared with 9,698 closings, for a net of 5,994 closings, according to Coresight. In 2021, there were only 180 net store closings, with a total of 5,228. In 2022, store openings soared, to 5,394 openings compared with 3,819 closings, for a net 1,575 openings. And last year, there were 5,843 openings versus 5,548 closings, for a net 295 openings.

![](https://costar.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e6c30d1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4664x3110+0+0/resize/2100x1400!/quality/100/?url=http%3A%2F%2Fcostar-brightspot.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2F6a%2F6b%2Fbb025090455a94b3a1d65cbd76b0%2Fgucci-american-dream-b741046-hr-v1-qc-r150.jpg)

Barrie Scardina, president of Americas Retail Services, Agency Leasing and Alliances for the brokerage Cushman & Wakefield, in an email said it's important to note that the square footage of the store openings is still ahead of that for closings, citing Coresight data. As of Aug. 2, announced store openings will result in an estimated 79.5 million square feet of new retail space, she said, compared with an estimated 67 million square feet of closed retail space.

# Home Improvement in Trouble

Svec and Daniel Gielchinsky, a partner at DGIM Law and a bankruptcy attorney, both said that retailers selling goods relating to homes and home improvements have been hit hard by high inflation and high interest rates that are putting a break on consumer spending in that sector.

On Tuesday, Home Depot, the world's largest home improvement retailer, [reported fiscal second-quarter earnings](https://product.costar.com/home/news/shared/1086305217?tag=24) and said it expects full-year, same-store sales to drop 3% to 4% in 2024.

"When people are unable to go out to the market and buy a house or invest in their house, it affects everything else," Gielchinsky told CoStar News. "Studies show that people who spend the most or invest the most in their newly purchased home in the first three years of their home ownership. But if home ownership is out of people's grasps, then they're never going to have that opportunity to invest."

He predicted that smaller home improvement retailers will be filing for Chapter 11.

The rise in store closings is a reflection of retail sector specific weakness, especially related to the slowdown in home sales, according to Svec.

"And it does reflect a true rotation and slowdown in sales growth that we're seeing amongst a lot of retailers," he said.

# 'Paying the Piper'

From an operational side, retailers are feeling the impact of slowing sales growth, higher costs, and fewer accommodating debt markets, according to Svec.

"All of those things are combining to reduce retailer profitability, to lead to this uptick in closures," he said. "But most of the closures we're seeing still can be classified really into a couple buckets. First and foremost, sector-specific weakness due to outside macro factors, and that's really your housing market, your furniture market, your appliance market. All of those sectors are are really still struggling, but that's really nothing to do with the overall macro environment."

Second, companies that were already standing in weak financial positions were thrown a temporary lifeline by the pandemic, according to Svec.

"Once sales normalized, once operations normalize, their poor merchandising, poor location strategies, what have you came back to roost," he said. "And we're now paying the piper that we should have and would have probably paid in 2021 had it not been for those tailwinds that they got from the pandemic."

Some retailers are relocating out of malls, resulting in store closings, he said.

There are plenty of bright spots in terms of store openings, with retailers such as Dollar General, Burlington Stores, and TJX Cos. debuting hundreds of new locations. And in an unusual turn of events, the new owner of teen apparel chain Rue21 that filed for Chapter 11 and closed more than 500 store, is [reopening dozens](https://product.costar.com/home/news/shared/864369536) of those shuttered locations.

In its recent report, Coresight cited 30 additional announced store openings were led by: Havertys, seven; Publix, five; Sleep Number’s, four; and Daiso, Murphy USA and Rag & Bone, three each. In addition, luxury retailer Gucci opened up shop at the [American Dream](https://product.costar.com/detail/lookup/9181694/summary) megamall in East Rutherford, New Jersey.

**"**We have too much retail space in certain locations," Svec said. "We have too much space in certain formats. But overall, I think we are still in a very tight space-balance position across most of the sector. And that's not changed by these more recent store closure announcements."

# 25,000 stores are predicted to close in 2020, as the coronavirus pandemic accelerates industry upheaval

![thumbnail](https://image.cnbcfm.com/api/v1/image/106497130-1587401879908img_0254.jpg?v=1587401920&w=60&h=60&ffmt=webp)

[Lauren Thomas](https://www.cnbc.com/lauren-thomas/)[@laurenthomas](https://twitter.com/laurenthomas)

[WATCH LIVE](/live-tv/)

Key Points

* U.S. retailers could announce between 20,000 and 25,000 closures this year, according to a tracking by Coresight Research, with 55% to 60% of those situated in America's malls.
* That would also mark a record for the industry.
* Coresight was previously forecasting there could be more than 15,000 store closures announced by retailers in 2020.

Spencer Platt | Getty Images

One result of the [coronavirus pandemic](https://www.cnbc.com/coronavirus/) could be as many as 25,000 store closures announced by retailers this year, as the crisis takes a toll on many businesses, and already has pushed some over the brink and into bankruptcy.

U.S. retailers could announce between 20,000 and 25,000 closures in 2020, according to a tracking by Coresight Research, with 55% to 60% of those situated in America's malls. That would also mark a record — which was previously [the more than 9,300 locations](https://www.cnbc.com/2019/12/20/sears-walgreens-among-retailers-that-closed-stores-in-2019.html) in 2019.

Coresight was [earlier this year forecasting there could be more than 15,000 store closures](https://www.cnbc.com/2020/03/16/retail-store-closures-in-the-us-could-explode-because-of-coronavirus.html) announced by retailers in 2020.

A glut of vacant storefronts will leave landlords scrambling to fill those spaces or find new uses for their real estate. There are not many retailers still growing via bricks and mortar today. And if they are, many are looking to downsize to smaller shops.

![Permanent changes to way consumers behave and spend': Retail analyst](https://image.cnbcfm.com/api/v1/image/106567253-permanentchangestothewayconsumersbehaveandspendmoneyoppenheimerretailanalyst.jpg?v=1591381593&w=750&h=422&vtcrop=y)

watch now

VIDEO3:2503:25

Permanent changes to way consumers behave and spend': Retail analyst

[Power Lunch](https://www.cnbc.com/power-lunch/)

In recent weeks, bankruptcy filings in retail have begun to mount. Coresight said it expects more liquidations, ticking up the closure tally. Department store chains Neiman Marcus, Stage Stores and J.C. Penney have filed for bankruptcy protection. So have the home goods chain Tuesday Morning and the apparel maker J.Crew. A number of these retailers will close some stores and begin operating again, but Stage Stores has warned it may need to shutter all of its locations if it doesn't find a buyer.

Coresight has, so far, recorded a total of 4,005 announced closures by retailers in 2020, including more than 900 by the home decor retailer Pier 1 Imports, roughly 300 by the health chain [GNC](/quotes/IGN-FF/), more than 200 by Tuesday Morning, and some from [L Brands](/quotes/LB/)' Victoria's Secret, Papyrus and Penney.

"We expect that a return to pre-crisis levels in offline discretionary retail sales overall will be gradual, as we expect consumer confidence, demand and spending to be short of normal for some time," Coresight founder and CEO Deborah Weinswig said in the report.

"Given that recovery to pre-crisis levels may be gradual, retailers that were struggling to stay in business pre-crisis are unlikely to have the wherewithal to stay the course on the road to recovery and could end up closing a number of stores," she said.

A separate report by eMarketer is forecasting total retail sales in the U.S. to fall more than 10% in 2020 and that they won't bounce back to pre-Covid-19 levels until 2022. Meantime, eMarketer is calling for e-commerce sales to surge 18% this year.

It expects all categories within retail except for food and beverage, and health and beauty, to see sales decline due to the pandemic.

"This is the sharpest consumer spending freeze in decades in the US," said eMarketer senior analyst Cindy Liu.

![Saks Fifth Avenue president on reopening and future of department stores](https://image.cnbcfm.com/api/v1/image/105958064-1560172244960gettyimages-1077094900.jpeg?v=1768403082&w=750&h=422&vtcrop=y)

Widespread decline in physical retail stores

|  |
| --- |
| The examples and perspectives in this article **deal primarily with the United States and do not represent a [worldwide view](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:WikiProject_Countering_systemic_bias "Wikipedia:WikiProject Countering systemic bias") of the subject**. Retail apocalypse

| Entrance to a former [Sears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sears "Sears") store at [Hudson Valley Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Valley_Mall "Hudson Valley Mall") in [Ulster, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulster,_New_York "Ulster, New York"), closed in 2018. It had been the mall's last [anchor store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anchor_store "Anchor store"). |
| Date | 2010 (2010) – present |
| Venue | Shopping malls, physical retail |
| Location | * [Northern America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_America "Northern America") |
| Cause | * Downsizing of retail chains caused by rise in global [e-commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E-commerce "E-commerce") operations related to the [2008 financial crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_financial_crisis "2008 financial crisis") * Accumulation of [corporate debt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporate_bond "Corporate bond") for retail overexpansion * Changes in spending habits * [Impact of COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_on_retail "Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on retail") * [2021–2023 inflation surge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021–2023_inflation_surge "2021–2023 inflation surge")[[1]](#cite_note-1) * Rise of e-commerce itself |
| Outcome | * Numerous bankruptcies ensued from early 2010s * Major decline in revenue from suppliers * Increase in the amount of [dead malls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_mall "Dead mall") * Bankruptcies accelerated from March 2020 as a result of the [COVID-19 recession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_recession "COVID-19 recession") and [Inflation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021-2023_inflation_surge "2021-2023 inflation surge") |

The **retail apocalypse** (also known as **retailpocalypse**[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3)) is the closing of numerous Northern American [brick and mortar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brick_and_mortar "Brick and mortar") [retail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retail "Retail") stores, especially those of large chains, starting in the 2010s.[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-atlantic-5)[*[failed verification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")*] The 2020s saw more store closures as a result of [COVID-19 lockdowns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_lockdowns "COVID-19 lockdowns") with customers using [online shopping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_shopping "Online shopping") as an alternative way to shop.

In 2017 alone, more than 12,000 physical stores closed. The reasons included debt and bankruptcy in the face of rising costs, [leveraged buyouts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leveraged_buyout "Leveraged buyout"), low quarterly profits outside [holiday binge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics_of_Christmas "Economics of Christmas") spending, delayed effects of the [Great Recession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Recession "Great Recession"),[[5]](#cite_note-atlantic-5) and changes in spending habits. American consumers have shifted their purchasing habits due to various factors, including [experience spending](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experience_economy "Experience economy") versus material goods and homes, casual fashion in relaxed [dress codes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dress_code "Dress code"), as well as the rise of [e-commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E-commerce "E-commerce")[[6]](#cite_note-6) and particularly [juggernaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juggernaut "Juggernaut") companies such as [Amazon.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon.com "Amazon.com") and [Walmart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walmart "Walmart"). A 2017 *[Business Insider](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business_Insider "Business Insider")* report dubbed this phenomenon the "Amazon effect" and calculated that Amazon.com was generating more than half of retail-sales growth.[[7]](#cite_note-business-insider-amazon-effect-1nov2017-7)

Not everyone agrees that a "retail apocalypse" exists. Dissenting economists and experts asserted that recent retail closures are a market correction, suggesting that the phrase is misleading and instills insecurity in the 16 million U.S. [retail workers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retail_workers_in_the_United_States "Retail workers in the United States").[[8]](#cite_note-Tech-8) Research published by global retail analyst IHL Group in 2019 suggests that the so-called retail apocalypse narrative was an exaggeration, with "more chains that are expanding their number of stores than closing stores."[[9]](#cite_note-IHL-9) That year, retailers in the United States announced 9,302 store closings, a 59% jump from 2018, and the highest number since tracking the data began in 2012.[[10]](#cite_note-closing_28-10)

Corporate bankruptcies and store closings increased in 2020. During the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_impact_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic "Financial impact of the COVID-19 pandemic"), most retail stores, especially struggling mall-based retailers, closed for extended periods of time.[[11]](#cite_note-11) Several large retail companies filed for bankruptcy during the pandemic, including [J. Crew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Crew "J. Crew"), [Century 21](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Century_21_(department_store) "Century 21 (department store)"), [Neiman Marcus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neiman_Marcus "Neiman Marcus"), [Lord & Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_&_Taylor "Lord & Taylor"), [Stage Stores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stage_Stores "Stage Stores"), [Stein Mart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stein_Mart "Stein Mart"), [JCPenney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JCPenney "JCPenney"), [Tuesday Morning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuesday_Morning "Tuesday Morning"), and [Pier 1 Imports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pier_1_Imports "Pier 1 Imports").[[12]](#cite_note-chicagotribune-12)

The most productive retailers in North America during the retail apocalypse are [discount](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discounter "Discounter") superstores[[13]](#cite_note-13) Walmart and [Target](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Target_Corporation "Target Corporation"), low-cost "[fast-fashion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast-fashion "Fast-fashion")" brands ([Zara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zara_(retailer) "Zara (retailer)"), [H&M](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H&M "H&M")), [dollar stores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dollar_stores "Dollar stores")[*[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")*] ([Dollar General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dollar_General "Dollar General"), [Dollar Tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dollar_Tree "Dollar Tree"), [Family Dollar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_Dollar "Family Dollar"), [Dollarama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dollarama "Dollarama")),[[14]](#cite_note-14) and [warehouse clubs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warehouse_club "Warehouse club") ([Costco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costco "Costco"), [Sam's Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam's_Club "Sam's Club"), and [BJ's Wholesale Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BJ's_Wholesale_Club "BJ's Wholesale Club")).[[15]](#cite_note-15)

A major consequence of the retail apocalypse has been the increase in vacant [retail space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retail_space "Retail space"), such as [big-box stores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big-box_stores "Big-box stores"), [strip malls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strip_malls "Strip malls") and [shopping malls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shopping_malls "Shopping malls")—with the latter becoming [dead malls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_malls "Dead malls") due to declining consumer traffic and store closures. Such vacant real estate, in turn, has become the site for [pop-up retail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop-up_retail "Pop-up retail") stores—a notable example being [Spirit Halloween](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spirit_Halloween "Spirit Halloween"), a seasonal retailer which sells Halloween merchandise and has set up stores at vacant retail buildings, including former big-box stores.[[16]](#cite_note-Saldana-16)[[17]](#cite_note-17)

## History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Retail_apocalypse&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f3/Closed_Grocery_Store_in_Port_Charlotte.jpg/250px-Closed_Grocery_Store_in_Port_Charlotte.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Closed_Grocery_Store_in_Port_Charlotte.jpg)

A permanently closed mom and pop health food store in [Port Charlotte, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Charlotte,_Florida "Port Charlotte, Florida")

The phrase "retail apocalypse" first appeared in print in an early 1990s essay by Peter Glen, author of *It's Not My Department!*[[18]](#cite_note-18) Media appropriated the term to refer to multiple brick-and-mortar store closures resulting from shifts in [consumer spending](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consumer_spending "Consumer spending").[[8]](#cite_note-Tech-8)

Since at least the [2008 financial crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_financial_crisis "2008 financial crisis"), various economic factors have resulted in the closing of many stores in North America, the United Kingdom, and Australia, particularly in the [department store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store "Department store") industry. For example, [Sears Holdings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sears_Holdings "Sears Holdings") had more than 3,500 stores and 355,000 employees in 2006.[[19]](#cite_note-19) By the end of 2016, Sears operated 1,430 stores.[[20]](#cite_note-20) In October 2018, Sears filed for bankruptcy and announced it would close an additional 142 of its 687 stores.[[21]](#cite_note-:0-21) At the time of filing, Sears had 68,000 employees.[[21]](#cite_note-:0-21)

The phrase "retail apocalypse" began gaining widespread usage in 2017 following multiple announcements from many major retailers of plans to either discontinue or greatly scale back a retail presence, including companies such as [H.H. Gregg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H.H._Gregg "H.H. Gregg"), [Family Christian Stores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_Christian_Stores "Family Christian Stores") and [The Limited](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Limited "The Limited") all going out of business entirely.[[22]](#cite_note-whioohioimpact-22) *[The Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Atlantic "The Atlantic")* described the phenomenon as "The Great Retail Apocalypse of 2017", reporting nine retail bankruptcies and several apparel companies having their stock hit new lows, including that of [Lululemon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lululemon "Lululemon"), [Urban Outfitters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_Outfitters "Urban Outfitters"), and [American Eagle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Eagle_Outfitters "American Eagle Outfitters").[[5]](#cite_note-atlantic-5) [Credit Suisse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credit_Suisse "Credit Suisse"), a major global financial services company, predicted that 25% of U.S. malls remaining in 2017 could close by 2022.[[23]](#cite_note-gymboree-23)

Since 2017, the phrase is frequently applied to brick-and-mortar closures in retail, with the retail apocalypse creating a [domino effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domino_effect "Domino effect") on manufacturers and suppliers; [Hasbro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasbro "Hasbro"), for example, cited the loss of the [Toys "R" Us](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toys_ "Toys ") chain as a major cause for lost revenue and layoffs the company imposed in October 2018.[[24]](#cite_note-24)

A 2019 analysis conducted by IHL Group international research and advisory firm found that when a retailer closes many stores, it indicates more about the individual retailer rather than the retail industry overall. In 2019, the 20 stores announcing the most closures [represent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pareto_principle "Pareto principle") 75% of all closures. IHL found that for each retailer closing stores in 2019, more than five retail chains are opening stores, an increase from the 3.7 ratio of 2018. IHL also reported that the number of chains adding stores in 2019 had increased 56%, while the number of closing stores decreased by 66% in the last year.[[9]](#cite_note-IHL-9)[[25]](#cite_note-25)

As of May 2020, bankruptcies and store closings were expected to intensify due to widespread business closures and the resulting [financial impact of the COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_impact_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic "Financial impact of the COVID-19 pandemic"). [J. Crew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Crew "J. Crew"), [Century 21](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Century_21_(department_store) "Century 21 (department store)"), [Neiman Marcus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neiman_Marcus "Neiman Marcus"), [Stage Stores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stage_Stores "Stage Stores"), [Stein Mart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stein_Mart "Stein Mart"), [Lord & Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_&_Taylor "Lord & Taylor"), [JCPenney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JCPenney "JCPenney"), [Tuesday Morning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuesday_Morning "Tuesday Morning"), and [Pier 1 Imports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pier_1_Imports "Pier 1 Imports") were among the first major retailers to file for bankruptcy during the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States "COVID-19 pandemic in the United States").[[12]](#cite_note-chicagotribune-12)

### Shift to e-commerce

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Retail_apocalypse&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Shift to e-commerce")]

Further information: [Online shopping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_shopping "Online shopping")

The main factor cited in the closing of retail stores in the retail apocalypse is the shift in consumer habits towards [online shopping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_shopping "Online shopping").[[26]](#cite_note-26) Holiday sales for e-commerce increased by an estimated 11% to 20% from 2015 to 2016. The same year, brick-and-mortar stores saw an overall increase of only 1.6%, with physical department stores experiencing a 4.8% decline.[[27]](#cite_note-practicale-27)

### Oversupply of shopping malls

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Retail_apocalypse&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Oversupply of shopping malls")]

Another factor is an over-supply of malls[[28]](#cite_note-28) as the growth rate of malls in North America between 1970 and 2015 was over twice the growth rate of the population. In 2004, [Malcolm Gladwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcolm_Gladwell "Malcolm Gladwell") wrote that investment in malls was artificially accelerated when the [United States Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress "United States Congress") introduced [accelerated depreciation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accelerated_depreciation "Accelerated depreciation") into the tax code in 1954.[[29]](#cite_note-29) Despite the construction of new malls, mall visits declined by 50% between 2010 and 2013 with further declines reported in each successive year.[[30]](#cite_note-30)

### Experience economy

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Retail_apocalypse&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Experience economy")]

Main article: [Experience economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experience_economy "Experience economy")

One idea presented in the 2010s for the supposed retail decline was a perceived ongoing "restaurant renaissance"— a shift in consumer spending habits for their [disposable income](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disposable_income "Disposable income") from material purchases such as clothing towards [dining out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Restaurant "Restaurant") and travel.[[5]](#cite_note-atlantic-5)

### Shrinking middle class

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Retail_apocalypse&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Shrinking middle class")]

Another cited factor is the "death of the [American middle class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_middle_class "American middle class")" represented by declining real wages and rising costs creating a [middle-class squeeze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle-class_squeeze "Middle-class squeeze"), resulting in large-scale closures of retailers such as [Macy's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macy's "Macy's"), [JCPenney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JCPenney "JCPenney"), and [Sears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sears "Sears") which traditionally relied on spending from this market segment.[[31]](#cite_note-middleclass-31) Particularly in rural areas, [variety stores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_store "Variety store") such as [Dollar General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dollar_General "Dollar General"), [Dollar Tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dollar_Tree "Dollar Tree"), and [Family Dollar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_Dollar "Family Dollar"), once thought to be unaffected by the apocalypse since they have continued growing rapidly, are now perceived as being at best a symptom of the phenomenon, and at worst a direct cause of rural, independent retailers collapsing, unable to compete with the lower margins that national chains can sustain.[[32]](#cite_note-32)[[33]](#cite_note-33)

### Poor management

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Retail_apocalypse&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Poor management")]

Poor retail management coupled with an overcritical eye towards quarterly dividends cause a lack of accurate inventory control, so the sales floor suffers from underperforming merchandise and out-of-stock merchandise, creating a poor shopping experience for customers. The focus on short-term balance sheets induces management to understaff retail stores to keep profits high.[[34]](#cite_note-34)[[35]](#cite_note-35) Furthermore, many long-standing chain retailers are [overloaded with debt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporate_debt_bubble "Corporate debt bubble"),[[36]](#cite_note-bloomberg_retail_beginning-36) often from [leveraged buyouts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leveraged_buyout "Leveraged buyout") from [private equity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_equity "Private equity") firms, which hinders the profitable operation of retail chains.[[37]](#cite_note-37)[[38]](#cite_note-38)

### COVID-19 pandemic

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Retail_apocalypse&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: COVID-19 pandemic")]

Main article: [Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on retail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_on_retail "Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on retail")

The [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic") exacerbated many issues affecting retailers, as many were forced to shut down due to non-pharmaceutical interventions that were issued in an effort to mitigate the pandemic.[[39]](#cite_note-39)

At the same time, [online shopping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_shopping "Online shopping") boomed during the coronavirus-related lockdown, even though it came back down starting in 2022.[[40]](#cite_note-40) Most of the major [e-commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E-commerce "E-commerce") retailers in the United States were classified as essential businesses and were not required to shut down. Buyers stated that they would deliberately buy products from such categories as food and drinks, hygiene, household cleaning, clothing, health, and consumer electronics online rather than in person due to COVID-19. The outbreak is said to have changed shopping behavior permanently: in the US, 29% of surveyed consumers stated that they had no intention to ever go back to offline shopping. In the UK, this number reached 43%.[[41]](#cite_note-41)

In June 2020, retail research firm Coresight reported that they estimated that the number of store closures due to the pandemic and ensuing recession would exceed the 2019 record of 9,302.[[42]](#cite_note-42)[[43]](#cite_note-43)

Coresight Research data later indicated that store closures had reduced by 49% from 2020 to 2021, with store openings increased by 36% over the previous year.[[44]](#cite_note-Coresight-44) Clothing and accessories accounted for 43% of retail closures in 2021.[[44]](#cite_note-Coresight-44) In July 2022, the analytics firm published findings that store openings had exceeded store closings for the first half of 2022, and that there were 10% fewer closings and 3% fewer openings than in 2021.[[45]](#cite_note-45)

## Strategies

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Retail_apocalypse&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Strategies")]

Researchers say retailers' survival may be tied to [customer experience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Customer_experience "Customer experience") and brand reputation. In 2019, *[Forbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes "Forbes")* said brand reputation was the biggest factor.[[83]](#cite_note-Fertik-83) In 2020, [Monash University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monash_University "Monash University") in Australia said the three key factors were delivering a "great in-store retail experience", customer-targeted stock offerings, and "seamless [omnichannel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omnichannel "Omnichannel") integration".[[84]](#cite_note-84)

[Toys "R" Us](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toys_ "Toys ") may not have responded well to changing [consumer behavior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consumer_behavior "Consumer behavior").[[85]](#cite_note-forbes-85)

Some retail chains are trying robots and other technologies to reduce costs or improve customer experiences. [Ikea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ikea "Ikea") became one of the first retailers to use [Apple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc.")'s [ARKit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARKit "ARKit") to develop an [augmented reality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augmented_reality "Augmented reality") app that allowed customers to visualize 3D renderings of Ikea products as they would appear in a certain room or place.[[86]](#cite_note-86)[[87]](#cite_note-87) [Macy's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macy's "Macy's"), [American Eagle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Eagle_Outfitters "American Eagle Outfitters"), [Nike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nike,_Inc. "Nike, Inc.") and [Sephora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sephora "Sephora") were reported to be implementing various technologies to integrate digital experiences to improve consumers' physical shopping experiences. Sephora has installed [smart mirrors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smart_mirror "Smart mirror") that use augmented reality to allow customers to try on makeup.[[88]](#cite_note-88) [Walmart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walmart "Walmart") automated some aspects of its supply chain. [Kohl's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kohl's "Kohl's") reduced the size of some stores from 90,000 to between 60,000 and 35,000 square feet[[83]](#cite_note-Fertik-83) and uses [robots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robot "Robot") to help clean and stock shelves. [Lowe's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowe's "Lowe's") has been using LowesBot to help customers find items.[[85]](#cite_note-forbes-85) Company executives have said robots lower costs and improve efficiency, but employees report they don't like working with robots.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

A 2018 study from the [International Council of Shopping Centers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Council_of_Shopping_Centers "International Council of Shopping Centers") indicated that opening new stores can increase traffic to retailer websites.[[89]](#cite_note-89)

args.summary: The "retail apocalypse" (also "retailpocalypse") refers to the widespread closure of brick-and-mortar retail stores in Northern America (and the UK, Australia), particularly large chains, starting in the 2010s and continuing into the 2020s. More than 12,000 physical stores closed in 2017 alone. Key causes include: the rise of e-commerce (especially Amazon and Walmart, dubbed the "Amazon effect"), oversupply of shopping malls, shifting consumer spending toward experiences (restaurants, travel) rather than goods, the shrinking American middle class, poor management and high debt from leveraged buyouts by private equity firms, and the COVID-19 pandemic which accelerated closures and bankruptcies. Major retailers filing for bankruptcy during the pandemic include J. Crew, Neiman Marcus, JCPenney, Lord & Taylor, Stage Stores, Stein Mart, Tuesday Morning, and Pier 1 Imports. The most resilient retailers have been discount superstores (Walmart, Target), fast-fashion brands (Zara, H&M), dollar stores, and warehouse clubs (Costco, Sam's Club). A consequence has been the rise of "dead malls" and vacant retail space often filled by pop-up retailers like Spirit Halloween. Some experts dispute the "apocalypse" narrative, arguing it's a market correction; IHL Group's 2019 research found more chains were expanding than closing stores. The term was first used by Peter Glen in an early 1990s essay and gained widespread usage in 2017. Strategies for survival cited by researchers include enhancing customer experience, omnichannel integration, and using technology (AR, robots, smart mirrors).
args.key_excerpts: "In 2017 alone, more than 12,000 physical stores closed. The reasons included debt and bankruptcy in the face of rising costs, leveraged buyouts, low quarterly profits outside holiday binge spending, delayed effects of the Great Recession, and changes in spending habits."
