# 25% of U.S. malls are expected to shut within 5 years. Giving them a new life won't be easy

![thumbnail](https://image.cnbcfm.com/api/v1/image/106497130-1587401879908img_0254.jpg?v=1587401920&w=60&h=60&ffmt=webp)

[Lauren Thomas](https://www.cnbc.com/lauren-thomas/)[@laurenthomas](https://twitter.com/laurenthomas)

[WATCH LIVE](/live-tv/)

Key Points

* Coresight Research estimates 25% of America's roughly 1,000 malls will close over the next three to five years.
* The coronavirus pandemic has accelerated a demise that was already underway.
* "Just because retail space has gone vacant or remained fallow does not mean that it is automatically a good candidate for repurposing into industrial space," Moody's Analytics real estate analyst Victor Calanog said.
* According to data pulled by Moody's Analytics REIS, apartment development in the U.S. is expected to be down 15.6% in a post-Covid-19 world. Office development is set to drop 10%, it said, while retail falls 15.7%.
* Industrial development, meantime, is expected to pick up 3.6%.

One of Macy's department stores locations at an indoor shopping mall.

Mike Blake | Reuters

What is going to happen to America's dead malls? That's a million-dollar question plaguing retailers and real estate developers.

With a [report circulating earlier this month](https://www.cnbc.com/2020/08/10/mall-owner-simon-shares-jump-on-reported-real-estate-talks-with-amazon.html) that the biggest U.S. mall owner [Simon Property Group](/quotes/SPG/) has been in talks with [Amazon](/quotes/AMZN/) to convert some shuttered Sears and J.C. Penney department stores into fulfillment centers, many industry analysts have been pontificating on the future of malls as logistics hubs.

The consensus seems to be that turning old retail space into new warehouses might not be so easy, even though it might seem like a logical solution. Demand for logistics buildings is skyrocketing as e-commerce sales balloon. But the hurdles include the need to have properties rezoned, which could be met with pushback from local municipalities.

"Just because retail space has gone vacant or remained fallow does not mean that it is automatically a good candidate for repurposing into industrial space," the head of Moody's Analytics commercial real estate economics division, Victor Calanog, said in a report released Thursday.

"One cannot simply build industrial buildings in areas zoned for commercial use," he explained. "Often, that requires rezoning areas — a long and tedious process with a low probability of success."

"State and local governments typically tax industrial properties at anywhere from half to two-thirds the rate of commercial properties, so municipalities have little incentive to rezone areas from commercial to industrial use, as they will collect less tax revenues," Calanog said.

Demand for various commercial real estate asset types is expected to shift noticeably because of the [coronavirus pandemic](https://www.cnbc.com/coronavirus/), with more people now working from home, flocking to the suburbs for space and buying online things they used to browse for in stores.

According to data pulled by Moody's Analytics REIS, apartment development in the U.S. is expected to be down 15.6% in a post-Covid-19 world. Office development is set to drop 10%, it said, while retail falls 15.7%. Industrial development, meantime, is expected to pick up 3.6%.

The firm did find five markets where it said it would make the most sense to covert vacant retail space into warehouse space, based on where retail has been underperforming and where warehouse demand is hot. Those are: Central New Jersey, Northern New Jersey, Long Island, Memphis and Detroit.

But shopping malls are likely going to be shuttering in suburbs all across the country, as store closures grow in number and landlords capitulate.

Destiny USA mall reopens as the coronavirus disease (COVID-19) restrictions are eased in Syracuse, New York, U.S.

Maranie Staab | Reuters

Another new report out this week from Coresight Research estimates 25% of America's roughly 1,000 malls will close over the next three to five years, with the pandemic accelerating a demise that was already underway before the new virus emerged.

The malls most at risk of going dark are classified as so-called B-, C- and D-rated malls, meaning they bring in fewer sales per square foot than an A mall. An A++ mall could bring in as much as $1,000 in sales per square foot, for example, while a C+ mall does about $320.

There are roughly 380 C- and D-rated malls in the U.S., according to an analysis by the commercial real estate firm Green Street Advisors. It has said malls rated C and below "are not viable retail centers long term."

[CBL & Associates](/quotes/CBLAQ/), a Tennessee-based mall owner that has a number of B- and C-rated malls in its portfolio, has said it [plans to file for bankruptcy by Oct. 1](https://www.cnbc.com/2020/08/19/us-mall-owner-cbl-strikes-deal-with-lenders-avoiding-bankruptcy.html), highlighting just how much pressure these landlords are facing.

Even high-end malls are under pressure, though. No one is really immune. An upscale mall owner in Miami, Bal Harbour Shops, is currently moving to evict the luxury department store chain Saks Fifth Avenue for not paying rent since mid-March. It owes Bal Harbour roughly $1.9 million, according to court documents.

"Despite being given months to honor its past due rental obligations and despite Saks' impressive post-COVID sales at Bal Harbour Shops, Saks steadfastly refused to make any effort to pay any part of its rent," Bal Harbour Shops President and Chief Executive Matthew Whitman Lazenby said in a statement.

"Bal Harbour Shops has worked tirelessly to ensure our business and our tenants can survive and thrive in this environment," he said. "Regrettably, this injudicious behavior has left us with no other option than to terminate the Saks lease and sue to evict Saks from Bal Harbour Shops."

A representative from Hudson's Bay-owned Saks was not immediately available to comment.

About 90% of occupants in U.S. malls are either experiential tenants like movie theaters, or department store chains and apparel retailers, according to the Coresight analysis. This makes malls the most vulnerable type of shopping centers to the Covid-19 impact, it said, compared with other properties like strip centers that have grocery stores and outlet centers that offer consumers bargains.

During the pandemic, movie theaters and clothing shops have faced long windows of being closed, while consumers could still flock to strip centers for food, cleaning products and other essentials. In some states, such as New York and California, movie theaters remain closed to this day. And so with minimal revenue coming in, these are the businesses that are most likely requesting rent reductions, or not paying rent at all.

Mall developers had up until now been courting entertainment companies like [Dave & Buster's](/quotes/PLAY/) and iFly indoor skydiving, and restaurants like [Cheesecake Factory](/quotes/CAKE/), to lessen their dependence on shrinking retailers. But those businesses have also not fared well in an age of social distancing.

So, if not warehouses and entertainment complexes, analysts have pondered other potential use cases for so-called dead malls: Churches, medical facilities, office spaces and even apartment complexes.

But even office space is a risky bet now, as the working-from-home trend could become permanent for some. Workers in [JPMorgan Chase](/quotes/JPM/)'s corporate and investment bank, for example, will [cycle between days spent at the office and at home](https://www.cnbc.com/2020/08/25/jpmorgan-will-have-staff-cycle-between-office-and-remote-work-in-a-move-that-may-remake-wall-street.html), keeping the ability to work remotely on a part-time basis. The world's biggest Wall Street bank by revenue has said it could shutter backup trading floors located outside New York and London as a result of the move.

The outdoor retailer REI is also looking to sell its recently completed corporate campus in suburban Seattle, shifting instead to more satellite offices, as a result of the pandemic.

"Unfortunately, this whole Covid thing has thrown the experiential pitch out the window," Moody's Calanog said in a phone interview. "Until we resolve this pandemic, I suspect we are going to be in a holding pattern with hollow retail space."

"Then we will see what the most viable format is," he said.

![How shrinking American mall will impact local tax revenue](https://image.cnbcfm.com/api/v1/image/106587441-howtheskrinkingamericanmallwillimpactlocaltaxrevnue.jpg?v=1592847332&w=750&h=422&vtcrop=y)

Widespread decline in physical retail stores

|  |
| --- |
| The examples and perspectives in this article **deal primarily with the United States and do not represent a [worldwide view](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:WikiProject_Countering_systemic_bias "Wikipedia:WikiProject Countering systemic bias") of the subject**. Retail apocalypse

| Entrance to a former [Sears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sears "Sears") store at [Hudson Valley Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Valley_Mall "Hudson Valley Mall") in [Ulster, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulster,_New_York "Ulster, New York"), closed in 2018. It had been the mall's last [anchor store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anchor_store "Anchor store"). |
| Date | 2010 (2010) – present |
| Venue | Shopping malls, physical retail |
| Location | * [Northern America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_America "Northern America") |
| Cause | * Downsizing of retail chains caused by rise in global [e-commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E-commerce "E-commerce") operations related to the [2008 financial crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_financial_crisis "2008 financial crisis") * Accumulation of [corporate debt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporate_bond "Corporate bond") for retail overexpansion * Changes in spending habits * [Impact of COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_on_retail "Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on retail") * [2021–2023 inflation surge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021–2023_inflation_surge "2021–2023 inflation surge")[[1]](#cite_note-1) * Rise of e-commerce itself |
| Outcome | * Numerous bankruptcies ensued from early 2010s * Major decline in revenue from suppliers * Increase in the amount of [dead malls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_mall "Dead mall") * Bankruptcies accelerated from March 2020 as a result of the [COVID-19 recession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_recession "COVID-19 recession") and [Inflation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021-2023_inflation_surge "2021-2023 inflation surge") |

The **retail apocalypse** (also known as **retailpocalypse**[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3)) is the closing of numerous Northern American [brick and mortar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brick_and_mortar "Brick and mortar") [retail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retail "Retail") stores, especially those of large chains, starting in the 2010s.[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-atlantic-5)[*[failed verification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")*] The 2020s saw more store closures as a result of [COVID-19 lockdowns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_lockdowns "COVID-19 lockdowns") with customers using [online shopping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_shopping "Online shopping") as an alternative way to shop.

In 2017 alone, more than 12,000 physical stores closed. The reasons included debt and bankruptcy in the face of rising costs, [leveraged buyouts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leveraged_buyout "Leveraged buyout"), low quarterly profits outside [holiday binge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics_of_Christmas "Economics of Christmas") spending, delayed effects of the [Great Recession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Recession "Great Recession"),[[5]](#cite_note-atlantic-5) and changes in spending habits. American consumers have shifted their purchasing habits due to various factors, including [experience spending](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experience_economy "Experience economy") versus material goods and homes, casual fashion in relaxed [dress codes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dress_code "Dress code"), as well as the rise of [e-commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E-commerce "E-commerce")[[6]](#cite_note-6) and particularly [juggernaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juggernaut "Juggernaut") companies such as [Amazon.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon.com "Amazon.com") and [Walmart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walmart "Walmart"). A 2017 *[Business Insider](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business_Insider "Business Insider")* report dubbed this phenomenon the "Amazon effect" and calculated that Amazon.com was generating more than half of retail-sales growth.[[7]](#cite_note-business-insider-amazon-effect-1nov2017-7)

Not everyone agrees that a "retail apocalypse" exists. Dissenting economists and experts asserted that recent retail closures are a market correction, suggesting that the phrase is misleading and instills insecurity in the 16 million U.S. [retail workers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retail_workers_in_the_United_States "Retail workers in the United States").[[8]](#cite_note-Tech-8) Research published by global retail analyst IHL Group in 2019 suggests that the so-called retail apocalypse narrative was an exaggeration, with "more chains that are expanding their number of stores than closing stores."[[9]](#cite_note-IHL-9) That year, retailers in the United States announced 9,302 store closings, a 59% jump from 2018, and the highest number since tracking the data began in 2012.[[10]](#cite_note-closing_28-10)

Corporate bankruptcies and store closings increased in 2020. During the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_impact_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic "Financial impact of the COVID-19 pandemic"), most retail stores, especially struggling mall-based retailers, closed for extended periods of time.[[11]](#cite_note-11) Several large retail companies filed for bankruptcy during the pandemic, including [J. Crew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Crew "J. Crew"), [Century 21](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Century_21_(department_store) "Century 21 (department store)"), [Neiman Marcus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neiman_Marcus "Neiman Marcus"), [Lord & Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_&_Taylor "Lord & Taylor"), [Stage Stores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stage_Stores "Stage Stores"), [Stein Mart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stein_Mart "Stein Mart"), [JCPenney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JCPenney "JCPenney"), [Tuesday Morning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuesday_Morning "Tuesday Morning"), and [Pier 1 Imports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pier_1_Imports "Pier 1 Imports").[[12]](#cite_note-chicagotribune-12)

The most productive retailers in North America during the retail apocalypse are [discount](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discounter "Discounter") superstores[[13]](#cite_note-13) Walmart and [Target](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Target_Corporation "Target Corporation"), low-cost "[fast-fashion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast-fashion "Fast-fashion")" brands ([Zara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zara_(retailer) "Zara (retailer)"), [H&M](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H&M "H&M")), [dollar stores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dollar_stores "Dollar stores")[*[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")*] ([Dollar General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dollar_General "Dollar General"), [Dollar Tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dollar_Tree "Dollar Tree"), [Family Dollar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_Dollar "Family Dollar"), [Dollarama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dollarama "Dollarama")),[[14]](#cite_note-14) and [warehouse clubs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warehouse_club "Warehouse club") ([Costco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costco "Costco"), [Sam's Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam's_Club "Sam's Club"), and [BJ's Wholesale Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BJ's_Wholesale_Club "BJ's Wholesale Club")).[[15]](#cite_note-15)

A major consequence of the retail apocalypse has been the increase in vacant [retail space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retail_space "Retail space"), such as [big-box stores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big-box_stores "Big-box stores"), [strip malls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strip_malls "Strip malls") and [shopping malls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shopping_malls "Shopping malls")—with the latter becoming [dead malls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_malls "Dead malls") due to declining consumer traffic and store closures. Such vacant real estate, in turn, has become the site for [pop-up retail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop-up_retail "Pop-up retail") stores—a notable example being [Spirit Halloween](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spirit_Halloween "Spirit Halloween"), a seasonal retailer which sells Halloween merchandise and has set up stores at vacant retail buildings, including former big-box stores.[[16]](#cite_note-Saldana-16)[[17]](#cite_note-17)

## History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Retail_apocalypse&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f3/Closed_Grocery_Store_in_Port_Charlotte.jpg/250px-Closed_Grocery_Store_in_Port_Charlotte.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Closed_Grocery_Store_in_Port_Charlotte.jpg)

A permanently closed mom and pop health food store in [Port Charlotte, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Charlotte,_Florida "Port Charlotte, Florida")

The phrase "retail apocalypse" first appeared in print in an early 1990s essay by Peter Glen, author of *It's Not My Department!*[[18]](#cite_note-18) Media appropriated the term to refer to multiple brick-and-mortar store closures resulting from shifts in [consumer spending](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consumer_spending "Consumer spending").[[8]](#cite_note-Tech-8)

Since at least the [2008 financial crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_financial_crisis "2008 financial crisis"), various economic factors have resulted in the closing of many stores in North America, the United Kingdom, and Australia, particularly in the [department store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store "Department store") industry. For example, [Sears Holdings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sears_Holdings "Sears Holdings") had more than 3,500 stores and 355,000 employees in 2006.[[19]](#cite_note-19) By the end of 2016, Sears operated 1,430 stores.[[20]](#cite_note-20) In October 2018, Sears filed for bankruptcy and announced it would close an additional 142 of its 687 stores.[[21]](#cite_note-:0-21) At the time of filing, Sears had 68,000 employees.[[21]](#cite_note-:0-21)

The phrase "retail apocalypse" began gaining widespread usage in 2017 following multiple announcements from many major retailers of plans to either discontinue or greatly scale back a retail presence, including companies such as [H.H. Gregg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H.H._Gregg "H.H. Gregg"), [Family Christian Stores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_Christian_Stores "Family Christian Stores") and [The Limited](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Limited "The Limited") all going out of business entirely.[[22]](#cite_note-whioohioimpact-22) *[The Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Atlantic "The Atlantic")* described the phenomenon as "The Great Retail Apocalypse of 2017", reporting nine retail bankruptcies and several apparel companies having their stock hit new lows, including that of [Lululemon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lululemon "Lululemon"), [Urban Outfitters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_Outfitters "Urban Outfitters"), and [American Eagle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Eagle_Outfitters "American Eagle Outfitters").[[5]](#cite_note-atlantic-5) [Credit Suisse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credit_Suisse "Credit Suisse"), a major global financial services company, predicted that 25% of U.S. malls remaining in 2017 could close by 2022.[[23]](#cite_note-gymboree-23)

Since 2017, the phrase is frequently applied to brick-and-mortar closures in retail, with the retail apocalypse creating a [domino effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domino_effect "Domino effect") on manufacturers and suppliers; [Hasbro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasbro "Hasbro"), for example, cited the loss of the [Toys "R" Us](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toys_ "Toys ") chain as a major cause for lost revenue and layoffs the company imposed in October 2018.[[24]](#cite_note-24)

A 2019 analysis conducted by IHL Group international research and advisory firm found that when a retailer closes many stores, it indicates more about the individual retailer rather than the retail industry overall. In 2019, the 20 stores announcing the most closures [represent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pareto_principle "Pareto principle") 75% of all closures. IHL found that for each retailer closing stores in 2019, more than five retail chains are opening stores, an increase from the 3.7 ratio of 2018. IHL also reported that the number of chains adding stores in 2019 had increased 56%, while the number of closing stores decreased by 66% in the last year.[[9]](#cite_note-IHL-9)[[25]](#cite_note-25)

As of May 2020, bankruptcies and store closings were expected to intensify due to widespread business closures and the resulting [financial impact of the COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_impact_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic "Financial impact of the COVID-19 pandemic"). [J. Crew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Crew "J. Crew"), [Century 21](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Century_21_(department_store) "Century 21 (department store)"), [Neiman Marcus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neiman_Marcus "Neiman Marcus"), [Stage Stores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stage_Stores "Stage Stores"), [Stein Mart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stein_Mart "Stein Mart"), [Lord & Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_&_Taylor "Lord & Taylor"), [JCPenney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JCPenney "JCPenney"), [Tuesday Morning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuesday_Morning "Tuesday Morning"), and [Pier 1 Imports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pier_1_Imports "Pier 1 Imports") were among the first major retailers to file for bankruptcy during the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States "COVID-19 pandemic in the United States").[[12]](#cite_note-chicagotribune-12)

### Shift to e-commerce

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Retail_apocalypse&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Shift to e-commerce")]

Further information: [Online shopping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_shopping "Online shopping")

The main factor cited in the closing of retail stores in the retail apocalypse is the shift in consumer habits towards [online shopping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_shopping "Online shopping").[[26]](#cite_note-26) Holiday sales for e-commerce increased by an estimated 11% to 20% from 2015 to 2016. The same year, brick-and-mortar stores saw an overall increase of only 1.6%, with physical department stores experiencing a 4.8% decline.[[27]](#cite_note-practicale-27)

### Oversupply of shopping malls

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Retail_apocalypse&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Oversupply of shopping malls")]

Another factor is an over-supply of malls[[28]](#cite_note-28) as the growth rate of malls in North America between 1970 and 2015 was over twice the growth rate of the population. In 2004, [Malcolm Gladwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcolm_Gladwell "Malcolm Gladwell") wrote that investment in malls was artificially accelerated when the [United States Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress "United States Congress") introduced [accelerated depreciation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accelerated_depreciation "Accelerated depreciation") into the tax code in 1954.[[29]](#cite_note-29) Despite the construction of new malls, mall visits declined by 50% between 2010 and 2013 with further declines reported in each successive year.[[30]](#cite_note-30)

### Experience economy

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Retail_apocalypse&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Experience economy")]

Main article: [Experience economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experience_economy "Experience economy")

One idea presented in the 2010s for the supposed retail decline was a perceived ongoing "restaurant renaissance"— a shift in consumer spending habits for their [disposable income](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disposable_income "Disposable income") from material purchases such as clothing towards [dining out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Restaurant "Restaurant") and travel.[[5]](#cite_note-atlantic-5)

### Shrinking middle class

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Retail_apocalypse&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Shrinking middle class")]

Another cited factor is the "death of the [American middle class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_middle_class "American middle class")" represented by declining real wages and rising costs creating a [middle-class squeeze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle-class_squeeze "Middle-class squeeze"), resulting in large-scale closures of retailers such as [Macy's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macy's "Macy's"), [JCPenney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JCPenney "JCPenney"), and [Sears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sears "Sears") which traditionally relied on spending from this market segment.[[31]](#cite_note-middleclass-31) Particularly in rural areas, [variety stores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_store "Variety store") such as [Dollar General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dollar_General "Dollar General"), [Dollar Tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dollar_Tree "Dollar Tree"), and [Family Dollar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_Dollar "Family Dollar"), once thought to be unaffected by the apocalypse since they have continued growing rapidly, are now perceived as being at best a symptom of the phenomenon, and at worst a direct cause of rural, independent retailers collapsing, unable to compete with the lower margins that national chains can sustain.[[32]](#cite_note-32)[[33]](#cite_note-33)

### Poor management

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Retail_apocalypse&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Poor management")]

Poor retail management coupled with an overcritical eye towards quarterly dividends cause a lack of accurate inventory control, so the sales floor suffers from underperforming merchandise and out-of-stock merchandise, creating a poor shopping experience for customers. The focus on short-term balance sheets induces management to understaff retail stores to keep profits high.[[34]](#cite_note-34)[[35]](#cite_note-35) Furthermore, many long-standing chain retailers are [overloaded with debt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporate_debt_bubble "Corporate debt bubble"),[[36]](#cite_note-bloomberg_retail_beginning-36) often from [leveraged buyouts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leveraged_buyout "Leveraged buyout") from [private equity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_equity "Private equity") firms, which hinders the profitable operation of retail chains.[[37]](#cite_note-37)[[38]](#cite_note-38)

### COVID-19 pandemic

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Retail_apocalypse&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: COVID-19 pandemic")]

Main article: [Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on retail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_on_retail "Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on retail")

The [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic") exacerbated many issues affecting retailers, as many were forced to shut down due to non-pharmaceutical interventions that were issued in an effort to mitigate the pandemic.[[39]](#cite_note-39)

At the same time, [online shopping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_shopping "Online shopping") boomed during the coronavirus-related lockdown, even though it came back down starting in 2022.[[40]](#cite_note-40) Most of the major [e-commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E-commerce "E-commerce") retailers in the United States were classified as essential businesses and were not required to shut down. Buyers stated that they would deliberately buy products from such categories as food and drinks, hygiene, household cleaning, clothing, health, and consumer electronics online rather than in person due to COVID-19. The outbreak is said to have changed shopping behavior permanently: in the US, 29% of surveyed consumers stated that they had no intention to ever go back to offline shopping. In the UK, this number reached 43%.[[41]](#cite_note-41)

In June 2020, retail research firm Coresight reported that they estimated that the number of store closures due to the pandemic and ensuing recession would exceed the 2019 record of 9,302.[[42]](#cite_note-42)[[43]](#cite_note-43)

Coresight Research data later indicated that store closures had reduced by 49% from 2020 to 2021, with store openings increased by 36% over the previous year.[[44]](#cite_note-Coresight-44) Clothing and accessories accounted for 43% of retail closures in 2021.[[44]](#cite_note-Coresight-44) In July 2022, the analytics firm published findings that store openings had exceeded store closings for the first half of 2022, and that there were 10% fewer closings and 3% fewer openings than in 2021.[[45]](#cite_note-45)

## Strategies

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Retail_apocalypse&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Strategies")]

Researchers say retailers' survival may be tied to [customer experience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Customer_experience "Customer experience") and brand reputation. In 2019, *[Forbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes "Forbes")* said brand reputation was the biggest factor.[[83]](#cite_note-Fertik-83) In 2020, [Monash University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monash_University "Monash University") in Australia said the three key factors were delivering a "great in-store retail experience", customer-targeted stock offerings, and "seamless [omnichannel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omnichannel "Omnichannel") integration".[[84]](#cite_note-84)

[Toys "R" Us](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toys_ "Toys ") may not have responded well to changing [consumer behavior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consumer_behavior "Consumer behavior").[[85]](#cite_note-forbes-85)

Some retail chains are trying robots and other technologies to reduce costs or improve customer experiences. [Ikea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ikea "Ikea") became one of the first retailers to use [Apple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc.")'s [ARKit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARKit "ARKit") to develop an [augmented reality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augmented_reality "Augmented reality") app that allowed customers to visualize 3D renderings of Ikea products as they would appear in a certain room or place.[[86]](#cite_note-86)[[87]](#cite_note-87) [Macy's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macy's "Macy's"), [American Eagle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Eagle_Outfitters "American Eagle Outfitters"), [Nike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nike,_Inc. "Nike, Inc.") and [Sephora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sephora "Sephora") were reported to be implementing various technologies to integrate digital experiences to improve consumers' physical shopping experiences. Sephora has installed [smart mirrors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smart_mirror "Smart mirror") that use augmented reality to allow customers to try on makeup.[[88]](#cite_note-88) [Walmart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walmart "Walmart") automated some aspects of its supply chain. [Kohl's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kohl's "Kohl's") reduced the size of some stores from 90,000 to between 60,000 and 35,000 square feet[[83]](#cite_note-Fertik-83) and uses [robots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robot "Robot") to help clean and stock shelves. [Lowe's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowe's "Lowe's") has been using LowesBot to help customers find items.[[85]](#cite_note-forbes-85) Company executives have said robots lower costs and improve efficiency, but employees report they don't like working with robots.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

A 2018 study from the [International Council of Shopping Centers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Council_of_Shopping_Centers "International Council of Shopping Centers") indicated that opening new stores can increase traffic to retailer websites.[[89]](#cite_note-89)

args.summary:
The "retail apocalypse" (also known as "retailpocalypse") refers to the widespread closing of North American brick-and-mortar retail stores, especially large chains, beginning in the 2010s and continuing through the present (2026). The phenomenon spans from 2010 to present and is primarily centered in Northern America, with effects also seen in the UK and Australia.

KEY FACTORS:
- Shift to e-commerce: Online shopping is the main cited factor. Holiday e-commerce sales increased 11-20% from 2015-2016, while brick-and-mortar stores saw only 1.6% growth and physical department stores declined 4.8%. Amazon generates more than half of retail-sales growth (the "Amazon effect").
- Oversupply of shopping malls: Mall growth (1970-2015) was over twice the population growth rate. Accelerated depreciation tax incentives from 1954 artificially accelerated mall investment. Mall visits declined 50% between 2010-2013.
- Experience economy: Consumers shifting disposable income from material goods toward dining out and travel.
- Shrinking middle class: Declining real wages and rising costs creating a "middle-class squeeze," affecting retailers like Macy's, JCPenney, and Sears. Dollar stores (Dollar General, Dollar Tree, Family Dollar) grew but are seen as both symptom and cause of rural independent retailer collapse.
- Poor management: Focus on short-term quarterly dividends, understaffing, inventory mismanagement, and heavy debt from leveraged buyouts by private equity firms.
- COVID-19 pandemic: Exacerbated closures; many retailers filed for bankruptcy. Online shopping boomed during lockdowns—29% of US and 43% of UK consumers said they'd never return to offline shopping.

KEY STATISTICS:
- 2017: more than 12,000 physical stores closed.
- 2019: 9,302 store closings announced (59% jump from 2018), the highest since tracking began in 2012.
- Credit Suisse predicted 25% of US malls could close by 2022.
- Sears fell from 3,500+ stores and 355,000 employees in 2006 to 1,430 stores by 2016, filing bankruptcy in October 2018 with 68,000 employees.
- IHL Group (2019) disputed the "apocalypse" narrative, finding 5+ chains opening stores for every one closing, and that 20 retailers accounted for 75% of all closures.
- Coresight estimated closures would exceed the 2019 record in 2020; by 2022 store openings had again exceeded closings.

MAJOR BANKRUPTCIES (from table): Borders Books (2011), The Bon-Ton (2018), Sears Holdings (2013-2021), JCPenney (2015-2020), Toys "R" Us (2018), J. Crew (2020), Barneys New York (2019), Forever 21 (2019 & 2025), A.C. Moore (2019-2020), Payless ShoeSource (2019-2020), Pier 1 Imports (2020), Neiman Marcus (2020), Tuesday Morning (2020 & 2023), GNC (2020), True Religion (2017 & 2020), Brooks Brothers (2020), Bed Bath & Beyond (2023), Express (2024), Big Lots (2024), Party City (2023 & 2024), Jo-Ann (2024 & 2025), 99 Cents Only Stores (2024), Rite Aid (2023 & 2025), Hudson's Bay (2025).

SURVIVORS/THRIVERS: Discount superstores (Walmart, Target), fast-fashion brands (Zara, H&M), dollar stores, and warehouse clubs (Costco, Sam's Club, BJ's).

CONSEQUENCES: Vacant retail space, dead malls, pop-up retail (e.g., Spirit Halloween in former big-box stores), and a domino effect on suppliers (e.g., Hasbro cited Toys "R" Us loss for lost revenue and layoffs).

STRATEGIES: Survival tied to customer experience, brand reputation, omnichannel integration, and technology adoption—Ikea (AR app), Sephora (smart mirrors), Walmart (supply chain automation), Kohl's (smaller stores + robots), Lowe's (LoweBot). A 2018 ICSC study found opening new stores increases website traffic.

DISSENTING VIEWS: Some economists argue closures are a market correction, not an "apocalypse," and the phrase instills insecurity in the 16 million US retail workers. The article notes its perspective deals primarily with the US and lacks a worldwide view.

The phrase "retail apocalypse" first appeared in print in a 1990s essay by Peter Glen, gaining widespread usage in 2017.

# More than 2,000 stores are set to close across the US in 2026. Here's the list.

Retailers and restaurants are gearing up for another wave of [store closures](https://www.businessinsider.com/stores-closing-in-2025-list).

It's shaping up to be the continuation of a retail pullback that Business Insider tracked in 2024 and 2025. Major chains, from [department stores like Macy's](https://www.businessinsider.com/macys-said-high-income-shoppers-are-driving-its-retail-comeback-2025-9) and [Saks Fifth Avenue](https://www.businessinsider.com/saks-stores-closing-off-5th-last-call-outlet-full-list-2026-1) to restaurant chains Pizza Hut and Wendy's, have already announced multiyear closure plans that extend into 2026, as have some niche stores.

Some companies, such as Macy's, are closing their physical stores to invest more resources into their online businesses.

In 2025, Business Insider tracked around 4,100 closures as of late December. Retail data and consultant firm Coresight Research predicted earlier in the year that roughly 15,000 retail locations would close in the year.

So far for 2026, Business Insider has identified more than 2,000 planned closures.

See the list of major closures below, ordered by the number of closures.

## 7-Eleven, Inc: 645 stores

![Image 2: REI store sign](blob:http://localhost/3f711207ef1410619eb8e4b36b1349ed)

7-Eleven's parent company said it planned to close over 600 stores.Deb Cohn-Orbach/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images

The parent company of 7-Eleven plans to close 645 stores in North America in its 2026 fiscal year, which runs through February 2027, according to an earnings document released by Seven & i Holdings in April. The company also said it plans to open 205 stores over the same period. As of the 2025 fiscal year, the company had 12,712 stores in North America.

The document said the closure number included stores being converted to wholesale fuel stores, but did not specify how many.

The closures, previously reported by [C-Store Dive](https://www.cstoredive.com/news/7-eleven-plans-to-close-645-c-stores-in-fiscal-2026/817294/), come as [7-Eleven continues to transition](https://www.businessinsider.com/7-eleven-japan-convenience-store-makeover-food-2024-7) some of its locations to more food-focused stores.

7-Eleven did not respond to a request for comment from Business Insider.

## Francesca's: over 400 stores

![Image 4: REI store sign](blob:http://localhost/3f711207ef1410619eb8e4b36b1349ed)

Francesca's will host sales at all of its store locations.Josh Brasted/Getty Images

After filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on February 5, apparel retailer Francesca's said it will conduct going-out-of-business sales at all of its roughly 400 stores across the US.

Francesca's previously filed for bankruptcy protection in 2020 before being acquired by TerraMar Capital and Tiger Group.

"This process provides a structured path to pursue the best outcome for all stakeholders," Curt Kroll, CFO, said in a February statement about the bankruptcy. "We remain focused on operating responsibly and supporting our teams, partners, and guests throughout this process."

## Wendy's: 300 stores

![Image 6: REI store sign](blob:http://localhost/3f711207ef1410619eb8e4b36b1349ed)

Wendy's is set to close hundreds of underperforming stores in 2026.Katy Blackwood/NurPhoto via Getty Images

In a February 13 earnings call, Wendy's interim CEO Ken Cook said the company planned to close underperforming restaurants in the US, representing 5% to 6% of its roughly 6,000 locations. An estimated 5% of Wendy's restaurants would come out to around 300 locations.

Cook told investors to expect the closings to take place in the first half of 2026.

## Pizza Hut: 250 stores

![Image 8: REI store sign](blob:http://localhost/3f711207ef1410619eb8e4b36b1349ed)

Pizza Hut operates about 20,000 stores globally.Jose Luis Torales/NurPhoto via Getty Images

Restaurant chain [Pizza Hut](https://www.businessinsider.com/why-pizza-hut-struggling-value-proposition-yum-brands-explores-sale-2025-11) is set to close 250 underperforming stores in the US during the first half of 2026, its parent company, Yum! Brands, said in February. The reduction comes as part of a program to accelerate the Pizza Hut brand in the long term.

The company said that the 250 targeted closures are a fraction of the 20,000 locations that Yum! Brands operates globally.

## Eddie Bauer: 175 stores

![Image 10: REI store sign](blob:http://localhost/3f711207ef1410619eb8e4b36b1349ed)

The operating entity behind Eddie Bauer's North American stores filed for Chapter 11 in February.Tim Boyle/Getty Images

Nearly 200 North American [Eddie Bauer](https://www.businessinsider.com/eddie-bauer-us-canada-stores-to-close-2026-3) storefronts are expected to shut down after the operating entity behind the stores failed to find a buyer during its [Chapter 11 restructuring](https://www.businessinsider.com/eddie-bauer-chapter-11-bankruptcy-protection-retail-stores-2026-2).

Liquidation sales have been underway at the 175 Eddie Bauer stores in the US and Canada.

Those store-closing sales are projected to wrap up before April 30, according to court filings in the company's bankruptcy case.

## Carter's: 100 stores

![Image 12: REI store sign](blob:http://localhost/3f711207ef1410619eb8e4b36b1349ed)

A Carter's store in New York.Diana Haronis/Getty Images

Carter's, one of North America's biggest children's and baby apparel retailers, said in October that it plans to close 150 stores across the region over the next three years as leases expire, including about 100 by the end of 2026.

## Macy's: 80 stores

![Image 14: REI store sign](blob:http://localhost/3f711207ef1410619eb8e4b36b1349ed)

Macy's announced a plan to close many stores.Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images

In January 2025, Macy's said it planned to close 150 locations through 2026, allowing it to focus on its best-performing locations and online experience. After the closures are complete, about 350 Macy's stores are expected to remain. Macy's closed at least 66 stores in 2025.

## Kroger: 60 stores

![Image 16: REI store sign](blob:http://localhost/3f711207ef1410619eb8e4b36b1349ed)

Kroger announced a wave of store closures beginning in 2025.Brandon Bell/Getty Images

[Grocery giant Kroger](https://www.businessinsider.com/ex-kroger-ceo-rodney-mcmullen-judge-order-questioning-resignation-jewel-2025-9) said in June 2025 that it planned to close 60 "unprofitable" stores across the US over the next 18 months. The company said in September that it had begun that process.

The company said in its last annual report that it operated 2,731 supermarkets in 35 states and Washington, DC, as of February 2025.

## Saks Off 5th: 57 stores

![Image 18: REI store sign](blob:http://localhost/3f711207ef1410619eb8e4b36b1349ed)

Saks Off 5th still operates several stores in the US.Kevin Carter/Getty Images

Saks Off 5th, a luxury outlet retailer offering discounted designer brands, plans to close 57 stores in early 2026. It announced plans to close nine of those stores last year, and the rest were announced in January.

[Saks Global](https://www.businessinsider.com/saks-bankruptcy-looms-how-crisis-unfolded-2026-1), the parent company of Saks Off 5th, as well as Saks Fifth Avenue, Neiman Marcus, and Bergdorf Goodman, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in early January. The outlet's website, a separate legal entity, is also winding down operations.

In addition to the Saks Off 5th closures, Saks Global is closing five Last Call locations, the off-price Neiman Marcus stores.

## Grocery Outlet: 36 stores

![Image 20: REI store sign](blob:http://localhost/3f711207ef1410619eb8e4b36b1349ed)

Grocery Outlet is a supermarket chain in the US.MediaNews Group/Orange County Register via Getty Images/MediaNews Group via Getty Images

[Supermarket chain Grocery Outlet](https://www.businessinsider.com/grocery-outlet-visit-expanding-store-locations-images-2025-9) is set to close 36 underperforming stores, representing about 6% of its fleet in 2026. CEO Jason Potter told analysts on March 4 that the company had identified stores that no longer had a "viable path to sustained profitability."

The closures come as the grocery chain has been expanding rapidly, particularly in Eastern states. The chain said in November that it planned to end 2025 with 37 new store openings. It plans to open another 30 to 33 net new stores in 2026, Potter said in the March call.

Of the 36 stores closing this year, 24 are located in the Eastern US. The closures make up about 30% of that region's stores, Potter said. He said Grocery Outlet won't be exiting any state completely.

"However, it's clear now that we expanded too quickly and these closures are a direct correction," Potter said.

Grocery Outlet saw a nearly $235 million operating loss and a more than $218 million net loss in its fourth-quarter earnings results.

## Torrid: 29 stores

![Image 22: REI store sign](blob:http://localhost/3f711207ef1410619eb8e4b36b1349ed)

Torrid closed 11 stores in the first quarter of 2025.Daniel Boczarski/Getty Images for Torrid

Torrid, a plus-size apparel retailer, told investors in March that it had previously identified 180 unproductive stores, of which it closed 151 locations by the end of 2025. CEO Lisa Harper said the company plans to close the remaining stores in the first half of 2026.

Torrid closed 11 locations in the first quarter of 2026, Harper said.

## Allbirds: 23 stores

![Image 24: REI store sign](blob:http://localhost/3f711207ef1410619eb8e4b36b1349ed)

Allbirds said it would close remaining full-price stores in the first quarter.Scott Olson/Getty Images

[Shoe brand Allbirds](https://www.businessinsider.com/guides/deals/allbirds-sale-deal-2025-12) said in January that it would close its remaining full-price stores in the US by the end of February. The company said the closures would enable it to dedicate resources toward its e-commerce business.

As of December 2025, Allbirds' US retail presence consisted of 23 stores.

"By exiting these remaining unprofitable doors, we are taking actions to reduce costs and support the long-term health of the business," said Joe Vernachio, CEO.

In March, [Allbirds agreed to sell](https://www.businessinsider.com/what-happened-to-allbirds-rise-fall-2023-4) to American Exchange Group, a New York-based fashion and consumer goods company, for $39 million.

## Yankee Candle: 20 stores

![Image 26: REI store sign](blob:http://localhost/3f711207ef1410619eb8e4b36b1349ed)

Yankee Candle is owned by Newell Brands.Brandon Bell/Getty Images

Newell Brands said in December 2025 that it would close 20 [Yankee Candle](https://www.businessinsider.com/yankee-candle-daughter-memories-tiktok-23-million-compound-2022-11) stores in the US and Canada beginning in January 2026. The closures were announced alongside the reduction of its workforce by over 900 employees.

"This productivity plan is about taking the next, disciplined step to enhance efficiency, sharpen our strategic focus, and deliver stronger, more consistent performance," CEO Chris Peterson said in a press release.

## Saks Fifth Avenue: 18 stores

![Image 28: REI store sign](blob:http://localhost/3f711207ef1410619eb8e4b36b1349ed)

Saks Global is closing several of its stores.ANGELA WEISS / AFP via Getty Images

After [filing for bankruptcy](https://www.businessinsider.com/saks-global-selling-corporate-jet-gulfstream-bankruptcy-2026-4) in January, Saks Global announced a series of closures.

The first wave was announced in February, with the company saying it would optimize its Saks Fifth Avenue footprint by closing eight locations. In March, it announced that another 10 locations would close.

Those closures leave 15 Saks Fifth Avenue locations remaining.

## Wren Kitchens: 15 stores

![Image 30: REI store sign](blob:http://localhost/3f711207ef1410619eb8e4b36b1349ed)

Wren Kitchens had a partnership with Home Depot.Peter Dazeley/Getty Images

UK-based kitchen retailer Wren Kitchens said it shut down all of its US brick-and-mortar stores in April, as its US business filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy. It also shuttered the studios it operated in partnership with Home Depot.

As of April 28, its US website said that all of its showrooms and studios are closed.

Wren Kitchens had 15 showrooms in the US as of January 2025.

## Neiman Marcus: 4 stores

![Image 32: REI store sign](blob:http://localhost/3f711207ef1410619eb8e4b36b1349ed)

The Neiman Marcus in Topanga, California, is among four that are closing.Courtesy of Saks Global

In addition to many Saks Fifth Avenue and Off Fifth locations, Saks Global closed four Neiman Marcus locations. The company announced one of the closures — a Boston store —in February and another three in March.

## Apple: 3 stores

![Image 34: REI store sign](blob:http://localhost/3f711207ef1410619eb8e4b36b1349ed)

Apple plans to close three mall locations in June.Mike Kemp/In Pictures via Getty Images

Apple said on April 9 it would close three stores in June, including locations in Connecticut, California, and Maryland. All of the stores are located in struggling shopping malls, [MacRumors reported](https://www.macrumors.com/2026/04/09/three-apple-stores-permanently-closing/).

"Following the departure of several retailers and declining conditions at Trumbull Mall, the Shops at North County, and Towson Town Center, we've made the difficult decision to close our stores at these locations," Apple said in the statement to MacRumors.

The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider.

In its statement, Apple said that employees at its Trumbull, Connecticut, and North County, California, locations would continue their roles at nearby stores. Employees at the Towson, Maryland, store — which has unionized workers — would be eligible to apply for open roles at Apple in accordance with the collective bargaining agreement.

The International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers, which represents retail employees at the Maryland store, said it was "outraged" by the decision.

"We are exploring all legal options and will work with elected officials and allies to hold Apple accountable," the IAM Union said in a statement.

## REI: 3 stores

![Image 36: REI store sign](blob:http://localhost/3f711207ef1410619eb8e4b36b1349ed)

REI is an outdoor gear retailer.Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images

REI confirmed to Business Insider that it plans to close three stores, starting with a location in New Jersey, in the first quarter of 2026. Its stores in New York City's SoHo neighborhood and Boston are set to follow in late 2026.

"As markets and customer needs evolve, we must adapt to position the co-op for long-term success," the company said in a statement.

Business Insider reports that more than 2,000 stores are set to close across the US in 2026, continuing a retail pullback tracked in 2024 and 2025. In 2025, Business Insider tracked approximately 4,100 closures, and Coresight Research predicted roughly 15,000 retail locations would close that year. The closures span major department stores, restaurant chains, and niche retailers. The article lists major closures ordered by number of stores closing:

- **7-Eleven, Inc.: 645 stores** — Parent company Seven & i Holdings plans to close 645 North American stores in fiscal 2026 (through February 2027) while opening 205, according to April earnings documents. The company had 12,712 stores in North America as of fiscal 2025. Some closures include conversions to wholesale fuel stores.
- **Francesca's: over 400 stores** — The apparel retailer filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on February 5 and will conduct going-out-of-business sales at all roughly 400 US locations. It previously filed for bankruptcy in 2020 before being acquired by TerraMar Capital and Tiger Group.
- **Wendy's: 300 stores** — Interim CEO Ken Cook said on a February 13 earnings call the company would close underperforming restaurants representing 5-6% of its roughly 6,000 US locations (~300 stores), expected in the first half of 2026.
- **Pizza Hut: 250 stores** — Parent company Yum! Brands said in February it would close 250 underperforming US stores in the first half of 2026, part of a program to accelerate the Pizza Hut brand long term.
- **Eddie Bauer: 175 stores** — The operating entity behind its North American stores filed for Chapter 11 in February and failed to find a buyer. Liquidation sales at 175 US and Canada stores are projected to wrap up before April 30.
- **Carter's: 100 stores** — The children's apparel retailer said in October it plans to close 150 stores across North America over three years as leases expire, including about 100 by end of 2026.
- **Macy's: 80 stores** — Announced in January 2025 plans to close 150 locations through 2026 to focus on best-performing locations and online. About 350 Macy's stores expected to remain. Macy's closed at least 66 stores in 2025.
- **Kroger: 60 stores** — Announced in June 2025 plans to close 60 "unprofitable" stores over 18 months, beginning in September. Operated 2,731 supermarkets in 35 states and DC as of February 2025.
- **Saks Off 5th: 57 stores** — Plans to close 57 stores in early 2026. Parent Saks Global filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in early January. Saks Global is also closing five Last Call (off-price Neiman Marcus) locations.
- **Grocery Outlet: 36 stores** — Closing about 6% of its fleet in 2026 (24 in Eastern US, ~30% of that region's stores). CEO Jason Potter acknowledged the chain "expanded too quickly." Company saw ~$235 million operating loss and >$218 million net loss in Q4.
- **Torrid: 29 stores** — Had identified 180 unproductive stores, closed 151 by end of 2025, plans to close the remaining in first half of 2026.
- **Allbirds: 23 stores** — Closing all remaining full-price US stores by end of February to focus on e-commerce. In March, Allbirds agreed to sell to American Exchange Group for $39 million.
- **Yankee Candle: 20 stores** — Newell Brands announced in December 2025 it would close 20 stores in US and Canada starting January 2026, alongside workforce reduction of over 900 employees.
- **Saks Fifth Avenue: 18 stores** — After January bankruptcy filing, Saks Global announced closures in waves (8 in February, 10 in March), leaving 15 Saks Fifth Avenue locations remaining.
- **Wren Kitchens: 15 stores** — UK-based kitchen retailer shut down all US brick-and-mortar stores in April as US business filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy, including Home Depot partnership studios.
- **Neiman Marcus: 4 stores** — Saks Global closed four locations (one Boston store announced in February, three more in March).
- **Apple: 3 stores** — Announced April 9 it would close three mall stores in June (Connecticut, California, and Maryland), all in struggling shopping malls. The Maryland store has unionized workers; the IAM Union said it was "outraged" and exploring legal options.
- **REI: 3 stores** — Plans to close stores in New Jersey (Q1 2026), NYC SoHo, and Boston (late 2026).

Some companies, like Macy's, are closing physical stores to invest more in their online businesses.

# Why the Death of Malls Is About More Than Shopping

Personalized Content

## Josh Sanburn

Follow this author to personalize your feed and get instant alerts.

WHY FOLLOW?

Update your preferences in [Account Settings](/account/preferences/)

![The exterior of the Springdale Mall in Mobile, AL on July 9, 2017.](https://static.time.com/v3/assets/bltea6093859af6183b/bltbafa84a6b5fc61bc/6988d641656a3f09bfbd0e42/malls-usa-retail-02.jpg?branch=production&width=3840&quality=75&auto=webp&crop=3:2)

The exterior of the Springdale Mall in Mobile, AL on July 9, 2017.

Personalized Content

## Josh Sanburn

Follow this author to personalize your feed and get instant alerts.

WHY FOLLOW?

The Schuylkill Mall in Frackville, Pa., is open for business, but you have to look hard to know it. The stores that have shuttered–Sears, Kmart, Spencer Gifts, Hallmark Cards–far outnumber the dozen businesses that remain. The customer-service office is cordoned off by a metal gate. The plants underneath the skylight droop toward a ring of yellow caution tape, and the piped-in music echoes off barren walls. The mall used to have a dance club. Now it’s a dialysis center.

A decade ago, the Schuylkill Mall and its 90 stores, restaurants and knickknack kiosks was a nexus of daily life in this part of Pennsylvania coal country, where teenagers met to flirt as warm-up-suited seniors walked laps around them. Crowds thronged to the annual Easter egg hunt and Lithuanian Days festival, a nod to the region’s ancestral ties. “I had to say excuse me a million times to get to work,” says Jane Krick, a waitress at Suglia’s Pizzeria & Restaurant, the last full-service restaurant standing. “It was full of people. Now we get a million phone calls a day asking, Are you still open?”

It won’t be for long. In early May, management gave the remaining tenants 60 to 90 days to close up shop. Tenants expect the property to be demolished. The wrecking ball will put the mall in good company around the nation. By 2022, analysts estimate that 1 out of every 4 malls in the U.S. could be out of business, victims of changing tastes, a widening wealth gap and the embrace of online shopping for everything from socks to swing sets.

Advertisement

This year alone, more than 8,600 stores could close, according to industry estimates, many of them the brand-name anchor outlets that real estate developers once stumbled over themselves to court. Already there have been 5,300 retail closings this year, including Sears, Macy’s, JCPenney and Kmart stores. Sears Holdings–which owns Kmart–said in March that there’s “substantial doubt” it can stay in business altogether, and will close 300 stores this year. In April, Payless Inc. announced it would close 400 of its shoe stores as part of its bankruptcy plan–on top of a separate 400 it had already scheduled to close. The mall staple RadioShack has filed for Chapter 11 twice in two years. So far this year, nine national retail chains have filed for bankruptcy.

Advertisement

Local jobs are a major casualty of what analysts are calling, with only a hint of hyperbole, the retail apocalypse. Since 2002, department stores have lost 448,000 jobs, a 25% decline, while the number of store closures this year is on pace to surpass the worst depths of the Great Recession. The growth of online retailers, meanwhile, has failed to offset those losses, with the e-commerce sector adding just 178,000 jobs over the past 15 years. Some of those jobs can be found in the massive distribution centers Amazon has opened across the country, often not too far from malls the company helped shutter. One of them is in Breinigsville, Pa., 45 miles from Schuylkill.

But those are workplaces, not gathering places. The mall is both. And in the 61 years since the first enclosed one opened in suburban Minneapolis, the shopping mall has been where a huge swath of middle-class America went for far more than shopping. It was the home of first jobs and blind dates, the place for family photos and ear piercings, where goths and grandmothers could somehow walk through the same doors and find something they all liked. Sure, the food was lousy for you and the oceans of parking lots encouraged car-heavy development, something now scorned by contemporary planners. But for better or worse, the mall has been America’s public square for the last 60 years.

So what happens when it disappears?

Think of your mall. Or think of the one you went to as a kid. Think of the perfume clouds in the department stores. The floating Muzak. The fountains splashing below the skylights. The cinnamon wafting from the food court. As far back as ancient Greece, societies have congregated around a central marketplace. In medieval Europe, they were outside cathedrals. For half of the 20th century and almost 20 years into the new one, much of America has found their agora on the terrazzo between Orange Julius and Sbarro, Waldenbooks and the Gap, Sunglass Hut and Hot Topic.

That mall was an ecosystem unto itself, a combination of community and commercialism peddling everything you needed and everything you didn’t: Magic Eye posters, wind catchers, Air Jordans, slap bracelets. The giant department stores that held its flanks–Saks, the Bon-Ton, Bloomingdale’s, Elder-Beerman–were miniature malls unto themselves, with their own escalators and sections and scents.

Advertisement

This was an experience replicated around the country from a single archetype: Southdale Center in Edina, Minn. Opened in 1956, it was the brainchild of Austrian architect Victor Gruen, a socialist appalled by American sprawl he described as “avenues of horror.”

![An interior scene in Santa Rosa Mall in Mary Esther, FL on July 10, 2017](https://static.time.com/v3/assets/bltea6093859af6183b/blt4f79a1036fb202e0/6988d6400a4a220cb99cf18f/malls-usa-retail-01.jpg?branch=production&width=3840&quality=75&auto=webp)

An interior scene in Santa Rosa Mall in Mary Esther, FL on July 10, 2017 Brian Ulrich for TIME

Gruen’s response was America’s first modern mall, something he envisioned as a hub for dense suburban developments that would include apartment buildings, hospitals and office space. The building was fully enclosed, the storefronts faced in, and large anchor stores were placed at separate ends to attract customers and promote foot traffic to the smaller shops in between. In the middle was a European-style central court with sculptures, an open-air café and an aviary. “Southdale set the tone for most malls after that,” says Thomas Fisher, a professor of architecture at the University of Minnesota.

Advertisement

It didn’t take long for thousands of acres of farmland to be converted into massive centers for buying stuff, surrounded by blacktop–“pyramids to the boom years,” the writer Joan Didion called them. Their construction was helped along by the Interstate Highway System and enormous commercial investments aided by changing tax laws. The white flight from cities during the 1960s and ’70s assured a customer base (and further isolated those left behind in city centers).

By the 1980s and into the ’90s, malls had vanquished Main Street and colonized pop culture. They became grist for board games (Mall Madness), TV game shows (Shop ‘Til You Drop) and concert tours. (Tiffany’s 1987 mall road show helped the teen star reach No. 1 on the pop charts; Britney Spears replicated the strategy a decade later.) Fast Times at Ridgemont High, the seminal 1982 film about high school life, set much of its angsty action inside Los Angeles’ Sherman Oaks Galleria. Seven years later, the time-traveling slackers in Bill and Ted’s Excellent Adventure brought Joan of Arc, Abraham Lincoln, Genghis Khan and other historical icons to hang out at their local mall. Because where else would you go in suburban California in 1989?

Advertisement

Malls had become “the new Main Streets of America,” as William Kowinski wrote in his 1985 book The Malling of America. Indeed, legal cases throughout the decade tested the argument that malls should not be seen as private spaces because so much public life happened there. (The courts didn’t always agree.)

By 1992, the New York Times could count 48 malls within a 90-minute drive of Times Square. That same year, the Mall of America opened its doors in Bloomington, Minn., with an amusement park at the center of 5.6 million sq. ft. of retail that eventually grew into more than 500 stores. All told, 1,500 malls were built in the U.S. between 1956 and 2005, and their rate of growth often outpaced that of the population.

Like all booms, this one couldn’t last. The decline began slowly, in the mid-2000s. The rise of online shopping and the blow of the Great Recession led to a drop in sales and foot traffic at big-brand retailers like JCPenney and Macy’s that anchored many of the country’s malls. Between 2010 and ’13, mall visits during the holiday season, the busiest shopping time of the year, dropped by 50%.

Advertisement

Some of the great mall die-off is what economists refer to as a market correction. “We are over-retailed,” says Ronald Friedman, a partner at Marcum LLP, which researches consumer trends. There is an estimated 26 sq. ft. of retail for every person in the U.S., compared with about 2.5 sq. ft. per capita in Europe. Roughly 60% of Macy’s stores slated to close are within 10 miles of another Macy’s.

A growing number of Americans, however, don’t see the need to go to any Macy’s at all. Our digital lives are frictionless and ruthlessly efficient, with retail and romance available at a click. Malls were designed for leisure, abundance, ambling. You parked and planned to spend some time. Today, much of that time has been given over to busier lives and second jobs and apps that let you swipe right instead of haunt the food court. Malls, says Harvard business professor Leonard Schlesinger, “were built for patterns of social interaction that increasingly don’t exist.”

Advertisement

![An interior scene in Santa Rosa Mall in Mary Esther, FL on July 10, 2017.](https://static.time.com/v3/assets/bltea6093859af6183b/bltd2cdad71d4688a91/6988d6418fd2ee0f0a3580a3/malls-usa-retail-03.jpg?branch=production&width=3840&quality=75&auto=webp)

An interior scene in Santa Rosa Mall in Mary Esther, FL on July 10, 2017. Brian Ulrich for TIME

Younger Americans “look at malls in an antiquated way,” says Dan Bell, a filmmaker who produces the Dead Mall Series on YouTube, an eerie record of the nation’s fading commercial temples. “They see it as, ‘That was my parents’ thing, and it’s not my thing.'”

Bell’s videos of abandoned and dying malls have received millions of views online, eliciting hundreds of messages a week from the same kids and teenagers who wouldn’t set foot inside a traditional mall. “When you go into a dead mall, it’s like shock and awe at the same time,” he says. “I think that’s really appealing for a lot of young people. It’s like watching the Titanic sink.”

Advertisement

There are still about 1,100 malls in the U.S. today, but a quarter of them are at risk of closing over the next five years, according to estimates from Credit Suisse. Other analysts predict the number will be even higher. Some ailing malls have already moved on to a second life. Austin Community College in Texas purchased Highland Mall in 2012 and converted part of it into a tech-driven learning lab and library. In Nashville, Vanderbilt University Medical Center moved into the second floor of the 100 Oaks Mall a few miles from downtown. The Southland Christian Church in Lexington, Ky., bought their nearby mall and transformed part of it into an auditorium.

Not all malls are failing, of course, and the ones that are thriving tend to share certain characteristics. Chief among them: luxury. From the 375-store Galleria in Houston to the Shops at Crystals in Las Vegas to the Bal Harbour Shops near Miami, complexes filled with runway brands such as Gucci and Louis Vuitton are reporting healthy revenues. As a greater percentage of America’s wealth is concentrated in a smaller share of its population, these elite malls partly avoid competition with Amazon by catering to those who don’t need to scour for deals.

Advertisement

Others have found success by updating what the best malls have always done: give people a reason to come beyond filling shopping bags. The Grove in Los Angeles has a mini main street and trolley running down its center, meant to evoke an urban boulevard, and hosts a summer concert series. The Palisades Center in West Nyack, N.Y., has a bowling alley, a comedy club and an indoor rope-climbing course. And at a moment when Instagramming one’s meal has become standard practice, malls in cities from Utah to Louisiana are pouring hundreds of thousands of dollars into upscaling their food courts. At Pennsylvania’s King of Prussia Mall, the country’s second largest, Auntie Anne’s now vies with stands hawking avocado toast and sushi burritos.

“Clearly there’s a shake-up going on,” Steven M. Lowy, co-CEO of Westfield, which operates dozens of malls around the world, told the Associated Press. “We understand the need to change and adapt.”

Advertisement

It also turns out that not everyone wants to spend their leisure time inside. Many of the new, millennial-focused malls are indoor/outdoor complexes designed as one cog of a suburban town center that includes apartments and office space–not unlike what Gruen envisioned more than a half-century ago. Easton Town Center outside of Columbus, Ohio, for example, includes 300 shops spread across a mix of enclosed mall and an open-air, car-free street grid. The development has become a magnet for millennials who are leaving downtowns for the suburbs but still want to live in a dense, walkable community.

Still, analysts say that only about 150 of these malls have figured out how to make it work. “Everybody else,” says Harvard’s Schlesinger, “is figuring out how to play catch-up.”

Two hours north of King of Prussia, “Up, Up and Away” is floating through the Schuylkill Mall as FYE, the CD and DVD retailer, prepares to close in five days. (Everything on sale! 30% TO 90% OFF!) Allen Reinert, an assistant manager, has 15 more minutes on his shift before he leaves the following day for Salem, Ore., where he’s going to work at another, hopefully better-off FYE.

Advertisement

“It’s tough,” says Reinert, 27, who’s worked for FYE off and on since he was 16. “This used to be a safe space where young people weren’t getting into trouble. But kids don’t hang out here on the weekend. Because there’s nothing here.”

He’s not joking. “It’s like something out of a horror movie,” says Maribeth Gantt, 37, a mother of four who visited the mall recently. “I got nervous when I walked in, like I’m waiting for a guy to jump out at me.”

Gantt can recall going to Schuylkill with her grandparents in the 1980s, when the building was humming. “It’s sad. I remember being a kid, and you go to the mall. My kids never say, ‘Let’s go to the mall.'”

Neither does the man who invented it. Late in life, Victor Gruen, the Southdale architect, became disillusioned with his creation, which never lived up to his vision. “I would like to take this opportunity to disclaim paternity once and for all,” he said in 1978. “I refuse to pay alimony for those bastard developments.”

Advertisement

He had a point. Very few malls turned into engines of smart development, with people working, learning and living in addition to shopping. The locations tended to promote sprawl, not reduce it. And as a private space devoted to consumption, it placed disposable income at the center of things.

But for all its flaws, the mall did manage to bring people together in ways that, in the era of personal devices, even Gruen might appreciate: the grandmothers and goths, the flirting teens, the mall walkers and mall rats. They’re all online now, face-to-screen, interacting in ways impersonal and impulsive. It’s a different sort of marketplace, unsurpassed in its efficiency and with its own code and culture, but without the skylights, the sweet smells, the splashing fountains, the ethereal Muzak–all of which are still around, but you have to look hard to know it.

This is a TIME magazine article by Josh Sanburn titled "Why the Death of Malls Is About More Than Shopping," examining the decline of American shopping malls and the broader cultural and economic implications. The article uses the Schuylkill Mall in Frackville, Pennsylvania, as a case study—a once-thriving 90-store mall in coal country that is now nearly empty, with tenants given 60-90 days to close and the property expected to be demolished.

Key statistics: By 2022, analysts estimate 1 out of every 4 U.S. malls could be out of business. More than 8,600 stores could close in 2017 alone, with 5,300 closings already recorded. Nine national retail chains filed for bankruptcy in 2017. Since 2002, department stores have lost 448,000 jobs (a 25% decline), while e-commerce added just 178,000 jobs over 15 years. Between 2010 and 2013, holiday-season mall visits dropped by 50%. There are about 1,100 malls in the U.S., with a quarter at risk of closing over the next five years. The U.S. has roughly 26 sq. ft. of retail per person vs. 2.5 sq. ft. in Europe. About 1,500 malls were built between 1956 and 2005.

Historical context: The first modern mall, Southdale Center in Edina, Minnesota, opened in 1956, designed by Austrian architect Victor Gruen, a socialist who opposed American sprawl. Malls grew via the Interstate Highway System, favorable tax laws, and white flight from cities. By the 1980s-90s, malls dominated pop culture (Mall Madness game, Shop 'Til You Drop, Fast Times at Ridgemont High, Bill and Ted's Excellent Adventure). The Mall of America opened in 1992 in Bloomington, Minnesota. Malls declined starting mid-2000s due to online shopping and the Great Recession.

The article notes some malls have found second lives: Austin Community College converted Highland Mall, Vanderbilt University Medical Center moved into 100 Oaks Mall in Nashville, and a church in Lexington, KY purchased a mall. Thriving malls tend to be luxury-focused (Galleria in Houston, Shops at Crystals in Las Vegas, Bal Harbour Shops near Miami) or those that added experiences (The Grove in LA with trolley and concerts, Palisades Center in NY with bowling and rope-climbing, upgraded food courts at King of Prussia Mall). Millennial-focused malls are becoming indoor/outdoor town center complexes with apartments and offices, echoing Gruen's original vision. Only about 150 malls have figured out how to succeed.

The article concludes by noting Gruen himself disowned his creation in 1978, saying "I refuse to pay alimony for those bastard developments," and reflects on how the mall was America's public square for 60 years, now replaced by online interactions lacking the physical communal experience.
