## **Major Retail Store Closures, Bankruptcies & Reopenings in 2026**

**The [retail world](https://passionatepennypincher.com/category/store_deals/) is going through major changes in 2026, and it’s affecting shoppers across the country.** From beloved craft stores and fashion chains to pharmacies and big-box retailers, companies are rethinking their future—whether that means shutting down, filing for bankruptcy, or making a bold comeback.

Whether you’re trying to plan your next shopping trip or hunting for liquidation deals, this updated list of retail store closures, reopenings, and transitions will help you stay one step ahead.

> **Here’s a breakdown of the biggest retail changes happening now—and what they might mean for you.**

### **[HSN](https://brandcycle.shop/rl67k) & [QVC](https://brandcycle.shop/r7lec)**

QVC Group (The parent company of both HSN and QVC) [announced yesterday](https://investors.qvcgrp.com/news-media/press-releases/detail/667/qvc-group-to-significantly-strengthen-financial-position-as) April 16th that it’s filed Chapter 11 Bankruptcy.  This is part of their plan to restructure the company’s $6.6 Billion in debt – and hopefully doesn’t mean an ACTUAL end to the home shopping mainstays we know and love.   Both online retailers will continue business as usual in the meantime, as the 90-day restructuring plan should wrap up late July.

You can still **s[hop at HSN](https://brandcycle.shop/rl67k)** and [at QVC](https://brandcycle.shop/r7lec) as normal – but it might not be a terrible idea to use up any giftcards or credit you have just in case. 😉

### [**Eddie Bauer**](https://brandcycle.shop/vhzcv)

**UPDATE – Gift cards will no longer be accepted, effective as of March 12th!**

Eddie Bauer recently [**filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection**](https://brandcycle.shop/vhzcv) for the operator of roughly 180 stores across the U.S. and Canada, citing declining sales and ongoing industry challenges.

An auction that was planned for **March 6th** to sell the retail operations of Eddie Bauer was canceled after no buyers stepped forward, according to recent bankruptcy court filings. As of now, all store-closing sales will continue at remaining locations and stores will close unless a buyer steps up soon.

**Have a gift card??** Court filings also stated that gift cards will no longer be accepted after **Thursday, March 12th** and returns or refunds will no longer be allowed.

---

### [**Amazon Go & Fresh**](https://amzn.to/4axbVih)

Amazon recently announced it is closing nearly all of its **Amazon Go** and [**Amazon Fresh stores**](https://amzn.to/4axbVih) as part of a broader strategy shift. The company is refocusing its efforts on food delivery services and expanding its established grocery brand, Whole Foods Market, signaling a move away from operating multiple physical store concepts in favor of strengthening areas with greater long-term growth potential.

---

### **[Francesca’s](https://brandcycle.shop/6ykd2)**

* **Status: Liquidating Inventory and Closing Soon (all locations)**

**Francesa’s has decided [after 25 years they will be closing](https://people.com/francescas-is-closing-after-25-years-what-shoppers-need-to-know-11887817) their doors.**  The retailer opened in 1999 and is known for their fashionable clothing and trendy accessories.   In 2020, they filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection with plans to sell.

Francesa’s is currently having a [“warehouse sale” online](https://brandcycle.shop/6ykd2).  Brick and Mortar stores haven’t yet announced their plans for clearing inventory, so keep an eye out if you have a local store for any sales and discounts.

---

### **[Claire’s](https://shopstyle.it/l/ctkFu)**

**NEW! Yikes. This is not looking good**! [Claire’s just filed for bankruptcy again, seven years after its last Chapter 11 restructuring](https://www.retaildive.com/news/labubus-gen-z-toy-collection-obsession/756625/?). The retailer plans to close at least 18 U.S. stores and is exploring selling some or all of its assets. Despite staying open for now, Claire’s is facing major debt (up to $10 billion) and struggling with declining mall traffic, online competition, and changing customer trends.

Experts say it’s getting harder for stores like Claire’s to keep up with fast-moving shoppers and low-cost online brands. While this bankruptcy could help them cut debt and reset, it may also be their last shot. If they can’t turn things around, they could end up shutting down for good.

---

### **[At Home](https://brandcycle.shop/ix76j)**

**NEW! Yikes — big news if you’re a fan of At Home!** The popular home décor chain that filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy back in June has upped their anticipated store closings to go from **26 to 32**, with 29 stores closing by Sept. 30. In an effort to reorganize its finances says it will remain open for business, but plans to **close underperforming stores** across 12 states as part of its restructuring – for now.

Known for its huge selection of affordable seasonal décor, wall art, furniture, and more, At Home operates 260 stores in 40 states — and for now, most locations will remain open. The company, however, is dealing with a heavy load of nearly $2 billion in debt, prompting this move to restructure and hopefully stabilize its operations.

All other stores will remain open and continue regular operations during the Chapter 11 reorganization. You can still [**shop online**](https://brandcycle.shop/ix76j) and in-store as usual, but if you’ve been holding onto a gift card, now might be a good time to use it – just in case more closures follow. Expect liquidation sales and clearance pricing at the closing locations – this is a great time to shop if you’re local to one of these outlets!

---

### **[Kroger](https://www.tkqlhce.com/click-7343086-15516630)**

Kroger recently announced it will be closing **60 locations** nationwide—and we’re starting to see specific stores pop up across the U.S. If you live near any of the cities below, here’s what we know so far:

#### **Georgia**

* **Alpharetta (Douglas Road):** Closing in August
* **Atlanta (Morosgo Way):** Closing July 19
* **Brookhaven (Buford Hwy):** Closing October
* **Decatur (Memorial Dr):** Closing September

#### **Indiana**

* **Elkhart (Johnson St.):** Closing early August
* **Dickinson:** Closed in June (Texas location)

#### **Kentucky**

* **Louisville (South Third St.):** Closed in June

#### **Texas**

* **McKinney (W University Dr):** Scheduled to close over the next 18 months
* **Dickinson, Texas (Gulf Fwy):** Closed June 10

#### **Virginia**

* **Abingdon, Charlottesville, Gassaway (WV), Bristol (TN):** Closures expected soon
* **Charlottesville, Virginia** (Emmett  St): Scheduled to close August 22

#### **Illinois**

* **Peoria (Sterling Ave):** Closing in August

**And that’s just the beginning—**there are reports of additional Harris Teeter and Pick ‘n Save closures coming to **Wisconsin, Maryland, North Carolina, Tennessee, West Virginia**, and possibly more.

If your store is affected, you’ll likely hear directly from Kroger. But for most shoppers, hopefully this means *better service, better stores, and better digital options* in the months to come.

**So what does this really mean?** Kroger isn’t in trouble — they’re just shifting their focus. With **2,700+ stores nationwide**, they’re still one of the largest grocery retailers in the country. This is all about streamlining, trimming the fat, and preparing for a more competitive future in the grocery game.

---

### **[JOANN](https://shopstyle.it/l/crb1r)**

* **Status:** Second Bankruptcy in a Year

JOANN has officially filed for bankruptcy for the second time in just one year. And this time, the news hits even harder: the beloved fabric and craft store is closing all of its remaining retail locations.

**BUT, we’re hearing two big updates since the announcement:**

* **Michaels** has struck a deal to acquire [**all of JOANN’s private label brands**](https://shopstyle.it/l/crb1r), including the beloved Big Twist. That means you might still see some familiar products pop up on shelves (and even with a special welcome page [**online here**](https://shopstyle.it/l/crb1r))… just under a different roof. Read more about this acquisition [here](https://www.michaelspressroom.com/news/detail/4972/the-michaels-companies-inc-acquires-joann-intellectual).
* **Burlington** will be taking over [**45+ former JOANN store locations**](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/burlington-snags-45-joann-store-121900707.html), likely repurposing them into their discount retail model.

---

### [Rite Aid Closing All Remaining Stores After Bankruptcy Filing](https://brandcycle.shop/msqdt)

Rite Aid filed for bankruptcy earlier this month — marking its second time doing so. Although the company initially stated that stores would remain open during the process, it has now confirmed that **all remaining locations will be shutting down**.

According to *Newsweek*, a total of **1,240 stores** are set to close across the country, including:

* 347 in California
* 345 in Pennsylvania
* 178 in New York
* 95 in Washington
* 60 in New Jersey
* 48 in New Hampshire
* 48 in Oregon
* 31 in Virginia
* 29 in Delaware
* 23 in Maryland
* 15 in Connecticut
* 8 in Idaho
* 5 in Vermont
* 4 in Massachusetts
* 4 in Ohio

The Rite Aid stores that remain will be acquired by competitors, with [**over 1,000 outlets**](https://brandcycle.shop/msqdt) being sold to companies such as CVS. So far, CVS Pharmacy has secured the largest share and is acquiring 625 Rite Aid stores across 15 states. Other buyers include Walgreens, Albertsons, Giant Eagle, and Kroger.

---

### **[WeightWatchers (WW)](https://trackcm.com/pbf/trackofr.asp?chnl=219220&ofr=1083556&uid=)**

* **Status:** [Officially filed for bankruptcy, as of May 6th](https://corporate.ww.com/news/news-details/2025/WeightWatchers-Takes-Strategic-Action-to-Eliminate-1-15-Billion-of-Debt-Strengthening-Financial-Position-for-Long-Term-Growth-and-Profitability/default.aspx)

WW International, known as WeightWatchers, has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy to eliminate $1.15 billion in debt and reposition itself for long-term growth. The move is supported by a majority of its lenders and aims to reduce the company’s total debt from $1.6 billion to approximately $465 million, cutting annual interest payments by half.

Despite the bankruptcy proceedings, WeightWatchers will continue operations without disruption to its 3.4 million members. The company expects to emerge from bankruptcy within 40 to 45 days.

The company has faced challenges due to the rising popularity of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy, which have impacted demand for traditional weight-loss programs. In response, WeightWatchers acquired the telehealth platform Sequence in 2023 to offer prescription-based weight-loss solutions, leading to a 57% increase in clinical subscription revenue year-over-year.

---

### **[Big Lots (Acquired by Variety Wholesalers)](https://biglots.com/)**

* **Status:** Bankrupt & Reacquired

Variety Wholesalers acquired 219 Big Lots stores. The first 9 stores reopened on April 10, 2025, with plans to reopen the remaining 210 stores in phases through early June. Think family apparel, electronics, and closeout deals galore!

**Reopened locations include:**

* **Tennessee:** 1041 S Riverside Dr, Clarksville | 744 Nashville Pike, Gallatin | 220 Dickson Plaza Dr, Dickson
* **Kentucky:** 1342 Indian Mound Dr, Mount Sterling
* **Louisiana:** 755 Veterans Memorial Blvd, Metairie
* **Mississippi:** 2605 W Main St, Tupelo | 5778 Hwy 80 E, Pearl
* **North Carolina:** 1432 E Dixie Dr, Asheboro
* **Virginia:** 2911 Hershberger Rd NW, Roanoke

---

### **[Forever 21](https://www.forever21.com/)**

* **Status:** In Bankruptcy

Stores and the website are still open (for now), but they’ve stopped accepting gift cards and store credits. A full phase-out of U.S. stores is likely on the horizon.

---

### **[Dollar General](https://www.dollargeneral.com/) & [pOpshelf](https://www.popshelf.com/)**

* **Status:** Strategic Closures

As part of a company-wide optimization, 96 Dollar General stores and 45 pOpshelf locations will close. Some pOpshelf stores will convert to DGs.

---

### **[Kohl’s](https://shopstyle.it/l/cpuk8)**

* **Status:** Downsizing

27 underperforming Kohl’s locations are closing this year. Most of their 1,100+ stores remain unaffected.

---

### **[Party City](https://www.partycity.com/)**

* **Status:** Massive Downsizing

Only 29 Party City stores will remain open. The company is refocusing on digital and profitable locations, and currently revamping their [online website](https://www.partycity.com/). Big party supply clearances are underway!

---

### **[Walgreens](https://go.magik.ly/ml/2bwtn/)**

* **Status:** Major Closures Ahead

Up to 25% of stores could be shut down, beginning with 500 locations this year alone.

---

### **[JCPenney](https://shopstyle.it/l/cpum7)**

* **Status:** 8 More Closures

This longtime retail staple is closing more doors in a continued effort to streamline.

---

### **[Macy’s](https://shopstyle.it/l/cpulz)**

* **Status:** Phasing Out 150 Stores

Part of their “Bold New Chapter” plan, Macy’s is shuttering underperforming stores while investing in stronger locations.

## **Other Retailers on the Chopping Block:**

* **Advance Auto Parts:** 727 stores closing

Store closures might mean fewer places to shop, but also more opportunities to save big. Liquidation sales, remodeled stores, and new concepts are popping up as brands evolve. This article from Passionate Penny Pincher (published around 2026) provides a comprehensive list of major retail store closures, bankruptcies, and reopenings affecting shoppers across the United States. The article is structured as a roundup of retailers undergoing significant changes, with specific details on each company's status.

KEY RETAILER DEVELOPMENTS:

1. **HSN & QVC** - QVC Group filed Chapter 11 Bankruptcy on April 16th to restructure $6.6 billion in debt. Both retailers continue operating normally during the 90-day restructuring plan expected to wrap up late July. Shoppers advised to use up gift cards/credits.

2. **Eddie Bauer** - Filed Chapter 11 bankruptcy for roughly 180 U.S. and Canada stores. An auction planned for March 6th was canceled after no buyers stepped forward. Gift cards no longer accepted as of March 12th; returns/refunds no longer allowed.

3. **Amazon Go & Fresh** - Closing nearly all locations as part of a strategy shift toward food delivery and expanding Whole Foods Market.

4. **Francesca's** - Liquidating inventory and closing all locations after 25 years (opened 1999). Previously filed Chapter 11 in 2020. Currently having a "warehouse sale" online.

5. **Claire's** - Filed bankruptcy again (second Chapter 11, seven years after last one). Plans to close at least 18 U.S. stores, exploring selling assets. Facing up to $10 billion in debt due to declining mall traffic, online competition, and changing trends.

6. **At Home** - Home décor chain (260 stores in 40 states) upped store closings from 26 to 32, with 29 closing by Sept. 30 across 12 states. Nearly $2 billion in debt.

7. **Kroger** - Closing 60 locations nationwide, including stores in Georgia (Alpharetta, Atlanta, Brookhaven, Decatur), Indiana, Kentucky, Texas, Virginia, and Illinois. Reports of additional Harris Teeter and Pick 'n Save closures in Wisconsin, Maryland, North Carolina, Tennessee, West Virginia. Kroger has 2,700+ stores and isn't in financial trouble, just streamlining.

8. **JOANN** - Second bankruptcy in a year, closing all remaining retail locations. Michaels acquired all JOANN private label brands (including Big Twist). Burlington taking over 45+ former JOANN locations.

9. **Rite Aid** - Filed bankruptcy second time; confirmed all remaining locations closing. Total of 1,240 stores closing (347 in California, 345 in Pennsylvania, 178 in New York, and others). Over 1,000 outlets sold to competitors, with CVS acquiring 625 stores across 15 states. Other buyers include Walgreens, Albertsons, Giant Eagle, and Kroger.

10. **WeightWatchers (WW)** - Filed Chapter 11 bankruptcy as of May 6th to eliminate $1.15 billion in debt. Debt to drop from $1.6 billion to ~$465 million, halving annual interest payments. 3.4 million members unaffected; expects to emerge from bankruptcy in 40-45 days. Challenges from GLP-1 weight-loss drugs (Ozempic, Wegovy); acquired telehealth platform Sequence in 2023, leading to 57% increase in clinical subscription revenue.

11. **Big Lots** - Acquired by Variety Wholesalers; 219 stores acquired, first 9 reopened April 10, 2025, remaining 210 reopening in phases through early June.

12. **Forever 21** - In bankruptcy; stores and website still open but gift cards/credits no longer accepted; full phase-out of U.S. stores likely.

13. **Dollar General & pOpshelf** - Strategic closures: 96 Dollar General and 45 pOpshelf locations closing; some pOpshelf stores converting to DG.

14. **Kohl's** - Downsizing; 27 underperforming locations closing this year; most of 1,100+ stores unaffected.

15. **Party City** - Massive downsizing; only 29 stores remaining; refocusing on digital and profitable locations.

16. **Walgreens** - Up to 25% of stores could shut down, beginning with 500 locations this year.

17. **JCPenney** - 8 more closures in continued streamlining effort.

18. **Macy's** - Phasing out 150 stores as part of "Bold New Chapter" plan.

OTHER RETAILERS ON THE CHOPPING BLOCK: Advance Auto Parts (727 stores), Bargain Hunt (all 91 locations), Denny's (100 closures), Foot Locker (100 closures), Dollar Tree (370 closures), GameStop (significant closures), Hudson's Bay Company (final 6 stores to liquidate).

The article notes that store closures mean fewer places to shop but more opportunities for liquidation savings, and encourages shoppers to check local listings and use gift cards promptly.

# Major department store chain shuts more locations across nation

Kirk O’Neil

4 min read

* [JWN](/quote/JWN/ "JWN")

Department stores have finished their 2025 holiday season and are regrouping by slashing product prices and also closing underperforming stores to cut costs.

Retailers are hoping to start the year with higher sales, though fashion industry executives have said they are not confident about performance for 2026.

A recent survey showed 46% of fashion executives expected industry conditions to worsen in 2026, compared to 39% in 2025, according to the 2026 Business of Fashion — McKinsey State of Fashion Executive Survey released by consulting firm [McKinsey & Company](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/retail/our-insights/state-of-fashion).

Only 25% of those surveyed believed industry conditions would improve, which was an improvement over 20% in 2025.

### Fashion industry expects challenging year

Fashion executives believe the year will be "challenging," with tariffs expected to be the top problem for retailers, the survey said.

To cut costs, several department store chains already closed stores in 2025, with [JCPenney](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/major-department-store-chain-shuts-010000653.html) closing about eight and Nordstrom dumping a couple.

### Marshall's shuts down stores

[Marshall's](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/discount-department-store-chain-closes-000300722.html) already started closing stores in 2026, closing two stores located in Los Angeles and San Jose, Calif., before Jan. 5.

And now a major department store chain will close over a dozen stores in 2026 as part of a multi-year restructuring.

[![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAIAAAAAAAP///ywAAAAAAQABAAACAUwAOw==)](https://s.yimg.com/lo/mysterio/api/2C8E00CD9AA7EE1482043F4425833ABB08767DCE6EEFC727F42DB2790AE5D6DC/subgraphmysterio/resizefit_w960;quality_80;format_webp/https:%2F%2Fmedia.zenfs.com%2Fen%2Fthestreet_881%2F238aff0b5d500a15519287b25844f665)

Shutterstock

 

### Macy's closes more locations

Huge department store chain Macy's has revealed that it will close 14 locations in 11 states in 2026 as part of its "Bold New Chapter" restructuring plan, which it launched in 2024, [Axios](https://www.axios.com/2026/01/09/macys-store-closing-list-2026-liquidation) reported.

The historic retailer, founded in New York in 1858, two years ago said it would close up to 150 underperforming locations, including about 50 by the end of its 2024 fiscal year, according to a February 2024 [Macy's](https://www.macysinc.com/newsroom/news/news-details/2024/Macys-Inc.-Announces-A-Bold-New-Chapter--Challenging-the-Status-Quo-to-Fundamentally-Reposition-the-Company-Enhance-the-Customer-Experience-Deliver-Growth-and-Unlock-Shareholder-Value/default.aspx) statement.

### Retailer closed 66 stores in 2025

Macy's closed 66 stores in 2025 and has not said whether it will close more than the 14 announced closures in 2026.

The stores on the 2026 chopping block include locations in La Mesa and Tracy, Calif.; Atlanta; Glen Burnie, Md.; Grandville, Mich.; St. Cloud, Minn.; Newington, N.H.; Livingston and Ramsey, N.J.; Amherst, N.Y.; Raleigh, N.C.; Tarentum, Pa.; Corpus Christi, Texas; and Tukwila, Wash.

"In executing our strategy, we continue to review our portfolio and make careful decisions about where and how we invest, including closing underproductive stores and streamlining operations," CEO Tony Spring said in a Jan. 8 [statement](https://www.macysinc.com/newsroom/news/news-details/2026/The-Office-of-Tony-Spring-Reflections-on-Our-Progress--2026-XEgQfh8Quy/default.aspx) on the company's progress. "These decisions are not made lightly."

**More closings:**

* [**Casual Mexican restaurant chain closes more locations**](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/another-struggling-mexican-restaurant-chain-033300457.html)
* [**79-year-old national trucking company closes down, no bankruptcy**](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/major-us-postal-trucking-company-023430432.html)
* [**65-year-old Home Depot rival shutters business permanently**](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/65-old-home-depot-rival-230700434.html)

Macy's offered employees affected by store closings the opportunity to transfer to stores remaining open, as well as severance and outplacement resources, Spring said.

The department store planned to reimagine its best stores, enhance customer service, expand its luxury business, and advance its [supply chain](https://www.thestreet.com/dictionary/s/supply-chain) capabilities.

### Macy's 14 stores closing:

* **La Mesa, Calif.**
* **Tracy, Calif.**
* **Atlanta**
* **Glen Burnie, Md.**
* **Grandville, Mich.**
* **St. Cloud, Minn.**
* **Newington, N.H.**
* **Livingston, N.J.**
* **Ramsey, N.J.**
* **Amherst, N.Y.**
* **Raleigh, N.C.**
* **Tarentum, Pa.**
* **Corpus Christi, Texas**
* **Tukwila, Wash.**

Macy's is seeking a successful restructuring to avoid financial distress that can lead to a bankruptcy filing, which its competitors JCPenney, Neiman Marcus, Lord & Taylor, and Sears could not avoid in recent years.

The historic retailer, founded in New York in 1858, previously committed to closing up to 150 underperforming locations, including about 50 by the end of fiscal 2024. Macy's closed 66 stores in 2025 and has not indicated whether more closures beyond the 14 will follow in 2026.

The closures are part of a broader cost-cutting wave in the department store sector. Retailers are regrouping after the 2025 holiday season by slashing prices and closing underperforming stores. <webpage_content>
# List of US Stores Closing in May

Published

May 02, 2026 at 05:00 AM EDT

updated

May 06, 2026 at 08:24 PM EDT

![Suzanne Blake](https://assets.newsweek.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/2286452-suzanne-blake.png?w=1600&quality=80&webp=1)

Reporter

A growing number of major [U.S. retailers](https://rankings.newsweek.com/americas-best-retailers-2025) are set to shutter locations in May, as financial pressures and [shifting consumer habits](https://www.newsweek.com/walmart-spots-change-in-how-americans-are-shopping-11750867) continue to reshape the brick‑and‑mortar lineup. “The retail reckoning we're seeing is incredibly unfortunate," a finance instructor told *Newsweek*.

Department stores, mall staples and specialty chains are among those trimming their footprints, with closures spanning multiple states and regions.

## Why It Matters

While some companies say the moves are part of broader turnaround strategies, the pace of store closures highlights ongoing challenges facing physical retail in 2026.

#### Read More on Shopping

[Store closures](https://www.newsweek.com/stores-closing-after-being-taken-over-private-equity-firms-2037523) can have ripple effects well beyond individual shopping centers. For consumers, shutdowns may reduce access to nearby pharmacies, grocery stores or department retailers, particularly in suburban or rural areas. For workers, closures can mean job losses or forced transfers.

![An Ikea store on February 25, 2011.](https://assets.newsweek.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/GettyImages-458642203.jpg?w=1600&quality=80&webp=1)

## What To Know

Several well‑known retail chains have confirmed store closures scheduled for May, though many have not released complete, finalized lists of every affected location.

Retailers with May closures include:

### Ikea

The furniture giant is closing its Memphis, Tennessee, store on May 3, citing a strategic shift to modernize its U.S. footprint and focus on higher‑growth markets and new store formats. Ikea has said it will continue investing in other U.S. locations despite the closure.

### Francesca’s

Women’s apparel retailer Francesca’s is completing the shutdown of its entire U.S. store fleet after filing for bankruptcy earlier this year. The company previously operated roughly 400 boutiques nationwide. Many locations are expected to close permanently in spring 2026, including May, as liquidation sales conclude.

### Saks OFF 5TH

About 57 Saks OFF 5TH locations are closing nationwide as part of Saks Global’s Chapter 11 bankruptcy restructuring. The discount chain’s shutdowns are rolling through early 2026, with some stores expected to shutter in May once inventory is sold.

### Neiman Marcus Last Call

All remaining Neiman Marcus Last Call outlet stores are being closed as the retailer’s parent company restructures. The shutdowns are occurring throughout spring 2026, with some locations expected to close during May depending on liquidation timelines.

### Macy’s

Macy’s continues to close underperforming department stores in 2026 as part of a multiyear plan to shutter up to 150 locations by the end of the year. Some stores are expected to close in late spring, including May, as leases expire.

### Kroger

Grocery chain Kroger is carrying out an 18‑month plan to close approximately 60 underperforming stores nationwide following the collapse of its proposed merger with Albertsons. The company has said closures are spread throughout 2026, with some stores expected to shutter during the spring months.

## Households Cutting Back

Retailers often announce closures at the local level or allow individual stores to close once inventory is depleted, meaning exact dates can vary and change with little notice.

Due to the closures, thousands of workers are likely to lose their jobs, and consumers will also face fewer options, especially in rural areas and smaller cities, said Alex Beene, a financial literacy instructor for the University of Tennessee at Martin.

“The retail reckoning we're seeing is incredibly unfortunate,” Beene told *Newsweek*. “As inflationary pressures have weighed on American households, many have cut back on spending for some items, while shifting to more affordable online options for others.”

## What Happens Next

Retail analysts expect store closures to continue throughout 2026, particularly as companies re-evaluate leases signed before the pandemic and shift more resources toward e‑commerce and smaller footprints.

Roughly 7,900 U.S. stores will close in 2026, according to an earlier CNBC report, and Business Insider reported that more than 1,200 [closures](https://www.newsweek.com/topic/closures) have already been publicly announced.

“These store closures aren't some big economic meltdown,” Michael Ryan, a finance expert and the founder of MichaelRyanMoney.com, previously told *Newsweek.*

“They're the retail sector finally admitting what we've all been watching happen in slow motion for years. They're all brands that never figured out how to matter in a world where people shop online and eat at home.”

This is the Transwestern Q4 2024 U.S. Commercial Real Estate Retail Market report, analyzing retail property market performance in the fourth quarter of 2024 and the full year.

**Economic Context:**
- Retail-using employment reached 29.6 million in Q4 2024, up 0.7% YoY

This Forbes article by Andria Cheng (October 2018) reports that the U.S. mall vacancy rate hit a seven-year high in Q3, but argues this is not cause for panic. Average mall rent dipped 0.3% from Q2 to $43.25 per square foot — the first decline since 2011. However, the article emphasizes a "bifurcation" in the retail landscape: lower-tier (B, C, D class) malls are struggling, while top-tier A malls are thriving and being redesigned as mixed-use lifestyle centers. Online-born brands like Casper and UNTUCKit, along with Apple, Tesla, gyms, coworking spaces (e.g., Macerich partnering with Industrious, Life Time Work at Southdale Center), movie theaters, and restaurants like Shake Shack are becoming new mall traffic drivers. Simon Property Group reported retail sales per square foot rose 4.6% to $646 (trailing 12 months ended June 30), with occupancy near 95%, and base minimum rent up 3.3% to $53.84. Outside malls, open-air and community shopping centers saw a net 2.3 million square feet occupied in Q3, reversing Q2's negative trend caused by Toys "R" Us closings (3.8 million sq ft vacated). Open-air vacancy held at 10.2%, but asking and effective rents both rose ~2% year-over-year to $21.11 and $18.48 per square foot (highest since at least 2013). New open-air occupants include trampoline parks, gyms, furniture, houseware, and grocery stores. Reis studied 77 primary metro markets.
</summary>

On February 6, 2026, CoStar Group released a revised U.S. office vacancy forecast from Arlington, Virginia, projecting stable vacancy rates through 2026. After reaching a cyclical peak in mid-2025 before slightly declining by year-end, the forecast anticipates stable office vacancy at 14.1% through the end of 2026, followed by a gradual decline bringing the rate near 13% by 2030. This revised outlook is more optimistic than the previous forecast, which had called for a continued rise in vacancy until late 2026 and rates well above 13% through the decade.

Key factors in the revised forecast include: approximately 10 million fewer square feet of occupancy gains expected in 2026 as job growth decelerates; about two-thirds of the remaining under-construction pipeline set to deliver in 2026; and rent growth expected to remain steady throughout 2026 but stay below 1% until acceleration in early 2027, coinciding with an expected pickup in job growth. The shift reflects recovering tenant demand during the back half of 2025, driven by stabilization in per-worker space needs even as traditional knowledge industry hiring lagged.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## U.S. Retail Real Estate Investment Benchmarks 2025

This report (published July 8, 2025, by MMCG Invest) analyzes U.S. retail real estate trends for 2025 across investment sales, vacancy, rent growth, and development, profiling five top investment markets. Data is sourced from the MMCG database, derived from the 2025 U.S. Retail National Report, with figures cross-validated against Colliers, Cushman & Wakefield, CoStar, MSCI, ICSC, CBRE, JLL, and PwC/ULI data.

### Investment Sales Trends
- Total retail sales reached **$59 billion in 2024**, an **8% YoY increase**, with each quarter outperforming the last
- **Q1 2025 investment volume rose 11%** vs. Q1 2024; preliminary April 2025 figures were **45% higher than April 2024**
- Cap rate expansion from 2022–2023 has tapered; cap rates have largely flattened since mid-2024
- Higher-yield transactions (dollar store/pharmacy at 7%+ caps) skewed averages upward, but prime single-tenant properties (especially essential retailers, ground-lease QSRs) still command **sub-5% cap rates**; most private net-lease buyers transact in the **5%–6% cap range**
- Grocery-anchored neighborhood centers stabilized (e.g., a Kroger-anchored center traded at **6.1% cap** in early 2025); power/community centers trade around **7% caps**
- Market outlook shifted from negative to **neutral-to-positive**; rising deal volume is freeing lending capacity

### Vacancy Rates by Asset Class (Q1 2025)
- **National retail vacancy: ~4.3%** (only slight uptick from record lows); **4.8%** of total retail space available for lease (15 bps above record low)
- Fastest backfill pace in nearly 15 years; quality space from bankruptcies re-leased quickly
- By asset type: **Malls 8.9%**, **Power Centers 4.7%**, **Neighborhood & Strip Centers 6.4%**, **Strip Centers 5.0%**, **General Retail 2.7%** (lowest, driven by single-tenant net-lease strength)
- Vacancy rates well below long-term averages in nearly every category

### Rent Growth
- National asking rents grew **~1.9% YoY** as of mid-2025 (moderating from 4%+ spikes in 2021–2022); forecast ~**1.7% for 2025** (return to 2010s average)
- **47 of 57 largest retail markets** (75M+ SF inventory each) saw positive rent growth
- Occupancy cost ratios near historical norms; core retail sales up 30%+ nominal since 2019 while occupied space grew <2%, meaning significantly higher sales per SF
- Strong Sunbelt/mountain west growth: **Raleigh, NC ~7.5% YoY**, **Tampa, FL ~4.7%**, **Orange County ~3.6%**; underperformers include Cleveland, Chicago (flat), and **East Bay/Oakland (-2.6%)**
- High rent spread on long-held spaces: tenants renewing leases from 5+ years ago face significantly higher rates; embedded rent upside persists into 2026

### Development Pipeline Constraints
- Only ~**81 million SF of new retail space annually** since 2020 (vs. ~300M SF/year in 2000–2009 and ~128M SF/year in the 2010s) — roughly one-quarter of early-2000s levels
- **165M+ SF of obsolete retail demolished since 2018**; total retail stock grew <2% from 2019–2024
- Retail under construction is at its **lowest level since 2011**; only ~**21 million SF of new space (since 2020) available for lease** — less than 5% of total availability
- Texas markets account for nearly one-third of new first-gen retail space
- New construction limited to build-to-suit pad sites and mixed-use ground-floor retail; supply additions projected below historical averages for next five years

### Top 5 Markets for Retail Investment 2025
1. **Dallas–Fort Worth (TX):** 468M+ SF inventory; **4.4% YoY rent growth** (top 10); **4.9% vacancy**; 7M+ SF under construction (most in country); strong population/job growth
2. **Atlanta (GA):** **4.2% YoY rent growth**; **~4.2% vacancy**; only 0.2% stock delivered in past year; rents in low-$20s PSF; strong REIT and private equity interest
3. **Tampa Bay (FL):** **~3.5% vacancy** (below national average); **~4.7% YoY rent growth** (top 5 nationally); only 0.3% under construction; driven by in-migration and tourism
4. **Phoenix (AZ):** **~3.8% YoY rent growth**; ~**1M SF net absorption** over 12 months (highest nationally); **~4.5% vacancy**; 5M+ population; 0.8% pipeline quickly leased
5. **Raleigh (NC):** **~7.5% YoY rent growth** (fastest of any large market); **~2.3% vacancy** (among lowest nationally); only 0.5% stock delivered; Research Triangle tech/life-sciences hub with fast-growing population

### Conclusion
U.S. retail real estate in 2025 is characterized by near-record occupancy, steady but modest rent growth, and reviving capital flows. The decade-long supply drought has created a tight equilibrium. Rent trends are bifurcated with Sunbelt/high-growth markets leading and older slow-growth regions lagging. The outlook is cautiously optimistic — limited new supply, steady consumer spending, and adaptive retailers should keep the sector positive, barring a major economic downturn.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 8: The State of the American Mall 2023 ---
URL: https://coresight.com/research/the-state-of-the-american-mall-competitive-attractive-and-here-to-stay

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Coresight Research report (published 2023, with a 2026 follow-up report referenced) examines the state of the American mall, challenging the popular narrative of "dying malls" by showing that top-tier malls are thriving. Key findings include:

- Physical retail bounced back after pandemic restrictions lifted, with 2022 seeing more store openings than closures for the first time since 2016.
- Retail sales at malls grew more than 11% in 2022 to nearly $819 billion.
- Malls capture a greater share of sales than their share of space, with high sales productivity especially pronounced at top-tier malls.

MARKET SCALE AND OPPORTUNITY:
- Malls make up a shrinking proportion of total US retail gross leasable area—down to 5.5% in 2023 from 5.7% in 2014, driven by low-tier mall closures.
- ICSC estimates 12.9% of US consumer expenditure on retail goods and services went through malls in Q1 2023.
- Mall expenditure totaled $728.9 billion in 2021 and $818.7 billion in 2022 (11.2% YoY increase).

CORESIGHT RESEARCH ANALYSIS:
- Occupancy: Top-tier malls averaged 95.1% occupancy in 2022 (based on public mall operators, S&P Capital IQ data), still slightly below pre-pandemic levels; non-top-tier malls lagged more meaningfully.
- Rent: Average minimum base rent at top-tier malls grew in the mid-teens percentage range for four consecutive quarters from Q4 2021.
- Revenue: Both top-tier and non-top-tier public mall operators saw CAGRs in the mid-to-high single digits between 2020 and 2022.
- Traffic: Based on a Placer.ai sampling of 120 malls, traffic at top-tier malls was up 12% on average in 2022 versus pre-pandemic 2019; non-top-tier malls were up 10%. Top-tier mall traffic growth was driven by long-distance visitors. Coresight's US Consumer Tracker found 40.3% of respondents visited a mall in the prior two weeks in the December 28, 2022 survey.

DRIVERS OF MALL GROWTH:
1. Multichannel halo effect: Brands with both online and offline presence see sales boosts, reduced customer acquisition costs, and better margins. Rising online advertising costs (driven partly by data privacy features like Apple's app tracking transparency) push brands to physical retail. 61% of retailers and 66% of digital-first retailers cite rising customer acquisition costs as the top obstacle to 2022 e-commerce goals (CommerceNext study). 45% of tracked DNVBs have opened physical stores (Coresight DNVB Databank). BORIS (buy online, return in-store) cuts shipping costs and boosts loyalty.
2. Brand synergy: Brands generate more value in proximity to other high-value brands, driving foot traffic.
3. Reinvestment: Top-tier mall operators like Simon Property Group (Phipps Plaza Atlanta redevelopment with Nobu Hotel/Restaurant, Life Time facility, Citizens Market, office tower) and Taubman ($200 million renovation of The Mall at Green Hills in Nashville, 2019, including 132,000 sq ft of inline retail, new Dillard's, and 70,000 sq ft RH store) continually reinvest.
4. Omnichannel investment by mall owners: Cadillac Fairview partnered with Swyft (CF Delivery same-day/next-day shipping) and ReturnBear (multi-retailer returns). Simon Property Group's Simon Search provides real-time mall inventory data; its Shop Premium Outlets (SPO) platform provides access to 35 million online shoppers and 2 billion in-store shoppers globally, and partnered with Tmall Global (Alibaba) in late October 2022 for Singles' Day. Simon also partnered with Leap (November 2022) to support DNVBs entering brick-and-mortar.

CONCLUSION: Top-tier malls are outperforming the average mall in revenues, occupancy, and foot traffic. The combination of physical retail and e-commerce creates a halo effect benefiting brands. Coresight expects that omnichannel strategies and investments will disproportionately benefit top-tier mall growth going forward.

Contributors: Charlotte Rothschild and Daniel Rodden, Analysts at Coresight Research.
</summary>

STRATEGIC RECOMMENDATIONS FOR OWNERS:

--- SOURCE 13: Dead mall - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_mall

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A "dead mall" (also known as a ghost mall or zombie mall) is a shopping mall with low consumer traffic or deteriorating conditions. The Wikipedia article covers the causes, effects, and redevelopment of dead malls, primarily in North America. Many malls are considered "dead" when they lose their anchor stores, causing sales volumes and rental revenues to decline below the cost of maintenance. Structural changes in the retail industry, including the rise of big-box chains (Walmart, Target, Best Buy), open-air lifestyle centers, and online shopping, have contributed significantly to mall decline. Newsweek declared the indoor mall format obsolete in 2008, and 2007 marked the first time since the 1950s that no new malls were built in the U.S.

Key causes of dead malls include: "demolition by neglect" (allowing malls to deteriorate without maintenance until demolition is necessary), demographic and socio-economic changes in surrounding neighborhoods, and the COVID-19 pandemic which exacerbated issues through temporary closures and retailer bankruptcies (including JCPenney, Lord & Taylor, Neiman Marcus, GNC, Brooks Brothers, and Ascena Retail Group). From 2006-2010, vacancy rates in U.S. malls increased significantly, with nearly 3% of malls considered "dying" (40%+ vacancy) and nearly one-fifth having "troubling" vacancy rates (10%+) by 2014. The U.S. has 40% more shopping space per capita than Canada and five times more than the U.K., contributing to an "extremely over-retailed" market.

Redevelopment of dead malls takes several forms: conversion to office/educational use (e.g., Windsor Park Mall became Rackspace's headquarters), transformation into open-air mixed-use centers, conversion to fulfillment centers by Amazon/FedEx/DHL/UPS, repurposing for homeless housing, and "mall-to-medicine" conversions by healthcare systems like Vanderbilt Health and University of Rochester Medical Center. Notable companies accused of neglect include Ashkenazy Acquisition Corporation, Namdar Realty Group, and Kohan Retail Investment Group. Some malls maintain profitability in areas with inclement weather or senior populations who engage in mall walking, with Simon Malls enjoying occupancy averages of 92%.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 14: The Death and Reinvention of American Malls ---
URL: https://sites.lsa.umich.edu/mje/2026/04/13/the-death-and-reinvention-of-american-malls

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the Michigan Journal of Economics, written by Reena Jari and published April 13, 2026, examines the decline and potential reinvention of American shopping malls. 

**Background/Context:** Malls are owned by real estate investment trusts (REITs) that lease retail spaces to tenants who pay base rent, operating expenses, and a percentage of sales. Large department stores like Macy's and Nordstrom serve as "anchor stores" that drive foot traffic and receive lower rents. Malls have faced declining retail sales due to multiple factors.

**Key Causes of Mall Decline:**
1. **E-commerce:** The rise of Amazon and other online retailers in the early 2010s shifted consumer behavior to online shopping due to convenience, accessibility, and product variety, reducing competitiveness of brick-and-mortar retail.
2. **COVID-19 pandemic:** Work-from-home trends reduced commuting and foot traffic. A JP Morgan Chase Institute report found grocery stores and restaurants recovered post-COVID, but retail spaces lagged due to e-commerce.
3. **Internal competition between malls:** Poorly managed malls struggle against newer malls with better amenities. Examples include a mall in Texas acquired by Dillard's after previous owners failed to pay utility bills and property taxes.
4. **Anchor store bankruptcies:** Forever 21's bankruptcy caused the loss of 200+ stores in the US, and large vacant spaces are difficult to fill. The San Francisco Centre mall entered a "death spiral" due to homelessness, shoplifting, and drug use, leading to anchor store closures (Nordstrom, Bloomingdale's) and collapse.

**Reinvention & Recovery:**
- Some investors see redevelopment potential; high-end malls are nearly fully occupied with rising rents according to the Wall Street Journal.
- Vacant spaces are being converted into restaurants, gyms, entertainment venues, and alternative uses — malls are evolving into entertainment centers.
- Dillard's purchased and renovated the Longview Mall in Texas to enhance consumer experience.
- Gen Z is driving a mall comeback: Circana data shows shoppers aged 18-24 bought 62% of total general merchandise in stores (vs. 52% for those 25+). Younger shoppers value instant gratification and in-store experiences, with the online clothing brand Edikted opening physical mall locations due to Gen Z demand.

**Conclusion:** While many malls have struggled to adapt to e-commerce, post-COVID changes, and bankruptcies, the industry may be making a comeback by adapting to consumer demand rather than disappearing entirely.
</summary>

"E-commerce sales are increasing because of how convenient online buying is, how accessible it is, and how many different things are available" (Kothari, 2018).
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Wikipedia article listing retailers in the United States and Canada that have either closed or announced plans to close large numbers of retail locations since 2010, in what media has dubbed the "retail apocalypse," accelerated by the rise of online shopping and the COVID-19 pandemic.

Key retailers and closures covered include:

**0-9:** 7-Eleven closed 592 US locations in 2024-2025 (26% drop in purchases since 2019), with 645 more closures planned for FY2026; 99 Cents Only Stores announced closure of all 371 locations in April 2024 (Dollar Tree acquired 170+ leases).

**A:** A.C. --- SOURCE 6: Retail Vacancy in New York City - Office of the New York City Comptroller
Mark Levine ---
URL: https://comptroller.nyc.gov/reports/retail-vacancy-in-new-york-city

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is from the New York City Comptroller's Office (comptroller.nyc.gov) and presents a comprehensive report titled "Retail Vacancy in New York City: Trends and Causes, 2007-2017." The report was authored by New York City Comptroller Scott Stringer and provides a data-driven analysis of retail vacancy across all five boroughs of NYC using administrative data from property tax filings (RPIE), commercial leasing data from Compstak, MasterCard merchant data, and regulatory approval data from the NY State Liquor Authority and NYC Department of Buildings.

KEY FINDINGS:
1. Vacancy Rates Have Risen: The citywide retail vacancy rate increased from a low of 4.0% in 2007 to 5.8% in 2017. Vacancy rates rose across all five boroughs, most dramatically in Staten Island (from 4.3% to nearly 11%). Reported vacant retail space roughly doubled from 5.6 million sq ft to 11.8 million sq ft over the decade. The highest vacancy rates are in the outer boroughs, particularly Staten Island, Queens, and the Bronx.

2. Internet Shopping Changed Retail Space Usage: Amazon sales rose from $14.8 billion in 2007 to $177.9 billion in 2017. NYC retail establishments grew 19%, but personal services grew ~50% and bars/restaurants rose 65%. Regression analysis shows Amazon sales positively and significantly associated with retail vacancy, driving vacant retail square footage higher by nearly 1 percentage point between 2007-2017.

3. Rising Rents Contributed to Vacancy: Average retail rents rose 22% citywide (from $42 to $51 per sq ft). Rents doubled in Soho (10012) from $60 to $126 and rose 87% on the Upper East Side (from $79 to $146). A 1% increase in average retail rents is associated with 0.33% increase in vacant retail square footage. Property taxes paid by retail tenants doubled from $1.1 billion in 2007 to $2.2 billion in 2017 (rising from 20% to 23% of total retail rents).

4. Regulatory Hurdles Impede Turnover: The share of Department of Buildings alteration permits unapproved after 30 days is a significant driver of vacancy (1% increase associated with 3.28% increase in vacant retail footage). Liquor license approval times rose from ~50 to ~75 days in 2018. A 1% increase in liquor license approval time is associated with 0.17% increase in retail vacancy.

5. Landmark status was NOT found to contribute to vacancy; in fact, regression analysis shows landmarked retail is associated with lower vacancy rates.

RECOMMENDED ACTIONS:
- Provide tax incentives (tax credits up to 20%) for independent merchandise retailers in high-vacancy retail corridors
- Create single point-of-contact customer service task force for businesses occupying retail space, and waive permitting/inspection fees for businesses taking over long-vacant space
- Incorporate retail demand analysis into neighborhood planning and rezoning decisions

The report includes appendices with regression methodology (fixed effects OLS regression of log vacant retail square footage on explanatory variables at zip code level), neighborhood definitions, and detailed notes on data sources and methodology. Key limitations noted: RPIE data excludes ~25% of retail square footage (smaller buildings under $40,000 assessed value); increased penalties for non-filing beginning in 2014 improved reporting by about 1 million sq ft.
</summary>

## U.S. Retail Investment Benchmarks 2025: Sales, Vacancy & Rent Trends

This MMCG Invest report (July 2025) analyzes national U.S. retail real estate trends across investment sales, vacancy, rent growth, and development supply, profiling five top markets for 2025 investment. All data is sourced from the MMCG database, derived from the 2025 U.S. Retail National Report.

### Investment Sales Trends
- Total retail investment sales reached **$59 billion in 2024** (8% YoY increase), with Q1 2025 volume rising 11% YoY and preliminary April 2025 figures 45% higher than April 2024.
- Cap rate expansion from 2022-2023 has tapered off; cap rates have largely flattened since mid-2024 with slight upward bias. Higher-yield deals (dollar stores, pharmacies at 7%+ caps) skew averages, but prime assets still command sub-5% caps; most private buyers transact in the 5%-6% cap range.
- Grocery-anchored centers have stabilized (e.g., a Kroger-anchored center traded at 6.1% cap in early 2025). Power centers trade around 7% caps (e.g., a 507,000 SF Arizona power center at 7.0% cap).
- Outlook shifted from negative to neutral-to-positive by mid-2025, with minimal new construction, low vacancy, and steady tenant demand supporting asset values.

### Vacancy Rates by Asset Class
- National retail vacancy: **~4.3%** as of early 2025; only 4.8% of total retail space available for lease at end of Q1 2025 (15 bps above record low). Fastest backfill pace in nearly 15 years.
- Vacancy by type: **Malls 8.9%** (highest), **Power Centers 4.7%**, **Neighborhood/Community Centers 6.4%**, **Strip Centers 5.0%**, **General Retail 2.7%** (lowest, driven by strong single-tenant net lease properties).

### Rent Growth
- National asking rents grew **~1.9% YoY** as of mid-2025, decelerating from 4%+ annual spikes in 2021-2022, in line with pre-pandemic historical average (~1.5-2% annually).
- Core retail sales (excluding e-commerce, gas, autos) rose over 30% nominally (10%+ real) since 2019, while occupied retail space grew under 2% — retail sales per SF has increased substantially.
- **47 of 57 largest retail markets** saw positive rent growth. Sunbelt markets lead; Northeast/Rust Belt and high-cost coastal markets lag.
- Notable market figures: Raleigh, NC (~7.5% YOY rent growth), Tampa, FL (~4.7%), Orange County (~3.6%), East Bay/Oakland (-2.6% decline), Dallas-Fort Worth (~4.4%), Atlanta (~4.2%), Phoenix (~3.8%).
- Forecast: national rent growth of ~1.7% in 2025, stabilizing at inflationary levels thereafter. Wide variation expected between high-growth and low-growth markets.

### Development Pipeline & Supply Constraints
- Since 2020, only ~81 million SF of new retail space added annually (vs. ~300 million SF/year in 2000-2009 and ~128 million SF/year in the 2010s) — roughly one-quarter of early 2000s levels.
- Over **165 million SF of older retail** demolished since 2018; total retail stock grew less than 2% from 2019-2024.
- Only ~21 million SF of newly built retail space (since 2020) is currently available for lease — less than 5% of total available space; 95%+ of availabilities are in older properties.
- Construction costs, financing costs, and cap rates have made ground-up development difficult; new construction is mostly niche (freestanding pad sites pre-leased to nationals, mixed-use ground-floor retail).
- Texas markets account for nearly one-third of all new first-generation retail space available.

### Top 5 Markets for Retail Investment in 2025
1. **Dallas-Fort Worth, TX**: 468+ million SF inventory, ~4.4% YOY rent growth (top 10 nationally), 4.9% vacancy, over 7 million SF under construction (most in country), strong population/job growth.
2. **Atlanta, GA**: ~4.2% YOY rent growth, ~4.2% vacancy, only 0.2% of stock delivered in past year, low-$20s PSF average rents, strong job market.
3. **Tampa Bay, FL**: ~3.5% vacancy (below national average), ~4.7% YOY rent growth (top 5 nationally), only 0.3% of inventory under construction, heavy in-migration and tourism.
4. **Phoenix, AZ**: ~3.8% YOY rent growth, ~4.5% vacancy, ~1 million SF absorbed over 12 months (one of highest nationally), ~0.8% of stock under construction.
5. **Raleigh, NC**: ~7.5% YOY rent growth (fastest of any large market), ~2.3% vacancy (among lowest nationally), minimal new construction (~0.5% delivered in past year), booming tech/life sciences hub.

### Conclusion
U.S. retail real estate in 2025 is characterized by near-record occupancy, steady (if modest) rent growth, and reviving capital flows, underpinned by a decade of constrained supply. The outlook is cautiously optimistic — limited new supply, steady consumer spending, and adaptive retailers should keep the sector positive barring a major downturn. The report emphasizes the importance of market selection, with Sunbelt and high-growth markets leading while older, slow-growth regions lag.

--- SOURCE 13: Unexpected Factors That Actually Determine A Shopping Center's Grade ---

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from RockStep Capital, dated March 10, 2025, is an educational blog article by Belen Worsham explaining the mall grading system used to classify shopping centers into Class A, B, or C categories. The article is aimed at beginner investors in shopping center/retail real estate.

**Origin of the Mall Grading System:** The concept emerged in the late 20th century. Malls were initially categorized by size (regional, super-regional, community centers). Investment research firms like Green Street Advisors pioneered revenue-based classification, and by the 1990s-2000s, REITs and firms like CBRE and JLL adopted these standards. The International Council of Shopping Centers (ICSC) continues to refine these standards today, and while not legally required, they are widely recognized as industry standard.

**Six Key Classification Factors:**
1. Sales Per Square Foot (most important metric)
2. Tenant Mix and Anchors (e.g., Apple, Gucci, Tesla vs. discount shops)
3. Location and Demographics
4. Occupancy Rates
5. Physical Condition and Amenities
6. Market Perception and Shopper Experience

**Class A Malls (Luxury High-Rises of Retail):** High sales exceeding $700-$1,000+ per square foot; premium tenants like Louis Vuitton, Gucci, Apple, and Nordstrom; occupancy at 95% or higher; located in major metro areas and affluent suburbs; offer experiential retail (fine dining, entertainment, unique attractions). Considered like blue-chip stocks—stable and resilient in downturns, but with high price tags that are less accessible to beginner investors.

**Class B Malls (Suburban Workhorses):** Moderate sales of $400-$700 per square foot; diverse tenant mix of national retailers, discount stores, and regional brands; occupancy around 85-95%; located in secondary markets (mid-sized cities or suburbs). More accessible to investors with value-add opportunities (renovations, re-tenanting), but require active management and face pressure from e-commerce trends.

**Class C Malls (Fixer-Uppers):** Low sales below $400 per square foot; high vacancy rates of 20% or more; declining foot traffic; outdated infrastructure; often viewed as redevelopment opportunities (mixed-use spaces, office hubs, or e-commerce logistics centers). High-risk, high-reward investments requiring heavy repositioning efforts and clear redevelopment strategy.

**Investor Takeaways:** The article recommends that beginner investors seek well-located Class A or B malls as the safest entry point, offering strong tenant demand and steady rental income. Those willing to take on more risk may pursue Class C repositioning, but success requires careful planning and market expertise. The page also promotes RockStep Capital's free webinar replay on "The Blueprint for Shopping Center Investments" and a free 50-page ebook on alternative investing. The article belongs to the "Investing Basics" topic category.
</summary>

The "retail apocalypse" (also known as "retailpocalypse") refers to the widespread closing of North American brick-and-mortar retail stores, especially large chains, beginning in the 2010s and continuing through the present (2026). - Shrinking middle class: Declining real wages and rising costs creating a "middle-class squeeze," affecting retailers like Macy's, JCPenney, and Sears. Dollar stores (Dollar General, Dollar Tree, Family Dollar) grew but are seen as both symptom and cause of rural independent retailer collapse.
- Poor management: Focus on short-term quarterly dividends, understaffing, inventory mismanagement, and heavy debt from leveraged buyouts by private equity firms.
- COVID-19 pandemic: Exacerbated closures; many retailers filed for bankruptcy. Online shopping boomed during lockdowns—29% of US and 43% of UK consumers said they'd never return to offline shopping.

KEY STATISTICS:
- 2017: more than 12,000 physical stores closed.
- 2019: 9,302 store closings announced (59% jump from 2018), the highest since tracking began in 2012.
- Credit Suisse predicted 25% of US malls could close by 2022.
- Sears fell from 3,500+ stores and 355,000 employees in 2006 to 1,430 stores by 2016, filing bankruptcy in October 2018 with 68,000 employees.
- IHL Group (2019) disputed the "apocalypse" narrative, finding 5+ chains opening stores for every one closing, and that 20 retailers accounted for 75% of all closures.
- Coresight estimated closures would exceed the 2019 record in 2020; by 2022 store openings had again exceeded closings.

SURVIVORS/THRIVERS: Discount superstores (Walmart, Target), fast-fashion brands (Zara, H&M), dollar stores, and warehouse clubs (Costco, Sam's Club, BJ's).

Both men and women saw gains in Nonstore Retailers, Motor Vehicle and Parts Dealers, and Building Material and Garden Supply Stores. The analysis notes that women's sustained retail job losses over the last year represent the longest stretch of losses in the industry for either gender since the Great Recession, with men's retail declines preceding women's before the recession and men's gains preceding women's during recovery. --- SOURCE 4: Retail trade employment: before, during, and after the ... ---
URL: https://www.bls.gov/opub/btn/volume-11/retail-trade-employment-before-during-and-after-the-pandemic.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics' "Beyond the Numbers" publication (Vol. 11, No. 4, April 2022) by Daniel Dorfman examines retail trade employment trends before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic, using data from the BLS Employment Projections program.

KEY TRENDS AND FINDINGS:

**Pre-Pandemic (2010-2019):**
- Retail employment grew from a Great Recession low of 14.4 million workers in 2010 to a peak of 15.8 million in 2017 (1.3% average annual growth), then declined by approximately 200,000 jobs from 2017-2019 (0.7% annual decline) due to e-commerce competition, thin sales margins, and technological disruption.
- Seven retail industries drove the 2017-19 contraction. General merchandise stores and clothing stores each accounted for ~29% of the decline; sporting goods, hobby, musical instrument, and bookstores accounted for 19.3%. These three together accounted for 77.6% of the sector's decline.
- Supporting industries grew significantly: couriers and messengers grew 54.4% and warehousing and storage grew 86.1% from 2010-2019, versus retail's 8.1% growth.

**During the Pandemic (2019-2020):**
- The retail sector lost almost 800,000 jobs in 2020 (vs. ~200,000 from 2017-19). E-commerce support industries (couriers/messengers, warehousing/storage) gained a combined ~300,000 jobs.
- Clothing stores accounted for 38.6% of total retail sector employment loss in 2020. Six industries (motor vehicle and parts dealers, gasoline stations, miscellaneous store retailers, clothing stores, furniture stores, and health/personal care stores) accounted for more than three-quarters of retail jobs lost.
- General merchandise stores fared relatively better (only 1.5% decline in 2020 vs. 29.2% in 2017-19), because warehouse clubs and supercenters selling essential goods experienced employment gains.

**Projections (2020-2030):**
- Retail trade is projected to lose ~587,000 jobs (4.0% of 2020 employment) over 2020-30, the largest projected employment decline of any sector. Retail trade's share of total employment is projected to fall from 9.7% (2020) to 8.6% (2030).
- Largest projected declines: food and beverage stores (-257,500 jobs, -8.3%) and general merchandise stores (-233,500 jobs, -7.7%), together accounting for 83.7% of retail jobs lost.
- Projected to gain employment: nonstore retailers (+85,600, +14.6%, the only industry projected to exceed prepandemic levels), motor vehicle and parts dealers (+76,100, +4.0%), clothing stores (+42,800, +4.5%), and furniture/home furnishings stores (+19,900, +4.9%).
- Other projected declines include: electronics and appliance stores (-15.0%), miscellaneous store retailers (-11.6%), sporting goods/hobby/book stores (-7.3%), gasoline stations (-4.7%), health/personal care stores (-4.0%), and building material dealers (-4.0%).
- By 2030, motor vehicle and parts dealers are projected to grow their share to 13.9% of retail employment (from 12.8%); nonstore retailers to 4.7% (from 3.9% in 2020). Clothing stores are projected to recover to 7.0% share (between prepandemic 8.5% and pandemic 6.4%).
- E-commerce sales increased 32.0% from Q4 2019 to Q4 2020, growing from 11.0% to almost 14.0% of total retail sales.

**Conclusions:**
The pandemic accelerated pre-existing trends driven by e-commerce and automation. Most retail industries will continue long-term declines, while those insulated from e-commerce (building material dealers, motor vehicle dealers) and those accelerated by e-commerce (nonstore retailers) will fare best. BLS projects 3.9% average annual productivity growth in retail trade from 2020-30, versus 2.3% from 2010-20.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 6: COVID-19 ends longest employment recovery and expansion in CES history, causing unprecedented job losses in 2020 : Monthly Labor Review : U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics ---
URL: https://www.bls.gov/opub/mlr/2021/article/covid-19-ends-longest-employment-expansion-in-ces-history.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a June 2021 Monthly Labor Review article by BLS economists Ryan Ansell and John P. Mullins documenting how COVID-19 ended the longest employment recovery and expansion in U.S. Current Employment Statistics (CES) history, causing unprecedented job losses in 2020.

KEY FINDINGS:
- Nonfarm payroll employment declined by 9.4 million in 2020, the largest calendar-year decline in the history of the CES employment series (which began in 1939).
- Total nonfarm employment ended 2020 at 10.0 million below its February 2020 peak of 152.5 million.
- The U.S. had experienced over 9 years of steady employment growth before the pandemic, the longest recovery/expansion in CES history.
- January and February 2020 added a combined 604,000 jobs before the pandemic hit.

CHRONOLOGY OF THE 2020 DOWNTURN:
- January 21, 2020: CDC announced the first U.S. COVID-19 case.
- March 11, 2020: WHO designated COVID-19 as a pandemic (312 new daily U.S. cases that day).
- March 2020: State/local governments imposed restrictions (stay-at-home orders, social distancing, travel restrictions, school closures, business capacity limits). Nonfarm employment fell by 1.7 million — a loss only surpassed by a 1945 post-WWII demobilization decline.
- February 2020 was designated as the economic peak (start of recession).
- April 2020: Employment plummeted by 20.7 million — the largest decline in CES history. Combined March-April losses totaled 22.4 million, a 15 percent decline. By contrast, job losses in the previous four recessions since 1981 averaged 3 percent (largest was 6 percent in the Great Recession of 2007–09).
- Recovery began May 2020 (+2.8 million) and June 2020 (+4.8 million). May, June, July, and August brought the four largest monthly job gains in CES history.
- As COVID-19 surged later in 2020 and restrictions tightened, gains shrank, and December ended with a job loss.

INDUSTRY IMPACTS (2020 employment changes):
- Leisure and hospitality: -3,677,000 (largest losses; fell 48.6% Feb–Apr, recovered 51.1% Apr–Dec)
- Government: -1,273,000
- Education and health services: -1,184,000
- Professional and business services: -860,000
- Manufacturing: -578,000
- Retail trade: -459,000
- Other services: -450,000
- Wholesale trade: -282,000
- Information: -238,000
- Construction: -157,000
- Mining and logging: -97,000
- Transportation and warehousing: -93,000
- Financial activities: -58,000
- Utilities: -10,000
- Every major industry lost jobs in 2020.

WOMEN'S EMPLOYMENT:
- Women's nonfarm employment fell 5.2 million in 2020.
- In March-April, women's employment declined by 12.2 million, accounting for 55 percent of total employment decline.
- Losses concentrated in industries with large female workforces (leisure and hospitality: women = 53% of employment; education/health services: 77%; government: 58%; other services: 53%; retail trade: 50%; professional/business services: 46%).
- In education/health services, women accounted for 84% of total employment declines in March-April; in leisure/hospitality, women accounted for 54% of job losses.

EARNINGS:
- Average hourly earnings of all private employees rose $1.55 (5.5%) in 2020; production/nonsupervisory rose $1.31 (5.5%) — largest annual changes in CES history.
- Earnings rose because job losses concentrated in low-wage industries. Leisure and hospitality (Feb avg hourly earnings $16.90, lowest of any industry) accounted for 39% of Feb–Apr private employment decline; retail trade ($20.18, second lowest) accounted for another 11%.
- This compositional effect pushed up average private earnings.

HOURS:
- Average weekly hours of all private employees rose 0.4 hour to 34.7 hours (largest annual increase since 2010); production/nonsupervisory rose 0.7 hour to 34.2 hours (largest in CES history).

DIFFUSION INDEXES (breadth of employment change):
- In April 2020, the 1-month total private diffusion index fell to 4.5 — lowest reading in 30-year history; manufacturing fell to 3.3 — lowest in its history.
- In March, 221 of 257 total private industries lost jobs; in April, 244 did. In manufacturing, 61 of 75 industries shed jobs in March, 72 in April.
- Index surged back above 50 from May onward, indicating most industries adding jobs monthly.
- However, December 2020 12-month index stood at 14.6 (total private) and 11.3 (manufacturing): 219 of 257 total private industries lost jobs during 2020 (only 37 gained); 66 of 75 manufacturing industries shed jobs (only 8 gained).

RELATED ARTICLES cited include: "Employment recovery in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic" (MLR, Dec 2020), "Employment projections in a pandemic environment" (MLR, Feb 2021), and "Employment expansion continued in 2019, but growth slowed in several industries" (MLR, Apr 2020).
</summary>

- Nearly 20.7 million people lost jobs in April 2020 alone; retail was hit particularly hard.

- Between February and April 2020, 2.4 million retail jobs were lost, with 1.4 million belonging to women. A partial recovery of 1.1 million jobs (April-June) gave 53.5% of gains to women, but jobs remain precarious amid COVID-19 surges.
- In nearly every retail subsector that saw losses, women's share of job losses exceeded their share of pre-pandemic subsector jobs. Examples: Food and Beverage Stores (100% of losses were women's despite being 50.3% of the subsector workforce), Health and Personal Care Stores (85% of losses; 71.9% share), General Merchandise Stores (74.8%; 58.3% share), and Clothing Stores (70.8%; 71.1% share).

WAGE AND BENEFIT DISPARITIES:
- Women in retail earn $34,000 annually vs. $42,000 for men (81 cents per dollar). Black women, Latinas, and Native American women earn $30,000 annually—just 61 cents per dollar paid to white, non-Hispanic men ($49,000). Women with disabilities and women born outside the U.S. earn 71 cents per dollar.
- In 2018, 32.5% of women in retail worked part-time vs. 20.1% of men. By June 2020, one in four women (25.2%) working part-time wanted full-time work but couldn't get it for economic reasons (up from 11% in February).
- 8.9% of women in retail lived in poverty in 2018—nearly double the overall worker poverty rate. Poverty rates were notably higher for Black women (12.5%), Latinas (12%), Native American women (10.5%), and women with disabilities (16.5%).
- Women hold 66% of cashier/retail salesperson jobs in grocery stores (paying ~$11.40/hour) and 71% in general merchandise stores (~$12.11/hour). Temporary $2-3/hour hazard pay boosts largely expired.
- Only ~40% of workers in large retail/grocery stores had paid sick days pre-pandemic; companies with 500+ employees are exempt from federal emergency paid sick leave provisions.
- Fewer than 2 in 5 women (37.4%) in retail had employer-provided health insurance in 2018.
- Only about one-quarter of large retail/grocery workers had access to masks in March-April 2020. Retail workers faced retaliation (including firing) for requesting PPE or protesting unsafe conditions; Black workers were more than twice as likely to report punishment or firing for raising COVID concerns.

POLICY RECOMMENDATIONS:
The NWLC calls for: extending and strengthening emergency unemployment insurance; shoring up nutrition, child care, and public benefits; halting evictions/foreclosures; enacting the Paycheck Recovery Act; ensuring access to testing, PPE, and stronger workplace safety standards; requiring premium pay for essential workers; extending paid sick leave provisions; preventing employer liability shields; and strengthening worker protections against retaliation and organizing rights.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Were small businesses more likely to permanently close in the pandemic? ---
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11187-022-00662-1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed research article published in Small Business Economics (Volume 60, pages 1613-1629, 2023) titled "Were small businesses more likely to permanently close in the pandemic?" by Robert Fairlie, Frank M. Fossen, Reid Johnsen, and Gentian Droboniku. The open-access paper was published on August 8, 2022 and has 13,000+ accesses and 55 citations.

The study provides the first analysis of permanent business closures during the COVID-19 pandemic using confidential administrative firm-level panel data covering the universe of businesses filing sales taxes from the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration (CDTFA). The paper addresses three questions: (1) what percentage of businesses with taxable sales closed in the first quarters of the pandemic, (2) whether closure rates differ by initial business size, and (3) the resulting effects on market share concentration.

Key findings:
- Large increases in closure rates in the first two quarters of 2020, with a strong reversal in the third quarter of 2020.
- The increase in closures in the pandemic was substantially larger for small businesses than large businesses, but the rebound was also larger.
- Small business closure rates increased from 4.6% in 2019Q2 to 8.5% in 2020Q2, while large businesses increased from 1.3% to 2.7%.
- Pre-pandemic, small businesses closed at an average rate of 5.4% per quarter versus 1.4% for large businesses (2015Q1-2019Q4).
- In 2020Q2, COVID increased business closures by 2.7 percentage points overall; small businesses experienced a 3.3 percentage point total increase vs. 1.3 percentage points for large businesses.
- In 2020Q1, COVID increased closures by 1.2 percentage points overall (1.7 for small, 0.2 for large).
- In 2020Q3, closure rates rebounded below expected levels by 1.4 percentage points, with small businesses rebounding 1.5 percentage points more than large businesses.
- The disproportionate closing of small businesses led to increased market concentration (measured by the Herfindahl–Hirschman Index) among larger businesses, which only partially reversed.
- GDP fell by 31.2% in 2020Q2 (with a 5.1% drop in 2020Q1) and rebounded 33.8% in 2020Q3—unprecedented volatility.

Methodology: The study defines permanent closure as a business with taxable sales in one quarter but no taxable sales in the next four consecutive quarters (following Census/BLS definitions). Small businesses are defined as those with average quarterly taxable sales annualized to less than $500,000. Regression models control for pre-pandemic time trends, seasonality, and business characteristics using linear probability models with over 7 million observations across 22 quarters (2015Q2–2019Q4 pre-COVID, plus three post-COVID quarters).

The study fills three literature gaps: limited information on small business impacts, little evidence on permanent closures, and silence on effects of small business closures on market competitiveness. The findings imply small businesses may need additional support given the trend toward purchases from large online retailers, and demonstrate the fragility of small businesses during large adverse shocks and negative consequences for market competitiveness.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Small businesses were more likely to close permanently during the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic than large businesses. Although they rebounded strongly thereafter, market concentration remains higher than before the pandemic."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: High-frequency data from the U.S. Census Bureau during the COVID-19 pandemic: small vs. new businesses ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8247100

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed research article published in Business Economics (July 2021) by Catherine Buffington, Daniel Chapman, Emin Dinlersoz, Lucia Foster (U.S. Census Bureau) and John Haltiwanger (University of Maryland). The paper examines two new high-frequency U.S. Census Bureau data products launched during the COVID-19 pandemic to track the impact on existing small businesses versus new business formations.

**Key findings from the Small Business Pulse Survey (SBPS):**
- Small businesses experienced very sharp declines in activity, sentiment, and expectations early in the pandemic (April 2020–January 2021, covering first three phases).
- The Overall Sentiment Index (OSI) was negative everywhere throughout the period, though negativity decreased over time. Only ~6.4% of businesses reported positive impacts by the last week of Phase 3.
- In the first week of Phase 1, 74.0% of businesses saw decreased revenue; this fell to 42.6% by the last week of Phase 1 but worsened again in Phase 3.
- Accommodation and Food Services was hit hardest (64.9% reported large negative effects at end of Phase 3 vs. 13.7% for Finance and Insurance).
- By end of Phase 3, 26.7% of Accommodation and Food Services businesses had declining employment vs. 5.5% for Finance and Insurance.
- 72.4% of SBPS respondents received Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) assistance and 21.3% received Economic Injury Disaster Loans (EIDL) by late June 2020.
- Patterns suggest a K-shaped recovery — no sector showed positive range across all indicators for small businesses, even where the broader economy had recovered.
- Sectoral dispersion grew over time (average max-min OSI difference rose from 0.35 in Phase 1 to 0.42 in Phase 3) while state dispersion remained flatter.
- Sector rankings were persistent (correlation 0.90 between first week Phase 1 and last week Phase 3) while state rankings were less so (correlation 0.54).

**Key findings from Business Formation Statistics (BFS):**
- In sharp contrast to existing small businesses, new business applications surged after an initial decline, with 2020 being the highest year for business applications since the series began in 2004.
- The COVID-19 recession differed sharply from the Great Recession: applications fell sharply but briefly, exhibiting a strong V-shaped recovery (vs. slow, protracted decline in the Great Recession).
- The surge was especially large for likely nonemployers (Non-High-Propensity Business Applications) but also present for likely employers (High-Propensity Business Applications).
- Applications surged especially in Retail Trade, particularly Non-store Retailers (NAICS 454, internet-based retail), which rose over 200% from its early-2020 low by mid-2020.

5. Adverse impact on revenue was greater than impact on employment, partly due to decreases in hours rather than employment (suggestive of labor hoarding). By the last week of Phase 3, 84.1% of businesses did not change employment.
6. About 74% of small businesses in the SBPS received PPP loans. Cash on hand was limited, highlighting the precarious nature of small business operations.
7. Remote work increased significantly but varied by sector (Information had highest at 79.6%; Accommodation and Food Services lowest at 21.7%). - Sample drawn from 2017 Economic Census for single-location businesses with 1-499 employees and $1000+ revenue

- Three phases: April-June, August-October, November-January
- Overall Sentiment Index (OSI) ranges from -1 (most negative) to +1 (most positive)
- Sectors consistently at top of OSI: Finance and Insurance, Construction, Retail Trade. At bottom: Arts/Entertainment/Recreation, Educational Services, Accommodation and Food Services
- By end of Phase 3, 64.9% of Accommodation and Food Services businesses had large negative effects vs. 13.7% in Finance and Insurance
