URL: https://www.cambridgeassociates.com/insight/thoughts-on-the-retail-apocalypse

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Cambridge Associates, written by Managing Director Wade O'Brien, argues that the "retail apocalypse" narrative has been overhyped and that investment implications for most investors are limited. Key points include: (1) US total retail sales rose 5.7% year-over-year in Q4 2017 to $1.3 trillion, with e-commerce growing 17% to $119 billion, reaching $452 billion for the full year (about 9% of total retail sales, double the level from six years prior); (2) Despite headlines about store closures (over 10,000 stores shuttered in 2017), roughly 4,100 stores were actually opened on a net basis, with mass merchandisers, convenience stores, and supermarkets opening significant numbers; (3) E-commerce was not the only culprit in retail struggles — elevated debt burdens, fast fashion competition, and over-malling (US has 23.5 sq ft of retail space per capita vs 16.4 in Canada and 4.6 in the UK) also played roles; (4) Most investors have limited direct retail exposure — retail represents only about 7% of the Russell 1000 index weight; (5) Retailers as a group actually outperformed broad equity indexes recently, driven by Amazon, Home Depot, and Lowe's, while struggling department stores have tiny market caps (Sears and JCPenney combined are under $1.5 billion; Macy's is barely 1% of Amazon's size); (6) Retail REITs underperformed peers by over 1,300 basis points in 2017 (returning -4.8%), but some higher-quality A mall operators may present contrarian value opportunities as their share declines don't seem justified by positive FFO growth; (7) In credit markets, high-yield retailers returned 3.1% (underperforming by ~100 bps) and investment-grade retailers returned 1.9% (trailing by ~20 bps), with sector weights under 4% in high-yield and 3% in investment-grade indexes; (8) Tax reform could create some retail winners and losers, with highly levered retailers impacted by reduced interest expense deductibility. The author concludes that misplaced concerns about retail may create a few opportunities, particularly in higher-quality mall REITs, but overall investment implications are limited given small index exposures and stable fundamentals.

--- SOURCE 6: The Unmalling of America: How Municipalities Are Navigating the Changing Retail Landscape ---
URL: https://www.lincolninst.edu/publications/articles/2019-12-unmalling-america-municipalities-navigating-changing-retail-landscape

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy examines how U.S. municipalities are adapting to the decline of traditional shopping malls amid changing retail habits driven by e-commerce. The piece uses the Bangor Mall in Maine as a central case study: opened in 1978 on a former dairy farm, it once served up to two-thirds of Maine's population and contributed $1.2 million annually to the local tax base. However, its assessment fell roughly 25% per year from $60.9 million (2017) to $46.3 million (2018) to $34.6 million (2019), and its tax bill dropped below $1 million for the first time in two decades. The mall was sold at auction in February 2019 for $12.6 million after owner Simon Property Group defaulted on an $80 million loan. Despite this, Bangor's downtown (anchored by a new $22 million Bangor Savings Bank campus and apartment redevelopment) has compensated for the loss, demonstrating a successful downtown revitalization plan dating to the 1990s.

The article covers several key themes: (1) Retail's importance to municipal finances—property taxes account for 72% of total local taxes collected in 2015, with retail representing about one-quarter of commercial property value; sales and non-property taxes account for about 12% of municipal tax revenue. (2) Case studies of other struggling malls, including ShoppingTown Mall in Onondaga County, New York, where owner Moonbeam LLC faced foreclosure over $9.7 million in back taxes; Sheboygan, Wisconsin's Memorial Mall, which lost the city $1.3 million annually when it challenged its assessment (Walmart also sought $90,000 and $180,000 tax reductions there for 2017-2018); and Hickory Hollow Mall in Nashville, which failed to revive even after $50 million in investment. (3) Successful mall transformations, including University Place in Chapel Hill, North Carolina (now hosting a children's museum, health club, CrossFit studio, and specialty food store) and Colin Creek Mall in Plano, Texas (where a $10 million property is being recast into $1 billion in commercial development with a local tax incentive). (4) The growing preference for walkable urban environments—the U.S. has 8.5 billion square feet of retail space (24.5 sq ft per capita vs. Europe's 4.5), and walkable urban places are gaining market share. (5) The shift toward service-oriented retail (bars, restaurants, gyms, salons) that cannot be replicated online, supported by data showing online shoppers reduce grocery spending by 4.5% but increase coffee shop spending by 7.6%.

Experts cited include Lincoln Institute Fellow Ron Rakow (former Boston assessor), Marc Moffitt of the Denton Central Appraisal District, and Lindsay Relihan of the London School of Economics. E-commerce currently accounts for only 10-11% of retail sales, projected to reach just over 15% by 2022. The article concludes that malls' land ("dirt") retains value for redevelopment, and that navigating changing retail requires municipal flexibility, creativity, and foresight, as demonstrated in Bangor, Sheboygan, and Chapel Hill.
</summary>

"In some communities dependent on malls, they can make up 20 to 30 percent of their tax base and other taxpayers may have been paying relatively less," says Lincoln Institute of Land Policy Fellow Ron Rakow. "If the mall isn't doing as well, the community is either going to have to reduce services or increase taxes for others."

--- SOURCE 8: The 'Retail Apocalypse' Doesn't Need a Government Fix | Cato Institute ---
URL: https://www.cato.org/commentary/retail-apocalypse-doesnt-need-government-fix

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Cato Institute commentary by Scott Lincicome (published February 26, 2025 in The Dispatch) argues that the "retail apocalypse" narrative is a myth and that the market doesn't need government intervention. The piece draws on a new National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) paper by economist Yue Cao and colleagues that tested the retail apocalypse thesis by examining 25 national chains and several regional outlets in 18 metro areas between 2010 and 2019, using smartphone geolocation data from over 2.7 million devices.

Key findings from the NBER paper include: (1) the number of general merchandise stores actually increased from 49,089 to 52,807 during the 2010s, as dollar stores, supercenters, and discount department stores more than replaced traditional department stores and regional chains; (2) Americans' access to retail chains (within 10 miles) improved from 2010 to 2019; (3) Walmart was the most preferred general merchandise store among both low-income and high-income Americans, while traditional department stores were widely disliked; (4) consumer surplus per trip to general merchandise stores did not significantly decline from 2010 to 2019—higher-income consumers were better off, and lowest-income Americans' welfare was basically unchanged because losses from department stores were offset by gains at Walmart and discount/dollar stores.

The article argues the same story holds today, citing evidence that e-commerce receded to pre-pandemic trends by 2022, brick-and-mortar retail has been making a comeback (Toys "R" Us and Barnes & Noble reopened locations; Burlington, Ross, and TJ Maxx collectively opened 339 stores in 2024; Nordstrom Rack grew 8.5%), and retail availability sits near record lows with rising commercial rents. The piece also criticizes the federal government's December 2024 block of the Kroger-Albertsons merger, arguing grocery competition is thriving through Walmart, Costco, Aldi (now the third-largest grocery chain at 2,400+ stores), and dollar stores—noting supermarkets' grocery share of food-at-home spending fell from two-thirds in 2000 to 54% in 2023 while warehouse clubs and supercenters nearly doubled to 23%. The article concludes that government regulations restricting big-box stores or dollar stores could disproportionately harm low-income consumers, and that "market 'apocalypses' might make for great headlines, but it's usually the government fixes doing the real damage."

--- SOURCE 9: Retail apocalypse - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retail_apocalypse

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The "retail apocalypse" (also "retailpocalypse") refers to the widespread closure of brick-and-mortar retail stores in Northern America (and the UK, Australia), particularly large chains, starting in the 2010s and continuing into the 2020s. More than 12,000 physical stores closed in 2017 alone. Key causes include: the rise of e-commerce (especially Amazon and Walmart, dubbed the "Amazon effect"), oversupply of shopping malls, shifting consumer spending toward experiences (restaurants, travel) rather than goods, the shrinking American middle class, poor management and high debt from leveraged buyouts by private equity firms, and the COVID-19 pandemic which accelerated closures and bankruptcies. Major retailers filing for bankruptcy during the pandemic include J. Crew, Neiman Marcus, JCPenney, Lord & Taylor, Stage Stores, Stein Mart, Tuesday Morning, and Pier 1 Imports. The most resilient retailers have been discount superstores (Walmart, Target), fast-fashion brands (Zara, H&M), dollar stores, and warehouse clubs (Costco, Sam's Club). A consequence has been the rise of "dead malls" and vacant retail space often filled by pop-up retailers like Spirit Halloween. Some experts dispute the "apocalypse" narrative, arguing it's a market correction; IHL Group's 2019 research found more chains were expanding than closing stores. The term was first used by Peter Glen in an early 1990s essay and gained widespread usage in 2017. Strategies for survival cited by researchers include enhancing customer experience, omnichannel integration, and using technology (AR, robots, smart mirrors).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 10: The unintended consequences of brick-and-mortar’s decline | Costello College of Business ---
URL: https://business.gmu.edu/news/2024-10/unintended-consequences-brick-and-mortars-decline

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from George Mason University's Costello College of Business (published October 8, 2024, by Delaiah Iyob) discusses research by Taotao Ye, assistant professor of marketing at the Donald G. Costello College of Business, on the unintended consequences of brick-and-mortar retail store closures during the "retail apocalypse." The research paper, forthcoming in Marketing Science and co-authored by Venkatesh Shankar of Southern Methodist University, analyzed comprehensive online and offline transaction data from a major video game and electronics retailer from July 2015 to July 2017. During this period, the retailer closed more than 200 stores (over 5% of its physical presence), and the researchers analyzed the effects at per-county and per-customer levels.

Key findings: Net losses to the retailer far exceeded the average sales of the shuttered locations. The retailer experienced an average net monthly sales loss of approximately $209,317 per shuttered location—18% of the average monthly per-county sales total. Brands were failing to redirect consumer activity to remaining locations or digital options, and the closure itself sent a negative signal about the brand, causing consumers to transfer loyalty to competitors appearing more stable. Ye suggests this may be a form of stability-seeking behavior. Brands have also been ineffective at onboarding "orphaned" consumers to e-commerce due to complex registration and navigation processes.

Ye's recommendations: (1) Retailers should simplify onboarding and smooth the pathway between in-person and online channels, communicating more with customers to engage them through apps to decouple brand loyalty from any single location; (2) consider alternatives to closure such as small-format stores (as seen with Macy's, Nordstrom, Best Buy, and IKEA) and localized use of customer data; (3) thoroughly analyze the total impact of closing a store before deciding, considering mitigating factors such as short distance to another location, high percentage of in-store discounts in the county (indicating brand loyalty among price-sensitive customers), and low value of product returns.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 15: Business exit during the COVID-19 pandemic - PMC - NIH ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8938302

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a research paper published in the Journal of Macroeconomics (March 2022) by Federal Reserve Board economists Leland D. Crane, Ryan A. Decker, Aaron Flaaen, Adrian Hamins-Puertolas, and Christopher Kurz. The paper examines business exit (permanent business death) during the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic (March 2020–February 2021) using non-traditional or "alternative" data sources, placing these measures in historical context.

Key findings and methodology:
- Official statistics on business dynamics are released with substantial lags (BLS establishment death data available mid-2022; Census firm death data not until 2023), prompting reliance on alternative data sources.
- Historically, business exit is common in the U.S.: about 7.5% of firms (roughly 400,000) and 8.5% of establishments (roughly 600,000) exit annually. Exit is countercyclical and driven primarily by very small firms (fewer than 5 employees). Temporary closures affect about 2% of establishments per quarter.
- The paper constructs novel measures of business exit using ADP payroll data (based on paycheck issuance) and SafeGraph cell phone geolocation data, in addition to reviewing existing measures from Womply, Homebase, and the Census Bureau's Small Business Pulse Survey.
- ADP data show business shutdown was elevated in late spring 2020 (shutdown spells of 25+ days were nearly 12 percentage points above historical averages by late April 2020), but shutdown returned to or fell below normal by late August 2020. Elevated shutdowns were driven largely by smaller units and appeared to be largely temporary.
- SafeGraph-based measures show substantially elevated establishment exit in full-service restaurants (13.5% cumulative 12-month exit rate, about 70% above the ~8% historical rate), and other services (NAICS 81, including barber shops and nail salons) saw more than 100,000 excess establishment exits. Other services alone accounted for roughly 123,000 excess exits.
- Industry-level variation aligns with intuition: high excess exit in other services, automotive repair, clothing stores, and personal care services; lower-than-normal exit in grocery stores, electronics/appliance stores, and outdoor recreation.
- The paper estimates economy-wide excess establishment exit was likely below 200,000 during the first year of the pandemic (exit rate about one-quarter to one-third above normal), which is roughly consistent with preliminary BED official data suggesting about 185,000 excess establishment exits in calendar year 2020.
- The authors note that the widely cited figure of ~400,000 permanently closed businesses by July 2020 (from Hamilton 2020) is likely an overestimate.
- The authors emphasize their evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive due to dataset limitations, and highlight the importance of timely official data production.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"For the U.S., business exit is fairly common, with about 7.5 percent of firms exiting annually in recent years."

- Only ~**81 million SF of new retail space annually** since 2020 (vs. ~300M SF/year in 2000–2009 and ~128M SF/year in the 2010s) — roughly one-quarter of early-2000s levels

<summary>
This Coresight Research report (published 2023, with a 2026 follow-up report referenced) examines the state of the American mall, challenging the popular narrative of "dying malls" by showing that top-tier malls are thriving. Key findings include:

- Physical retail bounced back after pandemic restrictions lifted, with 2022 seeing more store openings than closures for the first time since 2016.
- Retail sales at malls grew more than 11% in 2022 to nearly $819 billion.
- Malls capture a greater share of sales than their share of space, with high sales productivity especially pronounced at top-tier malls.

MARKET SCALE AND OPPORTUNITY:
- Malls make up a shrinking proportion of total US retail gross leasable area—down to 5.5% in 2023 from 5.7% in 2014, driven by low-tier mall closures.
- ICSC estimates 12.9% of US consumer expenditure on retail goods and services went through malls in Q1 2023.
- Mall expenditure totaled $728.9 billion in 2021 and $818.7 billion in 2022 (11.2% YoY increase).

CORESIGHT RESEARCH ANALYSIS:
- Occupancy: Top-tier malls averaged 95.1% occupancy in 2022 (based on public mall operators, S&P Capital IQ data), still slightly below pre-pandemic levels; non-top-tier malls lagged more meaningfully.
- Rent: Average minimum base rent at top-tier malls grew in the mid-teens percentage range for four consecutive quarters from Q4 2021.
- Revenue: Both top-tier and non-top-tier public mall operators saw CAGRs in the mid-to-high single digits between 2020 and 2022.
- Traffic: Based on a Placer.ai sampling of 120 malls, traffic at top-tier malls was up 12% on average in 2022 versus pre-pandemic 2019; non-top-tier malls were up 10%. Top-tier mall traffic growth was driven by long-distance visitors. Coresight's US Consumer Tracker found 40.3% of respondents visited a mall in the prior two weeks in the December 28, 2022 survey.

DRIVERS OF MALL GROWTH:
1. Multichannel halo effect: Brands with both online and offline presence see sales boosts, reduced customer acquisition costs, and better margins. Rising online advertising costs (driven partly by data privacy features like Apple's app tracking transparency) push brands to physical retail. 61% of retailers and 66% of digital-first retailers cite rising customer acquisition costs as the top obstacle to 2022 e-commerce goals (CommerceNext study). 45% of tracked DNVBs have opened physical stores (Coresight DNVB Databank). BORIS (buy online, return in-store) cuts shipping costs and boosts loyalty.
2. Brand synergy: Brands generate more value in proximity to other high-value brands, driving foot traffic.
3. Reinvestment: Top-tier mall operators like Simon Property Group (Phipps Plaza Atlanta redevelopment with Nobu Hotel/Restaurant, Life Time facility, Citizens Market, office tower) and Taubman ($200 million renovation of The Mall at Green Hills in Nashville, 2019, including 132,000 sq ft of inline retail, new Dillard's, and 70,000 sq ft RH store) continually reinvest.
4. Omnichannel investment by mall owners: Cadillac Fairview partnered with Swyft (CF Delivery same-day/next-day shipping) and ReturnBear (multi-retailer returns). Simon Property Group's Simon Search provides real-time mall inventory data; its Shop Premium Outlets (SPO) platform provides access to 35 million online shoppers and 2 billion in-store shoppers globally, and partnered with Tmall Global (Alibaba) in late October 2022 for Singles' Day. Simon also partnered with Leap (November 2022) to support DNVBs entering brick-and-mortar.

CONCLUSION: Top-tier malls are outperforming the average mall in revenues, occupancy, and foot traffic. The combination of physical retail and e-commerce creates a halo effect benefiting brands. Coresight expects that omnichannel strategies and investments will disproportionately benefit top-tier mall growth going forward.

Contributors: Charlotte Rothschild and Daniel Rodden, Analysts at Coresight Research.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Dying shopping malls have become cultural symbols in the US, evoking nostalgia among Americans who reminisce about their experiences in these once vibrant centers. However, the reality of the American mall landscape is more nuanced than the popular narrative suggests."
</key_excerpts>

This Coldwell Banker Commercial article (published March 11, 2026) examines the bifurcation of the American mall industry—why some malls thrive while others collapse. KEY STATISTICS AND DATA:
- Roughly 1,200 malls remain in the U.S. as of 2025, with projections suggesting only 900 will operate by 2028 (Capital One Shopping Research)
- Over 8,100 stores closed in 2025, up ~12% from 2024, with projections up to 15,000 closures (Coresight Research)

SUCCESSFUL MALL EXAMPLES:
- Houston's Galleria: 30+ million annual visitors; 2017 renovation added luxury wing anchored by Saks Fifth Avenue and Nobu; 2024 plans included 155,000 sq ft of new flooring and LED lighting upgrades
- King of Prussia: 22 million annual visitors, 450 stores; 2016 expansion added 155,000 sq ft including Savor dining hub; recognized for luxury retailers Gucci, Cartier, Dior

STRATEGIC RECOMMENDATIONS FOR OWNERS:
- SELL when: property lacks capital, location, or tenant mix to compete on experience; declining trade area; prohibitive repositioning costs
- REPOSITION when: solid location but outdated tenant mix; growing suburban markets with affluent demographics; examples include Houston Galleria's new tenants (Rothy's, Skims, Ring Concierge)
- CONVERT when: retail math no longer works; lower-tier malls in strong markets may convert to mixed-use, logistics, medical, or residential. The article warns that the worst strategy is inaction, as the gap between thriving and struggling properties will only widen, and the window for optimal timing is closing. Successful centers are shifting from pure retail to mixed-use experiential destinations—asking "how retail anchors a much broader ecosystem of uses."
</summary>

--- SOURCE 13: Dead mall - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_mall

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A "dead mall" (also known as a ghost mall or zombie mall) is a shopping mall with low consumer traffic or deteriorating conditions. The Wikipedia article covers the causes, effects, and redevelopment of dead malls, primarily in North America. Many malls are considered "dead" when they lose their anchor stores, causing sales volumes and rental revenues to decline below the cost of maintenance. Structural changes in the retail industry, including the rise of big-box chains (Walmart, Target, Best Buy), open-air lifestyle centers, and online shopping, have contributed significantly to mall decline. Newsweek declared the indoor mall format obsolete in 2008, and 2007 marked the first time since the 1950s that no new malls were built in the U.S.

Key causes of dead malls include: "demolition by neglect" (allowing malls to deteriorate without maintenance until demolition is necessary), demographic and socio-economic changes in surrounding neighborhoods, and the COVID-19 pandemic which exacerbated issues through temporary closures and retailer bankruptcies (including JCPenney, Lord & Taylor, Neiman Marcus, GNC, Brooks Brothers, and Ascena Retail Group). From 2006-2010, vacancy rates in U.S. malls increased significantly, with nearly 3% of malls considered "dying" (40%+ vacancy) and nearly one-fifth having "troubling" vacancy rates (10%+) by 2014. The U.S. has 40% more shopping space per capita than Canada and five times more than the U.K., contributing to an "extremely over-retailed" market.

Redevelopment of dead malls takes several forms: conversion to office/educational use (e.g., Windsor Park Mall became Rackspace's headquarters), transformation into open-air mixed-use centers, conversion to fulfillment centers by Amazon/FedEx/DHL/UPS, repurposing for homeless housing, and "mall-to-medicine" conversions by healthcare systems like Vanderbilt Health and University of Rochester Medical Center. Notable companies accused of neglect include Ashkenazy Acquisition Corporation, Namdar Realty Group, and Kohan Retail Investment Group. Some malls maintain profitability in areas with inclement weather or senior populations who engage in mall walking, with Simon Malls enjoying occupancy averages of 92%.
</summary>

"A dead mall, also known as a ghost mall or zombie mall, is a shopping mall that has low consumer traffic or is deteriorating in some manner."

--- SOURCE 14: The Death and Reinvention of American Malls ---
URL: https://sites.lsa.umich.edu/mje/2026/04/13/the-death-and-reinvention-of-american-malls

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the Michigan Journal of Economics, written by Reena Jari and published April 13, 2026, examines the decline and potential reinvention of American shopping malls. 

**Background/Context:** Malls are owned by real estate investment trusts (REITs) that lease retail spaces to tenants who pay base rent, operating expenses, and a percentage of sales. Large department stores like Macy's and Nordstrom serve as "anchor stores" that drive foot traffic and receive lower rents. Malls have faced declining retail sales due to multiple factors.

**Key Causes of Mall Decline:**
1. **E-commerce:** The rise of Amazon and other online retailers in the early 2010s shifted consumer behavior to online shopping due to convenience, accessibility, and product variety, reducing competitiveness of brick-and-mortar retail.
2. **COVID-19 pandemic:** Work-from-home trends reduced commuting and foot traffic. A JP Morgan Chase Institute report found grocery stores and restaurants recovered post-COVID, but retail spaces lagged due to e-commerce.
3. **Internal competition between malls:** Poorly managed malls struggle against newer malls with better amenities. Examples include a mall in Texas acquired by Dillard's after previous owners failed to pay utility bills and property taxes.
4. **Anchor store bankruptcies:** Forever 21's bankruptcy caused the loss of 200+ stores in the US, and large vacant spaces are difficult to fill. The San Francisco Centre mall entered a "death spiral" due to homelessness, shoplifting, and drug use, leading to anchor store closures (Nordstrom, Bloomingdale's) and collapse.

**Reinvention & Recovery:**
- Some investors see redevelopment potential; high-end malls are nearly fully occupied with rising rents according to the Wall Street Journal.
- Vacant spaces are being converted into restaurants, gyms, entertainment venues, and alternative uses — malls are evolving into entertainment centers.
- Dillard's purchased and renovated the Longview Mall in Texas to enhance consumer experience.
- Gen Z is driving a mall comeback: Circana data shows shoppers aged 18-24 bought 62% of total general merchandise in stores (vs. 52% for those 25+). Younger shoppers value instant gratification and in-store experiences, with the online clothing brand Edikted opening physical mall locations due to Gen Z demand.

**Conclusion:** While many malls have struggled to adapt to e-commerce, post-COVID changes, and bankruptcies, the industry may be making a comeback by adapting to consumer demand rather than disappearing entirely.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"E-commerce sales are increasing because of how convenient online buying is, how accessible it is, and how many different things are available" (Kothari, 2018).
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Bed Bath & Beyond is closing hundreds of stores. But they won’t be empty for long | CNN Business ---
URL: https://www.cnn.com/2023/04/24/business/bed-bath-beyond-stores-bankruptcy-real-estate/index.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
CNN article (updated from an original March 21 piece) reports on Bed Bath & Beyond's bankruptcy and the real estate opportunities created by its store closures. The company filed for bankruptcy on Sunday and will close its remaining 360 Bed Bath & Beyond stores and 120 buybuy Baby locations, adding to 400 stores already closed over the past year. Rather than remaining vacant, these stores are being rapidly scooped up by other retailers and businesses due to historically tight commercial real estate conditions.

Key context: total new commercial retail construction hit a record low in 2022 (third consecutive year), and the retail space vacancy rate fell to 4.9% at the end of 2022 — the lowest since CBRE began tracking in 2005. Bed Bath & Beyond stores are attractive because they're located in all 50 states (most in California, Texas, New Jersey, and Florida), mostly in suburbs of mid-size and large cities, and average around 30,000 square feet (under 50,000 sq ft), aligning with the retail trend toward smaller spaces. In some cases, landlords are eager to replace old leases because Bed Bath & Beyond was paying below-market rent.

Chains already moving into former locations include TJ Maxx, HomeGoods, Ross, Burlington, Five Below, Nordstrom Rack, and budget gym Planet Fitness (which opens ~200 new gyms a year). Growth is most pronounced in the discount retail segment as budget-conscious shoppers seek low prices. Physical store openings exceeded closings last year for the first time since 2016 (Coresight Research), and Dollar General, Family Dollar, Dollar Tree, and Five Below lead opening announcements this year.

Federal Realty, a REIT owning nine Bed Bath & Beyond stores, is negotiating with chains like TJX, Burlington, Ross, Nordstrom Rack, and Container Store. Once agreements are finalized, new retailers typically take 18-24 months to open. Meanwhile, Tuesday Morning will also close more than 250 stores this year, with A&G Real Estate Partners auctioning off leases (10,000-20,000 sq ft spaces), with discount chains interested due to their small, already-built nature. With limited new development, growth is coming from "second-generation space."
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"E-commerce scared a lot of people off from building retail. A lot of great real estate is going to come available into a market where there's been no vacancies. It will not take long for retailers to occupy those spaces." — Brandon Isner, head of retail research at CBRE. "For us, the biggest source of new store locations comes from other retailers closing stores. So many of our most productive locations were formerly Circuit City or Toys 'R' Us or Sports Authority." — Burlington CEO Michael O'Sullivan. "There is good interest for Bed Bath & Beyond stores that are closing given desirable locations and an average size of around 30,000 square feet." — Telsey Advisory Group retail analysts. "We feel pretty bullish based on the demand that we've seen that we'll be able to release all of these spaces to other retailers." — Lance Billingsley, senior VP of anchor leasing at Federal Realty. "With not a lot of new development going on, everyone's growth will come from second-generation space." — Mike Matlat, A&G Real Estate Partners senior managing director.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Dead/Dying Malls in Your Area and Predictions ---

SUMMARY:

The thread was started on November 24, 2020, by user "architect" and contains 91 posts across 10 pages. The purpose is for users to share observations about dead or dying shopping malls in their regions and predict which malls will next decline. The thread opens with a prediction that up to 50% of malls could close over the next five years.

Key observations by region:

**Dallas-Fort Worth, TX (architect):** The Shops at Willow Bend in Plano has deteriorated noticeably, with 30-40% of in-line spaces vacant. It opened around 9/11 targeting an upscale demographic with anchors including Neiman Marcus, Saks, and Lord & Taylor. Apple closed its store there (the third to open in the nation) due to patent-troll litigation strategy, causing traffic to decline. Other dead/dying DFW malls include Music City Mall, Irving Mall, Ridgmar Mall, and Village at Fairview. Golden Triangle Mall and Hulen Mall are at risk long-term.

**Portland, OR (babs):** Lloyd Center, interior of Mall 205, interior of Cedar Hills Crossing (exterior businesses successful), and Three Rivers Mall in Kelso are all struggling.

**Phoenix, AZ (arizonaguy):** Dead malls include MetroCenter (only Harkins, Dillard's Clearance Center, Walmart remain), Fiesta Mall (fully closed, being converted to medical offices), and Paradise Valley Mall (Dillard's closing). Dying malls include ChrisTown Spectrum, Desert Sky/Westridge, and Superstition Springs Center (wounded by Macerich building SanTan Village nearby). Healthy malls include SanTan Village, Biltmore Fashion Park, and Scottsdale Fashion Square (the Phoenix area's flagship mall). Notably, nearly all Phoenix malls are owned by Macerich.

**Pacific Northwest (Super S, Brian Lutz):** Struggling malls include Shoppes at Riverside (Aberdeen, WA), Willamette Town Center (Salem), Lewis County Mall (Chehalis), and Yard Birds "Mall" (Chehalis). In Seattle, Northgate Mall is being converted from indoor to outdoor (with a Seattle Kraken practice facility and new light rail station). Healthy Seattle malls include Bellevue Collection, Alderwood, Southcenter, and Crossroads Bellevue. So-so malls include Pacific Place, Westlake Center, Marketplace at Factoria, Everett Mall, Redmond Town Center, and Commons at Federal Way.

**Texas (pseudo3d):** Post Oak Mall (College Station) has seen better days, with Macy's upper level converted to Backstage, an outdated JCPenney, closed Sears (partially converted to Conn's HomePlus), and former Bealls became Gordmans then closed. The mall is about 85% full, with a small food court and demographic shifts.

**Northern California (lake52, Alpha8472, storewanderer):** Strong malls include Galleria at Roseville, Stanford, and Hillsdale Mall. Struggling malls include Fountains at Roseville, Arden Fair (which experienced a mass shooting around the time of posting), Sunrise Mall (city of Citrus Heights planning redevelopment away from retail), Downtown Commons, Tanforan, and Stonestown (in transition). Sunvalley Mall in Concord is near death with 80% of stores closed, and Hilltop Mall in Richmond is near death (only kept alive by a Walmart). Crime is cited as a major factor in several Bay Area mall declines. Arden Fair is discussed in depth, with suggestions that it needs to pivot to a lower-middle-class tenant mix and mixed-use/housing redevelopment, including adding a grocery operator.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is from the New York City Comptroller's Office (comptroller.nyc.gov) and presents a comprehensive report titled "Retail Vacancy in New York City: Trends and Causes, 2007-2017." The report was authored by New York City Comptroller Scott Stringer and provides a data-driven analysis of retail vacancy across all five boroughs of NYC using administrative data from property tax filings (RPIE), commercial leasing data from Compstak, MasterCard merchant data, and regulatory approval data from the NY State Liquor Authority and NYC Department of Buildings.

KEY FINDINGS:
1. Vacancy Rates Have Risen: The citywide retail vacancy rate increased from a low of 4.0% in 2007 to 5.8% in 2017. Vacancy rates rose across all five boroughs, most dramatically in Staten Island (from 4.3% to nearly 11%). Reported vacant retail space roughly doubled from 5.6 million sq ft to 11.8 million sq ft over the decade. The highest vacancy rates are in the outer boroughs, particularly Staten Island, Queens, and the Bronx.

2. Internet Shopping Changed Retail Space Usage: Amazon sales rose from $14.8 billion in 2007 to $177.9 billion in 2017. NYC retail establishments grew 19%, but personal services grew ~50% and bars/restaurants rose 65%. Regression analysis shows Amazon sales positively and significantly associated with retail vacancy, driving vacant retail square footage higher by nearly 1 percentage point between 2007-2017.

3. Rising Rents Contributed to Vacancy: Average retail rents rose 22% citywide (from $42 to $51 per sq ft). Rents doubled in Soho (10012) from $60 to $126 and rose 87% on the Upper East Side (from $79 to $146). A 1% increase in average retail rents is associated with 0.33% increase in vacant retail square footage. Property taxes paid by retail tenants doubled from $1.1 billion in 2007 to $2.2 billion in 2017 (rising from 20% to 23% of total retail rents).

4. Regulatory Hurdles Impede Turnover: The share of Department of Buildings alteration permits unapproved after 30 days is a significant driver of vacancy (1% increase associated with 3.28% increase in vacant retail footage). Liquor license approval times rose from ~50 to ~75 days in 2018. A 1% increase in liquor license approval time is associated with 0.17% increase in retail vacancy.

5. Landmark status was NOT found to contribute to vacancy; in fact, regression analysis shows landmarked retail is associated with lower vacancy rates.

RECOMMENDED ACTIONS:
- Provide tax incentives (tax credits up to 20%) for independent merchandise retailers in high-vacancy retail corridors
- Create single point-of-contact customer service task force for businesses occupying retail space, and waive permitting/inspection fees for businesses taking over long-vacant space
- Incorporate retail demand analysis into neighborhood planning and rezoning decisions

The report includes appendices with regression methodology (fixed effects OLS regression of log vacant retail square footage on explanatory variables at zip code level), neighborhood definitions, and detailed notes on data sources and methodology. Key limitations noted: RPIE data excludes ~25% of retail square footage (smaller buildings under $40,000 assessed value); increased penalties for non-filing beginning in 2014 improved reporting by about 1 million sq ft.

## U.S. Retail Investment Benchmarks 2025: Sales, Vacancy & Rent Trends

This MMCG Invest report (July 2025) analyzes national U.S. retail real estate trends across investment sales, vacancy, rent growth, and development supply, profiling five top markets for 2025 investment. All data is sourced from the MMCG database, derived from the 2025 U.S. Retail National Report.

### Investment Sales Trends
- Total retail investment sales reached **$59 billion in 2024** (8% YoY increase), with Q1 2025 volume rising 11% YoY and preliminary April 2025 figures 45% higher than April 2024.
- Cap rate expansion from 2022-2023 has tapered off; cap rates have largely flattened since mid-2024 with slight upward bias. Higher-yield deals (dollar stores, pharmacies at 7%+ caps) skew averages, but prime assets still command sub-5% caps; most private buyers transact in the 5%-6% cap range.
- Grocery-anchored centers have stabilized (e.g., a Kroger-anchored center traded at 6.1% cap in early 2025). Power centers trade around 7% caps (e.g., a 507,000 SF Arizona power center at 7.0% cap).
- Outlook shifted from negative to neutral-to-positive by mid-2025, with minimal new construction, low vacancy, and steady tenant demand supporting asset values.

### Vacancy Rates by Asset Class
- National retail vacancy: **~4.3%** as of early 2025; only 4.8% of total retail space available for lease at end of Q1 2025 (15 bps above record low). Fastest backfill pace in nearly 15 years.
- Vacancy by type: **Malls 8.9%** (highest), **Power Centers 4.7%**, **Neighborhood/Community Centers 6.4%**, **Strip Centers 5.0%**, **General Retail 2.7%** (lowest, driven by strong single-tenant net lease properties).

### Rent Growth
- National asking rents grew **~1.9% YoY** as of mid-2025, decelerating from 4%+ annual spikes in 2021-2022, in line with pre-pandemic historical average (~1.5-2% annually).
- Core retail sales (excluding e-commerce, gas, autos) rose over 30% nominally (10%+ real) since 2019, while occupied retail space grew under 2% — retail sales per SF has increased substantially.
- **47 of 57 largest retail markets** saw positive rent growth. Sunbelt markets lead; Northeast/Rust Belt and high-cost coastal markets lag.
- Notable market figures: Raleigh, NC (~7.5% YOY rent growth), Tampa, FL (~4.7%), Orange County (~3.6%), East Bay/Oakland (-2.6% decline), Dallas-Fort Worth (~4.4%), Atlanta (~4.2%), Phoenix (~3.8%).
- Forecast: national rent growth of ~1.7% in 2025, stabilizing at inflationary levels thereafter. Wide variation expected between high-growth and low-growth markets.

### Development Pipeline & Supply Constraints
- Since 2020, only ~81 million SF of new retail space added annually (vs. ~300 million SF/year in 2000-2009 and ~128 million SF/year in the 2010s) — roughly one-quarter of early 2000s levels.
- Over **165 million SF of older retail** demolished since 2018; total retail stock grew less than 2% from 2019-2024.
- Only ~21 million SF of newly built retail space (since 2020) is currently available for lease — less than 5% of total available space; 95%+ of availabilities are in older properties.
- Construction costs, financing costs, and cap rates have made ground-up development difficult; new construction is mostly niche (freestanding pad sites pre-leased to nationals, mixed-use ground-floor retail).
- Texas markets account for nearly one-third of all new first-generation retail space available.

### Top 5 Markets for Retail Investment in 2025
1. **Dallas-Fort Worth, TX**: 468+ million SF inventory, ~4.4% YOY rent growth (top 10 nationally), 4.9% vacancy, over 7 million SF under construction (most in country), strong population/job growth.
2. **Atlanta, GA**: ~4.2% YOY rent growth, ~4.2% vacancy, only 0.2% of stock delivered in past year, low-$20s PSF average rents, strong job market.

4. **Phoenix, AZ**: ~3.8% YOY rent growth, ~4.5% vacancy, ~1 million SF absorbed over 12 months (one of highest nationally), ~0.8% of stock under construction.
5. **Raleigh, NC**: ~7.5% YOY rent growth (fastest of any large market), ~2.3% vacancy (among lowest nationally), minimal new construction (~0.5% delivered in past year), booming tech/life sciences hub.

### Conclusion
U.S. retail real estate in 2025 is characterized by near-record occupancy, steady (if modest) rent growth, and reviving capital flows, underpinned by a decade of constrained supply. The outlook is cautiously optimistic — limited new supply, steady consumer spending, and adaptive retailers should keep the sector positive barring a major downturn. SUMMARY:
<summary>
A CNBC article (by Lauren Thomas, August 2020) examines the future of America's struggling malls amid the coronavirus pandemic. Coresight Research estimates that 25% of America's roughly 1,000 malls will close within the next three to five years, with the pandemic accelerating a decline already underway. The article focuses on the question of what to do with "dead malls," particularly the idea (reportedly under discussion between Simon Property Group and Amazon) of converting shuttered department stores into fulfillment centers.

Key obstacles to converting retail space into warehouses include the need for rezoning, which is a lengthy process with low success probability, and the fact that municipalities tax industrial properties at roughly half to two-thirds the rate of commercial properties, giving local governments little financial incentive to rezone. Moody's Analytics real estate economist Victor Calanog emphasized that vacant retail space is not automatically a good candidate for industrial repurposing.

According to Moody's Analytics REIS data, in a post-Covid-19 world, apartment development is expected to fall 15.6%, office development 10%, and retail 15.7%, while industrial development is projected to rise 3.6%. Moody's identified five markets where retail-to-warehouse conversion makes most sense: Central New Jersey, Northern New Jersey, Long Island, Memphis, and Detroit.

The most vulnerable malls are B-, C-, and D-rated properties with lower sales per square foot (an A++ mall can generate up to $1,000 per square foot vs. about $320 for a C+ mall). Roughly 380 C- and D-rated malls exist in the U.S., with Green Street Advisors stating these are "not viable retail centers long term." Tennessee mall owner CBL & Associates planned to file for bankruptcy by October 1, 2020. Even high-end malls face pressure—Bal Harbour Shops in Miami moved to evict Saks Fifth Avenue for ~$1.9 million in unpaid rent since mid-March. About 90% of mall occupants are experiential tenants (movie theaters), department stores, or apparel retailers, making malls the most Covid-vulnerable property type. Alternative uses pondered for dead malls include churches, medical facilities, offices, and apartments—though office space is risky given the working-from-home trend (e.g., JPMorgan shifting to hybrid work, REI selling its Seattle campus).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Just because retail space has gone vacant or remained fallow does not mean that it is automatically a good candidate for repurposing into industrial space," Victor Calanog, head of Moody's Analytics commercial real estate economics division, said. "One cannot simply build industrial buildings in areas zoned for commercial use. Often, that requires rezoning areas — a long and tedious process with a low probability of success.", "State and local governments typically tax industrial properties at anywhere from half to two-thirds the rate of commercial properties, so municipalities have little incentive to rezone areas from commercial to industrial use, as they will collect less tax revenues," Calanog said., "Unfortunately, this whole Covid thing has thrown the experiential pitch out the window. Until we resolve this pandemic, I suspect we are going to be in a holding pattern with hollow retail space. --- SOURCE 8: Retail apocalypse - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retail_apocalypse

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The "retail apocalypse" (also known as "retailpocalypse") refers to the widespread closing of North American brick-and-mortar retail stores, especially large chains, beginning in the 2010s and continuing through the present (2026). The phenomenon spans from 2010 to present and is primarily centered in Northern America, with effects also seen in the UK and Australia.

KEY FACTORS:
- Shift to e-commerce: Online shopping is the main cited factor. Holiday e-commerce sales increased 11-20% from 2015-2016, while brick-and-mortar stores saw only 1.6% growth and physical department stores declined 4.8%. Amazon generates more than half of retail-sales growth (the "Amazon effect").
- Oversupply of shopping malls: Mall growth (1970-2015) was over twice the population growth rate. Accelerated depreciation tax incentives from 1954 artificially accelerated mall investment. Mall visits declined 50% between 2010-2013.
- Experience economy: Consumers shifting disposable income from material goods toward dining out and travel.
- Shrinking middle class: Declining real wages and rising costs creating a "middle-class squeeze," affecting retailers like Macy's, JCPenney, and Sears. Dollar stores (Dollar General, Dollar Tree, Family Dollar) grew but are seen as both symptom and cause of rural independent retailer collapse.
- Poor management: Focus on short-term quarterly dividends, understaffing, inventory mismanagement, and heavy debt from leveraged buyouts by private equity firms.
- COVID-19 pandemic: Exacerbated closures; many retailers filed for bankruptcy. Online shopping boomed during lockdowns—29% of US and 43% of UK consumers said they'd never return to offline shopping.

KEY STATISTICS:
- 2017: more than 12,000 physical stores closed.
- 2019: 9,302 store closings announced (59% jump from 2018), the highest since tracking began in 2012.
- Credit Suisse predicted 25% of US malls could close by 2022.
- Sears fell from 3,500+ stores and 355,000 employees in 2006 to 1,430 stores by 2016, filing bankruptcy in October 2018 with 68,000 employees.
- IHL Group (2019) disputed the "apocalypse" narrative, finding 5+ chains opening stores for every one closing, and that 20 retailers accounted for 75% of all closures.
- Coresight estimated closures would exceed the 2019 record in 2020; by 2022 store openings had again exceeded closings.

MAJOR BANKRUPTCIES (from table): Borders Books (2011), The Bon-Ton (2018), Sears Holdings (2013-2021), JCPenney (2015-2020), Toys "R" Us (2018), J. Crew (2020), Barneys New York (2019), Forever 21 (2019 & 2025), A.C. Moore (2019-2020), Payless ShoeSource (2019-2020), Pier 1 Imports (2020), Neiman Marcus (2020), Tuesday Morning (2020 & 2023), GNC (2020), True Religion (2017 & 2020), Brooks Brothers (2020), Bed Bath & Beyond (2023), Express (2024), Big Lots (2024), Party City (2023 & 2024), Jo-Ann (2024 & 2025), 99 Cents Only Stores (2024), Rite Aid (2023 & 2025), Hudson's Bay (2025).

SURVIVORS/THRIVERS: Discount superstores (Walmart, Target), fast-fashion brands (Zara, H&M), dollar stores, and warehouse clubs (Costco, Sam's Club, BJ's).

CONSEQUENCES: Vacant retail space, dead malls, pop-up retail (e.g., Spirit Halloween in former big-box stores), and a domino effect on suppliers (e.g., Hasbro cited Toys "R" Us loss for lost revenue and layoffs).

STRATEGIES: Survival tied to customer experience, brand reputation, omnichannel integration, and technology adoption—Ikea (AR app), Sephora (smart mirrors), Walmart (supply chain automation), Kohl's (smaller stores + robots), Lowe's (LoweBot). A 2018 ICSC study found opening new stores increases website traffic.

DISSENTING VIEWS: Some economists argue closures are a market correction, not an "apocalypse," and the phrase instills insecurity in the 16 million US retail workers. The article notes its perspective deals primarily with the US and lacks a worldwide view.

The phrase "retail apocalypse" first appeared in print in a 1990s essay by Peter Glen, gaining widespread usage in 2017.

<webpage_content>
[Business](https://www.theatlantic.com/business/)

# The Silent Crisis of Retail Employment

What to do when department-store jobs—or mining and manufacturing jobs—go away

By [Derek Thompson](https://www.theatlantic.com/author/derek-thompson/)

Mike Blake / Reuters

Brick-and-mortar retail is [having a meltdown](https://www.theatlantic.com/business/archive/2017/04/retail-meltdown-of-2017/522384/), and economists are starting to see the effects in the job market.

Overall retail employment has fallen every month this year. Department stores, including Macy’s and JC Penney, have shed [nearly 100,000 jobs](https://mobile.nytimes.com/2017/04/15/business/retail-industry.html) since October—more than the total number of coal miners or steel workers currently employed in the U.S. Even America’s richest areas are getting hit: Employment in New York City clothing stores has [fallen three years in a row](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/SMU36935614244810001A), the longest period of decline on record, going back to the early 1990s.

When some industries lose workers, they win the consolation prize of empty political promises to turn back time. During the presidential campaign, Donald Trump and Hillary Clinton went up and down Appalachia—and far beyond—to lament the job losses suffered by manufacturers and miners. The loss of these jobs has been devastating to many cities and towns. But department stores have lost [18 times](https://www.nytimes.com/2017/04/17/opinion/why-dont-all-jobs-matter.html) more workers than coal mining since 2001.

So, how has the retail bloodletting been so much quieter than the decline in mining and manufacturing? There are several plausible explanations. First, mining and manufacturing jobs are geographically concentrated. Sixty percent of coal-mining jobs are in [just four states](https://www.eia.gov/coal/annual/pdf/table18.pdf): West Virginia, Kentucky, Pennsylvania, and Wyoming. Retail is spread more evenly across the country, so there are “mining towns,” which politicians can visit and photographers can capture and where the pain runs especially deep, in a way there are not “mall towns.” Second, as Slate Chief Political Correspondent Jamelle Bouie [tweeted](https://twitter.com/jbouie/status/853283089598033920), the demographics of a job can determine its political salience. Coal mining is still 95 percent white and 95 percent male. Department store workers are 40 percent minority and just 40 percent male. The emphasis on work that is white, male, and burly may represent an implicit bias against the working class of the modern service economy, which is more diverse and female. Third, mining and manufacturing jobs feed into a national nostalgia for the mid-century economy, with its unionized workforce, economic growth, and high pay for men without much education.

But the decline of clothing-store jobs has something in common with the demise of manufacturing and mining jobs, too. They are both victims of the familiar forces of globalization and technology, which have conspired to make clothes cheaper and accessible online. Both forces can make the country richer while specific areas suffer. For example, the loss of Ohio manufacturing jobs or an exurban department store can have severe local costs—like high poverty in an eastern Ohio steel town, or the shuttering of a downtown mall—while elsewhere the country flourishes, with rising industrial productivity and better access to cheaper clothes.

Altogether, the destruction of jobs in retail, mining, and manufacturing raises a thorny question: Is it really so bad when one industry’s jobs go away, if the country as a whole is getting richer and the number of jobs is still growing?

Indeed, as retail has moved online, some economists argue that e-commerce has created more—and, perhaps, better paying—work. The economist Michael Mandel estimates that since the Great Recession began, the e-commerce sector has created [355,000 new jobs](https://www.forbes.com/sites/realspin/2017/04/03/how-e-commerce-is-raising-pay-and-creating-jobs-around-the-country/#726546d56dff), compared to about 50,000 total jobs lost in physical retail stores. Much of that growth has come from large fulfillment centers in warehouses. Warehousing is not used exclusively for e-commerce, but the change in warehousing jobs is [highly correlated with Amazon’s job growth in the state](https://twitter.com/MichaelMandel/status/840285859878445056); since 2009, warehousing employment has soared by almost 50 percent. Fulfillment centers pay [26 percent better](http://www.progressivepolicy.org/blog/ecommerce-added-almost-100k-jobs-past-year/) than general retail jobs, and warehouse wages are currently growing [twice as fast as the national average](https://www.wsj.com/articles/online-retailers-new-warehouses-heat-up-local-job-markets-1491739203).

Politicians are often nostalgia merchants, selling the irreplaceable virtues of whatever cultural or economic norm is in its twilight. In the 20th century, they [mourned](https://www.nytimes.com/2016/10/09/magazine/why-are-politicians-so-obsessed-with-manufacturing.html) the wilting of the agricultural industry, just as they currently lament the death of factories. But in an economy that will become increasingly digitized, automated, and otherwise inflected with new technologies like self-driving cars and artificial intelligence, Americans can’t get too precious about any particular job or industry.

Instead, lawmakers should be focused on reducing human suffering as some job sectors shrink or disappear altogether. That might include universal health care that isn’t tied to any one specific company and moving vouchers to help workers manage the transition to a new area for work. Overall it requires an approach that is the opposite of then-candidate Trump’s message on the campaign: Not “how can we rebuild the economy of about 40 years ago and freeze it in carbonite?” but rather “what sort of federal policies are best for an economy that might be embarking on a period of industrial churn?”

The former question probably makes for better politics. It is easier to build a coalition through demonization, the establishment of an evil *them*—like, Democrats and their environmental regulations—to crystallize a politically motivated *us*—like, West Virginia mining towns. It is much harder to say the truth: Technology and trade make America richer as a country, but the winnings are distributed unevenly, and it’s the responsibility of government to improve the distribution without making everybody poorer in the process.

### About the Author

[![](https://cdn.theatlantic.com/thumbor/X_1bfJ1Wyog_MgZ0yvyRliDMEbI=/300x0:1068x768/120x120/media/None/Derek_Thompson_grey/original.png)](https://www.theatlantic.com/author/derek-thompson/)

  # How Is Online Shopping Affecting Retail Employment?

  Jason Bram and Nicole Gorton

  It’s been said that if you want to know how the economy is doing, look at how many people are carrying shopping bags. That adage may not hold so well today. The rise of the internet and e-commerce over the past two decades has chipped away at the market share of “brick and mortar” retailers. But it’s only been in the past few years that this shift in market share has had a noteworthy effect on retail employment. In this post, we focus on national and local employment trends in two categories of retail—department stores and nonstore retailers—and try to assess how the surge in online shopping has affected local labor markets across the United States.

  First, let’s look at trends in online retail sales over the past two decades. As shown in the chart below, online sales have grown strongly, with their share of total retail sales increasing from 2.5 percent in the mid-1990s to around 5 percent in the mid-2000s, then doubling again to exceed 10 percent today.

  Next, let’s look at employment trends for traditional retailers and nonstore retailers. Since total retail employment includes job figures for gas stations, auto dealers, and other establishments that are less exposed to the e-commerce wave, we will focus our comparison here on department stores—a category of retail that employs a lot of people and seems particularly susceptible to competition from the internet. In addition, department stores have seen steeper job losses than other types of retailers in recent years and may be among the most vulnerable to the rise of online shopping.

  As the chart below illustrates, employment at both department stores and nonstore retailers cycled up and down with the economy until early 2012. At that point, however, there was an abrupt shift: the two series began moving in opposite directions. That year, department stores slashed over 200,000 jobs on net, while nonstore retail employment rose by a small fraction of that figure. Since early 2013, department stores have eliminated roughly 80,000 jobs, on net, while nonstore retailers have added roughly 100,000. Both of these trends show no sign of abating and, if anything, recent reports of widespread department store closings—such as these from [March](http://money.cnn.com/2017/03/17/news/companies/jcpenney-stores-closing/index.html), [May](http://www.businessinsider.com/macys-might-shut-down-more-stores-2017-5), [June](https://www.usatoday.com/story/money/2017/06/08/nordstrom-department-store-private/102622170/), and [July](https://www.usatoday.com/story/money/2017/07/07/sears-holdings-kmart-store-closures/459277001/)—suggest that this pattern may be intensifying in 2017.

  The overall employment picture is not all bad. While department stores have been shedding jobs, other segments of the retail sector have posted steady to rising job counts. Moreover, as noted above, much of this churn is just a shift of jobs from one industry to another: over the past year, nonstore retailers have added almost as many jobs (29,000) as department stores have cut (32,000). So why should this be a concern? One reason is that the geographic distribution of jobs is very different for online retailers versus brick-and-mortar outfits. In other words, areas that are losing a lot of department store jobs may not be the ones gaining online retail jobs.

  Department stores have an incentive to spread out their staff in proportion with the distribution of the general population: because they do their business in person and there is demand for their products throughout the country, they employ people everywhere.

  Online retailers don’t have the same geographic constraints—that is, they don’t have to be where their customers are to make a transaction. In this sense, they are more like wholesale distributors. In contrast with traditional retailers, online sellers tend to concentrate all or most of their staff in one or a few locations: it is more expensive to have people all over the place if they don’t need to be. Although the largest online retailers do have multiple distribution centers around the country, they still tend to have considerably fewer locations than the largest department store chains. Though total employment across department stores and e-tailers combined has not changed much at the national level since late 2012, there have been significant differences across counties: the areas that are losing department store jobs are often not the same ones gaining nonstore jobs.

  To examine these trends more closely, we looked at local employment data across the fifty states, as well as in Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico. We were able to analyze detailed retail industry employment data for roughly 700 counties, areas that account for 82 percent of jobs nationwide. Such data are not available for more than 2,000 rural counties, however; to include those areas in our analysis, we have combined statistics on rural counties by state. In New York, for example, we had detailed data for only thirty-five of the state’s sixty-two counties, so we combined the other twenty-seven into one area, which we can think of as a really big, sparsely populated county. When these amalgamations are added in, we have a nationwide data set spanning 742 “counties” (as we will call them for simplicity).

  Between 2012 and 2016, 561 (about 75 percent) of the counties we studied lost department store jobs. While a majority of those counties did see some increase in nonstore retail jobs, four-fifths of these counties lost out on net—that is, department stores shed more jobs than nonstore retailers added. Of those counties that came out ahead—that is, gained more in nonstore retail jobs than they lost in department store jobs—some came out way ahead: none did better than King County, Washington, home of Amazon.com. In 2012, King County’s nonstore employment represented 1.4 percent of the total employment in the county; by 2016, that share had doubled to 2.8 percent. This seems especially remarkable since, at the national level, nonstore retail jobs had merely edged up from 0.4 percent of total employment to 0.5 percent during the same period.

  But simple job counts are not the only relevant measure of labor market conditions. How do the jobs being lost at department stores compare to those being gained in online retailing? For people who lose department store jobs, is finding a new job simply a matter of relocating to areas where there are lots of nonstore job openings?

  If wages are a rough proxy of employers’ demand for certain skillsets, then these two categories of jobs would seem to have different skill requirements: in 2012, the average online retail job paid slightly over $50,000, while the average department store job paid just $20,500. By 2016, the average wage for nonstore workers exceeded $59,000, while the average wage for department store workers remained roughly the same. Part of this pay gap reflects the fact that department store jobs are more likely to be part-time. Nevertheless, the difference is staggering, suggesting that nonstore retailers demand a different type of worker than department stores do. So, even if laid-off department store workers were willing and able to move to, say, King County, they might lack the skillsets sought by e-tailers.

  What Does This Mean for Job Growth across Counties?

  As we’ve seen, many counties with steep declines in department store employment have not seen much, if any, offsetting gain in nonstore retail jobs. Moreover, these counties tend to be less urban and have lower levels of income. However, there does not seem to be much of a correlation between department store job losses and trends in overall employment; in other words, counties with sizable declines in department store jobs are not predominantly counties that are doing poorly in general. It remains to be seen how the widespread retail closures announced in 2017 break out geographically.

  Of course, it is important to remember that the labor market effects of online retailing go well beyond the retail sector. A more thorough analysis would consider the indirect effects of e-commerce on warehousing, local freight trucking, and couriers and messengers—three industries that have seen fairly robust job growth in recent years. Moreover, these types of jobs would likely be distributed a bit more evenly across the country. And finally, the trend toward online shopping may enable small manufacturers to flourish pretty much anywhere: given the ability to deal directly with customers, they would no longer need to develop distribution networks or build large inventories.

args.summary:
This webpage is a Liberty Street Economics blog post (October 5, 2017) by Jason Bram and Nicole Gorton of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's Research and Statistics Group, examining how the rise of online shopping has affected retail employment in the United States.

Key findings:
- Online sales' share of total retail sales grew from 2.5% in the mid-1990s to around 5% in the mid-2000s, then doubled to exceed 10% by 2017.
- Employment at department stores and nonstore retailers moved in tandem until early 2012, then diverged sharply. In 2012, department stores cut over 200,000 jobs on net. Since early 2013, department stores eliminated roughly 80,000 jobs while nonstore retailers added roughly 100,000.
- Over the past year, nonstore retailers added almost as many jobs (29,000) as department stores cut (32,000).
- The geographic distribution of jobs differs greatly: department stores spread staff proportionally with population, while online retailers concentrate staff in one or a few locations (similar to wholesale distributors).
- Data was analyzed across roughly 700 counties (82% of jobs nationwide), with rural counties combined by state to create a dataset of 742 "counties." Between 2012 and 2016, 561 (about 75%) of counties lost department store jobs; four-fifths of these lost out on net (department stores shed more jobs than nonstore retailers added).
- King County, Washington (home of Amazon.com) gained the most: nonstore employment grew from 1.4% of county employment in 2012 to 2.8% in 2016, versus a national rise from 0.4% to 0.5%.
- Wages differ starkly: average online retail job paid slightly over $50,000 in 2012 (exceeding $59,000 by 2016) versus $20,500 for department store jobs (roughly unchanged by 2016), reflecting different skill requirements and more part-time work in department stores.
- Counties with steep department store declines tend to be less urban with lower incomes, but there is little correlation between department store job losses and overall employment trends in those counties.
- The analysis notes indirect effects of e-commerce on warehousing, local freight trucking, and couriers/messengers (which have seen robust job growth), and notes online shopping may enable small manufacturers to flourish anywhere.

We were also mothers and fathers, professors and students, sharing experiences in nature, sharing what our fears (monsters) are and how to slay them. Ari Lightman Courtney Graybill Laura Cantor Karina Dolgin Anita Srinivasan Grant Anderson Saranathan Govindarajan Kathy Doyle Thomas Madhav Kondle Stephanie Leone Dave Finnegan Guillaume Ledieu Matt Ezyk [Likes: 33, Comments: 5]; **Kelly Goetsch** (2d): I had the pleasure of joining NRF’s Nexus event last week, which focused on agentic commerce. Dozens of C-levels from major U.S. retailers and brands. Here's where the industry is at with agentic commerce as of July 2026: In short: not very far. So many of the discussions over drinks / dinners were debates about what agentic commerce even is. On one side, you have people saying it’s just chatbots on a brand.com , while others say it’s an autonomous AI agent buying something proactively on behalf of a shopper. I’ve long-defined the spectrum as: 1) On-site chatbot 2) Human buying through AI chatbot (compare toasters with a “Buy it now” button) 3) Human tasking AI to buy something (buy this brand of dog food for me every month, don't care where it's from) 4) AI proactively buying something on behalf of a human (AI sees you’re going on vacation and orders sun screen) Lots of blind pressure from boards and CEOs to do more, without defining what “more” looks like, never mind the fact that 1 is largely fake AI and 2-4 doesn’t really exist (2 did for like 10 minutes…it’s complicated). I always think back to the quote from Paul Gaffney in which he said “This is what happens when the hype cycle invents a word like ’agentic’ with no actual meaning. An empty vessel into which is poured various flavors of hopes and dreams.” Fear of losing first party data was quite palpable. In a world where ChatGPT or Claude become the new browser, they become the ultimate arbiter of which retailers are even surfaced and what data those retailers get. It’s not at all a stretch to imagine a future five years out where 1) the brand.com is mostly dead, 2) ChatGPT / Claude become the new web / browser, 3) retailers have to pay to be surfaced at all, and 4) those retailers only get raw orders to ship, with no 1st party data. It was telling that nobody from OpenAI or Anthropic was there. A few smiling faces would have gone a long way in building good will and relationships. This is a small clubby world that runs on trust and reputation. Interlopers from big tech have historically not done well. In practical terms, most in attendance are cleaning up their product catalogs and just starting to publish their catalog to LLMs. A few were doing actual enrichment for LLMs. A few were working with Stripe ACS. More experimentation at this point. If you look at the math of this - a retailer could dump $10m into agentic commerce and not see $1 in return - yet. Whether public or PE-owned, these execs have to deliver results tomorrow - not next year. I get it. If you're feeling lost and behind on agentic commerce - don't worry. You're in great company. We're all figuring this out together. As Jason Goldberg said in a recent episode of the Jason & Scot show: "When I’m retired, agentic commerce will probably go down as the most important thing that happened during my career." Big thanks to Jill Dvorak , Mary Kita , Susan Newman and the rest of the NRF team for an outstanding event. The page's recent posts center heavily on two major NRF events: #NRFNexus 2026 (focused on AI and agentic commerce, sponsored by American Express) and #NRF2026: Retail's Big Show Europe (scheduled for September 15, 2026 in Paris). Key themes from event posts include the current state of agentic commerce in retail, which appears to be in early experimentation stages. A detailed post by Kelly Goetsch outlines the industry's status on agentic commerce as of July 2026, noting that most retailers are not far along, with debates over what the term even means. He describes a spectrum from on-site chatbots to fully autonomous AI purchasing, and expresses concerns about retailers losing first-party data as AI chatbots become potential new browsers/arbiters of retail visibility. Other posts discuss leadership insights from Ryan Meyer (CEO of Hammitt), Jacob Elggren (co-founder of Andar), Julie Averill (author of "Chief Impact Officer"), and Brian Beitler of QVC Group. A post by Karissa Price highlights the importance of human connection at #NRFNexus despite the AI-focused theme.
