--- SOURCE 5: High Frequency Business Dynamics in the United States ... ---
URL: https://www2.census.gov/ces/wp/2021/CES-WP-21-06.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a CES research paper (CES 21-06, March 2021) by Catherine Buffington, Daniel Chapman, Emin Dinlersoz, Lucia Foster (U.S. Census Bureau) and John Haltiwanger (University of Maryland) examining high-frequency business dynamics during the COVID-19 pandemic using two new Census Bureau data products: the Small Business Pulse Survey (SBPS) and Business Formation Statistics (BFS).

KEY FINDINGS:
1. Existing small businesses experienced sharp declines in activity, sentiment, and expectations early in the pandemic. While indicators improved somewhat, they remained substantially negative through the first week of January 2021. The improvement was not monotonic—conditions improved in Summer 2020 but worsened at the end of 2020.
2. There is substantial sectoral variation: Accommodation and Food Services were hit especially hard compared to Finance and Insurance. Even in Finance and Insurance, small businesses exhibited negative growth indicators for all weeks from late April 2020 through early 2021.
3. After an initial decline, there was a strong surge in new business applications in 2020 (highest year on record), particularly in Retail Trade and Non-store Retailers (e-commerce). The surge was most apparent in the second half of 2020.
4. The pandemic may lead to lasting structural changes: sectors hit hard for existing small businesses are seeing surges in new business applications.
5. Adverse impact on revenue was greater than impact on employment, partly due to decreases in hours rather than employment (suggestive of labor hoarding). By the last week of Phase 3, 84.1% of businesses did not change employment.
6. About 74% of small businesses in the SBPS received PPP loans. Cash on hand was limited, highlighting the precarious nature of small business operations.
7. Remote work increased significantly but varied by sector (Information had highest at 79.6%; Accommodation and Food Services lowest at 21.7%). Some businesses pivoted to new goods/services (especially Educational Services, Accommodation and Food Services, Information) and many more pivoted to new delivery modes.
8. Geographically, the initial decline in business applications was concentrated in the Northeast and West, with recovery emphasized in the South and Midwest.

SBPS METHODOLOGY:
- Sample drawn from 2017 Economic Census for single-location businesses with 1-499 employees and $1000+ revenue
- ~100,000 emails sent weekly; ~25,000 responses weekly (25% response rate)
- Three phases: April-June, August-October, November-January
- Overall Sentiment Index (OSI) ranges from -1 (most negative) to +1 (most positive)
- Sectors consistently at top of OSI: Finance and Insurance, Construction, Retail Trade. At bottom: Arts/Entertainment/Recreation, Educational Services, Accommodation and Food Services
- By end of Phase 3, 64.9% of Accommodation and Food Services businesses had large negative effects vs. 13.7% in Finance and Insurance

KEY SECTOR STATISTICS:
- First week of Phase 1: 74.0% of businesses saw revenue decreases vs. 5.9% increases. Last week of Phase 3: 56.1% of Accommodation and Food Services had revenue decreases vs. 22.1% in Finance and Insurance.
- Employment: Finance and Insurance grew by ~50,000 jobs in 2020; Accommodation and Food Services shrank by ~3 million jobs (BLS data).
- By end of 2020, Finance and Insurance revenue was close to pre-pandemic levels; Accommodation and Food Services remained below.
- Supply chain issues: Retail Trade had largest percentage with domestic supplier issues (48.0%); Finance and Insurance smallest (5.0%).
- Operating capacity: about half of businesses noted decreased capacity relative to one year ago by end of Phase 3; 42.9% reported no change.

LIMITATIONS/CAVEATS: Seven considerations for interpreting SBPS results include non-response bias for business closures, reliance on email addresses, single-location business focus, willingness to respond to federal surveys, overrepresentation of adversely impacted businesses, and representation of young businesses.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Existing small businesses experienced very sharp declines in activity, business sentiment, and expectations early in the pandemic. While there has been some recovery since the early days of the pandemic, small businesses continued to exhibit indicators of negative growth, business sentiment, and expectations through the first week of January 2021."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: News | US Store Closings Outstrip Openings in Break From Past Two Years ---
URL: https://www.costar.com/article/1283357809/us-store-closings-outstrip-openings-in-break-from-past-two-years

SUMMARY:
<summary>
U.S. retail store closings have surpassed openings for the first time this year, according to a Coresight Research report dated August 9. Year to date, 4,548 store closings have outpaced 4,426 announced openings, resulting in 122 net store closings. This marks a shift from the previous two years when openings edged closings (2022: net 1,575 openings; 2023: net 295 openings). The surge is largely driven by Big Lots significantly increasing its planned closures by 258 locations, according to John Harmon, managing director of technology research at Coresight. The trend reflects a spurt of Chapter 11 bankruptcy filings in recent months, though the national retail vacancy rate remains very tight at 4.1% according to CoStar data. Retailers shuttering locations include Conn's HomePlus, Badcock's Home Furniture & More, LL Flooring Holdings (94 stores), Buca di Beppo, Rubio's, World of Beer, J.C. Penney (12 closed, plans for 3 more plus one in 2025), Target (one store in East Palo Alto, California), and Party City (18 closed year to date). However, Brandon Svec, national director of U.S. retail analytics for CoStar Group, said this is not a "resumption of the retail apocalypse" seen in 2018-2020, noting demand for retail space still outpaces supply. Home improvement retailers have been hit hardest by high inflation and high interest rates that are slowing home sales and consumer spending in that sector; Home Depot reported expected same-store sales to drop 3% to 4% in 2024. Barrie Scardina of Cushman & Wakefield noted that the square footage of openings (79.5 million sq ft) still exceeds that of closings (67 million sq ft). Bright spots include openings from Dollar General, Burlington Stores, TJX Cos., Havertys, Publix, Sleep Number, Daiso, Murphy USA, Rag & Bone, and Gucci (at American Dream mall in New Jersey). Svec attributed closures to sector-specific weakness (housing, furniture, appliances) and companies that were given temporary lifelines by the pandemic now "paying the piper" as operations normalize.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"It's not, in my opinion, a resumption of the retail apocalypse that we saw in 2018, 2019, 2020 where we were seeing so many stores closed," Brandon Svec, national director of U.S. retail analytics for CoStar Group, told CoStar News. "There are still a substantial amount of tenants from a broad range of sectors looking for space.", "Until two weeks ago, the lines [of closings and openings] were just tracking each other as expected," John Harmon, managing director of technology research at Coresight, said., "Once sales normalized, once operations normalize, their poor merchandising, poor location strategies, what have you came back to roost. And we're now paying the piper that we should have and would have probably paid in 2021 had it not been for those tailwinds that they got from the pandemic," Svec said., "We have too much retail space in certain locations. We have too much space in certain formats. But overall, I think we are still in a very tight space-balance position across most of the sector. And that's not changed by these more recent store closure announcements," Svec said., "When people are unable to go out to the market and buy a house or invest in their house, it affects everything else," Daniel Gielchinsky, a partner at DGIM Law and a bankruptcy attorney, told CoStar News.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: Coresight predicts record 25,000 retail stores will close in 2020 ---
URL: https://www.cnbc.com/2020/06/09/coresight-predicts-record-25000-retail-stores-will-close-in-2020.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This CNBC article (by Lauren Thomas) reports that U.S. retailers could announce between 20,000 and 25,000 store closures in 2020 due to the coronavirus pandemic, according to tracking by Coresight Research. This would mark a record for the industry, surpassing the more than 9,300 locations closed in 2019. Notably, 55% to 60% of the closures are expected to be in America's malls. --- SOURCE 11: Does Apple Anchor a Shopping Mall? The Effect of the ... ---
URL: https://www.hbs.edu/ris/download.aspx?name=20-066.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This working paper (20-066) by Doug J. Chung (Harvard Business School), Kyoungwon Seo (Seoul National University), and Reo Song (California State University, Long Beach) examines the effect of technology stores—company-owned Apple and Microsoft retail stores—on shopping mall configuration. The study uses a structural model that considers endogenous location decisions of retail stores, accounting for both market characteristics and spillover effects of co-location.

Key data and context: The retail sector generated over $5 trillion in U.S. sales in 2017 (approximately 26% of GDP), with e-commerce only accounting for 7.3% of total retail sales in 2015. The study analyzes 1,196 regional and super-regional shopping malls with 6,753 anchor stores, sourced from the Directory of Major Malls. Apple opened its first physical store in 2001 and had 506 retail stores across 25 countries by 2018 (272 in the U.S.). Apple and Microsoft stores were present in 168 and 84 malls respectively. 59.5% of Apple stores co-located with upscale stores, while only 9.5% co-located with discount stores.

Methodology: The paper employs a simultaneous-move discrete game of complete information with 11 players (anchor store types) and more than 100 parameters. Three key methodological innovations are introduced: (1) addressing multiple equilibria by estimating equilibrium selection from observed data using the Bajari, Hong, and Ryan (2010) selection function method; (2) developing an efficient "augmented simulator" that requires only 64 random draws to achieve higher accuracy than 1,000 draws from a traditional simple simulator; and (3) utilizing GPGPU (general-purpose computing on graphics processing units) technology, which runs estimation more than 10,000 times faster than traditional methods (reducing 3-hour computation from what would take 1,250 days). Bayesian estimation via MCMC (Metropolis algorithm) is used.

Key findings:
- Population and income are key drivers of retail store profits. New anchors (Apple, Microsoft) and traditional upscale anchors locate in affluent, populated areas with younger demographics and small household sizes (likely urban). Discount and midscale stores locate in lower-income, less-populated areas.
- Traditional upscale stores prefer high-income areas with higher average age (traditionally affluent areas), while new anchors prefer high-income regions with younger demographics.
- Competitive effects dominate within and across store categories for traditional department stores, except positive agglomeration effects exist within midscale and within upscale stores.
- Apple has a profound effect on many players: negative spillover to discount stores, positive spillover to upscale stores and Microsoft stores. However, no player—traditional or new—affects Apple's profits, establishing Apple as the "ultimate anchor store."
- No evidence that the highest joint-payoff equilibrium is more frequently selected (the coefficient for equilibrium selection was negative and statistically insignificant), contradicting common assumptions in prior literature.
- Counterfactual analyses show Apple's entry substantially increases the profit/entry probability of upscale department stores but decreases that of discount stores. Even under favorable market conditions, some stores would not enter due to competitive entry of other stores.
- Mall developers should carefully consider whether to lure new anchor stores: while they increase foot traffic and mall performance (sales productivity rose from $383/sq ft in 2009 to $513 in 2018), they may change mall configuration by attracting high-income consumers and pushing out midscale and discount stores.

The paper differs from Vitorino (2012), which used an incomplete-information framework, MPEC estimation, did not address multiple equilibria, and examined only traditional anchor stores.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The results show that competitive effects dominate within and across store categories for traditional department stores, but agglomeration effects exist between technology stores and upscale department stores. The presence of an Apple store, for example, attracts high-income consumers, promoting the entry of upscale stores and the exit of midscale and discount stores."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 14: The Economic History of the Shopping Mall — and Its Future (Yes, It Does Have One) | Richmond Fed ---
URL: https://www.richmondfed.org/publications/research/econ_focus/2022/q3_economic_history

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an Econ Focus article (Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, Third Quarter 2022) by Matthew Wells examining the economic history, decline, and future of the American shopping mall.

**Early History:**
- Baltimore's Roland Park Business Block (1907) is recognized by Guinness World Records as the world's first shopping center, offering six shops in an English Tudor-style complex.
- Early outdoor shopping areas followed with parking, including Richmond's Cary Court (1938), Kansas City's Country Club Plaza (1923), and Dallas' Highland Park Shopping Village (1931).
- Northland Center in Southfield, Michigan (1954), was the first planned shopping mall pairing a department store with smaller retail stores, but declined in the 1980s-90s and closed fully by 2015, remaining vacant.

**Key Figures & Developments:**
- Victor Gruen, an Austrian-born architect, designed Northland Center (1954) and Southdale Shopping Center in Edina, Minn. (1956), the first enclosed, temperature-controlled mall in the U.S. He aimed to bring downtown shopping to suburbs, which he saw as chaotic "avenues of horror."
- Southdale had 5,200 parking spaces; Northland had 8,344. Malls featured inward-facing shops, enclosed atriums, public art, fishponds, and live trees.
- The Community Builders' Handbook (Urban Land Institute, 1947) classified malls into neighborhood centers (up to 20 shops), community centers (20-40 stores), and regional centers (40-100 stores with full-size department stores).
- James Rouse introduced the food court at New Jersey's Paramus Park Mall (1974); JLL reported in 2019 that malls with good food courts enjoy ~25% more sales.
- Architect Jon Jerde designed Horton Plaza (1985), Mall of America (1992), and Universal CityWalk (1993), influenced by Ray Bradbury's "fun house logic" manifesto — malls with winding walkways, multiple levels, and integrated entertainment.

**Decline:**
- Over 1,500 malls were built between 1956 and 2005. Average monthly mall time per consumer fell from 12 hours in 1980 to 4 hours in 1990.
- Green Street Advisors (2014) predicted 15% of malls would close within a decade; Credit Suisse (2017) predicted over 25% (200+ malls) would close by 2022.
- ~7,000 retail stores closed in 2017; CoStar reported a record 145 million square feet of vacant retail space in 2018.
- Three causes of decline cited: (1) overbuilding (24 sq ft of retail per American vs. 4.6 in UK and 2.8 in China), (2) rise of online shopping, (3) middle-class consumers abandoning department stores for discounters like Target and Kohl's during the Great Recession (360 mall-based department stores closed 2016-2020).
- COVID-19: Moody's Analytics reported regional mall vacancy spiked to a record 11.4% in Q1 2021 (up from 10.5%); forecasters suggested over one-third of malls would permanently close.

**Resilience & Future:**
- Despite predictions, the ~1,150 malls in the U.S. have stayed consistent over the past three years. ~86% of retail sales still occur in physical stores (down from 88% pre-pandemic).
- Retailers announced 3,694 store openings vs. 1,385 closures as of April 2022 (Coresight Research).
- Malls are adapting by adding diverse/higher-end food options (e.g., Westfield Santa Anita in Arcadia, Calif., added Asian offerings including the first U.S. Uncle Tetsu Japanese Cheesecake), and repurposing vacant department store spaces into "experiential" uses like theaters, arcades, libraries, and gyms (fitness space in malls up 70% since 2013).
- Mixed-use redevelopment is a growing trend: if just 10% of Greater Boston's 3,000 strip malls were retrofitted, it could add 124,000 new housing units. Northland Center is being redeveloped into a mixed-use development with 1,500 apartments, 254 lofts, and "Hudson City Market."

**Key Expert Quotes:**
- Tom McGee (ICSC President/CEO): "If the pandemic didn't cause a dramatic decline in the number of these centers, then almost nothing will."
- McGee: "Ultimately, it's a marketplace. People want to go to a place that has the best collection of retailers and restaurants that fit their needs."
- Alexandra Lange (author, Meet Me by the Fountain): thriving malls "continue to feel special, like they are up to date in terms of their décor and their offerings."
- June Williamson (CUNY professor): "We've got all this land that's already distributed within existing neighborhoods and cities. I think there's a lot of potential there."
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: The Silent Crisis of Retail Employment - The Atlantic ---
URL: https://www.theatlantic.com/business/archive/2017/04/the-silent-crisis-of-retail-employment/523428

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This opinion piece by Derek Thompson (published in The Atlantic, April 2017) examines why the crisis in retail employment has received far less political and media attention than job losses in mining and manufacturing, despite being far larger in scale. Key points include:

- Retail employment fell every month in 2017, with department stores like Macy's and JC Penney shedding nearly 100,000 jobs since October—more than the total number of coal miners or steel workers currently employed in the U.S.
- Department stores have lost 18 times more workers than coal mining since 2001.
- New York City clothing store employment has fallen three years in a row, the longest decline on record since the early 1990s.

The author offers three explanations for why retail job losses have been quieter than mining/manufacturing declines: (1) mining and manufacturing jobs are geographically concentrated (60% of coal-mining jobs are in just four states: West Virginia, Kentucky, Pennsylvania, and Wyoming), creating "mining towns" with visible pain, unlike retail which is spread evenly; (2) demographics—coal mining is 95% white and 95% male, while department store workers are 40% minority and 40% male, suggesting implicit bias against the more diverse and female modern service workforce; and (3) mining and manufacturing feed national nostalgia for the mid-century unionized economy.

However, all three industries are victims of globalization and technology. The author notes that economist Michael Mandel estimates e-commerce has created 355,000 new jobs since the Great Recession compared to ~50,000 jobs lost in physical retail. Warehousing employment has soared nearly 50% since 2009, highly correlated with Amazon's job growth. Fulfillment centers pay 26% better than general retail and warehouse wages are growing twice as fast as the national average.

Thompson argues politicians are "nostalgia merchants" who lament dying industries rather than addressing the reality that technology and trade make America richer but distribute winnings unevenly. He recommends policies like universal healthcare not tied to employers and moving vouchers to help workers transition, instead of trying to freeze the economy in a past era. He concludes the Trump campaign's approach of demonization (e.g., blaming environmental regulations) is politically easier but less honest than acknowledging the need for government to improve distribution of economic gains without making everyone poorer.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: Decline in Retail Jobs Felt Entirely by Women ---
URL: https://iwpr.org/articles/decline-in-retail-jobs-felt-entirely-by-women

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the Institute for Women's Policy Research (IWPR), published December 18, 2017, analyzes U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) employment data to examine gender disparities in retail job losses. Over the year from November 2016 to November 2017, women gained 985,000 jobs overall while men gained 1,086,000. Retail Trade suffered the greatest job losses of any industry during this period, and women shouldered the entirety of those losses—women lost 160,300 retail jobs between October 2016 and October 2017, while men actually gained 106,000 retail jobs. Women's share of all retail trade jobs fell from 50.4 to 49.6 percent. The losses were concentrated in general merchandising stores, where women lost jobs while men gained 87,800 positions; women fell from 64 percent to 60.4 percent of General Merchandise Store workers. Women also saw losses in Clothing and Clothing Accessories stores, while men experienced losses in Food and Beverage Stores and Sporting Goods, Hobby, Book, and Music Stores. Both men and women saw gains in Nonstore Retailers, Motor Vehicle and Parts Dealers, and Building Material and Garden Supply Stores. The analysis notes that women's sustained retail job losses over the last year represent the longest stretch of losses in the industry for either gender since the Great Recession, with men's retail declines preceding women's before the recession and men's gains preceding women's during recovery. The report was prepared by Jennifer Clark, Emma Williams-Baron, and Heidi Hartmann, Ph.D., at IWPR.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 3: Retail trade employment: before, during, and after the ... ---
URL: https://www.bls.gov/opub/btn/volume-11/retail-trade-employment-before-during-and-after-the-pandemic.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics' "Beyond the Numbers" publication (Vol. 11, No. 4, April 2022) by Daniel Dorfman examines retail trade employment trends before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic, using data from the BLS Employment Projections program.

KEY TRENDS AND FINDINGS:

**Pre-Pandemic (2010-2019):**
- Retail employment grew from a Great Recession low of 14.4 million workers in 2010 to a peak of 15.8 million in 2017 (1.3% average annual growth), then declined by approximately 200,000 jobs from 2017-2019 (0.7% annual decline) due to e-commerce competition, thin sales margins, and technological disruption.
- Seven retail industries drove the 2017-19 contraction. General merchandise stores and clothing stores each accounted for ~29% of the decline; sporting goods, hobby, musical instrument, and bookstores accounted for 19.3%. These three together accounted for 77.6% of the sector's decline.
- Supporting industries grew significantly: couriers and messengers grew 54.4% and warehousing and storage grew 86.1% from 2010-2019, versus retail's 8.1% growth.

**During the Pandemic (2019-2020):**
- The retail sector lost almost 800,000 jobs in 2020 (vs. ~200,000 from 2017-19). E-commerce support industries (couriers/messengers, warehousing/storage) gained a combined ~300,000 jobs.
- Clothing stores accounted for 38.6% of total retail sector employment loss in 2020. Six industries (motor vehicle and parts dealers, gasoline stations, miscellaneous store retailers, clothing stores, furniture stores, and health/personal care stores) accounted for more than three-quarters of retail jobs lost.
- General merchandise stores fared relatively better (only 1.5% decline in 2020 vs. 29.2% in 2017-19), because warehouse clubs and supercenters selling essential goods experienced employment gains.

**Projections (2020-2030):**
- Retail trade is projected to lose ~587,000 jobs (4.0% of 2020 employment) over 2020-30, the largest projected employment decline of any sector. Retail trade's share of total employment is projected to fall from 9.7% (2020) to 8.6% (2030).
- Largest projected declines: food and beverage stores (-257,500 jobs, -8.3%) and general merchandise stores (-233,500 jobs, -7.7%), together accounting for 83.7% of retail jobs lost.
- Projected to gain employment: nonstore retailers (+85,600, +14.6%, the only industry projected to exceed prepandemic levels), motor vehicle and parts dealers (+76,100, +4.0%), clothing stores (+42,800, +4.5%), and furniture/home furnishings stores (+19,900, +4.9%).
- Other projected declines include: electronics and appliance stores (-15.0%), miscellaneous store retailers (-11.6%), sporting goods/hobby/book stores (-7.3%), gasoline stations (-4.7%), health/personal care stores (-4.0%), and building material dealers (-4.0%).
- By 2030, motor vehicle and parts dealers are projected to grow their share to 13.9% of retail employment (from 12.8%); nonstore retailers to 4.7% (from 3.9% in 2020). Clothing stores are projected to recover to 7.0% share (between prepandemic 8.5% and pandemic 6.4%).
- E-commerce sales increased 32.0% from Q4 2019 to Q4 2020, growing from 11.0% to almost 14.0% of total retail sales.

**Conclusions:**
The pandemic accelerated pre-existing trends driven by e-commerce and automation. Most retail industries will continue long-term declines, while those insulated from e-commerce (building material dealers, motor vehicle dealers) and those accelerated by e-commerce (nonstore retailers) will fare best. BLS projects 3.9% average annual productivity growth in retail trade from 2020-30, versus 2.3% from 2010-20.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Retail trade is projected to decline by nearly 587,000 jobs from 2020 to 2030 (the largest projected employment decline of any sector)... the retail trade sector is expected to make up 8.6 percent of total employment in 2030, down from 9.7 percent in 2020 and 10.2 percent in 2010."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: How Is Online Shopping Affecting Retail Employment? - Liberty Street Economics ---
URL: https://libertystreeteconomics.newyorkfed.org/2017/10/how-is-online-shopping-affecting-retail-employment

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a Liberty Street Economics blog post (October 5, 2017) by Jason Bram and Nicole Gorton of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's Research and Statistics Group, examining how the rise of online shopping has affected retail employment in the United States.

Key findings:
- Online sales' share of total retail sales grew from 2.5% in the mid-1990s to around 5% in the mid-2000s, then doubled to exceed 10% by 2017.
- Employment at department stores and nonstore retailers moved in tandem until early 2012, then diverged sharply. In 2012, department stores cut over 200,000 jobs on net. Since early 2013, department stores eliminated roughly 80,000 jobs while nonstore retailers added roughly 100,000.
- Over the past year, nonstore retailers added almost as many jobs (29,000) as department stores cut (32,000).
- The geographic distribution of jobs differs greatly: department stores spread staff proportionally with population, while online retailers concentrate staff in one or a few locations (similar to wholesale distributors).
- Data was analyzed across roughly 700 counties (82% of jobs nationwide), with rural counties combined by state to create a dataset of 742 "counties." Between 2012 and 2016, 561 (about 75%) of counties lost department store jobs; four-fifths of these lost out on net (department stores shed more jobs than nonstore retailers added).
- King County, Washington (home of Amazon.com) gained the most: nonstore employment grew from 1.4% of county employment in 2012 to 2.8% in 2016, versus a national rise from 0.4% to 0.5%.
- Wages differ starkly: average online retail job paid slightly over $50,000 in 2012 (exceeding $59,000 by 2016) versus $20,500 for department store jobs (roughly unchanged by 2016), reflecting different skill requirements and more part-time work in department stores.
- Counties with steep department store declines tend to be less urban with lower incomes, but there is little correlation between department store job losses and overall employment trends in those counties.
- The analysis notes indirect effects of e-commerce on warehousing, local freight trucking, and couriers/messengers (which have seen robust job growth), and notes online shopping may enable small manufacturers to flourish anywhere.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"It's been said that if you want to know how the economy is doing, look at how many people are carrying shopping bags. That adage may not hold so well today."

--- SOURCE 7: Dead mall ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_mall

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A "dead mall" (also known as a ghost mall or zombie mall) is a shopping mall with low consumer traffic or deteriorating conditions. The Wikipedia article covers the causes, effects, and redevelopment of dead malls, primarily in North America. Many malls are considered "dead" when they lose their anchor stores, causing sales volumes and rental revenues to decline below the cost of maintenance. Structural changes in the retail industry, including the rise of big-box chains (Walmart, Target, Best Buy), open-air lifestyle centers, and online shopping, have contributed significantly to mall decline. Newsweek declared the indoor mall format obsolete in 2008, and 2007 marked the first time since the 1950s that no new malls were built in the U.S.

Key causes of dead malls include: "demolition by neglect" (allowing malls to deteriorate without maintenance until demolition is necessary), demographic and socio-economic changes in surrounding neighborhoods, and the COVID-19 pandemic which exacerbated issues through temporary closures and retailer bankruptcies (including JCPenney, Lord & Taylor, Neiman Marcus, GNC, Brooks Brothers, and Ascena Retail Group). From 2006-2010, vacancy rates in U.S. malls increased significantly, with nearly 3% of malls considered "dying" (40%+ vacancy) and nearly one-fifth having "troubling" vacancy rates (10%+) by 2014. The U.S. has 40% more shopping space per capita than Canada and five times more than the U.K., contributing to an "extremely over-retailed" market.

Redevelopment of dead malls takes several forms: conversion to office/educational use (e.g., Windsor Park Mall became Rackspace's headquarters), transformation into open-air mixed-use centers, conversion to fulfillment centers by Amazon/FedEx/DHL/UPS, repurposing for homeless housing, and "mall-to-medicine" conversions by healthcare systems like Vanderbilt Health and University of Rochester Medical Center. Notable companies accused of neglect include Ashkenazy Acquisition Corporation, Namdar Realty Group, and Kohan Retail Investment Group. Some malls maintain profitability in areas with inclement weather or senior populations who engage in mall walking, with Simon Malls enjoying occupancy averages of 92%.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"A dead mall, also known as a ghost mall or zombie mall, is a shopping mall that has low consumer traffic or is deteriorating in some manner."

--- SOURCE 12: National Retail Federation ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Retail_Federation

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The National Retail Federation (NRF) is the world's largest retail trade association, headquartered in Washington, D.C. at 1101 New York Avenue. Formed in June 1911 as the National Retail Dry Goods Association (NRDGA), it was renamed the National Retail Merchants Association in 1958, and in 1990 merged with the American Retail Federation to become the NRF. The organization represents the largest private-sector industry in the U.S., covering over 3.8 million retail establishments and supporting more than 52 million employees. Its members include department stores, specialty, discount, catalog, internet, and independent retailers, chain restaurants, grocery stores, multi-level marketing companies, and vendors, plus over 100 state, national, and international retail associations.

**History & Recent Controversies:** In 2023, NRF retracted inaccurate claims about organized shoplifting after its report showed external theft levels consistent with the prior 20 years, accounting for roughly one-third of retail shrink. In 2024, NRF replaced its data collection method with a survey of senior security executives, reporting significantly higher theft levels—a conclusion challenged by multiple sources. The 2024 report was sponsored by Sensormatic, a company selling shoplifting prevention technology. In February 2025, U.S. retail sales declined 0.22% month-over-month but rose 3.38% year-over-year, attributed to tariff concerns, economic uncertainty, and adverse winter weather. NRF forecasts 2025 retail sales growth of 2.7% to 3.7%, reaching between $5.42 trillion and $5.48 trillion.

**Lobbying Activities:** NRF lobbied for retailer relief during COVID-19, advocating for CARES Act programs and the Paycheck Protection Program, including expedited loan forgiveness for loans up to $150,000. NRF's educational arm, the NRF Foundation, offered its Retail Industry Fundamentals course for free during the pandemic. The organization called for a "uniform and fair framework" for data handling in 2019 via the Main Street Privacy Coalition. NRF has been involved in long-running interchange fee litigation since 2011, suing the Federal Reserve over fee caps; a $30 billion settlement was rejected by a federal judge in June 2024. NRF lobbied for the INFORM Consumers Act (2022) and the Combating Organized Retail Crime Act (2023). It was a founding member of the United for Patent Reform coalition and wrote an amicus brief in the Oil States Energy Services case. NRF has argued against the trade war with China, launched the "S.O.S: Save Our Shipments" campaign in 2021, advocated for the Ocean Shipping Reform Act of 2022, and led 177 trade associations calling to resolve the 2024 U.S. port strike. NRF opposed the border-adjustment tax in 2017, opposed the Affordable Care Act while supporting the American Health Care Act of 2017, and lobbied for online sales tax reform via the South Dakota v. Wayfair case.

**Conferences & Leadership:** NRF hosts Retail's Big Show annually; the 2025 conference had approximately 40,000 attendees and 1,000 exhibitors. Its fourth annual State of Retail & the Consumer discussion took place March 20, 2024, featuring CEO Matthew Shay, Walmart U.S. CEO John Furner, and Chief Economist Jack Kleinhenz. Matthew Shay became NRF president and CEO in May 2010, replacing Tracy Mullin (who joined NRF in 1976 and became president in 1993). Under Shay, NRF's revenue doubled, net assets quadrupled, and Walmart became a member in 2013.

**Retail Sales Data:** NRF releases annual retail sales forecasts each spring. The 2025 forecast of 2.7%-3.7% growth compares with 3.6% growth ($5.29 trillion) in 2024 and aligns with the 10-year pre-pandemic average of 3.6%. The 2024 November-December holiday season grew 4% over 2023 to a record $994.1 billion.
</summary>

## U.S. Retail Real Estate Investment Benchmarks 2025

This report (published July 8, 2025, by MMCG Invest) analyzes U.S. retail real estate trends for 2025 across investment sales, vacancy, rent growth, and development, profiling five top investment markets. Data is sourced from the MMCG database, derived from the 2025 U.S. Retail National Report, with figures cross-validated against Colliers, Cushman & Wakefield, CoStar, MSCI, ICSC, CBRE, JLL, and PwC/ULI data.

### Investment Sales Trends
- Total retail sales reached **$59 billion in 2024**, an **8% YoY increase**, with each quarter outperforming the last
- **Q1 2025 investment volume rose 11%** vs. Q1 2024; preliminary April 2025 figures were **45% higher than April 2024**
- Cap rate expansion from 2022–2023 has tapered; cap rates have largely flattened since mid-2024
- Higher-yield transactions (dollar store/pharmacy at 7%+ caps) skewed averages upward, but prime single-tenant properties (especially essential retailers, ground-lease QSRs) still command **sub-5% cap rates**; most private net-lease buyers transact in the **5%–6% cap range**
- Grocery-anchored neighborhood centers stabilized (e.g., a Kroger-anchored center traded at **6.1% cap** in early 2025); power/community centers trade around **7% caps**
- Market outlook shifted from negative to **neutral-to-positive**; rising deal volume is freeing lending capacity

### Vacancy Rates by Asset Class (Q1 2025)
- **National retail vacancy: ~4.3%** (only slight uptick from record lows); **4.8%** of total retail space available for lease (15 bps above record low)
- Fastest backfill pace in nearly 15 years; quality space from bankruptcies re-leased quickly
- By asset type: **Malls 8.9%**, **Power Centers 4.7%**, **Neighborhood & Strip Centers 6.4%**, **Strip Centers 5.0%**, **General Retail 2.7%** (lowest, driven by single-tenant net-lease strength)
- Vacancy rates well below long-term averages in nearly every category

### Rent Growth
- National asking rents grew **~1.9% YoY** as of mid-2025 (moderating from 4%+ spikes in 2021–2022); forecast ~**1.7% for 2025** (return to 2010s average)
- **47 of 57 largest retail markets** (75M+ SF inventory each) saw positive rent growth
- Occupancy cost ratios near historical norms; core retail sales up 30%+ nominal since 2019 while occupied space grew <2%, meaning significantly higher sales per SF
- Strong Sunbelt/mountain west growth: **Raleigh, NC ~7.5% YoY**, **Tampa, FL ~4.7%**, **Orange County ~3.6%**; underperformers include Cleveland, Chicago (flat), and **East Bay/Oakland (-2.6%)**
- High rent spread on long-held spaces: tenants renewing leases from 5+ years ago face significantly higher rates; embedded rent upside persists into 2026

### Development Pipeline Constraints
- Only ~**81 million SF of new retail space annually** since 2020 (vs. ~300M SF/year in 2000–2009 and ~128M SF/year in the 2010s) — roughly one-quarter of early-2000s levels
- **165M+ SF of obsolete retail demolished since 2018**; total retail stock grew <2% from 2019–2024
- Retail under construction is at its **lowest level since 2011**; only ~**21 million SF of new space (since 2020) available for lease** — less than 5% of total availability
- Texas markets account for nearly one-third of new first-gen retail space
- New construction limited to build-to-suit pad sites and mixed-use ground-floor retail; supply additions projected below historical averages for next five years

### Top 5 Markets for Retail Investment 2025
1. **Dallas–Fort Worth (TX):** 468M+ SF inventory; **4.4% YoY rent growth** (top 10); **4.9% vacancy**; 7M+ SF under construction (most in country); strong population/job growth
2. **Atlanta (GA):** **4.2% YoY rent growth**; **~4.2% vacancy**; only 0.2% stock delivered in past year; rents in low-$20s PSF; strong REIT and private equity interest
3. **Tampa Bay (FL):** **~3.5% vacancy** (below national average); **~4.7% YoY rent growth** (top 5 nationally); only 0.3% under construction; driven by in-migration and tourism
4. **Phoenix (AZ):** **~3.8% YoY rent growth**; ~**1M SF net absorption** over 12 months (highest nationally); **~4.5% vacancy**; 5M+ population; 0.8% pipeline quickly leased
5. **Raleigh (NC):** **~7.5% YoY rent growth** (fastest of any large market); **~2.3% vacancy** (among lowest nationally); only 0.5% stock delivered; Research Triangle tech/life-sciences hub with fast-growing population

### Conclusion
U.S. retail real estate in 2025 is characterized by near-record occupancy, steady but modest rent growth, and reviving capital flows. The decade-long supply drought has created a tight equilibrium. Rent trends are bifurcated with Sunbelt/high-growth markets leading and older slow-growth regions lagging. The outlook is cautiously optimistic — limited new supply, steady consumer spending, and adaptive retailers should keep the sector positive, barring a major economic downturn.

--- SOURCE 8: The State of the American Mall 2023 ---
URL: https://coresight.com/research/the-state-of-the-american-mall-competitive-attractive-and-here-to-stay

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Coresight Research report (published 2023, with a 2026 follow-up report referenced) examines the state of the American mall, challenging the popular narrative of "dying malls" by showing that top-tier malls are thriving. Key findings include:

- Physical retail bounced back after pandemic restrictions lifted, with 2022 seeing more store openings than closures for the first time since 2016.
- Retail sales at malls grew more than 11% in 2022 to nearly $819 billion.
- Malls capture a greater share of sales than their share of space, with high sales productivity especially pronounced at top-tier malls.

MARKET SCALE AND OPPORTUNITY:
- Malls make up a shrinking proportion of total US retail gross leasable area—down to 5.5% in 2023 from 5.7% in 2014, driven by low-tier mall closures.
- ICSC estimates 12.9% of US consumer expenditure on retail goods and services went through malls in Q1 2023.
- Mall expenditure totaled $728.9 billion in 2021 and $818.7 billion in 2022 (11.2% YoY increase).

CORESIGHT RESEARCH ANALYSIS:
- Occupancy: Top-tier malls averaged 95.1% occupancy in 2022 (based on public mall operators, S&P Capital IQ data), still slightly below pre-pandemic levels; non-top-tier malls lagged more meaningfully.
- Rent: Average minimum base rent at top-tier malls grew in the mid-teens percentage range for four consecutive quarters from Q4 2021.
- Revenue: Both top-tier and non-top-tier public mall operators saw CAGRs in the mid-to-high single digits between 2020 and 2022.
- Traffic: Based on a Placer.ai sampling of 120 malls, traffic at top-tier malls was up 12% on average in 2022 versus pre-pandemic 2019; non-top-tier malls were up 10%. Top-tier mall traffic growth was driven by long-distance visitors. Coresight's US Consumer Tracker found 40.3% of respondents visited a mall in the prior two weeks in the December 28, 2022 survey.

DRIVERS OF MALL GROWTH:
1. Multichannel halo effect: Brands with both online and offline presence see sales boosts, reduced customer acquisition costs, and better margins. Rising online advertising costs (driven partly by data privacy features like Apple's app tracking transparency) push brands to physical retail. 61% of retailers and 66% of digital-first retailers cite rising customer acquisition costs as the top obstacle to 2022 e-commerce goals (CommerceNext study). 45% of tracked DNVBs have opened physical stores (Coresight DNVB Databank). BORIS (buy online, return in-store) cuts shipping costs and boosts loyalty.
2. Brand synergy: Brands generate more value in proximity to other high-value brands, driving foot traffic.
3. Reinvestment: Top-tier mall operators like Simon Property Group (Phipps Plaza Atlanta redevelopment with Nobu Hotel/Restaurant, Life Time facility, Citizens Market, office tower) and Taubman ($200 million renovation of The Mall at Green Hills in Nashville, 2019, including 132,000 sq ft of inline retail, new Dillard's, and 70,000 sq ft RH store) continually reinvest.
4. Omnichannel investment by mall owners: Cadillac Fairview partnered with Swyft (CF Delivery same-day/next-day shipping) and ReturnBear (multi-retailer returns). Simon Property Group's Simon Search provides real-time mall inventory data; its Shop Premium Outlets (SPO) platform provides access to 35 million online shoppers and 2 billion in-store shoppers globally, and partnered with Tmall Global (Alibaba) in late October 2022 for Singles' Day. Simon also partnered with Leap (November 2022) to support DNVBs entering brick-and-mortar.

CONCLUSION: Top-tier malls are outperforming the average mall in revenues, occupancy, and foot traffic. The combination of physical retail and e-commerce creates a halo effect benefiting brands. Coresight expects that omnichannel strategies and investments will disproportionately benefit top-tier mall growth going forward.

Contributors: Charlotte Rothschild and Daniel Rodden, Analysts at Coresight Research.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 13: Dead mall - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_mall

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A "dead mall" (also known as a ghost mall or zombie mall) is a shopping mall with low consumer traffic or deteriorating conditions. The Wikipedia article covers the causes, effects, and redevelopment of dead malls, primarily in North America. Many malls are considered "dead" when they lose their anchor stores, causing sales volumes and rental revenues to decline below the cost of maintenance. Structural changes in the retail industry, including the rise of big-box chains (Walmart, Target, Best Buy), open-air lifestyle centers, and online shopping, have contributed significantly to mall decline. Newsweek declared the indoor mall format obsolete in 2008, and 2007 marked the first time since the 1950s that no new malls were built in the U.S.

Key causes of dead malls include: "demolition by neglect" (allowing malls to deteriorate without maintenance until demolition is necessary), demographic and socio-economic changes in surrounding neighborhoods, and the COVID-19 pandemic which exacerbated issues through temporary closures and retailer bankruptcies (including JCPenney, Lord & Taylor, Neiman Marcus, GNC, Brooks Brothers, and Ascena Retail Group). From 2006-2010, vacancy rates in U.S. malls increased significantly, with nearly 3% of malls considered "dying" (40%+ vacancy) and nearly one-fifth having "troubling" vacancy rates (10%+) by 2014. The U.S. has 40% more shopping space per capita than Canada and five times more than the U.K., contributing to an "extremely over-retailed" market.

Redevelopment of dead malls takes several forms: conversion to office/educational use (e.g., Windsor Park Mall became Rackspace's headquarters), transformation into open-air mixed-use centers, conversion to fulfillment centers by Amazon/FedEx/DHL/UPS, repurposing for homeless housing, and "mall-to-medicine" conversions by healthcare systems like Vanderbilt Health and University of Rochester Medical Center. Notable companies accused of neglect include Ashkenazy Acquisition Corporation, Namdar Realty Group, and Kohan Retail Investment Group. Some malls maintain profitability in areas with inclement weather or senior populations who engage in mall walking, with Simon Malls enjoying occupancy averages of 92%.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 14: The Death and Reinvention of American Malls ---
URL: https://sites.lsa.umich.edu/mje/2026/04/13/the-death-and-reinvention-of-american-malls

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the Michigan Journal of Economics, written by Reena Jari and published April 13, 2026, examines the decline and potential reinvention of American shopping malls. 

**Background/Context:** Malls are owned by real estate investment trusts (REITs) that lease retail spaces to tenants who pay base rent, operating expenses, and a percentage of sales. Large department stores like Macy's and Nordstrom serve as "anchor stores" that drive foot traffic and receive lower rents. Malls have faced declining retail sales due to multiple factors.

**Key Causes of Mall Decline:**
1. **E-commerce:** The rise of Amazon and other online retailers in the early 2010s shifted consumer behavior to online shopping due to convenience, accessibility, and product variety, reducing competitiveness of brick-and-mortar retail.
2. **COVID-19 pandemic:** Work-from-home trends reduced commuting and foot traffic. A JP Morgan Chase Institute report found grocery stores and restaurants recovered post-COVID, but retail spaces lagged due to e-commerce.
3. **Internal competition between malls:** Poorly managed malls struggle against newer malls with better amenities. Examples include a mall in Texas acquired by Dillard's after previous owners failed to pay utility bills and property taxes.
4. **Anchor store bankruptcies:** Forever 21's bankruptcy caused the loss of 200+ stores in the US, and large vacant spaces are difficult to fill. The San Francisco Centre mall entered a "death spiral" due to homelessness, shoplifting, and drug use, leading to anchor store closures (Nordstrom, Bloomingdale's) and collapse.

**Reinvention & Recovery:**
- Some investors see redevelopment potential; high-end malls are nearly fully occupied with rising rents according to the Wall Street Journal.
- Vacant spaces are being converted into restaurants, gyms, entertainment venues, and alternative uses — malls are evolving into entertainment centers.
- Dillard's purchased and renovated the Longview Mall in Texas to enhance consumer experience.
- Gen Z is driving a mall comeback: Circana data shows shoppers aged 18-24 bought 62% of total general merchandise in stores (vs. 52% for those 25+). Younger shoppers value instant gratification and in-store experiences, with the online clothing brand Edikted opening physical mall locations due to Gen Z demand.

**Conclusion:** While many malls have struggled to adapt to e-commerce, post-COVID changes, and bankruptcies, the industry may be making a comeback by adapting to consumer demand rather than disappearing entirely.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"E-commerce sales are increasing because of how convenient online buying is, how accessible it is, and how many different things are available" (Kothari, 2018).
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Bed Bath & Beyond is closing hundreds of stores. But they won’t be empty for long | CNN Business ---
URL: https://www.cnn.com/2023/04/24/business/bed-bath-beyond-stores-bankruptcy-real-estate/index.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
CNN article (updated from an original March 21 piece) reports on Bed Bath & Beyond's bankruptcy and the real estate opportunities created by its store closures. The company filed for bankruptcy on Sunday and will close its remaining 360 Bed Bath & Beyond stores and 120 buybuy Baby locations, adding to 400 stores already closed over the past year. Rather than remaining vacant, these stores are being rapidly scooped up by other retailers and businesses due to historically tight commercial real estate conditions.

Key context: total new commercial retail construction hit a record low in 2022 (third consecutive year), and the retail space vacancy rate fell to 4.9% at the end of 2022 — the lowest since CBRE began tracking in 2005. Bed Bath & Beyond stores are attractive because they're located in all 50 states (most in California, Texas, New Jersey, and Florida), mostly in suburbs of mid-size and large cities, and average around 30,000 square feet (under 50,000 sq ft), aligning with the retail trend toward smaller spaces. In some cases, landlords are eager to replace old leases because Bed Bath & Beyond was paying below-market rent.

Chains already moving into former locations include TJ Maxx, HomeGoods, Ross, Burlington, Five Below, Nordstrom Rack, and budget gym Planet Fitness (which opens ~200 new gyms a year). Growth is most pronounced in the discount retail segment as budget-conscious shoppers seek low prices. Physical store openings exceeded closings last year for the first time since 2016 (Coresight Research), and Dollar General, Family Dollar, Dollar Tree, and Five Below lead opening announcements this year.

Federal Realty, a REIT owning nine Bed Bath & Beyond stores, is negotiating with chains like TJX, Burlington, Ross, Nordstrom Rack, and Container Store. Once agreements are finalized, new retailers typically take 18-24 months to open. Meanwhile, Tuesday Morning will also close more than 250 stores this year, with A&G Real Estate Partners auctioning off leases (10,000-20,000 sq ft spaces), with discount chains interested due to their small, already-built nature. With limited new development, growth is coming from "second-generation space."
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"E-commerce scared a lot of people off from building retail. A lot of great real estate is going to come available into a market where there's been no vacancies. It will not take long for retailers to occupy those spaces." — Brandon Isner, head of retail research at CBRE. "For us, the biggest source of new store locations comes from other retailers closing stores. So many of our most productive locations were formerly Circuit City or Toys 'R' Us or Sports Authority." — Burlington CEO Michael O'Sullivan. "There is good interest for Bed Bath & Beyond stores that are closing given desirable locations and an average size of around 30,000 square feet." — Telsey Advisory Group retail analysts. "We feel pretty bullish based on the demand that we've seen that we'll be able to release all of these spaces to other retailers." — Lance Billingsley, senior VP of anchor leasing at Federal Realty. "With not a lot of new development going on, everyone's growth will come from second-generation space." — Mike Matlat, A&G Real Estate Partners senior managing director.
</key_excerpts>

The thread was started on November 24, 2020, by user "architect" and contains 91 posts across 10 pages. The purpose is for users to share observations about dead or dying shopping malls in their regions and predict which malls will next decline. The thread opens with a prediction that up to 50% of malls could close over the next five years.

Key observations by region:

**Dallas-Fort Worth, TX (architect):** The Shops at Willow Bend in Plano has deteriorated noticeably, with 30-40% of in-line spaces vacant. It opened around 9/11 targeting an upscale demographic with anchors including Neiman Marcus, Saks, and Lord & Taylor. Dying malls include ChrisTown Spectrum, Desert Sky/Westridge, and Superstition Springs Center (wounded by Macerich building SanTan Village nearby). Healthy malls include SanTan Village, Biltmore Fashion Park, and Scottsdale Fashion Square (the Phoenix area's flagship mall). Notably, nearly all Phoenix malls are owned by Macerich.

In Seattle, Northgate Mall is being converted from indoor to outdoor (with a Seattle Kraken practice facility and new light rail station). Healthy Seattle malls include Bellevue Collection, Alderwood, Southcenter, and Crossroads Bellevue. So-so malls include Pacific Place, Westlake Center, Marketplace at Factoria, Everett Mall, Redmond Town Center, and Commons at Federal Way.

--- SOURCE 4: The Great American Store Closure Tracker, 2026 Edition - MMCG Invest ---
URL: https://www.mmcginvest.com/post/the-great-american-store-closure-tracker-2026-edition

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive citation-grade research article (April 2026, "The Great American Store Closure Tracker, 2026 Edition") analyzing the 2025 U.S. retail closure cycle. The central thesis is counterintuitive: while media portrayed American retail as "collapsing," the data show a CONCENTRATED contraction, not a broad collapse.

KEY HEADLINE DATA:
- Coresight Research counted 8,270 U.S. store closures in 2025 vs. 5,270 openings (net loss ~3,000), far below the projected 15,000
- National retail vacancy was 5.7% (Q4 2025), only 40 bps above the cyclical low of 5.3%
- Simon Property Group ended 2025 at 96.4% mall/outlet occupancy with rents up 4.7%
- Five bankrupt brands (Joann, Party City, Big Lots, New Rite Aid, Forever 21) drove more than half of all 2025 closure square footage (~127M sf closed through July 2025)
- Top ten chains accounted for ~5,500 of 8,270 closures (~two-thirds)

MAJOR BANKRUPTCIES AND CLOSURES:
- Rite Aid: second Chapter 11 (May 5, 2025), full liquidation of all ~1,240 stores by Oct 3, 2025; ~15.5M sf vacated
- Joann: second Chapter 11 (Jan 15, 2025), full liquidation of all ~800 stores; ~18M sf
- Party City: Chapter 22 (Dec 21, 2024), ~700 stores liquidated; ~8.4M sf
- Big Lots: converted to Chapter 7 (Nov 10, 2025), ~340 net closures after Variety Wholesalers rescue; ~9M sf
- Forever 21: Chapter 22 (Mar 16, 2025), all 354 U.S. stores liquidated
- Saks Global: Chapter 11 (Jan 13, 2026, Southern District of Texas), $3.4B funded debt, ~5.6M sf coming off market; post-closure footprint ~13 Saks Fifth Avenue, 32 Neiman Marcus, 2 Bergdorf Goodman stores
- Walgreens: ~500 closures FY2025; Sycamore Partners $23.7B take-private (Aug 28, 2025) decelerated closures to <100 in 2026
- CVS: ~271 closures in 2025, ending its 900-store program; first net-add year in five
- Starbucks: ~520 North American closures (Q1 FY26 only 3 more)
- Advance Auto Parts: 727 closures (5.45M sf), exited 5 Western states entirely
- GameStop: 727 closures FY2025, cumulative >50% of fleet since FY2023

STRUCTURAL INSIGHTS:
- Chapter 22s (second filings) dominated — companies emerged from prior Chapter 11 but failed to restore trade credit/vendor terms
- 71% of largest consumer discretionary bankruptcies of 2025 involved private equity ownership at filing
- Casual dining in worst distress since 2009 (Red Lobster, TGI Fridays, Hooters, FAT Brands/Twin Hospitality filing Jan 2026 with $1.3-1.4B debt, QVC Group prepackaged Chapter 11 Apr 16, 2026 targeting $5.3B debt reduction)
- 9% of full-service restaurant units and 4% of limited-service units flagged "at risk" of 2026 closure

GEOGRAPHIC BIFURCATION:
- Most stressed markets: New Orleans (+240 bps to 6.3%), Buffalo (+240 bps to 10.8%), Pittsburgh (+200 bps to 6.4%), Providence (+170 bps), Milwaukee (+170 bps)
- Sun Belt winners: Charlotte (+7.6% rent growth to $27.29/sf, 3.4% vacancy), Raleigh-Durham (3.1% vacancy), Phoenix (+964,553 sf absorption)
- Heavy closure concentration in California, Florida, Ohio, New York, Michigan
- Stagnant/declining population states lose retail; high-growth Sun Belt states gain it

BACKFILL COHORT (who absorbed closed boxes):
- Aldi: ~180 new stores 2025 toward 800-store target
- Burlington: 104 net new stores 2025, >40% from bankrupt-tenant recaptures
- Planet Fitness: 181 new clubs 2025 (highest ever); Crunch Fitness: 91 clubs, leased 4.27M sf
- Dollar Tree: +388 net stores to 9,269; Dollar General: +196
- AutoZone: 304 net new stores (record); O'Reilly: 207 net new with 225-235 guided for 2026
- Dave's Hot Chicken: Roark Capital $1B valuation majority stake (June 2025)
- Dick's Sporting Goods: 16 new House of Sport + 20 Field House in 2025

LANDLORD OUTCOMES:
- Best landlords turned bankruptcy into alpha: Brixmor full-year 2025 new-lease cash spreads 38.7%; Kimco ~90% of Party City/Joann/Big Lots/Rite Aid space re-leased at 30-40% releasing spreads; Simon re-tenanted Saks Off 5th at +67% mark-to-market spread
- Kimco upgraded to A- (S&P) and A3 (Moody's)
- 2025 saw the largest embedded rent mark-to-market in a decade driven by bankruptcy recapture
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Ask a casual observer what happened to American retail in 2025 and the answer is usually some version of 'it collapsed.' The images from the year support the impression. Joann liquidated. Party City liquidated. Rite Aid liquidated for the second time in nineteen months. Forever 21 liquidated. Big Lots collapsed into Chapter 7. Starbucks shuttered more than five hundred North American stores in a single fiscal quarter. Advance Auto Parts walked away from five Western states entirely. The data tell a different and more useful story."

--- SOURCE 5: List of Retail Company Bankruptcies & Closing Stores - CB Insights ---
URL: https://www.cbinsights.com/research/retail-apocalypse-timeline-infographic

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a CB Insights research report (published April 26, 2023) that analyzes 154 retail bankruptcies from 2015 through early 2023, examining why major retailers failed. The report argues that Amazon is not the only cause of physical retail's troubles—mounting debt, retailers' own missteps, and lack of adaptability are also to blame.

Key context: The Covid-19 pandemic accelerated the fall of many retailers facing dwindling sales and growing debt. Department stores proved most vulnerable (e.g., Neiman Marcus, JCPenney). There were 52 retail bankruptcies in 2020, 21 in 2021 (a 60% drop YoY), and only a handful in 2022. Reports indicated bankruptcies may flare up again in 2023 due to rising prices and pullback in consumer spending.

Notable 2023 bankruptcies:
- Bed Bath & Beyond (April, home goods): Lagged competitors in e-commerce, faced declining revenue, debt, supply chain disruption; closed stores to sell parts of the business.

This webpage is from the New York City Comptroller's Office (comptroller.nyc.gov) and presents a comprehensive report titled "Retail Vacancy in New York City: Trends and Causes, 2007-2017." The report was authored by New York City Comptroller Scott Stringer and provides a data-driven analysis of retail vacancy across all five boroughs of NYC using administrative data from property tax filings (RPIE), commercial leasing data from Compstak, MasterCard merchant data, and regulatory approval data from the NY State Liquor Authority and NYC Department of Buildings.

KEY FINDINGS:
1. Vacancy Rates Have Risen: The citywide retail vacancy rate increased from a low of 4.0% in 2007 to 5.8% in 2017. Vacancy rates rose across all five boroughs, most dramatically in Staten Island (from 4.3% to nearly 11%). Reported vacant retail space roughly doubled from 5.6 million sq ft to 11.8 million sq ft over the decade. The highest vacancy rates are in the outer boroughs, particularly Staten Island, Queens, and the Bronx.

2. Internet Shopping Changed Retail Space Usage: Amazon sales rose from $14.8 billion in 2007 to $177.9 billion in 2017. NYC retail establishments grew 19%, but personal services grew ~50% and bars/restaurants rose 65%. Regression analysis shows Amazon sales positively and significantly associated with retail vacancy, driving vacant retail square footage higher by nearly 1 percentage point between 2007-2017.

3. Rising Rents Contributed to Vacancy: Average retail rents rose 22% citywide (from $42 to $51 per sq ft). Rents doubled in Soho (10012) from $60 to $126 and rose 87% on the Upper East Side (from $79 to $146). A 1% increase in average retail rents is associated with 0.33% increase in vacant retail square footage. Property taxes paid by retail tenants doubled from $1.1 billion in 2007 to $2.2 billion in 2017 (rising from 20% to 23% of total retail rents).

4. Regulatory Hurdles Impede Turnover: The share of Department of Buildings alteration permits unapproved after 30 days is a significant driver of vacancy (1% increase associated with 3.28% increase in vacant retail footage). Liquor license approval times rose from ~50 to ~75 days in 2018. A 1% increase in liquor license approval time is associated with 0.17% increase in retail vacancy.

5. Landmark status was NOT found to contribute to vacancy; in fact, regression analysis shows landmarked retail is associated with lower vacancy rates.

RECOMMENDED ACTIONS:
- Provide tax incentives (tax credits up to 20%) for independent merchandise retailers in high-vacancy retail corridors
- Create single point-of-contact customer service task force for businesses occupying retail space, and waive permitting/inspection fees for businesses taking over long-vacant space
- Incorporate retail demand analysis into neighborhood planning and rezoning decisions

## U.S. Retail Investment Benchmarks 2025: Sales, Vacancy & Rent Trends

This MMCG Invest report (July 2025) analyzes national U.S. retail real estate trends across investment sales, vacancy, rent growth, and development supply, profiling five top markets for 2025 investment. All data is sourced from the MMCG database, derived from the 2025 U.S. Retail National Report.

### Investment Sales Trends
- Total retail investment sales reached **$59 billion in 2024** (8% YoY increase), with Q1 2025 volume rising 11% YoY and preliminary April 2025 figures 45% higher than April 2024.
- Cap rate expansion from 2022-2023 has tapered off; cap rates have largely flattened since mid-2024 with slight upward bias. Higher-yield deals (dollar stores, pharmacies at 7%+ caps) skew averages, but prime assets still command sub-5% caps; most private buyers transact in the 5%-6% cap range.
- Grocery-anchored centers have stabilized (e.g., a Kroger-anchored center traded at 6.1% cap in early 2025). Power centers trade around 7% caps (e.g., a 507,000 SF Arizona power center at 7.0% cap).
- Outlook shifted from negative to neutral-to-positive by mid-2025, with minimal new construction, low vacancy, and steady tenant demand supporting asset values.

### Vacancy Rates by Asset Class
- National retail vacancy: **~4.3%** as of early 2025; only 4.8% of total retail space available for lease at end of Q1 2025 (15 bps above record low). Fastest backfill pace in nearly 15 years.
- Vacancy by type: **Malls 8.9%** (highest), **Power Centers 4.7%**, **Neighborhood/Community Centers 6.4%**, **Strip Centers 5.0%**, **General Retail 2.7%** (lowest, driven by strong single-tenant net lease properties).

### Rent Growth
- National asking rents grew **~1.9% YoY** as of mid-2025, decelerating from 4%+ annual spikes in 2021-2022, in line with pre-pandemic historical average (~1.5-2% annually).
- Core retail sales (excluding e-commerce, gas, autos) rose over 30% nominally (10%+ real) since 2019, while occupied retail space grew under 2% — retail sales per SF has increased substantially.
- **47 of 57 largest retail markets** saw positive rent growth. Sunbelt markets lead; Northeast/Rust Belt and high-cost coastal markets lag.
- Notable market figures: Raleigh, NC (~7.5% YOY rent growth), Tampa, FL (~4.7%), Orange County (~3.6%), East Bay/Oakland (-2.6% decline), Dallas-Fort Worth (~4.4%), Atlanta (~4.2%), Phoenix (~3.8%).
- Forecast: national rent growth of ~1.7% in 2025, stabilizing at inflationary levels thereafter. Wide variation expected between high-growth and low-growth markets.

### Development Pipeline & Supply Constraints
- Since 2020, only ~81 million SF of new retail space added annually (vs. ~300 million SF/year in 2000-2009 and ~128 million SF/year in the 2010s) — roughly one-quarter of early 2000s levels.
- Over **165 million SF of older retail** demolished since 2018; total retail stock grew less than 2% from 2019-2024.
- Only ~21 million SF of newly built retail space (since 2020) is currently available for lease — less than 5% of total available space; 95%+ of availabilities are in older properties.
- Construction costs, financing costs, and cap rates have made ground-up development difficult; new construction is mostly niche (freestanding pad sites pre-leased to nationals, mixed-use ground-floor retail).
- Texas markets account for nearly one-third of all new first-generation retail space available.

### Top 5 Markets for Retail Investment in 2025
1. **Dallas-Fort Worth, TX**: 468+ million SF inventory, ~4.4% YOY rent growth (top 10 nationally), 4.9% vacancy, over 7 million SF under construction (most in country), strong population/job growth.
2. **Atlanta, GA**: ~4.2% YOY rent growth, ~4.2% vacancy, only 0.2% of stock delivered in past year, low-$20s PSF average rents, strong job market.
3. **Tampa Bay, FL**: ~3.5% vacancy (below national average), ~4.7% YOY rent growth (top 5 nationally), only 0.3% of inventory under construction, heavy in-migration and tourism.
4. **Phoenix, AZ**: ~3.8% YOY rent growth, ~4.5% vacancy, ~1 million SF absorbed over 12 months (one of highest nationally), ~0.8% of stock under construction.
5. **Raleigh, NC**: ~7.5% YOY rent growth (fastest of any large market), ~2.3% vacancy (among lowest nationally), minimal new construction (~0.5% delivered in past year), booming tech/life sciences hub.

### Conclusion
U.S. retail real estate in 2025 is characterized by near-record occupancy, steady (if modest) rent growth, and reviving capital flows, underpinned by a decade of constrained supply. The outlook is cautiously optimistic — limited new supply, steady consumer spending, and adaptive retailers should keep the sector positive barring a major downturn. The report emphasizes the importance of market selection, with Sunbelt and high-growth markets leading while older, slow-growth regions lag.

--- SOURCE 13: Unexpected Factors That Actually Determine A Shopping Center's Grade ---

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from RockStep Capital, dated March 10, 2025, is an educational blog article by Belen Worsham explaining the mall grading system used to classify shopping centers into Class A, B, or C categories. The article is aimed at beginner investors in shopping center/retail real estate.

**Origin of the Mall Grading System:** The concept emerged in the late 20th century. Malls were initially categorized by size (regional, super-regional, community centers). Investment research firms like Green Street Advisors pioneered revenue-based classification, and by the 1990s-2000s, REITs and firms like CBRE and JLL adopted these standards. The International Council of Shopping Centers (ICSC) continues to refine these standards today, and while not legally required, they are widely recognized as industry standard.

**Six Key Classification Factors:**
1. Sales Per Square Foot (most important metric)
2. Tenant Mix and Anchors (e.g., Apple, Gucci, Tesla vs. discount shops)
3. Location and Demographics
4. Occupancy Rates
5. Physical Condition and Amenities
6. Market Perception and Shopper Experience

**Class A Malls (Luxury High-Rises of Retail):** High sales exceeding $700-$1,000+ per square foot; premium tenants like Louis Vuitton, Gucci, Apple, and Nordstrom; occupancy at 95% or higher; located in major metro areas and affluent suburbs; offer experiential retail (fine dining, entertainment, unique attractions). Considered like blue-chip stocks—stable and resilient in downturns, but with high price tags that are less accessible to beginner investors.

**Class B Malls (Suburban Workhorses):** Moderate sales of $400-$700 per square foot; diverse tenant mix of national retailers, discount stores, and regional brands; occupancy around 85-95%; located in secondary markets (mid-sized cities or suburbs). More accessible to investors with value-add opportunities (renovations, re-tenanting), but require active management and face pressure from e-commerce trends.

**Class C Malls (Fixer-Uppers):** Low sales below $400 per square foot; high vacancy rates of 20% or more; declining foot traffic; outdated infrastructure; often viewed as redevelopment opportunities (mixed-use spaces, office hubs, or e-commerce logistics centers). High-risk, high-reward investments requiring heavy repositioning efforts and clear redevelopment strategy.

**Investor Takeaways:** The article recommends that beginner investors seek well-located Class A or B malls as the safest entry point, offering strong tenant demand and steady rental income. Those willing to take on more risk may pursue Class C repositioning, but success requires careful planning and market expertise. The page also promotes RockStep Capital's free webinar replay on "The Blueprint for Shopping Center Investments" and a free 50-page ebook on alternative investing. The article belongs to the "Investing Basics" topic category.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 6: 25% of U.S. malls are set to shut within 5 years. What comes next? ---
URL: https://www.cnbc.com/2020/08/27/25percent-of-us-malls-are-set-to-shut-within-5-years-what-comes-next.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A CNBC article (by Lauren Thomas, August 2020) examines the future of America's struggling malls amid the coronavirus pandemic. Coresight Research estimates that 25% of America's roughly 1,000 malls will close within the next three to five years, with the pandemic accelerating a decline already underway. The article focuses on the question of what to do with "dead malls," particularly the idea (reportedly under discussion between Simon Property Group and Amazon) of converting shuttered department stores into fulfillment centers.

Key obstacles to converting retail space into warehouses include the need for rezoning, which is a lengthy process with low success probability, and the fact that municipalities tax industrial properties at roughly half to two-thirds the rate of commercial properties, giving local governments little financial incentive to rezone. Moody's Analytics real estate economist Victor Calanog emphasized that vacant retail space is not automatically a good candidate for industrial repurposing.

According to Moody's Analytics REIS data, in a post-Covid-19 world, apartment development is expected to fall 15.6%, office development 10%, and retail 15.7%, while industrial development is projected to rise 3.6%. Moody's identified five markets where retail-to-warehouse conversion makes most sense: Central New Jersey, Northern New Jersey, Long Island, Memphis, and Detroit.

The most vulnerable malls are B-, C-, and D-rated properties with lower sales per square foot (an A++ mall can generate up to $1,000 per square foot vs. about $320 for a C+ mall). Roughly 380 C- and D-rated malls exist in the U.S., with Green Street Advisors stating these are "not viable retail centers long term." Tennessee mall owner CBL & Associates planned to file for bankruptcy by October 1, 2020. Even high-end malls face pressure—Bal Harbour Shops in Miami moved to evict Saks Fifth Avenue for ~$1.9 million in unpaid rent since mid-March. About 90% of mall occupants are experiential tenants (movie theaters), department stores, or apparel retailers, making malls the most Covid-vulnerable property type. Alternative uses pondered for dead malls include churches, medical facilities, offices, and apartments—though office space is risky given the working-from-home trend (e.g., JPMorgan shifting to hybrid work, REI selling its Seattle campus).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Just because retail space has gone vacant or remained fallow does not mean that it is automatically a good candidate for repurposing into industrial space," Victor Calanog, head of Moody's Analytics commercial real estate economics division, said. "One cannot simply build industrial buildings in areas zoned for commercial use. Often, that requires rezoning areas — a long and tedious process with a low probability of success.", "State and local governments typically tax industrial properties at anywhere from half to two-thirds the rate of commercial properties, so municipalities have little incentive to rezone areas from commercial to industrial use, as they will collect less tax revenues," Calanog said., "Unfortunately, this whole Covid thing has thrown the experiential pitch out the window. Until we resolve this pandemic, I suspect we are going to be in a holding pattern with hollow retail space. Then we will see what the most viable format is," Calanog said in a phone interview., "Despite being given months to honor its past due rental obligations and despite Saks' impressive post-COVID sales at Bal Harbour Shops, Saks steadfastly refused to make any effort to pay any part of its rent," Bal Harbour Shops President and CEO Matthew Whitman Lazenby said in a statement.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 8: Retail apocalypse - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retail_apocalypse

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The "retail apocalypse" (also known as "retailpocalypse") refers to the widespread closing of North American brick-and-mortar retail stores, especially large chains, beginning in the 2010s and continuing through the present (2026). The phenomenon spans from 2010 to present and is primarily centered in Northern America, with effects also seen in the UK and Australia.

KEY FACTORS:
- Shift to e-commerce: Online shopping is the main cited factor. Holiday e-commerce sales increased 11-20% from 2015-2016, while brick-and-mortar stores saw only 1.6% growth and physical department stores declined 4.8%. Amazon generates more than half of retail-sales growth (the "Amazon effect").
- Oversupply of shopping malls: Mall growth (1970-2015) was over twice the population growth rate. Accelerated depreciation tax incentives from 1954 artificially accelerated mall investment. Mall visits declined 50% between 2010-2013.
- Experience economy: Consumers shifting disposable income from material goods toward dining out and travel.
- Shrinking middle class: Declining real wages and rising costs creating a "middle-class squeeze," affecting retailers like Macy's, JCPenney, and Sears. Dollar stores (Dollar General, Dollar Tree, Family Dollar) grew but are seen as both symptom and cause of rural independent retailer collapse.
- Poor management: Focus on short-term quarterly dividends, understaffing, inventory mismanagement, and heavy debt from leveraged buyouts by private equity firms.
- COVID-19 pandemic: Exacerbated closures; many retailers filed for bankruptcy. Online shopping boomed during lockdowns—29% of US and 43% of UK consumers said they'd never return to offline shopping.

KEY STATISTICS:
- 2017: more than 12,000 physical stores closed.
- 2019: 9,302 store closings announced (59% jump from 2018), the highest since tracking began in 2012.
- Credit Suisse predicted 25% of US malls could close by 2022.
- Sears fell from 3,500+ stores and 355,000 employees in 2006 to 1,430 stores by 2016, filing bankruptcy in October 2018 with 68,000 employees.
- IHL Group (2019) disputed the "apocalypse" narrative, finding 5+ chains opening stores for every one closing, and that 20 retailers accounted for 75% of all closures.
- Coresight estimated closures would exceed the 2019 record in 2020; by 2022 store openings had again exceeded closings.

MAJOR BANKRUPTCIES (from table): Borders Books (2011), The Bon-Ton (2018), Sears Holdings (2013-2021), JCPenney (2015-2020), Toys "R" Us (2018), J. Crew (2020), Barneys New York (2019), Forever 21 (2019 & 2025), A.C. Moore (2019-2020), Payless ShoeSource (2019-2020), Pier 1 Imports (2020), Neiman Marcus (2020), Tuesday Morning (2020 & 2023), GNC (2020), True Religion (2017 & 2020), Brooks Brothers (2020), Bed Bath & Beyond (2023), Express (2024), Big Lots (2024), Party City (2023 & 2024), Jo-Ann (2024 & 2025), 99 Cents Only Stores (2024), Rite Aid (2023 & 2025), Hudson's Bay (2025).

SURVIVORS/THRIVERS: Discount superstores (Walmart, Target), fast-fashion brands (Zara, H&M), dollar stores, and warehouse clubs (Costco, Sam's Club, BJ's).

CONSEQUENCES: Vacant retail space, dead malls, pop-up retail (e.g., Spirit Halloween in former big-box stores), and a domino effect on suppliers (e.g., Hasbro cited Toys "R" Us loss for lost revenue and layoffs).

STRATEGIES: Survival tied to customer experience, brand reputation, omnichannel integration, and technology adoption—Ikea (AR app), Sephora (smart mirrors), Walmart (supply chain automation), Kohl's (smaller stores + robots), Lowe's (LoweBot). A 2018 ICSC study found opening new stores increases website traffic.

DISSENTING VIEWS: Some economists argue closures are a market correction, not an "apocalypse," and the phrase instills insecurity in the 16 million US retail workers. The article notes its perspective deals primarily with the US and lacks a worldwide view.

The phrase "retail apocalypse" first appeared in print in a 1990s essay by Peter Glen, gaining widespread usage in 2017.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In 2017 alone, more than 12,000 physical stores closed. The reasons included debt and bankruptcy in the face of rising costs, leveraged buyouts, low quarterly profits outside holiday binge spending, delayed effects of the Great Recession, and changes in spending habits."
</key_excerpts>
