This report from The Sycamore Institute (a Tennessee nonpartisan public policy research organization), authored by Mandy Spears and published May 20, 2020, examines which Tennessee counties might see the largest drops in sales tax revenue due to the COVID-19 recession. It is the second in a series exploring state and local government relationships in Tennessee.

KEY FINDINGS:
- Sales taxes are most counties' 2nd largest local tax revenue source and a large funding source for schools. Local option sales taxes (up to 2.75% on top of the state's 7% general sales tax and 4% grocery tax) provided about 11% of counties' total FY 2017 budgets on average, while property taxes accounted for 20%. In 17 counties, local option sales taxes generated 15% or more of all FY 2017 revenue.
- In FY 2017, local option sales tax ranged from ~1% of revenues in Trousdale and McMinn Counties to 33% in Sevier County, totaling $2.3 billion statewide.
- State law requires at least half of local sales tax revenues go to K-12 education. Local option sales taxes made up 10% of revenues for the average Tennessee school district in 2018-19 (ranging from 0% in Morgan County to 38% in Sevier County).
- Tennessee's April 2020 sales tax collections were down 6% from the prior year. By end of April 2020, consumer spending fell 35% in restaurants/hotels, nearly 69% in entertainment/recreation, and nearly 65% in transportation.
- During and after the Great Recession, inflation-adjusted local sales tax revenues fell in 75 of Tennessee's 95 counties, averaging a 7% decline below FY 2007 levels (ranging from -1.4% in Union County to -20% in Trousdale County and -15% in Van Buren, Clay, and Davidson Counties).
- Most counties did not hit bottom until FY 2010 or later, after the recession officially ended. Only 16 counties (one in five) recovered within three years. Five counties (Cumberland, Greene, McMinn, Scott, Warren) still had not regained prior highs by FY 2016.
- Sales tax rate increases in 14 counties between FY 2008-2018 appear to have prevented or mitigated declines.
- One in four counties collected less inflation-adjusted local sales tax in FY 2018 than in FY 2007, even as the statewide average grew by 15%. Grundy County saw the largest drop at 9%.
- Counties most at risk from a drop in local sales tax revenue include: Sevier, Cumberland, Dyer, Blount, Knox, Carroll, Dickson, Sullivan, and Greene. Sevier County is especially vulnerable due to its 33% reliance on local option sales tax and tourism dependence.
- Hamilton and Shelby Counties were excluded from most analyses due to significant local policy changes (Hamilton's 1966 sales tax agreement with Chattanooga ended in FY 2012; Shelby County school districts underwent major reorganization in FY 2014) that prevent accurate year-to-year comparisons.

# Tracking the Fallout From State Tax Cuts

Updated

July 16, 2026

States are in the midst of a years-long tax-cutting spree that is undermining funding for key community investments like schools, housing, child care, and infrastructure.More than half in recent years have slashed income taxes primarily for wealthy people and corporations, in some cases by extraordinary amounts. Many others have added further harm through a proliferation of property tax cuts and caps and costly new school voucher programs.

And much of that was underway before President Trump and congressional Republicans enacted the harmful federal megabill in July 2025. That law paired enormous tax breaks for wealthy households and corporations with historically deep cuts that will take away people’s vital health care and food assistance, all while foisting considerable new costs and responsibilities onto states and localities that will [intensify their budget pressures](https://www.cbpp.org/research/state-budget-and-tax/sound-state-revenue-choices-essential-to-counteract-harmful-policies).

This resource, Tracking the Fallout of State Tax Cuts, covers the story as it unfolds and traces the impact of these decisions on critical goals like enhancing economic opportunity, advancing racial equity, and protecting democracy.

It features:

*   stories about cuts to public services and disinvestment stemming from revenue losses;
*   case studies on states that should serve as a warning to others; and
*   analysis of tax cut trends.

Stay informed on the latest state tax developments. By signing up for email updates, you will be notified when we post new entries that analyze the latest news out of statehouses, track emerging policy trends, and explain how they impact people and communities. You can unsubscribe at any time.

## Oklahoma Faces a Child Care Crisis Made Worse by Income Tax Cuts

July 16, 2026

#### More than 400[](https://www.cbpp.org/research/state-budget-and-tax/tracking-the-fallout-from-state-tax-cuts#more-than-400-cbpp-anchor)

Number of child care centers closed since November 2025 in Oklahoma

Oklahoma is staring down a child care crisis as more than 400 child care centers, such as [Kids of Faith](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/04/13/us/childcare-daycare.html) and [Integris Health](https://kfor.com/news/local/out-of-left-field-families-react-to-integris-health-daycare-closures/?ipid=promo-link-block1) in Oklahoma City, have closed since November 2025. With the expiration of [federal pandemic-era aid](https://www.koco.com/article/oklahoma-child-care-centers-losing-covid19-era-funding/70941539) that enabled many providers to stay open and a long [history of paltry state investment](https://www.readfrontier.org/stories/short-state-funding-oklahoma-is-losing-child-care-providers/) in affordable child care, the number of available providers in Oklahoma — [as in many states](https://tcf.org/content/commentary/still-unaffordable-child-cares-rising-prices-stretched-supply-and-staffing-shortages/) — has begun to fall sharply from its post-pandemic high, and even those managing to stay open are [struggling to survive](https://tulsaflyer.org/2026/04/16/schools-families/post/child-care-centers-shift-over-funding-crisis/).

Late last year, the agency administering the program [requested](https://kfor.com/news/local/okdhs-cuts-childcare-subsidy-budget-by-50-million/) about $70 million in the upcoming state budget to help stem the crisis, but that appeal appears to have been ignored. Although the agency then [cut its request](https://kfor.com/news/local/okdhs-cuts-childcare-subsidy-budget-by-50-million/) by $50 million, lawmakers went even further in the state’s final budget, only investing [about $12 million](https://okpolicy.org/oklahoma-takes-a-closer-look-at-its-early-childhood-services-capitol-update/) in child care overall. That choice cements the financial strain on providers, leaving families with fewer and more expensive child care options.

At the same time, Oklahoma’s leaders keep showing where their fiscal priorities truly lie. In May 2025, Governor Kevin Stitt [signed](https://okpolicy.org/new-report-oklahoma-enacted-one-of-the-five-biggest-tax-cuts-for-millionaires-in-2025/#:~:text=Gov.,the%20state's%20six%20tax%20brackets.) a bill significantly reducing the state’s personal income tax rate, at an estimated annual cost of $397 million in lost revenue. The bill also includes triggers that will further cut or even eliminate the income tax if certain revenue requirements are met in the future. If the triggered tax cuts are fully phased in, the state could lose nearly $6 billion annually in revenue. This new tax cut follows years of costly, regressive tax-cutting that had already put Oklahoma on [an unsustainable trajectory](https://okpolicy.org/tax-cuts-now-crisis-later-oklahomas-unsustainable-budget/).

Oklahoma needs investments in child care programs that will ease the burden on families rather than irresponsible tax cuts that will only benefit the wealthiest Oklahomans and leave working families behind. To maintain crucial child care support along with other vital services Oklahomans count on, the state should consider revenue-generating sources to fill this funding gap, as many other states [chose to do this year](https://itep.org/2026-state-legislative-sessions-tax-the-rich/).

In May, Georgia Governor Brian Kemp [signed](https://georgiarecorder.com/2026/05/12/governor-cuts-budget-after-income-tax-bill-creates-1-3-billion-hole/) a bill that cut the state’s flat income tax rate from 5.19 percent to 4.99 percent, scheduled additional rate cuts in the future, increased the standard deduction, and exempted some income from overtime and tips. The new law creates a $1.2 billion revenue shortfall and is expected to cost more than $6 billion annually once fully implemented. Rather than continuing on a path of deep tax cuts that primarily benefit wealthy households and corporations, Georgia lawmakers could have used the revenue to provide better health care, quality education, and safety for communities.

#### $344 million[](https://www.cbpp.org/research/state-budget-and-tax/tracking-the-fallout-from-state-tax-cuts#344-million-cbpp-anchor)

Public spending Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp vetoed and disregarded to help make up for lost revenue and balance the budget due to new tax cut law

To partially make up for the lost revenue and balance the state budget, Governor Kemp vetoed and disregarded $344 million in public spending. He [said](https://roughdraftatlanta.com/2026/05/17/kemp-vetoes-tax-cut-impact/), “The General Assembly failed to account for this loss of revenue in the appropriations process, instead prioritizing general taxpayer relief.”

Simply put, Governor Kemp said the quiet part out loud: he acknowledged that to pay for these expensive and skewed tax cuts, lawmakers are ready and willing to sacrifice key services that Georgians depend on. That tradeoff has been [a recurring theme](https://www.cbpp.org/research/state-budget-and-tax/tracking-the-fallout-from-state-tax-cuts-0?item=30600) among anti-tax policymakers in numerous states in the past few years.

Here are some of the [specific investments](https://gbpi.org/governor-kemp-unilaterally-issues-344-million-in-spending-cuts-to-fund-tax-cuts-for-corporations-high-income-earners/) Governor Kemp removed in favor of tax cuts:

*   $48 million in new Medicaid reimbursement rate increases to support providers and facilities, including primary care, dental care, and psychiatric residential treatment.

*   $30.7 million for additional school transportation and support for bus operations.

*   $9.4 million in funding for domestic violence shelters and $3.3 million for sexual assault centers.

Deeper spending cuts are inevitable as the new tax cut law will continue to reduce the state’s personal income tax by one-eighth of a percentage point each year for eight years if certain [revenue triggers](https://www.cbpp.org/research/state-budget-and-tax/tracking-the-fallout-from-state-tax-cuts-0?item=30615) are hit. These cuts to the tax rate will further skew Georgia’s upside-down tax code to benefit the wealthy and provide only minimal gain for everyday Georgians. [Middle-income households](https://gbpi.org/governor-kemp-unilaterally-issues-344-million-in-spending-cuts-to-fund-tax-cuts-for-corporations-high-income-earners/) in Georgia will see an average tax cut of just $119 in the first full year of the plan, compared to $3,411 for the state’s highest-income 1 percent.

Georgia had [an opportunity to deliver](https://www.cbpp.org/research/state-budget-and-tax/sound-state-revenue-choices-essential-to-counteract-harmful-policies) for communities who are currently dealing with rising prices and loss of medical care and food assistance due to the fallout from last July’s Republican reconciliation law. But instead, the new Georgia law will deliver more tax cuts to the top 1 percent and wealthy corporations than to the first 60 percent of Georgia households combined – while further jeopardizing the public investments that allow everyday Georgians to have the best chance to succeed.

## Some States Continue Down Tax Cut Path, Compounding Harms of Republican Megabill

May 4, 2026

West Virginia Gov. Patrick Morrisey recently [cited an $11 million cost](https://apnews.com/article/west-virginia-morrisey-vetoes-foster-care-tax-cuts-53d7999ddf3a82d91776669678d6ecf9) when vetoing a program that would have helped youth transitioning out of foster care to live independently, find work, and enroll in higher education. Yet Morrisey also just greenlit $230 million in annual costs — with outsized benefits going to wealthier people and corporations — by signing a 5 percent reduction to the state’s personal income tax and by [linking the state’s tax code](https://itep.org/how-does-federal-state-tax-conformity-work/) to expanded federal tax cuts.

West Virginia is just one of many states wrestling with the budgetary fallout from the harmful Republican megabill. That law shifted more responsibilities and costs to states and cut federal funding for essentials like Medicaid health coverage and SNAP’s grocery benefits for millions of people from coast to coast.

These budgetary pressures and dramatic benefit cuts pose significant harm for people in every state. States can minimize the impacts by implementing [revenue-raising policies](https://www.cbpp.org/research/state-budget-and-tax/sound-state-revenue-choices-essential-to-counteract-harmful-policies) to partially offset the federal funding cuts to health care and food assistance, while protecting funding for quality public schools, safe infrastructure, and other essential services.

But in West Virginia and elsewhere, some lawmakers are instead doubling down on a [recent wave of income tax cuts](https://www.propublica.org/article/food-stamps-crisis-snap-big-beautiful-bill-state-tax-cuts), even if it means billions in lost revenue and even less ability to invest in people and communities:

*   **Georgia**. In April the state legislature passed a law accelerating a planned income tax cut, which will benefit wealthiest Georgians the most at an enormous cost to everyday people struggling to get by. If fully implemented, the measure would eliminate about one-third of Georgia’s income tax by 2034, reducing state revenues by [more than $6.5 billion](https://gbpi.org/racing-to-the-bottom/?_gl=1*f3plax*_up*MQ..*_ga*NjczODE0MDQ4LjE3NzUyNDY4MzE.*_ga_ZWZC5HZ1YJ*czE3NzUyNDY4MzAkbzEkZzAkdDE3NzUyNDY4MzAkajYwJGwwJGgw) each year.
*   **Missouri**. State lawmakers recently approved a constitutional amendment that would put the state on a path to eliminating its income tax entirely — paid for in part by raising sales taxes — which would [likely cost billions](https://x.com/WCTharpe/status/2049501241168859500?s=20) in lost revenue while also _raising_ taxes on many lower- to middle-income people. The measure will now go before Missouri voters later this year.
*   **South Carolina**. In March, lawmakers approved legislation that could eliminate the state’s individual income tax over time, with short- and long-term benefits [enormously weighted toward the wealthy](https://itep.org/south-carolina-h4216-eliminate-state-income-tax/). This will reduce revenue in South Carolina by $309 million this year, while full income tax elimination would cost over $6.6 billion a year if fully implemented — nearly 45 percent of the current state general fund.

Rather than continuing these regressive and harmful tax cuts, states should prioritize policies that offer relief to people facing harm due to the unpopular Republican megabill (and in many cases, to recent harmful state policy choices, as well).

Ideally, more states would choose the path of raising new revenues from those most able to pay — as [Washington State](https://itep.org/historic-millionaires-tax-in-washington-will-make-states-tax-code-fairer-raise-critical-revenue/) and [Maine](https://www.mecep.org/news/maine-enacts-millionaire-tax-in-historic-win-for-working-families/) recently approved and [others are also considering](https://stateline.org/2026/04/29/millionaire-taxes-gain-steam-as-states-face-budget-crunches/). We know from [states’ recent experience](https://www.cbpp.org/research/state-budget-and-tax/states-that-raised-revenue-offer-brighter-roadmap-for-others) that such policies can help residents from all backgrounds better access economic opportunities and achieve a higher quality of life.

But at the very least, states should reconsider wasteful tax cuts that mostly help those who don’t need it. For example, [Hawai’i](https://itep.org/state-rundown-4-30-aloha-to-tax-cuts-hawaii-lawmakers-address-revenue-gap-with-high-end-tax-changes/) lawmakers this year appear likely to reclaim some lost revenue by partially trimming an enormous tax cut approved two years ago, and [North Carolina](https://www.wunc.org/politics/2026-03-24/nc-revenue-surplus-tax-cuts-decrease-state-funding) may revisit some prior tax cuts, too. And in [Louisiana](https://www.theadvertiser.com/story/news/2026/03/31/louisiana-lawmakers-urge-caution-before-further-cutting-state-income-tax/89401355007/), state legislators recently chose to forgo any additional cuts without at least reviewing prior ones.

## Kentucky District Weighs Payroll Loan as State Aid Shrinks and Tax Cuts Tighten Budgets

August 25, 2025

Kentucky’s Woodford County Public Schools, which serves [middle-income families](https://data.census.gov/profile/Woodford_County,_Kentucky?g=050XX00US21239#income-and-poverty) in rural communities outside of Lexington, may need a short-term state loan to make payroll before its November property tax distribution arrives — a red flag for broader school finance instability in a state that has cut revenue sources for schools [three](https://www.cbpp.org/research/state-budget-and-tax/states-recent-tax-cut-spree-creates-big-risks-for-families-and)[times](https://kentuckylantern.com/briefs/democrat-beshear-signs-gops-top-priority-another-income-tax-cut-into-kentucky-law/) in the last four years.

Schools in Kentucky, as in most states, are supported by both state and local revenue sources. But state support for schools never recovered from the Great Recession, falling by [24 percent](https://kypolicy.org/education-funding-in-kentucky-remains-inadequate-inequitable-and-uncertain-as-kids-head-back-to-school/) since 2008, adjusting for inflation, leading districts to rely more heavily on local property tax revenue with inequitable consequences for students and communities.

Woodford ended FY 2025 with $5.1 million on hand, but officials warn it [may not cover payroll and bills](https://www.taxnotes.com/tax-notes-today-state/property-taxation/kentucky-school-district-says-loan-may-be-needed-make-payroll/2025/08/06/7sx13) until the expected $20 million property tax payment comes. As Woodford Chief Financial Officer Shane Smith told the school board, the district could “get to a point where we don’t have enough cash in the bank to cover the payroll outflow,” leading to instability for teachers and administrators and the students they support.

The funding crunch is not unique to Woodford. Kentucky’s [SEEK formula](https://www.taxnotes.com/tax-notes-today-state/property-taxation/kentucky-school-district-says-loan-may-be-needed-make-payroll/2025/08/06/7sx13) (Support Education Excellence in Kentucky) reduces state aid as local property values rise, leaving districts to backfill with local property taxes. Woodford projects over [$3.1 million in SEEK losses](https://www.taxnotes.com/tax-notes-today-state/property-taxation/kentucky-school-district-says-loan-may-be-needed-make-payroll/2025/08/06/7sx13) from 2022 to 2026, while inflation in salaries, transportation, utilities, and materials keeps pushing costs up. Funding instability in Woodford does not bode well for poorer districts across the state: about 50 percent of students in Woodford live in poverty compared to 60 percent across the state, and the district boasts the 9th highest property value per student [in the state](https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/lrc/publications/ResearchReports/RR487.pdf). In the face of declining state investment, districts with fewer local resources could fail to meet the needs of all students.

In neighboring Fayette County (Lexington), the school board [voted to raise its occupational tax](https://www.kentucky.com/news/local/education/article307150961.html) from 0.5 percent to 0.75 percent to fill a $16 million budget hole but was [forced to pull the increase](https://kentuckylantern.com/2025/06/04/ky-attorney-general-says-fayette-school-board-didnt-give-public-notice-before-tax-vote/) after the attorney general said the vote lacked proper notice — underscoring how fragile and contested local funding solutions can be.

Layered on top of this are Kentucky’s ongoing [personal income tax rate cuts](https://kypolicy.org/another-income-tax-cut-will-dig-the-hole-deeper/), which lawmakers can continue when certain revenue conditions are met. These cuts shrink the General Fund that funds SEEK and other core services, leaving schools increasingly dependent on property taxes and short-term fixes. The result is [growing inequity](https://kypolicy.org/education-funding-in-kentucky-remains-inadequate-inequitable-and-uncertain-as-kids-head-back-to-school/) between communities with different tax bases: the funding gap between low- and high-poverty school districts has increased by almost 14 percent to $4,247 since 1990. To illustrate the inequities produced by increased reliance on property tax revenue for school funding, consider two counties serving similar numbers of students with different property values: a one-cent increase in taxes levied per $100 of property would have resulted in about [three times as much revenue](https://kypolicy.org/kentucky-school-funding-returns-to-pre-kera-levels/) raised in Bourbon County outside Lexington as in Bell County in rural Appalachia in 2022. And districts like Woodford may turn to borrowing just to make payroll — a stark signal that the state’s tax cut-driven revenue policies are leaving classrooms, staff, and students in increasingly precarious territory.

Statewide, experts note that Kentucky’s education funding remains both [inadequate and inequitable](https://kypolicy.org/education-funding-in-kentucky-remains-inadequate-inequitable-and-uncertain-as-kids-head-back-to-school/), with long-standing gaps among districts. Repeated income tax reductions, including the most recent cuts, further shrink state revenues, intensifying pressure on districts to rely on [property taxes or short-term borrowing](https://kypolicy.org/another-income-tax-cut-will-dig-the-hole-deeper/). Experts warn that without restoring state aid, the fiscal strain could force more districts into precarious cash-flow situations, widen disparities, and prevent critical investments in supports for students.

## Wyoming Passes 25% Property Tax Cut for Homeowners — Without Replacing Lost Revenue for Local Services

July 30, 2025

Wyoming lawmakers enacted a sweeping [25 percent property tax cut](https://cowboystatedaily.com/2025/02/28/property-tax-cut-bill-headed-to-govs-desk-but-not-without-senator-calling-it-fertilizer/) this year for homes valued up to $1 million. But the legislation passed without any plan to replace the critical funding it will strip from public safety, K-12 education, higher education, libraries, and essential local services like road maintenance and legal services.

Despite warnings from some lawmakers and local officials about the fiscal cliff the bill creates, SF 69 moved forward after backfill provisions were removed — which would have made up for the lost local revenue at the state level — to ensure the governor’s support. Gov. Mark Gordon previously vetoed a similar bill that included backfill.

Sen. Ogden Driskill, R-Devils Tower, was among the few to [sound the alarm](https://www.wyomingnews.com/news/local_news/proposal-would-redistribute-8-of-state-sales-tax-to-local-governments-based-on-need/article_c7386309-224c-4f8e-b493-da175bb08e4f.html): “We’re about to lose our only ambulance service,” he said of Crook County. “We’re going to lose part of our firefighting.”

Sen. Larry Hicks, R-Baggs, blasted the legislation for prioritizing a headline-making cut over sustainable local governance, [describing the final deal as “fertilizer](https://cowboystatedaily.com/2025/02/28/property-tax-cut-bill-headed-to-govs-desk-but-not-without-senator-calling-it-fertilizer/).”

The tax cuts come as Wyoming communities face growing needs — aging infrastructure, [volunteer-run emergency response](https://www.wyomingnews.com/news/local_news/proposal-would-redistribute-8-of-state-sales-tax-to-local-governments-based-on-need/article_c7386309-224c-4f8e-b493-da175bb08e4f.html), rising costs, and shrinking resources. Yet the state has now locked in a permanent 25 percent reduction in its largest local revenue source — property taxes — without new tools for counties or municipalities to fill the gap. As a result, local officials are having to cut their budgets by [up to 23 percent](https://wyofile.com/fremont-county-library-flap-a-symptom-of-broader-property-tax-pains-angers-patrons/), and the state is now facing a [$686 million school funding deficit](https://www.wyomingnews.com/news/local_news/wyoming-predicted-to-have-686m-deficit-in-education-spending-by-2029-30-biennium/article_f12aac85-e27f-4a83-a839-66743f3a0e7f.html) by 2030.

Adding to the pressure, lawmakers also passed a [universal school voucher program](https://cowboystatedaily.com/2025/02/28/property-tax-cut-bill-headed-to-govs-desk-but-not-without-senator-calling-it-fertilizer/) this session, diverting millions of public dollars to private schools — with no income limits for K–12 families and limited accountability for how the vouchers are spent.

SF 69 is part of a broader national trend: state legislatures pushing aggressive tax cuts without corresponding plans to sustain vital public services. In Wyoming’s case, lawmakers opted for a short-term win over long-term stability — leaving local governments to do more with far less.

## Iowa to Use Over $900M in Reserves to Cover Tax-Cut Fallout

July 10, 2025

Iowa lawmakers have approved a [new state budget](https://www.iowapublicradio.org/state-government-news/2025-05-15/iowas-2025-legislative-session-ends) that lays bare the growing cost of the state’s tax-cut agenda: to balance the books, they’re now planning to use over [$900 million in state reserves](https://www.iowapublicradio.org/state-government-news/2025-03-13/iowa-legislature-use-state-savings-budget-gap) to cover declining revenue. The gap is largely due to major personal and corporate income tax cuts enacted in recent years — with more reductions still phasing in.

Gov. Kim Reynolds and legislative leaders touted the $9.4 billion budget as balanced and responsible, but beneath that label is a troubling and unsustainable pattern: using one-time cash to fund ongoing expenses.

While Republicans insist that the state’s $6 billion in savings will cover temporary shortfalls until revenues grow, that optimism is built on shaky assumptions. The long-term cost of Iowa’s flat tax and other reductions is expected to reach over [$2 billion annually](https://www.commongoodiowa.org/policy-areas/state-budget--taxes/tax-cuts-whats-at-stake-for-iowans?), threatening the state’s ability to meet future budget needs without deep cuts to essential services.

The budget maneuvering comes at a time when Iowa has already dropped below the national average in [education investment](https://www.axios.com/newsletters/axios-des-moines-4ac81a30-a34a-11ef-9413-c1fe03c477b3?) and faced scrutiny for [underfunding state services](https://iowacapitaldispatch.com/2023/05/08/lawmakers-in-both-parties-disappointed-by-shortfalls-in-8-5-billion-state-budget/?), including health care and infrastructure.

By using reserves to backfill lost revenue — rather than reversing course on tax cuts — Iowa is pushing the hard decisions further down the road. And when the reserve funds run out, the pressure to cut services, raise other taxes, or borrow will only grow.

Let Iowa’s case serve as a warning: when states commit to permanent tax cuts without sustainable revenue plans, even the largest cash reserves won’t last forever.

## Missouri Poised to Enact Appalling Giveaway to its Richest Residents

June 30, 2025

Missouri legislators in May approved an alarming tax policy change: eliminating the state income tax on capital gains, a first-of-its-kind move that will deliver enormous gains to wealthy households and little to no benefit for almost everyone else. Widely expected to be signed by the governor in the next two weeks, the change is part of a broader pattern of tax reductions over the past decade that have weakened the state's ability to fund essential services that all Missourians count on.

The capital gains cut will completely exempt all income from stocks, bonds, cryptocurrency, real estate, and other investments from Missouri state taxes — something that no state with an income tax currently does. The vast majority of this benefit will go to the wealthiest Missourians, who are far more likely to earn significant capital gains. The state’s highest-income 5 percent will receive [an estimated 80 percent of the tax cut](https://www.epi.org/blog/missouri-republican-state-lawmakers-are-pushing-a-radical-anti-worker-tax-plan/), while the state’s richest 1 percent will reap about two-thirds of it.

Meanwhile, the top-heavy policy will likely spell serious trouble for Missouri’s ability to fund key services, especially now that significant federal budget cuts are likely on the way as well. The exemption could reduce state revenues by around $600 million [each year](https://missouriindependent.com/2025/04/22/missouri-is-sleepwalking-into-a-half-billion-dollar-tax-cut-for-the-rich/), according to the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, roughly equal to the cost of funding 11,000 [public school teachers’ salaries](https://www.mnea.org/news/missouri-falls-49th-teacher-pay). That comes on top of a series of tax reductions in recent years that have already impacted Missouri's fiscal health. The Missouri Budget Project notes that when fully implemented, prior tax cuts will reduce state general revenue by [$3 billion annually](https://mobudget.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Intro-MO-Budget-2025.pdf) — more than the amount the state sends via formula to local public schools.

As state revenues show continued [signs of strain nationwide](https://www.governing.com/finance/state-tax-revenues-are-dropping-below-long-term-trends) and a torrent of harmful federal budget cuts for health care, food assistance, and other essential needs [now looming over state finances](https://www.cbpp.org/research/state-budget-and-tax/house-republican-reconciliation-bill-would-force-states-to-cut-food) nationwide, the recent capital gains giveaway raises serious concern about Missouri's futures. State policymakers there should reverse the reckless and regressive cuts as soon as possible, and shift course toward an approach that prioritizes education, health care, infrastructure, and stable revenues for all Missourians over tax cuts for the rich.

## Idaho Swaps Support for Public School Families for Private School Vouchers

June 23, 2025

Idaho lawmakers have [dismantled](https://www.propublica.org/article/idaho-vouchers-public-school-funding-cuts?emci=133d51c4-a01e-f011-8b3d-0022482a9fb7&emdi=74e7a5dd-b61e-f011-8b3d-0022482a9fb7&ceid=604746) a widely used grant program that supported public school families — just weeks after creating a $50 million school voucher program for private school tuition and related expenses. The change reflects a deeper trend in states’ priorities: public funds increasingly flowing toward private education, while [support for public school students stagnates or shrinks](https://idahofiscal.org/private-school-tax-credit-vouchers-lead-to-decreased-public-school-investment/).

The now-defunct Empowering Parents grant program offered families up to $1,000 per child ($3,000 per household) to pay for education-related items like laptops, tutoring, internet, and school supplies. While the program wasn’t a solution to Idaho’s lack of public school funding, at least 81 percent of the program’s funds went to public school students this year, supporting more than 24,000 kids — many from low-income, rural communities.

And while the funding for Empowering Parents could have been distributed more equitably by investing it directly in technology and tutoring at public schools, eliminating prohibitive application processes, this stop-gap program provided important resources to students:

*   A fifth grader in Nampa School District received her first laptop, finally able to do homework at home.
*   A student in southern Idaho raised her math grade from a D to a B+ with paid tutoring.
*   In rural districts, the grants covered basic needs like backpacks and laptops.

That program is now gone. In its place is [a new tax credit voucher](https://idahofiscal.org/idaho-parental-choice-tax-credit-program-uses-taxpayer-dollars-to-pay-for-private-school-expenses/), $5,000 that private-school families can use on any number of things with little oversight. Unlike Empowering Parents, the new tax credit voucher is off-limits to public school students, and accountability is minimal — families must only prove how they used the money if audited.

State lawmakers funneled a total of $50 million into private school vouchers and shortchanged [94 percent](https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/sites/default/files/2025-03/pub_private_Idaho_MAP.pdf) of students who attend Idaho public schools. All the while, Idaho comes in dead last for per-pupil funding out of all 50 states and the District of Columbia, spending [one-third less](https://edlawcenter.org/research/making-the-grade-state-profiles/) than the national average. This failure to invest in the state’s future has resulted in inadequate education for many Idaho students, including subjecting them to [abysmal learning environments](https://www.propublica.org/series/state-of-disrepair) like freezing classrooms and leaky, soggy ceilings at risk of collapse. The portion of Idaho’s gross state product that goes toward K-12 funding, or its “effort,” has [fallen by 25 percent since 2006](https://www.schoolfinancedata.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/profiles25_ID.pdf), suggesting that the state has the capacity to increase investments in the public schools that most students attend, if lawmakers choose to.

The Idaho Freedom Foundation, a vocal backer of the school voucher program, openly proposed shifting the $30 million from Empowering Parents to expand the private school voucher — suggesting public education dollars be used to subsidize 6,000 more non-public students.

The repeal of Empowering Parents creates a stark double standard: public school families who relied on modest grants for essentials like internet or calculators are now told there’s no money for them, while families already in private schools may claim thousands in state-funded school vouchers.

This shift reflects a growing [national trend](https://www.cbpp.org/blog/states-should-reverse-course-on-defunding-public-education-through-private-school-vouchers-and): school voucher policies that steadily divert public funds into private, less accountable alternatives. The long-term risk isn’t just fiscal — it’s the erosion of equitable, inclusive support for the 94 percent of students who attend Idaho’s public schools.

## Nebraska’s Surplus Turns to Shortfall After Tax Cuts and One-Time Windfall Fades

June 17, 2025

Just two years ago, Nebraska lawmakers entered the 2023 session with a record $1.9 billion budget surplus — equal to nearly 17 percent of this year’s total budget. Today, that surplus has vanished, leaving lawmakers scrambling to close a $432 million budget shortfall. And with future deficits already projected, the state’s long-term fiscal outlook is dimming fast.

What caused the [swing from abundance to scarcity](https://www.openskypolicy.org/punctuating-the-state-budget/)? In large part, it’s a case of lawmakers using temporary federal aid as a vehicle to shortsightedly justify permanent tax cuts. The surplus was driven by one-time federal pandemic relief funds, not recurring growth. But [in 2023](https://nebraskaexaminer.com/2023/05/25/lawmakers-pass-nebraska-income-tax-cuts-property-tax-offsets-child-tax-credits/), lawmakers used that windfall to pass LB 754, a sweeping tax package that lowers both personal and corporate income tax rates to 3.99 percent by 2027. They also passed LB 243, which expanded property tax credits and took funding away from public schools.

Supporters claimed the cuts would jumpstart the economy, but the boom hasn’t materialized. Instead, Nebraska has faced slowing revenues and rising costs. And while [federal Medicaid match rate (FMAP) reductions](https://nebraskaexaminer.com/briefs/decrease-in-federal-share-of-nebraska-medicaid-costs-increases-state-budget-shortfall/) have been blamed for the shortfall, those changes were anticipated and reflect a stronger state economy — not a sudden drop in federal support.

To avoid immediate agency cuts this year, lawmakers [resorted to flat budgets](https://nebraskaexaminer.com/2025/05/15/nebraska-passes-11-billion-two-year-budget-closes-major-projected-deficit-for-now/) for most state agencies and raided $150 million from cash funds, including the rainy day fund. These one-time fixes paper over the deeper problems of declining revenues and rising costs without addressing growing structural imbalances.

Meanwhile, the Legislature declined to consider LB 171, which would have [paused the next phase of income tax cuts](https://nebraskaexaminer.com/2025/03/13/nebraska-lawmakers-told-easiest-way-to-dig-out-of-budget-deficit-is-to-pause-income-tax-cuts/). That decision could prove costly, as more revenue reductions are set to phase in, even as the state braces for additional shortfalls in the next budget cycle.

Nebraska’s experience is a case study in fiscal whiplash: a temporary surplus misused to justify permanent tax cuts with long-term negative consequences for the public services Nebraskans rely on. As the federal funds fade and revenue growth slows, policymakers may soon face painful choices — cutting essential programs, draining reserves further, or shifting costs to local governments and families.

The lesson for other states is clear: when one-time money is used to fund permanent tax cuts, the math doesn’t hold — and the bill eventually comes due.

## Backing Vouchers and Tax Cuts, Texas Lawmakers Fuel a Perfect Storm of Underfunding

June 6, 2025

Texas is hurtling toward fiscal instability, driven by a sweeping school voucher program and lawmakers’ support of massive, untargeted property tax cuts — both funded by fleeting budget surpluses.

At the same time, public schools serving the vast majority of Texas students remain drastically underfunded, and the state has no income tax to stabilize revenues when they fall. These decisions risk locking in structural imbalances that will be difficult — and painful — to undo.

## School vouchers divert public dollars as public schools struggle[](https://www.cbpp.org/research/state-budget-and-tax/tracking-the-fallout-from-state-tax-cuts#school-vouchers-divert-public-dollars-cbpp-anchor)

[Against the public’s wishes](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1nas166lRYI_VVSk8CpYVRo18z_UeIndJ/view) and after years of failed attempts, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott [signed into law](https://www.texasobserver.org/abbott-trump-house-vouchers-pass/) a universal school voucher bill that will drain public funds from public schools to subsidize private school tuition. The [new la w](https://hro-dfr.house.texas.gov/bill-analysis?legislature=89&session=R&billNumber=SB2) appropriates $1 billion for the program’s first two years; it’s projected to cost [$7 billion](https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/89R/fiscalnotes/pdf/SB00002F.pdf#navpanes=0) in its second two years. That price tag is nearly equivalent to what the state would have needed this year to provide the same level of basic education funding [students](https://everytexan.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Count-Every-Student-2025.pdf) received in 2019 when accounting for inflation.

Most voucher funding is expected to go to families already enrolled in private schools, and the program excludes students without a documented immigration status. That’s even though the [U.S. Supreme Court ruled](https://www.uscourts.gov/educational-resources/educational-activities/access-education-rule-law) that all students, regardless of immigration status, must be able to attend public schools without cost.

Even as [88 percent of Texas students](https://www.schoolfinancedata.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/profiles25_TX.pdf) attend schools that are underfunded to meet national average test scores, [lawmakers passed](https://www.texastribune.org/2025/06/04/texas-public-education-schools-funding-bill-explained/) only a modest increase to the state’s basic funding formula that falls far short of keeping up with inflation.

## Property tax giveaways now rival the state’s largest budget priorities[](https://www.cbpp.org/research/state-budget-and-tax/tracking-the-fallout-from-state-tax-cuts#property-tax-giveaways-now-rival-cbpp-anchor)

Meanwhile, lawmakers are doubling down on property tax cuts. Cuts already on the books are costing Texas $44.5 billion in this biennium, and lawmakers have proposed giving away another $6.5 billion this session.

The scale of these cuts is staggering. If property tax cuts were their own agency, it would be the third-largest in the state budget — more than double what Texas spends on public safety and criminal justice combined, more than the entire two-year operating budget of the Texas A&M University System, and enough to build a high-speed rail line from Dallas to Houston, according to the [Texas Tribune](https://www.texastribune.org/2025/04/10/texas-property-tax-cuts-budget/).

Taken together, vouchers and property tax cuts are creating mounting strain in Texas: a deeply underfunded public school system, ballooning voucher and tax cut costs, reliance on temporary surpluses, and no income tax to fall back on when revenues decline.

With state surpluses expected to dwindle and [federal funding at risk](https://www.multistate.us/insider/2025/2/28/state-budgets-in-the-shadow-of-federal-uncertainty), these costly, untargeted tax breaks will be difficult to sustain. When the surpluses dry up, Texas could face devastating cuts to education and local services.

Instead of locking in billions for tax cuts that benefit wealthy homeowners and businesses and paying private school tuition while underfunding public schools, lawmakers could make [meaningful, cost-effective investments](https://everytexan.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Report_-Halbook_Alternatives-to-property-tax-cuts.pdf) in Texans’ well-being. These investments include a meaningful boost in the K-12 funding formula, rebates for renters, property-tax [circuit breakers](https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/86R/handouts/C4902020072900001/32c9d82b-aa52-4e95-99d2-175d8c4a8e83.PDF), or enacting a state Earned Income Tax Credit.

This is a Center on Budget and Policy Priorities (CBPP) tracking resource documenting the negative fallout from state tax cuts across the United States. The page, updated July 16, 2026, covers how more than half of states have slashed income taxes primarily benefiting wealthy people and corporations, plus property tax cuts, caps, and school voucher programs that undermine funding for schools, housing, child care, infrastructure, and other public services. It notes that the harmful federal Republican "megabill" of July 2025 exacerbated these pressures by shifting more costs onto states while cutting federal health care and food assistance.

KEY STATE CASE STUDIES (chronological):

**Mississippi (April 2025):** Gov. Tate Reeves signed a law phasing out the personal income tax entirely. Full repeal will cost roughly one-third of the state's general fund. The highest-income 5% receive nearly 40% of the tax cut; the top 1% get annual breaks of nearly $42,000.

**Texas (June 2025):** Gov. Greg Abbott signed a universal school voucher bill costing $1 billion in its first two years and projected at $7 billion in its second two years. Property tax cuts cost Texas $44.5 billion this biennium with another $6.5 billion proposed — if they were an agency, property tax cuts would be the third-largest in the state budget. Texas has no income tax to stabilize revenues.

**Nebraska (June 2025):** A record $1.9 billion surplus (2023) has turned into a $432 million shortfall after permanent tax cuts were funded with one-time federal pandemic aid. Lawmakers raided $150 million from cash funds and declined to pause further income tax cuts.

**Idaho (June 2025):** Lawmakers dismantled the Empowering Parents grant program (up to $1,000/child for public school families, supporting 24,000+ kids, 81% public school students) and replaced it with a $50 million private school voucher program with minimal accountability. Idaho ranks last nationally in per-pupil funding, spending one-third less than the national average.

**Missouri (June 2025):** Lawmakers approved eliminating the state income tax on capital gains — a first-of-its-kind move. The richest 1% reap about two-thirds of the benefit; the cut reduces revenues by ~$600 million/year. Prior tax cuts already reduce general revenue by $3 billion annually.

**Iowa (July 2025):** Approved a budget using over $900 million in reserves to cover revenue gaps from tax cuts. Long-term cost of the flat tax and reductions expected to exceed $2 billion annually.

**Wyoming (July 2025):** Passed a 25% property tax cut for homes valued up to $1 million with no backfill for local services. Local officials face budget cuts up to 23%; the state faces a $686 million school funding deficit by 2030. Also passed a universal school voucher program with no income limits.

**Kentucky (August 2025):** Woodford County Public Schools may need a short-term payroll loan due to shrinking state aid. State support for schools fell 24% since 2008. Funding gap between low- and high-poverty districts increased ~14% to $4,247 since 1990.

**Georgia (June 2026):** Gov. Brian Kemp signed a bill cutting the flat income tax from 5.19% to 4.99%, creating a $1.2 billion revenue shortfall. He vetoed/disregarded $344 million in spending, including $48M in Medicaid rate increases, $30.7M for school transportation, $9.4M for domestic violence shelters. Middle-income households see ~$119 average tax cut vs. $3,411 for the top 1%.

**Oklahoma (July 2026):** More than 400 child care centers closed since November 2025. Lawmakers invested only ~$12 million in child care despite a $70 million request. Gov. Kevin Stitt signed a personal income tax cut costing $397 million annually, with triggers that could lead to nearly $6 billion in annual revenue loss if fully phased in.

**West Virginia (May 2026):** Gov. Patrick Morrisey vetoed an $11 million foster care transition program while signing $230 million in annual tax cuts benefiting the wealthy.

**Multi-state trend (May 2026):** Georgia, Missouri (constitutional amendment to eliminate income tax), and South Carolina (potential income tax elimination costing over $6.6 billion/year, ~45% of the general fund) continued tax-cutting paths, compounding the harms of the federal Republican megabill.

The resource contrasts these trends with revenue-raising alternatives, citing Washington State and Maine's millionaire taxes as positive models, and notes states like Hawai'i, North Carolina, and Louisiana are reconsidering prior tax cuts.
