**List of Queries and Tool Calls Made**

To research this topic, the following Tavily web searches were conducted:

1. "US mall vacancy rate history 2005 2020 2024 CoStar percent"; "enclosed mall vacancy rate COVID CoStar Coresight percentage"; "how many US malls closed dead dying malls 2023 2024 2025 projections"
2. "anchor store closures Sears JCPenney Macy's Bed Bath Beyond store closing numbers"; "US retail square footage vacant mall strip mall vacancy statistics"; "Class A mall vs Class B C mall vacancy rate health"
3. "mall vacancy rate 2005 2008 2010 2015 2020 history Reis Moody's Analytics peak 11.2% 2020"; "how many US enclosed malls closed permanently Coresight Moody's 1000 1500 forecast 25% malls close Green Street"; "Bed Bath Beyond stores closed 2023 Sears JCPenney Macy's 150 stores closure 2026 department store bankruptcies"
4. "mall vacancy rate 2017 2018 2019 retail apocalypse percentage enclosed malls Cushman Wakefield historical"; "total US retail square footage 2023 2024 billion square feet retail vacancy statistics national"; "Moody's Analytics mall vacancy 2022 2023 2024 2025 rate decline recovery"
5. "number of enclosed malls United States 700 1000 2024 Coresight Moody's closure count"; "US retail total square footage 7 billion 10 billion square feet mall space percentage"; "mall vacancy rate 2022 2023 recovery Moody's CoStar percent Class A top tier"

---

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

**PART A: NATIONAL MALL VACANCY RATES OVER TIME (2005–2026)**

**COVID-Era Peak (Moody's Analytics / Reis Data):**
- U.S. regional and super-regional mall vacancy rates hit a **record 11.4% in Q1 2021**, according to Moody's Analytics REIS data. This was a **90-basis-point jump from Q4 2020** (10.5%), marking the **largest quarterly increase ever recorded** by Moody's Analytics' commercial real estate division, surpassing the previous record 80-basis-point spike during Q1 2009 (Great Recession). (Sources: CNBC, Retail Dive)
- Victor Calanog, lead of Moody's commercial real estate economics division, stated: "Malls are absolutely still on the ropes... They were on the ropes even before Covid. ... It's almost passe now to say that we have a record vacancy rate for malls because we've been breaking that record all year." (CNBC)
- Moody's Analytics tracks roughly **700 of the approximately 1,000 malls** in the U.S. for its analysis. (CNBC)
- In Q1 2021, mall vacancy was up 0.4% year over year, with asking rents down 1% and effective rents down 1.5%. (Retail Dive)
- Moody's Analytics Senior Economist Thomas LaSalvia noted: "Both office and retail are going through a structural change that will continue to cause many firms to look closely at their respective footprints. As their leases expire, it is likely some will move or downsize, putting further downward pressure on rents and vacancy rates through this year and into 2022." He also said: "[R]etail is slogging through the evolutionary process that started well before the pandemic... Malls are of more concern than neighborhood centers, but even then, it is unlikely that we will close down every single mall in the US." (Retail Dive)
- A separate UBS report predicted roughly **80,000 retail store closures nationwide in the five years following 2021** (by 2026), impacting about 9% of all retail stores, with apparel, sporting goods, and office supplies driving the closures. UBS counted **115,000 shopping centers across the U.S. at the end of 2020**, up from 112,000 in 2010 and 90,000 in 2000. (CNBC)

**Pre-COVID "Retail Apocalypse" Period (2010s):**
- The "retail apocalypse" refers to the widespread closing of North American brick-and-mortar retail stores, especially large chains, beginning in the 2010s and continuing through 2026. (Wikipedia)
- **Q3 2018:** The U.S. mall vacancy rate in enclosed regional malls **rose to 9.1%**, the highest since Q4 2011, up from 8.6% in Q2, driven by Sears and Bon-Ton store closings. Average mall rent dipped 0.3% from Q2 to **$43.25 per square foot** — the first decline since 2011. (Forbes, citing Reis)
- **Q4 2015:** U.S. shopping center vacancy was **8.0%**, the lowest in six years, marking the 15th consecutive quarter of steady or declining vacancy. Since peaking at **10.3% in Q1 2010**, vacancy had fallen in 20 of the last 23 quarters. Total inventory was over **3.9 billion SF across 65+ major U.S. markets**. (Cushman & Wakefield Q4 2015 MarketBeat)
- **Q4 2015 shopping center subtype vacancy data** (Cushman & Wakefield): Community/Neighborhood centers 8.7%, Strip centers 8.7%, Power centers 5.1%, Lifestyle centers 7.0%. Regional breakdown: Atlantic 7.0%, Midwest 9.9%, Mountain 10.4%, Pacific 6.7%, South 7.9%. (Cushman & Wakefield)
- **2015 retail snapshot:** Overall retail vacancy of 6.0%, average asking rent of $15.70 psf (six-year high). (Cushman & Wakefield)
- **Q1 2019:** U.S. shopping center vacancy rate was **6.4%** (down 10 bps from 6.5% in Q1 2018). Average asking rent (NNN) was **$17.26/SF** (up from $16.74). Over 5,000 closure announcements had already been made by end of Q1 2019. All 66 tracked markets had single-digit vacancy. (Cushman & Wakefield Q1 2019 MarketBeat)
- **Historical context:** The strip mall vacancy rate data begins in 1980. In the 1980s there was overbuilding in the mall sector amid rising vacancy rates due to loose commercial lending (S&L crisis). In the mid-2000s, mall investment picked up following residential boom "rooftops," leading to higher vacancy rates even before the recession, followed by a sharp increase during the recession and financial crisis. (Calculated Risk blog on Moody's data)
- **Moody's broader retail (non-mall) data:** Within retail excluding malls, 40 of 77 metros recorded effective rent declines in Q1 2021, with vacancy at **10.6%** (up from 10.5% in Q4). (CNBC)
- **Moody's strip/shopping center data:** The retail vacancy rate remained stable at **10.3% in Q4 2024**, down slightly from 10.4% in Q4 2023. Both asking and effective rent increased 0.3%, reaching **$21.90/sqft** and **$19.19/sqft** respectively. (Calculated Risk, January 2025)
- **Moody's Q1 2026 preliminary data:** Retail delivered "mild upside surprises" with a **flat vacancy rate of 10.4%**, supported by strong consumer spending. (Bisnow)
- **DoorLoop/Moody's data:** Mall vacancy rate was **8.7%** in Q2 2022 (Q4 2022 figure cited as 8.7%); retail vacancy flatlined at **10.3% in Q1 2023** with asking rents at $21.52/SF and effective rents at $18.81/SF. General retail space occupied 6.4 billion of 11.8 billion sq ft of retail space. (DoorLoop)

**Post-2023 Mall Vacancy Data (Colliers, MMCG, CoStar):**
- **Q1 2025:** National retail vacancy was **~4.3%** (only slight uptick from record lows); **4.8%** of total retail space was available for lease (15 bps above record low). By asset type: **Malls 8.9%**, **Power Centers 4.7%**, **Neighborhood & Strip Centers 6.4%**, **Strip Centers 5.0%**, **General Retail 2.7%** (lowest, driven by single-tenant net-lease strength). (MMCG Invest, cross-validated against Colliers, Cushman & Wakefield, CoStar, MSCI, ICSC, CBRE, JLL, and PwC/ULI data)
- **Q4 2024 (Transwestern):** Vacancy rate was **4.1%**, up 10 basis points from the previous year (slightly increased from 4.0%). Net absorption was 6.8 million SF in Q4, marking the 16th consecutive quarter of positive absorption; 2024 total was 23.1 million SF (down significantly from 50.2 million SF in 2023). Asking rent was $25.40/SF, up 2.0% annually. (Transwestern Q4 2024 Retail Report)
- **Q2 2025 (Colliers):** National vacancy rate **rose to 4.3%**, up 10 basis points from Q1. Net absorption turned negative with 6.4 million square feet returned to the market; leasing activity down 5.2%. Coresight tracked 5,822 store closures as of end of June 2025 (~123.7 million square feet). Nearly 40% of available space is rated 2 Stars or below, and less than a quarter was built after 2000. Asking rents dipped slightly to $25.46 per square foot (a 0.39% decrease). Since end of 2019, occupied U.S. retail space has grown only 1.3%, yet monthly sales per square foot reached a record $24.96 in the first half of 2025 — more than 30% above pre-pandemic levels. (Colliers Knowledge Leader)
- **Q4 2025 (Colliers):** The national retail vacancy rate **held at 4.3% for a third consecutive quarter** as the market absorbed late 2024 and early 2025 bankruptcies. Move-ins surged past 91 million square feet (highest since Q2 2022). **Mall vacancy improved to 8.5%** and shopping centers to **5.2%**, each improving by 10 basis points quarter-over-quarter. The market recorded 11.1 million square feet of positive net absorption despite a 17.3% decline in leasing activity, with lease-up times averaging under seven months. Average asking rents rose to **$26.13 per square foot**, a modest 0.27% gain. Construction remained muted at 50.1 million square feet total in Q4, with 8.1 million square feet delivered; under-construction volume fell to its lowest level since 2021. (Colliers Knowledge Leader, January 21, 2026)
- **Q2 2026 (Cushman & Wakefield):** National retail vacancy held essentially steady, up just 3 basis points to **6.0%** — well below the 7.4% historical average. Asking rents grew 2.2% year-over-year to **$25.65 per square foot** nationally. Only 2.3 million square feet was delivered in Q2, and the development pipeline represents less than 0.3% of existing inventory. Retail net absorption totaled 708,000 sf. (Cushman & Wakefield U.S. Shopping Center MarketBeat Q2 2026)
- **Q4 2025 (MMCG Invest):** National retail vacancy was **5.7%**, only 40 bps above the cyclical low of 5.3%. (MMCG Invest, April 2026)
- **PwC/ULI Emerging Trends 2026:** Retail vacancy rose from 4.0% to 4.1% in 2024, then jumped to **4.3% by Q3 2025**, with 10.6M sq ft of negative net absorption in the first nine months of 2025. New development deliveries fell to 19.6M sq ft in 2025, on pace to be the third weakest year for new development this century. Rent growth remained positive at 1.8% through Q3 2025. Retail real estate recorded positive net absorption of 21.2 million square feet in 2024 (vs. 71.7M sq ft annual average since 2013). Retail sales growth slowed from 3.6% average annual gains in 2023 to just 0.7% across 2024. (PwC)
- **CBRE Investment Management:** Neighborhood and community center (NCC) retail vacancies **fell to the lowest levels on record since the late 1980s (5.6% as of Q1 2025)**. Asking rents for NCC retail rose at the fastest rate in 15 years post-pandemic. Above-trend asking rent growth of 3.1% per year is projected over the next five years. More than 400 million SF of retail space was demolished since 2009. Retail values fell cumulatively 24% since 2017 but have plateaued since late 2024. (CBRE IM, May 30, 2025)

**PART B: ENCLOSED MALL CLOSURES AND DEAD/DYING MALLS**

**Mall Counts and Closure Projections:**
- The U.S. has roughly **1,000 malls**, with Moody's tracking about 700 for its analysis. (CNBC, April 2021)
- **Coresight Research estimated that 25% of America's roughly 1,000 malls would close within three to five years** (i.e., by roughly 2023–2025), with the pandemic accelerating a decline already underway. (CNBC, August 2020)
- **Credit Suisse predicted 25% of US malls could close by 2022.** (Wikipedia, Retail apocalypse)
- **Capital One Shopping Research:** Roughly **1,200 malls remain in the U.S. as of 2025**, with projections suggesting **only 900 will operate by 2028**. Projections indicate that **up to 87% of large shopping malls may close over 10 years**; by some estimates, there were **as few as 700 large shopping malls left in the U.S. in 2022**. Shopping malls are twice as likely to be vacant as the average retail space. (Coldwell Banker Commercial; Capital One Shopping)
- The US has gone from about **2,500 malls in the 1980s to roughly 700–1,000 today**, with 10–20 shutting down each year and estimates that one in four could close. (Trends in US Mall Closures)
- **TIME (2017):** By 2022, analysts estimated **1 out of every 4 U.S. malls could be out of business**. There were about **1,100 malls in the U.S.**, with a quarter at risk of closing over the next five years. About 1,500 malls were built between 1956 and 2005. (TIME)
- **Green Street Advisors:** Roughly **380 C- and D-rated malls exist in the U.S.**, which Green Street stated "are not viable retail centers long term." An A++ mall can generate up to **$1,000 per square foot** vs. about **$320 for a C+ mall**. (CNBC, August 2020)
- The most vulnerable malls are **B-, C-, and D-rated properties** with lower sales per square foot. Tennessee mall owner CBL & Associates planned to file for bankruptcy by October 1, 2020. (CNBC)
- **Moody's post-Covid-19 development projections:** Apartment development expected to fall 15.6%, office development 10%, and **retail 15.7%**, while industrial development projected to rise 3.6%. Moody's identified five markets where retail-to-warehouse conversion makes most sense: Central New Jersey, Northern New Jersey, Long Island, Memphis, and Detroit. (CNBC, August 2020)

**Dead Mall Definitions and Historical Context:**
- A "dead mall" (ghost mall or zombie mall) is a shopping mall with low consumer traffic or deteriorating conditions. Many malls are considered "dead" when they lose their anchor stores, causing sales volumes and rental revenues to decline below the cost of maintenance. (Wikipedia)
- Newsweek declared the indoor mall format obsolete in 2008, and **2007 marked the first time since the 1950s that no new malls were built in the U.S.** (Wikipedia)
- From 2006–2010, vacancy rates in U.S. malls increased significantly, with **nearly 3% of malls considered "dying" (40%+ vacancy)** and **nearly one-fifth having "troubling" vacancy rates (10%+)** by 2014. (Wikipedia)
- The U.S. has **40% more shopping space per capita than Canada and five times more than the U.K.**, contributing to an "extremely over-retailed" market. (Wikipedia)
- The U.S. has roughly **26 sq. ft. of retail per person vs. 2.5 sq. ft. in Europe**. (TIME)
- The first modern mall, Southdale Center in Edina, Minnesota, opened in 1956, designed by Austrian architect Victor Gruen. Mall of America opened in 1992. (TIME)
- **IPX1031 survey (May 2023, 1,005 respondents):** 68% of Americans live within one hour of a "dead mall"; 2 in 5 live near two or more dead malls. 28% had an abandoned mall torn down in their area within the last 5 years. 61% of Americans want a revival of traditional shopping malls. Top reasons for mall closures: online shopping (78%), economic recession (46%), poor management (35%), competing shopping centers (31%), and COVID-19 pandemic (25%). (IPX1031)
- **Redevelopment forms:** Dead malls have been converted to office/educational use (e.g., Windsor Park Mall became Rackspace's headquarters), open-air mixed-use centers, Amazon/FedEx/DHL/UPS fulfillment centers, homeless housing, and "mall-to-medicine" conversions by healthcare systems like Vanderbilt Health and University of Rochester Medical Center. Austin Community College converted Highland Mall; Vanderbilt University Medical Center moved into 100 Oaks Mall in Nashville. (Wikipedia, TIME)
- The San Francisco Centre mall entered a "death spiral" due to homelessness, shoplifting, and drug use, leading to anchor store closures (Nordstrom, Bloomingdale's) and collapse. (Michigan Journal of Economics)
- **Coldwell Banker Commercial (March 2026):** "The American mall is not dying—it's dividing." Average vacant mall sells at **43% below acquisition price**; closed malls remain empty **~4 years on average**. About 90% of mall occupants are experiential tenants (movie theaters), department stores, or apparel retailers, making malls the most Covid-vulnerable property type. (Coldwell Banker Commercial; CNBC)
- Only about **150 malls have figured out how to succeed** (TIME, 2017). Simon Malls enjoy occupancy averages of 92%. (Wikipedia)

**Mall Count Evolution (Coresight):**
- Malls make up a shrinking proportion of total US retail gross leasable area—**down to 5.5% in 2023 from 5.7% in 2014**, driven by low-tier mall closures. (Coresight Research)
- ICSC estimates **12.9% of US consumer expenditure on retail goods and services went through malls in Q1 2023**. Mall expenditure totaled **$728.9 billion in 2021** and **$818.7 billion in 2022** (11.2% YoY increase). (Coresight Research)
- Physical retail bounced back after pandemic restrictions lifted, with **2022 seeing more store openings than closures for the first time since 2016**. Retail sales at malls grew more than 11% in 2022 to nearly $819 billion. (Coresight Research)

**PART C: ANCHOR STORE DEPARTURES AND BANKRUPTCIES**

**Department Store and Major Chain Bankruptcies/Closures:**
- **2020 bankruptcies (mall-based retailers):** J.C. Penney, Neiman Marcus, Lord & Taylor, Brooks Brothers, and J.Crew all filed for bankruptcy protection in 2020. (CNBC)
- **Sears:** Fell from 3,500+ stores and 355,000 employees in 2006 to 1,430 stores by 2016, filing bankruptcy in **October 2018** with 68,000 employees. Sears Holdings bankruptcy timeline spans 2013–2021. (Wikipedia)
- **JCPenney:** Filed Chapter 11 in **May 2020**; JCPenney bankruptcy timeline 2015–2020. JCPenney closed about eight stores in 2025 and continued with more closures in 2026 in continued streamlining effort. (Wikipedia; Passionate Penny Pincher; Yahoo Finance/TheStreet)
- **Bed Bath & Beyond:** Filed bankruptcy in **2023**. (Wikipedia)
- **Macy's:** Plans to close **150 underperforming stores through 2026** as part of its "Bold New Chapter" strategy launched in 2024. Macy's committed to closing up to 150 underperforming locations, including about 50 by the end of fiscal 2024. **Macy's closed 66 stores in 2025**, and announced 14 more store closures across 11 states in 2026 (January 2026 announcement). About 350 Macy's stores expected to remain. Macy's Inc. operates 424 full-size stores, 21 small-format locations, 5 freestanding Macy's Backstage stores, 32 Bloomingdale's, 25 Bloomingdale's outlet stores, 4 Bloomie's locations, and 174 Bluemercury stores. (Coldwell Banker Commercial; Business Insider; Yahoo Finance/TheStreet)
- **Forever 21:** Bankruptcy in 2019 caused the loss of 200+ stores in the US. Forever 21 filed **Chapter 22 on March 16, 2025**, liquidating all 354 U.S. stores. (Michigan Journal of Economics; MMCG)
- **Toys "R" Us:** Filed bankruptcy in 2018, causing 3.8 million sq ft of open-air center space to be vacated in Q3 2018. (Forbes; Wikipedia)
- **The Bon-Ton:** Filed bankruptcy in 2018; its store closings (along with Sears) drove the Q3 2018 mall vacancy rise to 9.1%. (Forbes; Wikipedia)
- **Other major bankruptcies (from Wikipedia list):** Borders Books (2011), Barneys New York (2019), A.C. Moore (2019–2020), Payless ShoeSource (2019–2020), Pier 1 Imports (2020), Tuesday Morning (2020 & 2023), GNC (2020), True Religion (2017 & 2020), Express (2024), Big Lots (2024), Party City (2023 & 2024), Jo-Ann (2024 & 2025), 99 Cents Only Stores (2024), Rite Aid (2023 & 2025), Hudson's Bay (2025).

**2024–2026 Major Closures and Liquidations (Coresight/MMCG/Business Insider/Newsweek/AARP):**
- **Coresight Research tracked 8,270 U.S. store closures in 2025 vs. 5,270 openings** (net loss ~3,000), far below the projected 15,000. As of June 27, 2025, Coresight had tracked **5,822 announced store closings (~123.7 million square feet)**, surpassing 3,960 store openings (74.5 million square feet). This compared to 3,496 closings in the comparable period in 2024. Coresight initially predicted a record ~15,000 store closures for all of 2025, which would exceed 2024's total of 7,325 closures (the highest since 2020 when nearly 10,000 closings were tracked during the pandemic peak). (CoStar News; MMCG)
- **2024:** U.S. retailers projected over **7,100 store closures by the end of November 2024**, a **69% increase** compared to the same period in 2023 — the largest surge since the start of the coronavirus pandemic. (Newsweek, citing Coresight; AARP)
- **Historical Coresight openings/closures:** 2020: 3,704 openings and 9,698 closures (net loss of 5,994); 2021: net closures dropped to 180; 2022: openings surged to 5,394 surpassing 3,819 closures (net gain of 1,575); 2023: 5,843 openings and 5,548 closures (net gain of 295). (Newsweek)
- **Retail apocalypse era closures:** 2017: more than 12,000 physical stores closed; 2019: 9,302 store closings announced (59% jump from 2018), the highest since tracking began in 2012. (Wikipedia)
- **2025 bankruptcies driving closures (MMCG "Great American Store Closure Tracker"):**
  - **Rite Aid:** second Chapter 11 (May 5, 2025), full liquidation of all ~1,240 stores by Oct 3, 2025; ~15.5M sf vacated. CVS acquired 625 stores across 15 states.
  - **Joann:** second Chapter 11 (Jan 15, 2025), full liquidation of all ~800 stores; ~18M sf. Michaels acquired all JOANN private label brands; Burlington took over 45+ former JOANN locations.
  - **Party City:** Chapter 22 (Dec 21, 2024), ~700 stores liquidated; ~8.4M sf. Only 29 stores remained thereafter.
  - **Big Lots:** converted to Chapter 7 (Nov 10, 2025), ~340 net closures after Variety Wholesalers rescue; ~9M sf. 219 stores acquired by Variety Wholesalers; first 9 reopened April 10, 2025.
  - **Forever 21:** Chapter 22 (Mar 16, 2025), all 354 U.S. stores liquidated.
  - **Saks Global:** Chapter 11 (Jan 13, 2026, Southern District of Texas), $3.4B funded debt, ~5.6M sf coming off market; post-closure footprint ~13 Saks Fifth Avenue, 32 Neiman Marcus, 2 Bergdorf Goodman stores. Saks Off 5th closed 57 stores; Neiman Marcus Last Call closed all remaining outlet stores.
  - **Walgreens:** ~500 closures FY2025; Sycamore Partners $23.7B take-private (Aug 28, 2025) decelerated closures to <100 in 2026. Walgreens confirmed it would shut down 1,200 stores over three years (from 2024 announcement).
  - **CVS:** ~271 closures in 2025, ending its 900-store program; CVS closed 586 stores in 2024.
  - **Starbucks:** ~520 North American closures.
  - **Advance Auto Parts:** 727 closures (5.45M sf), exited 5 Western states entirely.
  - **GameStop:** 727 closures FY2025, cumulative >50% of fleet since FY2023.
  - **7-Eleven:** Closed over 500 locations in 2024; parent Seven & i Holdings plans to close 645 North American stores in fiscal 2026 while opening 205.
  - **99 Cents Only:** Closed all 371 remaining stores; Dollar Tree acquired leases for 170 of its stores.
  - **Conn's HomePlus:** Filed bankruptcy July 2024, permanently closed all 174 locations across 15 southern states, owing about $530 million in debt.
  - **Family Dollar:** Shut down the most stores in 2024 with 718 closures as of mid-December.
  - **Francesca's:** Filed Chapter 11 on February 5, 2026; going-out-of-business sales at all roughly 400 US locations.
  - **QVC Group:** Filed Chapter 11 on April 16, 2026, to restructure $6.6 billion in debt.
  - **Claire's:** Filed second Chapter 11; plans to close at least 18 U.S. stores, facing up to $10 billion in debt.
  - **Eddie Bauer:** Filed Chapter 11 in February 2026; liquidation sales at 175 US and Canada stores.
  - **WeightWatchers (WW):** Filed Chapter 11 as of May 6, 2026, to eliminate $1.15 billion in debt.
- **2026 closure projections:** Roughly **7,900 U.S. stores are expected to close in 2026**, with over 1,200 closures already publicly announced (as of early May 2026). Business Insider tracked approximately 4,100 closures in 2025. (Newsweek; Business Insider)
- **Five bankrupt brands (Joann, Party City, Big Lots, New Rite Aid, Forever 21) drove more than half of all 2025 closure square footage** (~127M sf closed through July 2025). Top ten chains accounted for ~5,500 of 8,270 closures (~two-thirds). (MMCG)
- **Chapter 22s (second filings) dominated** 2025 — companies emerged from prior Chapter 11 but failed to restore trade credit/vendor terms. 71% of largest consumer discretionary bankruptcies of 2025 involved private equity ownership at filing. (MMCG)

**Anchor Store Impact on Mall Viability:**
- Large department stores like Macy's and Nordstrom serve as "anchor stores" that drive foot traffic and receive lower rents. Large vacant spaces from anchor departures are difficult to fill. (Michigan Journal of Economics)
- Power has shifted from landlords to retailers, who are securing more lease concessions. Department stores like Nordstrom and Macy's are increasingly avoiding malls. (Retail Dive)
- **Backfill cohort (who absorbed closed boxes):** Aldi (~180 new stores 2025), Burlington (104 net new stores 2025, >40% from bankrupt-tenant recaptures), Planet Fitness (181 new clubs 2025), Crunch Fitness (91 clubs, leased 4.27M sf), Dollar Tree (+388 net stores to 9,269), Dollar General (+196), AutoZone (304 net new stores), O'Reilly (207 net new), Dick's Sporting Goods (16 new House of Sport + 20 Field House in 2025). (MMCG)
- **Landlord outcomes:** Best landlords turned bankruptcy into alpha: Brixmor full-year 2025 new-lease cash spreads 38.7%; Kimco ~90% of Party City/Joann/Big Lots/Rite Aid space re-leased at 30-40% releasing spreads; Simon re-tenanted Saks Off 5th at +67% mark-to-market spread. Kimco was upgraded to A- (S&P) and A3 (Moody's). 2025 saw the largest embedded rent mark-to-market in a decade driven by bankruptcy recapture. (MMCG)
- **Simon Property Group** reported retail sales per square foot rose 4.6% to **$646** (trailing 12 months ended June 30, 2018), with occupancy near 95%, and base minimum rent up 3.3% to $53.84. Simon ended 2025 at **96.4% mall/outlet occupancy with rents up 4.7%**. (Forbes; MMCG)
- **Off-price and discount retailers** are the store growth leaders: Dollar General, Lidl, TJ Maxx, Burlington, Five Below, plus beauty chains Ulta and Sephora. (CNBC)

**PART D: TOTAL RETAIL SQUARE FOOTAGE AND VACANT RETAIL SPACE**

- **Total U.S. retail square footage:** The United States had a **total of 8.5 billion retail square feet as of December 2019**, equating to **24.5 square feet per capita**, compared to the European average of 4.5 square feet per capita. (Georgia COVID-19 archive, citing Lincoln Institute of Land Policy, CoStar Group, and U.S. Census Bureau)
- **Statista data (2023):** Most of the retail real estate stock in the U.S. in 2023 was **general retail space** (single-tenant freestanding commercial buildings with parking, such as drugstores, grocery stores, and street front urban retail stores), which also had the lowest vacancy rate among retail real estate types. Property categories include: General retail, Malls (Lifestyle Centers, Regional Malls, Superregional Malls), and Power centers (several freestanding anchors with minimal small tenants, 250,000–600,000 sq. ft.). (Statista)
- **DoorLoop data:** General retail space occupied **6.4 billion of 11.8 billion sq ft of retail space** (the 11.8B figure appears to be a broader total including all commercial retail building types). Retail accounts for only 9% of CRE buildings. (DoorLoop)
- **Development pipeline constraints:** Only ~**81 million SF of new retail space annually** since 2020 (vs. ~300M SF/year in 2000–2009 and ~128M SF/year in the 2010s) — roughly one-quarter of early-2000s levels. **165M+ SF of obsolete retail demolished since 2018**; total retail stock grew <2% from 2019–2024. Retail under construction is at its lowest level since 2011; only ~**21 million square feet of new space (since 2020) available for lease** — less than 5% of total availability. Texas markets account for nearly one-third of new first-gen retail space. (MMCG Invest; Colliers)
- From 2000–2008, retail space grew 2.1% annually (nearly double population growth), with space per capita rising from 52.4 SF to 57.2 SF. After 2009, annual retail construction completions averaged just 0.5% of inventory. More than 400 million SF of retail space was demolished. (CBRE IM)
- **Vacant square footage context:** In Q2 2025, Coresight tracked 5,822 store closures representing an estimated **123.7 million square feet** of retail space. Five bankrupt brands drove more than half of all 2025 closure square footage (~127M sf closed through July 2025). (CoStar News; Colliers; MMCG)
- Demand for office space dropped by **157 million square feet** since the start of the pandemic, with office vacancy rising to 13.2% (context for retail comparisons). (BakersfieldNow)
- Retail-using employment reached **29.6 million in Q4 2024**, up 0.7% YoY. Real retail sales totaled $226.8 billion in December 2024, up 1.2% YoY. (Transwestern)
- U.S. retail sales projected at roughly **$7.4 trillion in 2025** with tepid growth (~0.4% YoY). Retail industry employs ~18 million people across ~3 million establishments. (MMCG)

**PART E: CLASS A / TOP-TIER VS. CLASS B & C MALL HEALTH (BIFURCATION)**

- **Coresight Research "Great Mall Divide" report:** Top-tier U.S. malls average **95.5% occupancy** compared to **89% for lower-tier centers**. (RE Journals)
- **Coresight "State of the American Mall" (2023):** Top-tier malls averaged **95.1% occupancy in 2022** (based on public mall operators, S&P Capital IQ data), still slightly below pre-pandemic levels; non-top-tier malls lagged more meaningfully. Average minimum base rent at top-tier malls grew in the mid-teens percentage range for four consecutive quarters from Q4 2021. Both top-tier and non-top-tier public mall operators saw CAGRs in the mid-to-high single digits between 2020 and 2022. Based on Placer.ai sampling of 120 malls, **traffic at top-tier malls was up 12% on average in 2022 versus pre-pandemic 2019; non-top-tier malls were up 10%**. Top-tier mall traffic growth was driven by long-distance visitors. Coresight's US Consumer Tracker found 40.3% of respondents visited a mall in the prior two weeks in the December 28, 2022 survey. (Coresight Research)
- **Coldwell Banker Commercial (2026):** **Class A malls ($500+/sq ft annual sales) have 5.6% vacancy; Class C malls (<$300/sq ft) have 13.3% vacancy.** (Coldwell Banker Commercial)
- **Green Street Advisors (via CNBC):** The most vulnerable malls are B-, C-, and D-rated properties with lower sales per square foot. An A++ mall can generate up to $1,000 per square foot vs. about $320 for a C+ mall. Roughly 380 C- and D-rated malls exist in the U.S. and are "not viable retail centers long term." (CNBC, August 2020)
- **Forbes (2018) on bifurcation:** Lower-tier (B, C, D class) malls are struggling, while top-tier A malls are thriving and being redesigned as mixed-use lifestyle centers. Online-born brands like Casper and UNTUCKit, along with Apple, Tesla, gyms, coworking spaces (e.g., Macerich partnering with Industrious, Life Time Work at Southdale Center), movie theaters, and restaurants like Shake Shack are becoming new mall traffic drivers. (Forbes)
- **Cushman & Wakefield (Q4 2015):** A "Have vs. Have-Not" marketplace: **75% of national vacancy is in Class B or C product**; there is a shortage of Class A space. Rental growth is driven almost entirely by Class A projects, with Class B rents flat and Class C very tenant-favorable. (Cushman & Wakefield)
- **Cushman & Wakefield (Q1 2019):** Class A properties continuing to outperform; Class B properties struggling unless well-funded. (Cushman & Wakefield)
- **Placer.ai December 2025 Mall Index:** Indoor malls posted visit gains across all four quarters; open-air centers Q4 visits up 2.0% YoY; outlet malls saw annual traffic declines including 1.1% holiday drop. (Coldwell Banker Commercial)
- **Successful mall examples (Coldwell Banker Commercial):** Houston's Galleria (30+ million annual visitors; 2017 renovation added luxury wing anchored by Saks Fifth Avenue and Nobu); King of Prussia (22 million annual visitors, 450 stores; 2016 expansion added 155,000 sq ft including Savor dining hub); Mall of America (40+ million visitors); Aventura Mall (Florida; ranked No. 1 in USA Today's 2025 10Best). (Coldwell Banker Commercial)
- **Mall reinvestment examples (Coresight):** Simon Property Group's Phipps Plaza Atlanta redevelopment with Nobu Hotel/Restaurant, Life Time facility, Citizens Market, office tower; Taubman's $200 million renovation of The Mall at Green Hills in Nashville (2019) including 132,000 sq ft of inline retail, new Dillard's, and 70,000 sq ft RH store. (Coresight Research)
- **Traffic drivers for top-tier malls:** Multichannel halo effect (61% of retailers and 66% of digital-first retailers cite rising customer acquisition costs as the top obstacle to 2022 e-commerce goals); brand synergy; reinvestment; omnichannel investment by mall owners (Simon's Shop Premium Outlets platform provides access to 35 million online shoppers and 2 billion in-store shoppers globally; Simon partnered with Tmall Global/Alibaba in late October 2022). (Coresight Research)
- **Gen Z mall comeback:** Circana data shows shoppers aged 18–24 bought 62% of total general merchandise in stores (vs. 52% for those 25+). 60% of Gen Z and 53% of Millennials visited a mall in the past three months. (Michigan Journal of Economics; MMCG)
- **Regional bifurcation (MMCG):** Sun Belt winners: Charlotte (+7.6% rent growth to $27.29/sf, 3.4% vacancy), Raleigh-Durham (3.1% vacancy), Phoenix (+964,553 sf absorption). Most stressed markets: New Orleans (+240 bps to 6.3%), Buffalo (+240 bps to 10.8%), Pittsburgh (+200 bps to 6.4%), Providence (+170 bps), Milwaukee (+170 bps). Heavy closure concentration in California, Florida, Ohio, New York, Michigan. (MMCG)
- **Rent growth bifurcation:** National asking rents grew ~1.9% YoY as of mid-2025 (moderating from 4%+ spikes in 2021–2022); forecast ~1.7% for 2025. 47 of 57 largest retail markets saw positive rent growth. Strong Sunbelt/mountain west growth: Raleigh, NC ~7.5% YoY, Tampa, FL ~4.7%, Orange County ~3.6%; underperformers include Cleveland, Chicago (flat), and East Bay/Oakland (-2.6%). Sun Belt markets (Phoenix, Tampa, Orlando) saw rents increase 20%+ since pandemic start; San Francisco rental rate growth lags pre-pandemic levels at -3% since Q1 2021. (MMCG; Transwestern)
- **Simon Property Group example:** David Simon said "Demand from tenants for space in our highly productive centers is increasing" (July 2018 earnings call). (Forbes)

**ADDITIONAL CONTEXT: THE "RETAIL APOCALYPSE" NARRATIVE**

- The phrase "retail apocalypse" first appeared in print in a 1990s essay by Peter Glen, gaining widespread usage in 2017. (Wikipedia)
- 2017: More than 12,000 physical stores closed. Reasons included debt and bankruptcy in the face of rising costs, leveraged buyouts, low quarterly profits outside holiday binge spending, delayed effects of the Great Recession, and changes in spending habits. (Wikipedia)
- Mall visits declined **50% between 2010–2013**. Holiday-season mall visits dropped by 50% between 2010 and 2013. (Wikipedia; TIME)
- Since 2002, department stores have lost **448,000 jobs (a 25% decline)**, while e-commerce added just 178,000 jobs over 15 years. (TIME)
- IHL Group (2019) disputed the "apocalypse" narrative, finding 5+ chains opening stores for every one closing, and that 20 retailers accounted for 75% of all closures. (Wikipedia)
- Mall growth (1970–2015) was over twice the population growth rate. (Wikipedia)
- Consumer spending is bifurcated: the top 20% of earners now account for nearly 60% of personal outlays, favoring grocery, discount, and value-oriented retailers. (Cushman & Wakefield Q2 2026)

# Evolution of American Shopping Habits (2005–2026): Research Findings

## List of Queries and Tool Calls Made

1. **Census/e-commerce penetration (2 searches):** "U.S. Census Bureau quarterly e-commerce share of total retail sales 2005 2020 2024 history percentage"; "e-commerce penetration rate US retail sales 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 census data"
2. **Foot traffic (2 searches):** "Placer.ai mall foot traffic decline 2020 2021 recovery retail store visits data"; "COVID-19 store foot traffic decline physical retail Placer.ai ShopperTrak data"
3. **BOPIS/curbside/store closures:** "Placer.ai foot traffic 2024 2025 retail recovery mall visits pre-pandemic levels data"; "buy online pick up in store BOPIS curbside pickup adoption rate 2020 2021 2022 percent consumers statistics"; "retail store openings closures 2023 2024 2025 net new stores brick and mortar recovery Coresight"
4. **Demographics/resale:** "Gen Z millennials shopping habits physical stores experience economy retail 2024 2025 data"; "secondhand resale market growth thredUP 2024 2025 resale report billion statistics"; "store closings 2020 pandemic retail bankruptcies list 2021 2022 openings"
5. **Pandemic-era collapse & recovery:** "retail foot traffic pandemic 2020 plummeted percent shopper traffic physical stores March April 2020 decline Placer.ai ShopperTrak"; "retail store openings 2022 2023 net new stores recovery post pandemic Target Walmart Aldi opening numbers"; "thredUP resale report 2024 2025 secondhand market $ billion projected resale growth statistics"
6. **Experience economy/NRF:** "experience economy retail entertainment food beverage dining experiential retail growth 2023 2024 2025 data percentage"; "National Retail Federation 2024 2025 retail sales forecast consumer spending Gen Z physical stores study"
7. **Historical year-by-year & 2021-2022 rebound:** "census bureau ecommerce share retail sales by year 2005 2006 2007 2008 2009 2010 2011 2012 2013 2014 2015 2016 2017 2018 2019 full year percent history"; "shopping center foot traffic 2020 2021 recovery ShopperTrak mall visits declined 2020 rebound 2021 2022 percent"
8. **Omnichannel/experiential follow-up:** "experiential retail food and beverage entertainment share of mall tenants 2023 2024 data restaurants gyms anchors"; "omnichannel shoppers statistics 2023 2024 percent consumers use online research in store purchase shopping journey"
9. **Reflection tool call** summarizing findings across all five topic areas.

---

## Fully Comprehensive Findings

### (a) E-Commerce's Share of Total U.S. Retail Sales Over Time (Census Bureau Data)

**Long-term historical context (1998–2015):**
- Per IntechOpen (citing the U.S. Census Bureau's Annual Retail Trade Survey): "the U.S. retail sales from e-commerce grew from 0.19% (=5/2582 billion) in 1998 to 3.60% (=142/3935 billion) in 2008 to 9.66% (=508/5255 billion) in 2018." [17]
- Per the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration (CDTFA, December 2017): "Electronic commerce has grown at double-digit annual rates for nearly two decades, and shows no sign of slowing." From 2000 to 2015, average annual growth was 23.3% for e-commerce, 3.4% for mail order, and 10.1% for combined "remote sales." In 2015, total retail trade rose 1.9% while e-commerce sales increased 14.0%. Mail order's share of remote sales declined dramatically: in 2000, mail order was 77.4% of remote sales and e-commerce 22.6%; by 2015 the shares nearly reversed (e-commerce 68.0%, mail order 32.0%). Remote sales constituted 9.2% of total 2015 U.S. retail sales. Nonstore retailers increased their share of total retail sales by 5.6% from 1998 to 2015. The electronic shopping industry (NAICS 4541) accounts for 87% of all e-commerce sales; car sellers are second with 9%. E-commerce grew faster than average for clothing and furniture, and slower for food, cars, and sporting goods (2011–2015). [41]
- YCharts (Census-sourced indicator) notes the long-term average e-commerce penetration is 7.20%, with an average growth rate of 13.41%. Historical data shows a steady upward trend from roughly 6–7% in 2014–2015. [2]
- SellersCommerce provides this year-by-year e-commerce penetration of total U.S. retail sales: 5.88% in 2013, rising consistently to 16.04% in 2024 — "crossing 16% for the first time. The only drop was in 2022 (-0.22%)." [7]

**Annual U.S. e-commerce sales volumes (SellersCommerce, with YoY change):**
- 2013: $260.5B (+12.7%); 2014: $297.0B (+14%); 2015: $337.3B (+13.6%); 2016: $383.5B (+13.7%); 2017: $442.4B (+15.4%); 2018: $506.7B (+14.5%); 2019: $569.4B (+12.4%); 2020: $807.1B (+41.7%); 2021: $950.5B (+17.8%); 2022: $1,012.2B (+6.5%); 2023: $1,102.2B (+8.9%); 2024: $1,192.6B (+8.2%); 2025*: $1,298.7B (+8.9%) (*projected). The dramatic 41.7% growth in 2020 was largely driven by the COVID-19 pandemic. U.S. e-commerce crossed the $1 trillion mark for the first time in 2022 ($1.01 trillion). Q4 2024 reached $352.93 billion, accounting for 16.2% of all retail sales. [7]
- Digital Commerce 360 reports that in 2000, the first full year tracked, consumers spent about $27.6 billion online; 2005 e-commerce sales were ~$91 billion; 2015 sales were ~$338 billion; 2025 e-commerce sales were more than triple 2015 and more than 10 times greater than 2005. [8]

**The 2020 COVID surge:**
- YCharts (Census data): e-commerce penetration dipped to 11.9% in Q1 2020, then surged to a pandemic peak of 16.3% in Q2 2020. [2]
- Retail Dive (citing Coresight Research CEO Deborah Weinswig): "We estimate that the share of US e-commerce jumped to 19.0% in 2020, which would not have occurred until around 2023 based on the trajectory of e-commerce increasing 1.25% each year between 2017 and 2019." Retail Dive also projected a 32.4% year-over-year increase in retail e-commerce sales, reaching nearly $795 billion for 2020 (up from just over $600 billion in 2019). [23]
- ExportUSA gives alternative (broader-definition) figures: 2020 online sales at 21.3% of total retail; 2021 e-commerce market share of 19.1% (rising to 20.6% in 2022); 2023 e-commerce at 22% of total retail sales (+0.8% vs 2022), with total online sales hitting $1.119 trillion and Q4 2023 surpassing $320 billion (the highest quarterly revenue in U.S. history); 2024 e-commerce accounted for 22.7% of U.S. retail sales ($1,192.59 billion, +7.5%, vs total retail $5,246.78 billion, +2.6%); "E-commerce now accounts for about 23.5% of retail sales in the United States, with a projected peak of 30% by the end of the decade"; online sales expected to reach $1.27 trillion in 2025 (+8.5% YoY). In 2019, pre-pandemic e-commerce was only $571 billion. The explosive growth during COVID-19 was "largely an acceleration of existing trends, and the market has returned to a pre-pandemic trajectory." [6]

Wells Fargo economists called 2024 "a decent year for retailers." [9]

**2025 annual performance (Digital Commerce 360):** 2025 U.S. e-commerce sales totaled approximately $1.234 trillion, a 5.4% increase over 2024's $1.170 trillion — the fourth consecutive year of single-digit growth and the second-lowest YoY growth rate since the Great Recession (the slowest being 4.9% in 2022). E-commerce accounted for 23.1% of total U.S. retail sales in 2025 (up from 22.8% in 2024), with Q4 2025 being the first quarter where e-commerce reached 25% of sales. Total U.S. retail sales reached $5.339 trillion in 2025, up 4.0% from $5.134 trillion in 2024. Holiday season (Nov. 1–Dec. 31, 2025) online sales reached $257.8 billion, up 6.8% from $241.4 billion in 2024; 56.4% of transactions were completed on mobile devices. Cyber 5 (Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday) generated $44.2 billion, with Cyber Monday drawing the most single-day spending at $14.25 billion and Black Friday online sales at $11.8 billion. Consumers spent $20 billion online using buy now, pay later (BNPL) in the last two months of 2025. Generative AI-powered chat services and browsers drove 693.4% more traffic to retailers' websites during the 2025 holiday season versus the prior year. Since 1999, both the dollar amount and percentage share of e-commerce sales have increased every year; only 2002 (30.2%) and 2020 (42.0%) saw growth of at least 30%. E-commerce penetration surpassed 20% for the first time in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic. Digital Commerce 360's penetration calculation (23.1%) differs from the Commerce Department's raw figure (16.4% for 2025) because DC360 excludes spending in segments that don't typically sell online. [8]

**Methodology notes (Census Bureau):**
- Estimates come from the Monthly Retail Trade Survey (MRTS), a stratified simple random sample of approximately 10,800 retail firms (excluding food services), weighted and benchmarked to represent over two million retail firms. [3]
- As of the April 2025 annual revision, nonemployer firms (businesses without paid employees) are no longer included in the estimates, aligned with the Annual Integrated Economic Survey (AIES). This changed the time series. Because of this benchmark, Q1 2025 reads 16.0% on the restated basis vs. the original 16.2%, and the Q1 2025→Q1 2026 share gain of +0.9 points vs. only +0.1 points the prior year is partly a "benchmark artifact." [1][3]
- E-commerce is defined as sales where the buyer places an order or negotiates price/terms over the Internet, mobile device (M-commerce), extranet, EDI network, email, or comparable online system. Payment may or may not be made online. Online travel services, financial brokers/dealers, and ticket sales agencies are NOT classified as retail and are excluded. [3][4][5]
- Estimates are seasonally adjusted using the X-13ARIMA-SEATS program; adjusted for holiday/trading-day differences but not price changes. [3]
- Census 16.9% differs from Digital Commerce 360's 23.1% due to different definitions (Census excludes nonemployers post-April 2025 and covers retail NAICS 44-45; DC360 uses a broader goods-and-services basis). [1][8]

### (b) Foot Traffic at Physical Stores vs. Online Transactions

**The 2020 collapse:**
- Retail Dive (citing Placer.ai): Year-over-year foot traffic collapsed 26% in March, 45% in April, and 30% in May 2020. "From June onward, traffic remained down 13-18% monthly." Lingering effects from remote work, economic uncertainty, and shifts away from cities had major ongoing impact. [23]
- Retail Dive also reported: retail sales fell 1% (March) and 16% (April) before recovering with 11% YoY gains in June, July, and September; December 2020 holiday sales rose 6.7%. Apparel sales fell 53% in March, 89% in April, 64% in May, 25% in June, and 20% in July 2020 — and did not increase a single month after March. Coresight found U.S. clothing/accessories sales fell 30% from January to October 2020. [23]
- Store closures: 8,736 permanent store closures in 2020 (following 9,832 in 2019), marking the fourth consecutive year of net negative store openings. S&P Global Market Intelligence recorded 52 retail bankruptcies in 2020 — 63% higher than the previous year, exceeding the typical 32–34 per year. [23]

**Recovery trajectory (2021–2024):**
- Abakus Analytics: Footfall improved in 2021 but remained generally low; shopping mall foot traffic exceeded that of retail markets and groceries. 2022 saw only a 1% year-over-year increase in footfall, with significant drops in the last six months. Foot traffic continued declining in 2023 compared to the first half of 2022. "As Placer.ai revealed in its recent reports, foot traffic for physical retail stores has never been as high as in the pre-pandemic era." In 2024, most months saw footfall increases (despite a January dip from severe winter frost), with visits dropping in April, September, and December due to Easter, Halloween, and Christmas. [24]
- Placer.ai March 2025 Mall Index: Mall visits rebounded in March 2025 following a February drop. Indoor malls showed the strongest YoY growth at 1.8%, while open-air centers and outlets narrowed their YoY visit gaps to 1.1% and 0.7%. The rebound was partially driven by increased consumer confidence among younger consumers (under 35) and households earning over $125K annually. Indoor malls have led in visit strength since roughly Q1 2024, overtaking open-air centers (which outperformed between Q2 2023 and Q1 2024), attributed to a "survival of the fittest" effect (many weaker malls shuttered, redistributing traffic to remaining top-tier locations) and renewed demand for the indoor mall experience (e.g., Walmart's purchase of Monroeville Mall, Simon's redevelopment of Smith Haven Mall). COVID-19's lingering impact persists: In Q1 2025 vs. Q1 2019, all three mall types saw fewer and shorter visits. Open-air centers saw traffic only 2.0% lower than pre-pandemic but visit duration down 4.4%. Indoor malls saw the strongest visit-duration recovery (only 2.9% shorter than pre-pandemic) but visit numbers down 7.4%. Outlet malls saw the largest drops in both metrics. [10]
- Placer.ai June 2025 Mall Index: June 2025 traffic declined across all mall formats after two months of YoY growth — indoor malls fell just 0.7%, open-air centers dropped 1.6%, outlets declined 4.4% — likely reflecting "natural demand normalization after tariff-driven spring shopping." H1 2025 overall was largely positive: indoor malls led with YoY visits up 1.8%, open-air centers grew 0.6%, outlets were relatively flat at −0.8%. All formats saw average visit duration rise, with indoor malls posting the largest dwell time increase of 3.3%. Open-air shopping centers are the only format to surpass pre-pandemic levels (H1 2025 visits up 0.3% vs. H1 2019). Open-air centers consistently met or exceeded pre-pandemic visits over the past two years (Q2 2025 visits 2.7% higher than Q2 2019). Indoor malls narrowed the gap significantly in Q2 2025, with visits just 1.1% lower than Q2 2019 — their strongest performance since 2020. [11][44]
- GrowthFactor mall foot traffic guide: "The 'retail apocalypse' story is now two years out of date." Indoor malls grew visits in all four quarters of 2025 (the first format to do so since the pandemic, per Placer.ai); open-air centers led the 2025 holiday season (+1.7% YoY for Nov/Dec); outlet malls were the only format to decline for the full year 2025. February 2026 readings: open-air centers up 7.3% YoY, outlet malls up 7.2%, indoor malls up 5% YoY. Recovery milestone: Q1 2024 open-air centers first to exceed 2019 visitor levels; March 2024 saw double-digit YoY gains across all three formats. [12]
- GrowthFactor retail foot traffic guide: In the first half of 2026, visits rose year-over-year across all three mall formats: open-air shopping centers led at +4.7%, indoor malls +1.9%, and outlet malls +1.0% (per Placer.ai's June 2026 Mall Index). June 2026 extended this to a third consecutive month of growth, with open-air centers up 5.1%. E-commerce accounted for only 16.9% of total U.S. retail sales in Q1 2026, meaning "roughly 83 cents of every retail dollar is still spent in physical locations." A commonly used planning range for retail foot traffic conversion rate is 20% to 40%. [27]
- PassBy (analysis of 36.9 billion modelled mall visits): Overall mall traffic grew 0.48% YoY but diverged sharply. Community centres led with +1.22% growth (adding 100M+ visits), neighbourhood centres +0.81%, strip/convenience +0.38%, power centres flat at 0.15%, regional centres +0.03%. Declining formats: lifestyle centres −0.68%, festival/entertainment −1.03%, super-regional centres −1.2%, outlet centres −3.24%. Holiday 2025 traffic fell 3.0% (7.09B to 6.88B visits). Regional leaders: Kansas (+3.72%), Missouri (+3.37%), Iowa (+3.13%), Kentucky (+2.85%), Oklahoma (+2.67%). Declining: Washington DC (−2.85%), New Jersey (−0.86%), Colorado (−0.84%), New York (−0.42%), California roughly flat. [43]
- QSR Magazine (Ashley Robinson, The Seaker Group): A significant decline in brick-and-mortar retail foot traffic began on June 6, 2025, marking the first material decline since COVID-19. After four years of steady gains (2021–2024), foot traffic had been running about 20 percent above pre-pandemic norms, but in the second half of 2025, weekly pedestrian traffic at store levels fell sharply — dropping 10 percent or more for the balance of the year, a 30-point swing from earlier gains. The decline appeared across large metros, smaller cities, outdoor centers, urban streets, and mixed-use districts. The author attributes the decline primarily to Hispanic consumers avoiding public spaces due to fears about immigration enforcement; Hispanics represent about 20% of the U.S. population and roughly 15% of total consumer spending. Data was compiled from mobile-location data covering roughly 500 U.S. shopping destinations over five years. [45]
- StreetLight Data (13 top malls, 2019–2022): In 2019, about 60% of mall visits occurred on weekdays; by 2022 this rose to over 70%, driven by the work-from-home era. Mall of America shifted from ~56% to ~70% weekday share; Roosevelt Field from ~60% to 74%. Thanksgiving-day mall visits effectively ended: about 15% of weekend mall traffic occurred on Thanksgiving in 2019, but this fell to near zero in subsequent years. Black Friday's dominance diminished but it still held a plurality share with a smoother distribution; peak arrival in 2022 was around 11 a.m. [44]
- Placer.ai "Physical Retail in 2026: How the Giants Are Winning" (May 11, 2026): The combined share of physical retail traffic captured by Walmart, Target, Costco, and Dollar General rose from 16.8% in 2019 to 17.5% in Q1 2026. In 2025, visits per store exceeded pre-pandemic levels by 18.1% for Costco and 10.2% for Dollar General. Walmart remains the largest player, accounting for 9.7% of traffic to major brick-and-mortar chains in 2025. Target's Q1 2026 visits were up 8.3% compared to Q1 2019 and up 5.1% YoY — its first positive visit growth in over a year. Walmart's average visits per location grew 3.5% YoY in Q1 2026. Dollar General: nearly a quarter of visitors frequented the chain at least four times per month in Q1 2026 (up from 21.2% in Q1 2022); 28.0% of visits come from within one mile. Costco sustained growth after raising membership fees in September 2024. [26]
- Thumbvista (Dec 10, 2025): "According to Placer.ai and NRF reports, U.S. retail foot traffic has dropped roughly 17% year-over-year, with apparel and big box stores seeing even sharper declines." Online shopping grew 56% since 2020; same-day delivery usage increased 3x; mobile shopping now influences 70% of in-store purchases; shoppers visit 5–7 fewer stores per month than in 2019 (McKinsey study); 46% prioritize "needs over wants." [25]
- Placer.ai Office Index (related context for downtown/urban foot traffic): June 2025 nationwide office visits were down 27.4% compared to June 2019 (improved from June 2024's −32.9%), up 8.3% YoY; April 2025 visits were down 30.7% vs April 2019; New York City led office recovery at just 5.5% below pre-pandemic levels (April 2025). [12][13]

### (c) Consumer Behavior Shifts: Omnichannel, BOPIS, Curbside Pickup, Click-and-Collect, Stores as Fulfillment Nodes

**BOPIS/click-and-collect adoption:**
- Capital One Shopping: 97.2 million Americans (34.2% of U.S. consumers) regularly use BOPIS; BOPIS is the third most-used fulfillment method among online shoppers. U.S. click-and-collect retail sales grew from $35 billion in 2019 to $154 billion in 2025, with projections to reach $292 billion by 2030. Year-over-year growth for this segment slowed from 49.5% (2019) to 16.2% (2025), with projections of 12.0% by 2030. Worldwide BOPIS share of eCommerce fluctuated from 18.8% (July 2025) to 19.1% (April 2026) per Signifyd. Demographically, BOPIS usage skews younger: Millennials (39.1%), Gen Z (35.9%), Gen X (17.8%), and Baby Boomers (7.2%). Nearly half of click-and-collect shoppers use curbside pickup as a fulfillment method. "During the COVID-19 pandemic of the 2020s, retailers dramatically expanded omnichannel ordering and fulfillment options to meet demand for reduced- and no-contact shopping." [15]
- Endear (citing Capital One Shopping Research): U.S. click-and-collect retail sales hit an estimated $154.3 billion in 2025 and are projected to reach $177.9 billion in 2026, a 15.3% YoY jump. 85% of U.S. BOPIS shoppers say they have made an additional purchase while collecting an order. Roughly 68% of U.S. shoppers used BOPIS at least once in 2024, up from 57% in 2022. [16]
- WeSupply: About one-third of consumers made an online purchase and chose BOPIS during the 2016 holiday season. 30% of BOPIS shoppers chose this option for the first time after the pandemic was declared. In 2019, less than a third of U.S. retailers had a digital transformation strategy, and only about 4% of the 500 largest retailers offered curbside pickup. In May 2020, BOPIS increased by over 554% year-over-year. Revenue from BOPIS sales was up an average of 35% during the 2019 holiday season. 56% of shoppers plan to continue using BOPIS after pandemic restrictions are lifted. U.S. BOPIS sales more than doubled in 2020 and were predicted to maintain double-digit growth rates. Click-and-collect buyers were projected to increase from 143.8 million people in 2020 to over 160 million in 2024. 83% of consumers find shopping convenience more important than in previous years, and 70% said BOPIS improved their shopping experience. Many large U.S. retailers promise BOPIS orders are ready for pickup in 30 minutes or less. The industry benchmark for curbside pickup is under 2 minutes. [17]

**Curbside pickup:**
- Red Stag Fulfillment: Approximately 72 million Americans (25.3% of U.S. consumers) used curbside pickup within the past year as of 2024, with U.S. curbside pickup retail sales projected to reach $54.3 billion in 2025. Only 24.8% of the Top 1,000 retail chains offered curbside pickup in 2024, down from a pandemic peak of 55.1% in 2021. Food & Beverage chains lead with 50% offering curbside pickup in 2024, with grocery usage doubling from 6% in 2022 to 12% in 2024. Virtually all major grocery and big-box retailers (Target, Walmart, Kroger, Home Depot) maintain the service. Target's "Drive Up" fulfills over half its digital orders through same-day services; Walmart's store-fulfilled models contributed to a $2.5 billion monthly e-commerce run rate by late 2024; Kroger reports 97% customer satisfaction. Retailers with curbside report higher online conversion rates (3.9% vs. 3.1% industry average). Millennials lead adoption, with two-thirds favoring curbside. Apparel retailers show more conservative adoption due to sizing, returns, and inventory complexities. [14]

**Stores as fulfillment nodes / omnichannel:**
- Endear: Target's same-day fulfillment ecosystem — spanning Drive Up, in-store pickup, and rapid delivery — generated more than $14 billion in sales and roughly two-thirds of Target's digital revenue in fiscal 2025, according to Retail Dive. Real-world examples of BOPIS-driven store models: Nordstrom Local (small neighborhood locations built entirely around services including online-order pickup, no sellable inventory); Lululemon (BOPIS via website and app with same-day pickup); The Reformation (web inventory filterable by immediate store pickup availability); Home Depot (same-day local availability search). [16]
- Modern Retail: Target's 2026 stores will fulfill 95% of its online orders, and Target is leaning into larger footprints (148,000-square-foot locations vs. its 125,000-square-foot average). [31]
- IntechOpen (academic chapter, published October 25, 2022): Proposes a digital-era retail channel typology including Brick-and-mortar (B&M), Ship-to-home (S2H), Ship-to-store (S2S), Home-delivery-from-store (HDFS), Pickup-from-store (PFS, with subtypes CPFS = curbside-pickup-from-store and ISPFS), Ship-to-third-place (S23P, e.g., Amazon lockers with ~15,000 units in the U.S.), and Third-place-delivery-from-store (3PDFS). Key findings: Adding curbside-pickup-from-store extends a store's competitive impact on rivals' in-store sales up to eight miles (vs. only 1.5–2 miles for traditional in-store competition). Consumers can order from stores much farther away (e.g., 33 miles in Charlotte, NC for a $5 long-distance fee). Median online grocery shopping duration (14.36 min) is over 25% shorter than in-store dwell time (19.52 min). During the pandemic: 45% shopped online for groceries more; 46% used HDFS more; 40% used CPFS more; 30% shopped less at grocery stores; average weekly grocery trips dropped from 2.7 pre-pandemic; consumers shopping for fresh food multiple times a week dropped by half; 36% of households changed who shopped, with a majority (24%) reducing to one shopper; 44% spent more per grocery visit; average weekly grocery spend surged from $121 (early 2020) to $161 (late March), settling around $126 by April. Post-pandemic predictions: CPFS and HDFS adoption will continue permanently — e-grocery expected to reach 21.5% of total grocery sales by 2025; CPFS predicted to remain the larger channel (75% of online orders fulfilled via pickup post-COVID, up from 69% during the pandemic), with HDFS only surpassing it in major markets; grocers expected to move from 3rd-party services (primarily Instacart) to 1st-party e-commerce channels. [19]
- Thumbvista (omnichannel behavior): Online shopping grew 56% since 2020; same-day delivery usage increased 3x; mobile shopping now influences 70% of in-store purchases — "customers still shop in-store, [but] decisions are made before visiting." [25]
- ExportUSA: Mobile e-commerce reached 40% of total online sales (2020–2021 estimates), and purchases INFLUENCED by smartphone research could be around 80%. [6]
